entries.text:
Scope

A pair-density wave (PDW) concerns finite-wavevector components of a superconducting pair field. A charge-density wave (CDW), a modulated tunneling spectrum and a modulated pair field are different observables. Specify the underlying lattice or superlattice, the electromagnetic gauge convention and whether a uniform condensate coexists. A single plane-wave phase has constant magnitude; periodic magnitude alone also need not establish a new spontaneous broken translation symmetry.  

The conventional Fulde–Ferrell–Larkin–Ovchinnikov (FFLO) problem uses spin imbalance to motivate finite-momentum pairing. Fulde and Ferrell's clean exchange-field model includes a compensating normal contribution to the current: a phase gradient must not be equated with an uncompensated equilibrium current. The Larkin–Ovchinnikov paper appeared in Russian in 1964 and English translation in 1965; its institutional publication record is checked here, but the original full text remains an access gap. Modern orbital-FFLO proposals require separate assumptions.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For a scalar illustration in a fixed gauge, write \Delta(x)=d0+d+e^{iQx}+d-e^{-iQx}. The Fourier coefficients of |\Delta|^2 are C0=|d0|^2+|d+|^2+|d-|^2, CQ=d+d0^+d0d-^ and C{2Q}=d+d-^, with negative-wavevector coefficients given by conjugation. Four independent discrete Fourier examples reproduce these identities. They are algebraic intensity identities, not a derivation of electronic charge density or a tunneling response.  

For d0=d-=0, the Fulde–Ferrell-type plane wave has constant |\Delta|. Equal real d+=d-=d/2 instead give the Larkin–Ovchinnikov-type standing wave d\cos Qx: the pair field has period 2\pi/Q, while its squared magnitude has period \pi/Q. Adding a real uniform component produces a Q harmonic through interference. A missing Q intensity harmonic therefore does not rule out a pure standing-wave pair field, and a detected 2Q charge harmonic does not uniquely identify one. These imposed examples do not compare free energies.   

Under an electron gauge phase \alpha, both pair components acquire e^{2i\alpha}. The product d+d-^ is neutral, whereas d+d- transforms with e^{4i\alpha} and has zero net wavevector. Three numerical phase checks confirm the distinction. A composite with charge 4e is not by itself evidence for a thermodynamically coherent charge-4e phase. Berg, Fradkin and Kivelson's 2009 melting theory proposes such a phase and fractional flux as a test; that proposal is distinct from the 2007 layer-decoupling paper. 

Berg and colleagues' 2007 stripe model suppresses leading interplane Josephson coupling through a particular antiphase pattern and stacking. An independent overlap calculation gives \langle\cos Qx\cos Qy\rangle=0 over complete periods for perpendicular stripes, but parallel stripes give 1/2. Adding a common uniform amplitude u gives u^2; a cropped window need not cancel. The quartic overlap remains \langle\cos^2Qx\cos^2Qy\rangle=1/4. This illustrates why cancellation of the lowest coupling does not mean all coupling vanishes. The paper retains higher-order/further-neighbor terms and discusses defects that spoil exact cancellation. 

An illustrative vortex-halo envelope A(r)=e^{-r/\xi} produces a Q amplitude proportional to A\Delta0^ and a 2Q amplitude proportional to A^2. If \Delta0 is approximately constant, the latter decays twice as fast. Four independent logarithmic-slope checks verify this and show failure of that ratio when the uniform component recovers from zero. The relation is conditional, especially near the core; it is not a universal PDW diagnostic. 

 Experimental criteria

Tranquada and colleagues' 1995 neutron study concerns static spin/charge stripes in Nd-substituted La–Sr–Cu–O at x=0.12. That diffraction evidence does not directly measure a superconducting pair field. Layer decoupling and charge harmonics are useful cross-checks only when competing charge, magnetic and structural explanations are addressed.  

Hamidian and colleagues' 2016 experiment used a superconducting Bi2212 nanoflake tip for scanned Josephson tunneling microscopy below 50 mK. It reported modulations near QP=(0.25\pm0.02)\,2\pi/a0, superposed on a stronger uniform component. It is not the later field-induced vortex-halo spectroscopy experiment. Their phase-diffusion model uses I(V)=IJ^2 ZV/[2(V^2+Vc^2)], with Vc=2eZkBT^/\hbar. The measured peak Ic=\hbar IJ^2/(8ekBT^) differs from the underlying Josephson critical current IJ; three independent numerical peak searches verify this relation. The effective noise temperature T^ must not simply be replaced by refrigerator temperature. 

Edkins and colleagues' 2019 study used single-electron STM, explicitly without scanned Josephson tunneling microscopy. At 2 K it compared 0 and 8.25 T in the same Bi2212 field of view using the same tip. Approximately eight-cell and four-cell electronic modulations support a PDW interpretation within the authors' model. The fitted Fourier widths are not exactly in a two-to-one ratio. Sublattice form factors belong to the measured electronic response and must not be copied directly onto the pair field. The core region is excluded from the simple envelope argument. Raw-data fitting and the complete supplement are not reproduced here. 

Chen and colleagues' 2021 CsV3Sb5 work reports spatial gap/conductance modulations and Josephson spectroscopy on prepared surfaces. Bulk and surface temperature scales differ, and the author manuscript explicitly says roton excitations were not directly observed. Its proposed complex PDW interpretation is not a direct phase measurement or a universal statement about kagome superconductors. The selected manuscript and methods check is inherited from the chiral-pairing entry. 

In May 2026, Cao and colleagues reported a hysteretic tunneling-gap transition in multilayer NbSe2 under an in-plane field, consistent with a possible orbital FFLO state. Their reported angle, disorder and thickness dependences matter; the selected theoretical discussion neglects vortices in its energy comparison. This is evidence for a transition with a proposed interpretation, not a direct image of finite pair momentum. Only the publisher abstract, introduction and selected model passage have been checked here. 

 Limits and disputes

Keep four distinctions explicit: pair tunneling versus single-electron tunneling; induced modulation versus a primary instability; field-induced versus spontaneous behavior; and a surface observation versus a bulk thermodynamic phase. A particular gap map cannot alone determine the pair phase. A nonzero composite amplitude, a half-vortex proposal or an unusual transport curve likewise needs a separate coherence and alternative-explanation analysis.   

The 2026 report by Wang and colleagues deliberately calls its moiré result Cooper-pair density modulation (CPDM): the authors describe periodic order-parameter variation without additional translation-symmetry breaking. That distinction prevents treating every periodic pairing texture as a spontaneous PDW. This entry has checked the institutional abstract and publication identity, not the complete measurement or microscopic model. 

 Discovery implications

Store the probe, temperature, magnetic-field magnitude and orientation, surface preparation, Fourier convention, uniform component and normalization with every candidate. Compare observations with an explicit response model before assigning an order parameter. Our local algebra, peak and overlap checks test stated examples; they do not reproduce the experiments, establish a material ground state, or close full scientific acceptance.    

 Related topics

entries.title: Singlet and triplet pairing: spin, parity and spin–orbit coupling
entries.summary: Classify pairing with orbital and frequency exchange, and distinguish measured correlations from a proposed order parameter.
entries.text:
Scope

Spin singlet and spin triplet describe antisymmetric and symmetric two-electron spin states. They do not, by themselves, identify a crystal representation, a pairing mechanism, chirality or topology. The familiar even-parity singlet / odd-parity triplet rule assumes even-frequency pairing and a symmetric orbital or band exchange sector. State these assumptions before applying it to a material.  

Spin–orbit coupling (SOC) makes physical spin different from a band label. In a time-reversal-invariant centrosymmetric normal state, inversion combined with time reversal produces a degenerate pair at each momentum. Such a doublet need not transform under crystal rotations as an ordinary spin-1/2 pseudospin: Samokhin identifies exceptional twofold bands where the usual axial-vector transformation of the triplet component fails. His classification retains even/odd intraband components in its static convention; the exception concerns crystal transformation rules, not the Pauli principle. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For a homogeneous pair correlation with combined spin and orbital indices a,b, fermion exchange requires F{ab}(\mathbf k,i\omegan)=-F{ba}(-\mathbf k,-i\omegan). If spin, momentum, orbital and frequency exchange can each be diagonalized, their signs obey sSsPsOs\omega=-1. Here frequency exchange is not the physical time-reversal operation. For sO=s\omega=+1, spin singlet implies even momentum parity and triplet implies odd momentum parity. Reversing either the orbital or frequency sign reverses that implication. An independent matrix check tests all 16 sign combinations, accepting eight and rejecting eight. These are allowed symmetry sectors, not evidence that all are stable phases. 

In a chosen spin-1/2 basis, write the static gap matrix \Delta=(\psi+\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)i\sigmay. The scalar is the spin-antisymmetric component; the vector multiplies symmetric spin matrices. An analogous decomposition in a band doublet must retain that basis's actual symmetry matrices. In higher-angular-momentum low-energy bands, coupled angular-momentum sectors replace a simple singlet/triplet classification; microscopic fermion antisymmetry still applies. Leggett's helium framework and crystal symmetry classifications are useful references, with their respective physical settings kept separate. The 1976 Leggett correction withdraws a historical factor-of-two discrepancy claim.     

For the illustrative noncentrosymmetric Hamiltonian h=\xi I+\alpha\mathbf g\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma, take real odd \mathbf g(-\mathbf k)=-\mathbf g(\mathbf k) and an imposed even singlet gap \psi i\sigmay. The anomalous Green function can contain a triplet component even though the imposed triplet gap is zero. Twelve independent matrix inversions reproduce the helicity-projector expression, in the specified Nambu convention, F=-\sum{\lambda=\pm}\psi P\lambda i\sigmay/[\omegan^2+(\xi+\lambda\alpha|\mathbf g|)^2+|\psi|^2], where P\lambda=(I+\lambda\hat{\mathbf g}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)/2. Different denominators generate a triplet correlation; they coincide at the particle-hole-symmetric test point. This distinguishes a pair correlation from a self-consistent triplet order parameter. The calculation is an imposed mean-field example, not a prediction of a material's mixing ratio. 

With an imposed aligned component \mathbf d=d\hat{\mathbf g}, the two gap magnitudes are |\psi+d| and |\psi-d| in this simple model. Five direct gap-matrix checks recover the squared magnitudes, including complex relative phase. A zero in one branch requires the appropriate cancellation, not merely the absence of inversion symmetry. The interaction, band structure and gap equation must determine the actual amplitudes. At points where \mathbf g=0, its unit vector and this helicity construction require separate treatment.  

Frigeri and colleagues' weak-coupling calculation neglects small singlet–triplet coupling terms associated with particle-hole asymmetry and analyzes the channels separately. Its leading triplet suppression contains |\mathbf d|^2-|\hat{\mathbf g}\cdot\mathbf d|^2: alignment avoids this particular suppression. The erratum adds an omitted linear term to the MnSi SOC vector, \mathbf g=\alpha1\mathbf k+\alpha2[kx(ky^2-kz^2),ky(kz^2-kx^2),kz(kx^2-ky^2)]. Thus a conclusion about suppression of a p-wave component depends on the relative coefficients; alignment alone does not choose the stable state. Three independent angular examples check that dependence without calculating a transition temperature. The erratum also rescales the original Fig. 2 SOC parameter by dividing it by \sqrt{3/2}.  

 Experimental criteria

A Knight shift includes spin and orbital contributions and depends on field direction, SOC, hyperfine coupling and the superconducting measurement conditions. Pustogow and colleagues' 2019 Sr2RuO4 study used reduced radio-frequency excitation to address heating and reported a spin-susceptibility reduction. The selected author-version passages checked here do not establish every possible representation. The 2026 muon result adds a low-field constraint, with a finite temperature floor and extrapolation assumptions; it also does not constitute a complete order-parameter identification. Compare the actual susceptibility tensor and conditions with competing states.  

An upper critical field above a simple weak-coupling Pauli estimate is not a stand-alone triplet test. Orbital depairing, SOC, strong coupling, multiband effects and field direction must be addressed. In particular, Frigeri's field calculation neglects orbital depairing and considers a continuous instability: its formally large paramagnetic limit is not an unlimited physical upper critical field. In UTe2, the discovery paper's measured field range and higher extrapolated scale must remain distinct.  

UGe2, URhGe and UCoGe motivate triplet and equal-spin pairing through superconductivity associated with ferromagnetism, but discovery evidence does not determine a complete odd-parity representation. Check microscopic coexistence and sample volume rather than infer them solely from two transition anomalies. UTe2 must not be placed in the same category of established long-range ferromagnetic superconductors; its historical interpretation is not a substitute for a current material-specific review. The uranium discovery abstracts and selected UTe2 text have different review depths here.    

Phase-sensitive junctions, impurity response and spin-sensitive probes can provide complementary constraints, but interfaces can select or generate correlations absent from the bulk gap. Tanaka and Golubov's proximity theory explicitly permits odd-frequency, even-parity triplet correlations in a diffusive normal metal. That is not by itself an intrinsic odd-frequency bulk superconducting phase. The publisher abstract has been checked; the full junction derivation remains open. 

 Limits and disputes

Do not infer a singlet–triplet mixing fraction from crystal inversion breaking. Symmetry permits compatible components; microscopic interactions decide their magnitude. Conversely, an orbital-antisymmetric spin-triplet sector can have even momentum parity at even frequency. Physical-spin pairing and the intraband pseudospin gap can therefore carry different descriptions after projection. Clepkens and colleagues' interorbital “shadowed-triplet” construction illustrates this distinction as a model proposed for Sr2RuO4, not an experimentally established assignment. Only its author abstract and publication identity are checked here.   

Neither an unchanged Knight shift nor a measured decrease alone fixes all SOC-coupled possibilities. A ferromagnetic background, a large critical field, nodes or broken time reversal similarly fails to identify a unique representation. Keep spin structure, momentum parity, orbital exchange, frequency dependence, crystal representation and topology as separate questions. The finite tests on this page validate specified algebra; they do not establish energetic stability or reproduce susceptibility data.    

 Discovery implications

For each candidate, record inversion and magnetic symmetries, the electronic basis, orbital or band indices, frequency convention, field direction, temperature, heating controls, measured observables and alternative explanations. Report a proposed gap only at the level supported by mutually consistent probes and a stated response model. Retain both Frigeri papers when using the corrected SOC argument. Full scientific acceptance, complete version comparisons and experimental reproduction remain open.    

 Related topics

entries.text:
Scope

An elemental superconductor contains one chemical element, but that label does not specify its crystal structure, bands, coupling strength or pressure history. Elemental systems provide useful benchmarks for electron–phonon theory; they do not all reduce to one weak-coupling model. Niobium's approximately 9.2 K transition is a useful conventional scale, not a ceiling on elemental superconductivity or a certified value for every sample.  

The mercury discovery is associated with Onnes's 1911 report. His later Nobel lecture describes the abrupt resistance decrease near 4.2 K, explicitly qualified by measurement accuracy, and a current threshold above which voltage reappeared. The lecture scan includes subsequent notes and a 1914 addendum; those later observations should not be dated to 1911. It is a firsthand account, not a substitute for a modern magnetic-volume or heat-capacity measurement. 

 Mathematical assumptions

The isotope coefficient is \alpha=-d\ln Tc/d\ln M. If harmonic frequencies scale as M^{-1/2} while the dimensionless pairing parameters remain fixed, the corresponding transition scale has \alpha=1/2. This is a conditional model statement, not a value certified here for the original mercury datasets. Maxwell and Reynolds are retained as the historical experimental sources; their full datasets still require direct review. An isotope substitution may also change structure or anharmonic motion, so a measured coefficient must retain its sample and phase conditions.   

The weak-coupling isotropic BCS benchmark is 2\Delta(0)/(kBTc)\simeq3.53. Lead is a strong-coupling benchmark, so that number is not a compulsory fit to its tunneling spectrum. Retardation makes the gap energy dependent; a full gap alone does not establish its sign structure or the microscopic pairing interaction.  

For an illustrative McMillan-type estimate, write Tc=(\omega{\log}/1.2)\exp[-A/D], with A=1.04(1+\lambda) and D=\lambda-\mu^(1+0.62\lambda)>0, taking \omega{\log} in kelvin. If \mu^=\mu/[1+\mu\ln(E{\mathrm{el}}/\omega{\log})], with the two cutoff scales in the same units, fixed \lambda,\mu,E{\mathrm{el}} give \alpha=\tfrac12[1-A(1+0.62\lambda)(\mu^)^2/D^2]. Three finite-difference mass substitutions independently confirm this derivative and its difference from the fixed-\mu^ limit. These examples are not mercury fits. The estimate omits the full Allen–Dynes shape factors and is not a universal upper bound.   

In the Sc paper's Table I, six printed estimates are consistent with the input rounding intervals. Sc-IV printed inputs yield 21.37/18.72 K, versus listed 21.5/18.8 K; exact reproduction needs unrounded inputs. Sc-V at 260 GPa gives 30.07/26.38 K for \mu^=0.10/0.13. These are calculations, not the measured 37.6 K onset at a different pressure. The reported extrapolated B{c2}(0)=21.3 T implies \xi=\sqrt{\Phi0/(2\pi B{c2})}=39.31 angstrom; this checks units, not the extrapolation model. 

 Experimental criteria

Tunneling is valuable when the measured superconducting conductance is normalized by an appropriate normal reference. Rowell's 1970 account states the crucial conditions: the current must be tunneling current and the barrier must remain effectively unchanged through the transition. Unnormalized structure can instead reflect the barrier or its excitations. The 1965 McMillan–Rowell paper establishes the historical lead inversion reference, but its original quantitative inversion has not been independently rerun here. A phonon density of states alone is not the coupling-weighted spectrum \alpha^2F.   

Lithium illustrates why conditions cannot be dropped from a material label. Shimizu and colleagues reported compressed Li reaching about 20 K at 48 GPa in 2002; Tuoriniemi and colleagues reported an ambient-pressure transition around 0.4 mK in 2007, with a Meissner-state figure. The latter is 0.0004 K, not 0.4 K. These source checks cover abstracts and selected captions; they do not establish an entire phase diagram or independently validate the underlying data.  

Wang and colleagues reported Sc onset at 37.6 K and 243 GPa, distinct from the plotted 37.3 K at 244 GPa. Four-probe warming measurements used diamond Raman pressure calibration; onset means departure from the normal-state line. Field/current suppression supports the transport assignment, but no Meissner measurement was supplied. Phase boundaries were inferred from transition trends and compared with earlier diffraction. Applied fields reached 9 T; 21.3 T is an extrapolation. 

Sakata and colleagues reported Ca-VII near 29 K at 216 GPa. Their selected methods describe room-temperature diffraction and transport; a room-temperature structure measurement does not automatically determine the low-temperature phase. An Andersson comment is part of the source trail, but its contents have not yet been obtained in this review. The reported result remains attributed to its authors, with that reconciliation open.  

Iron is another warning against classification by ambient behavior. Shimizu and colleagues reported a resistance drop and Meissner signal below 2 K under 15–30 GPa in the non-magnetic state. This abstract-level evidence does not identify the pairing interaction or justify transferring a simple weak-coupling description from an unrelated element. Magnetic history, structure and purity need their own assessment. 

 Limits and disputes

A finite resistive transition, instrument-limited zero resistance, field suppression, magnetic shielding and a bulk thermodynamic anomaly answer different questions. Compare them on the same sample or explain why samples differ. Report the thermometer, onset/midpoint/zero criterion, pressure calibration, pressure medium, compression path and structural measurement temperature. Missing information stays unknown rather than being inferred from the chemical formula.    

The September 2026 Sc theory paper connects compression, increasing overlap of 3d orbitals and band broadening to stronger electron–phonon coupling. Its phrase “electronic mechanism” does not mean a demonstrated nonphonon pairing glue. This page has checked the publisher abstract only: no new experimental transition, full calculation or universal elemental record is inferred from that description. Historical “highest” claims must be dated to the publication and its comparison set. 

 Discovery implications

Treat an element as a collection of phase-specific test cases. Useful screening combines a dynamically and thermodynamically plausible structure, electron–phonon matrix elements, electronic energy scales and a stated Coulomb treatment, then asks which experimental observable could falsify the prediction. Agreement with one transition temperature does not validate the whole spectral function, numerical convergence or phase assignment. Keep calculated values separate from experimental transition records and preserve negative or incomplete evidence.

entries.text:
Scope

Organic charge-transfer salts provide distinct low-dimensional settings for superconductivity. The Bechgaard salts (TMTSF)₂X have strongly anisotropic electronic motion; the κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂X family has conducting molecular layers and is widely studied near a pressure-controlled Mott transition. The anion, molecular packing, sample history and field direction are part of the material identity. A pairing assignment for one salt or field regime is not a classification of the entire family.   

The 1980 Jérome report identifies superconductivity in (TMTSF)₂PF₆. Its bibliographic identity is checked here, while the original experimental text remains an access gap. For κ-Br, the 1990 Kini paper explicitly distinguishes an inductive onset of 11.6 K from a resistive onset of 12.5 K in its title. Those criteria should survive quotation and database export. Its original publication is July 1990; the publisher's 2002 online date does not move the discovery into a later decade.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Izawa's rotating-field thermal-conductivity analysis separates \kappa(\theta)=C0+C2\cos(2\theta)+C4\cos(4\theta), where the angle is between the heat current and the in-plane field. The large twofold term has a substantial phonon-scattering contribution, whereas the low-temperature fourfold term is interpreted through nodal quasiparticles. An independent synthetic harmonic-recovery check confirms the decomposition algebra, not the original fit or the inferred gap symmetry. A 45° rotation reverses the sign of the fourfold basis function, so node labels require a stated crystallographic convention. 

The normal-state anisotropic shift used by Shinagawa is K=K{\mathrm{iso}}+K{\mathrm{ax}}(3\cos^2\theta-1), with K{\mathrm{iso}}=3.9\times10^{-4} and K{\mathrm{ax}}=10.5\times10^{-4}. Substitution gives 2,490 ppm at 0° and −660 ppm at 90°. These are signed model contributions, not directly the observed superconducting change. Reducing the spin contribution can move resonance shifts in opposite directions for two orientations. Hyperfine calibration, chemical shifts, screening fields and pulse heating must therefore accompany a spin-pairing inference. 

Kagawa's transport analysis found approximate exponents (\delta,\beta,\gamma)=(2,1,1), satisfying \delta=1+\gamma/\beta. Checking that identity does not independently validate a universality class. The analysis maps conductance onto an order parameter and treats pressure/temperature mixing within stated approximations; it excludes the closest region to the endpoint because of calibration and sample limitations. A later theoretical treatment shows how conductivity can couple to singular quantities other than the thermodynamic order parameter. Transport exponents and thermodynamic exponents must not be equated automatically.  

 Experimental criteria

Lefebvre's κ-Cl phase diagram combines proton NMR with AC susceptibility under helium-gas pressure. NMR uses a 0.5 T field perpendicular to the layers; susceptibility uses an approximately 0.05 Oe oscillating field parallel to them, without a static field. Slow pressure and temperature sweeps, restricted to helium's fluid region, resolve hysteresis and changing phase fractions. The reported meeting region near 282 bar and 13.1 K is not evidence that antiferromagnetism and superconductivity occupy every microscopic volume together: the paper explicitly discusses inhomogeneous coexistence. 

In the separate κ-Cl conductance experiment, a critical endpoint occurs near 39.7 ± 0.1 K and 24.8 ± 0.1 MPa. Here the paper's symbol Tc denotes the Mott endpoint, not a superconducting transition. Four-probe measurements, helium pressure sweeps near 3 MPa per hour and a current-independence check over two orders of magnitude underpin this assignment. The endpoint pressure is 0.0248 GPa; confusing MPa with GPa would introduce a factor of one thousand. 

Izawa studies κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu(NCS)₂ with a reported resistive transition near 10.4 K. Heat flows along the b axis, with in-plane field alignment better than 0.01°. At 2 T the fourfold component becomes visible around 0.52 and 0.43 K, at approximately 0.2% of the normal-state total conductivity. These low temperatures are probe conditions, not additional transition temperatures. Extracting such a small electronic modulation requires separating phonons, vortex scattering and the field/temperature regime; the sign cannot be interpreted without that model. 

For (TMTSF)₂ClO₄, Shinagawa's samples were cooled at 7 mK per minute through anion ordering near 24 K and showed resistive/rf onset near 1.4 K. NMR pulses with tip angles below 3° were checked for heating using simultaneous resistance measurements. Low-field shifts support reduced spin susceptibility, while relaxation near 100 mK changes sharply around 15 kOe. That crossover field is neither a superconducting temperature nor, by itself, a unique identification of an FFLO or triplet state. 

 Limits and disputes

The earlier Lee result concerns a different salt, (TMTSF)₂PF₆, at 7 kbar with field along the conducting a axis; its abstract reports little Knight-shift change and argues for triplet pairing. The later ClO₄ study finds a low-field singlet-compatible response and leaves its high-field state unresolved. These are condition-specific observations. High upper critical fields, unchanged shifts in one regime or proximity to spin-density-wave order cannot alone establish family-wide p-wave superconductivity.  

For κ-(BEDT-TTF)₂Cu₂(CN)₃, absence of magnetic ordering down to 32 mK motivated a spin-liquid interpretation, while pressure studies found a neighboring superconducting region. Subsequent spin-gap work supports a valence-bond interpretation but does not uniquely exclude a gapped chiral spin liquid. Mounting strain and microcracks complicate comparison with a nominally hydrostatic experiment. Neither an exchange scale nor a spin-gap anomaly should become a superconducting Tc record.   

The original κ-Br reference in the pinned draft had an unrelated DOI. The correct identifier is 10.1021/ic00339a004; 10.1021/ic00331a012 identifies a metal-complex structural-analysis paper. This public article corrects the citation while preserving the fixed source file. Discovery-era methods, complete supplements, final-version comparisons and original-data refits remain outside parts of this scoped review. 

 Discovery implications

Compare pressure, chemical substitution and strain through measured phase diagrams rather than treating them as interchangeable tuning knobs. Report the exact salt, cooling protocol, pressure medium, field orientation and transition criterion before comparing performance. A useful next measurement should distinguish competing explanations—for example by combining bulk thermodynamics, low-heating spin probes and controlled-disorder studies on the same specimen. A nearby Mott state constrains a mechanism without identifying it uniquely.   

Molecular superconductors also provide a warning against copying symmetry names between coordinate systems. The κ-NCS thermal-conductivity paper discusses nodal directions relative to b and c as well as a rotated convention. Preserve those directions and the observable itself when comparing with theories. Fullerides belong to a separate molecular family with different orbital degeneracy and vibronic physics; the shared word “organic” does not make their pairing evidence interchangeable.

entries.summary: Separate pairing, phase coherence and interface tuning. A gap-closing scale, resistance onset and BKT transition are not interchangeable temperatures.

entries.text:
Scope

Two-dimensional geometry and interface location describe different properties. Weak out-of-plane dispersion does not alone establish a two-dimensional phase transition. An interface can support a superconducting region between constituents that are not superconducting separately. Charge redistribution, oxygen defects, strain, orbital structure and disorder can change together, so an enhanced transition does not identify one universal interface mechanism.  

Pair formation and macroscopic phase coherence need not coincide. Every temperature below retains its probe and criterion: a spectral gap, resistance onset, noise-floor zero, magnetic screening or BKT analysis. An ultrathin film may also have finite lateral size, nonuniform current paths and coupling to its substrate. These conditions matter when comparing it with an ideal phase model.   

 Mathematical assumptions

In the convention F=(Js/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2, the ideal BKT jump is kBT{\mathrm{BKT}}=\pi Js(T{\mathrm{BKT}}^-)/2. Here Js is the long-wavelength, renormalized total phase stiffness, with units of energy. It is not the bare pairing amplitude or a separately measured geometric contribution. Magnetic screening, finite size and interlayer coupling limit the length scales over which the logarithmic-vortex description applies. BCS-like amplitude formation and BKT phase ordering are not mutually exclusive microscopic pairing mechanisms.  

For a homogeneous local sheet response, Js=\hbar^2/(4e^2Lk) relates the same stiffness to sheet kinetic inductance. Combining it with the jump gives Lk=\Phi0^2/(8\pi kBT{\mathrm{BKT}}), where \Phi0=h/(2e). Independent electron-density and pair-density conventions give the same conversion. At a hypothetical 0.188 K jump it predicts approximately 65.5 nH per square; this is a model conversion, not an inductance measured in Reyren's device. Finite-frequency response must not be silently identified with the asymptotic equilibrium stiffness.  

 Experimental criteria

A convincing BKT comparison combines current–voltage behavior, an appropriate resistance-fluctuation regime and stiffness where available. An apparent cubic law over a chosen current interval is insufficient: the synthetic response V=I+I^3 has nearly cubic high-current behavior while retaining finite low-current resistance. Likewise, an activated resistor can mimic a linearized BKT plot in a narrow window. These checked counterexamples test logical uniqueness, not the validity of any cited experiment. Heating, current window, finite size and inhomogeneity need independent controls. 

Reyren's 2007 LaAlO3/SrTiO3 measurements distinguish eight-unit-cell and fifteen-unit-cell LaAlO3 overlayers, with resistance reaching the noise floor below approximately 200 and 100 mK respectively at 100 nA. Those overlayer thicknesses are not measured superconducting-sheet widths. The field-dependent transition uses 50% of the 1 K resistance; extrapolated zero-temperature fields of 65 and 30 mT are therefore criterion-dependent estimates. 

For the eight-unit-cell sample, the current–voltage exponent reaches three near 188 mK and the resistance-tail analysis yields about 190 mK. Figure 4 also shows an ohmic low-current regime attributed to finite size. Agreement between these analyses is informative without eliminating their assumptions. The paper's roughly 10 nm thickness bound relies on an oxygen-defect/carrier-profile scenario and bulk carrier requirements, rather than direct spatial imaging or a unique explanation of carrier origin. 

 Oxide interface controls

The Reyren specimens use TiO2-terminated SrTiO3, pulsed-laser growth and oxygen treatment during cooling. A two-unit-cell reference remains insulating within the reported measurement window. These controls constrain oxygen-vacancy interpretations but do not prove that defects are absent. Later electrostatic gating requires nonlinear capacitance integration and attention to conditioning history; a dome does not establish carrier density as the only variable or identify a unique quantum critical pairing interaction.  

In Gozar's author manuscript, I denotes insulating La2CuO4, M denotes metallic La1.55Sr0.45CuO4 and S denotes oxygenated superconducting La2CuO4+δ. Reversing I–M to M–I changes the characteristic transition from roughly 15 to 30 K; oxygenating M–I produces M–S near 50 K. The thickness-series figure uses a resistance midpoint. Its separate screening figure reports 33.2 K for S and 51.6 K for M–S, measured with 10 kHz mutual inductance. Screening and transport criteria must remain distinct. 

The layer-thickness and screening-current analyses constrain an interfacial region approximately one to two unit cells thick, subject to their structural and electrodynamic models. Microscopy bounds cation interdiffusion at roughly one unit cell; it does not establish perfectly abrupt chemistry. Logvenov's original abstract describes layer-selective Zn markers that suppress superconductivity and locate the response within a single CuO2 plane. That selected abstract supports the localization statement, while its full methods and calibration remain unchecked here.  

 FeSe spectra and annealing

He and colleagues' 2012 author version, associated with the 2013 journal article, follows annealing-dependent electronic phases in single-layer FeSe/SrTiO3. Figure 3 extracts gaps from symmetrized energy-distribution curves and compares them with BCS-form temperature fits. Sequence 10 has an approximately 10 meV gap closing around 40 K; sequence 15 reaches roughly 19 meV and 65 ± 5 K. The latter is an ARPES gap scale, not a measured zero-resistance temperature. 

The inferred electron count assumes two degenerate electron sheets, and the observed band evolution is not a simple rigid shift. Annealing may alter selenium or oxygen content and atomic configuration; later annealing also degrades sample quality. The selected author text describes direct single-layer transport and magnetic measurements as still underway. A BCS-shaped fit is compatible with a superconducting interpretation but does not independently demonstrate global phase coherence. 

Lee's later replica-band study supports coupling between FeSe electrons and a substrate-related phonon, while its estimated pairing enhancement depends on the assumed background interaction. Its 58 ± 7 K fitted gap closing belongs to that specimen and analysis, not to He's annealing sequence. Replica bands alone do not partition every contribution to the pairing kernel. See  for the source-specific model limitations. 

 Limits and disputes

A superconducting single layer establishes sufficiency under its preparation and measurement conditions, not that interlayer coupling is universally irrelevant. Interface records should not be merged with bulk, transient or high-pressure records. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: selected original passages and figures, inherited named checks and model arithmetic are documented, while full supplements, final-author comparisons, raw-data reanalysis and independent replication are incomplete.    

 Discovery implications

Separate thickness, termination, oxygen history, strain and electrostatics in a controlled comparison. Report the current and frequency window, temperature criterion, sample variation and structural uncertainty. A useful mechanism should predict which intervention changes a gap and which changes phase stiffness, with observations that can distinguish competing explanations. Keep those outcomes separate in prose, search filters and exported evidence.

entries.title: Topological superconductor candidates: materials and devices
entries.summary: Compare bulk crystals, superconducting surfaces, vortex spectra and semiconductor devices while preserving the boundary between candidate signals, topological interpretation and demonstrated operations.

materialCases.temperatureNote: 0.55K vortex-STM measurement; not a superconducting transition temperature.

entries.text:
Scope

Topological superconductivity concerns the superconducting quasiparticle state, not merely a topological normal-state band next to a superconducting transition. Candidate platforms include intrinsically paired crystals, proximitized surfaces and engineered semiconductor devices. This comparison separates measured superconductivity, a proposed topological phase and evidence for localized Majorana modes. Their criteria and relevant dimensionality differ; a surface result does not automatically classify an entire three-dimensional bulk.    

For a fully gapped Bogoliubov–de Gennes description, topology depends on dimensionality, symmetries and the occupied quasiparticle states. This restricted framework does not exhaust interacting or nodal superconductivity. A local zero-bias peak is neither a universal requirement for every topological superconductor nor sufficient proof of a Majorana mode. Demonstrating non-Abelian operations is a further question; it is not the definition of every bulk topological superconducting phase.    

 Mathematical assumptions

One clean single-subband wire model uses H(k)=\xik\tauz+\alpha k\tauz\sigmay+VZ\sigmax+\Delta\taux, where \xik=\hbar^2k^2/(2m)-\mu, \sigma acts on spin and \tau on particle–hole space. Here \Delta is real induced pairing, spin–orbit and Zeeman axes are perpendicular, and VZ=|g\muB B|/2 is an energy rather than a magnetic field. With a=\alpha k, diagonalization yields E\pm^2=\xik^2+a^2+VZ^2+\Delta^2\pm2\sqrt{VZ^2(\xik^2+\Delta^2)+\xik^2a^2}.  

The zero-momentum gap closes at VZ^2=\mu^2+\Delta^2. In the stated gapped wire model, the side with VZ^2>\mu^2+\Delta^2 supports the topological phase. The inequality alone is not a material diagnostic: setting spin–orbit coupling to zero can leave finite-momentum gapless excitations even when it holds. Independent checks compare 54 matrix spectra, three closure points and that counterexample. They do not simulate multiband disorder, orbital depairing, interfaces or a complete material invariant.  

Fu–Berg supplies a sufficient criterion for fully gapped, time-reversal-invariant odd-parity pairing in an inversion-symmetric weak-pairing setting, using the parity of enclosed time-reversal-invariant momenta. It is not a necessary criterion for every topological superconductor, nor proof that a particular doped crystal realizes odd parity. Fu–Kane's proximitized helical surface is a different construction: its uniform superconducting surface and a vortex carrying a localized mode must be distinguished.  

 Experimental criteria

Hor's Cu-intercalated Bi2Se3 study reports a transition near 3.8 K. In the checked author manuscript, Cu0.12Bi2Se3 has a magnetic response roughly one-fifth of ideal diamagnetism at the lowest accessible temperature, which the authors treat as a lower bound because the transition is incomplete. The resistance does not reach zero. This establishes why sample preparation and connected superconducting paths matter; neither a universal superconducting volume nor topological pairing can be inferred from those numbers alone. 

Butch's YPtBi crystals show a resistive transition near 0.77 K with an AC diamagnetic response. The critical-field curve uses a 50% resistive criterion, with 10–90% bounds, and field perpendicular to [001]. The often-quoted 1.5 T is a zero-temperature extrapolation. Converting it with B{c2}=\Phi0/(2\pi\xi^2) gives about 14.8 nm as a consistency estimate. Superconductivity in a candidate topological semimetal does not itself identify its pairing topology or establish a calibrated superconducting volume. 

Two iron-chalcogenide papers require separate attribution. Zhang's ARPES study resolves a spin-helical surface band and a superconducting surface gap around 1.8 meV, interpreted as surface topological superconductivity. Its low-temperature measurement at 2.4 K is not the reported 14.5 K transition temperature. The study's surface interpretation must not be replaced by a statement that all bulk pairing is topological. In its angular-gap figure, hollow mirrored markers are not additional independent measurements. 

Wang's distinct vortex-STM paper studies FeTe0.55Se0.45. Figure 2 spectra at 0.55 K and 0.5 T parallel to c are normalized by integrated spectral area; they cannot be read as an absolute quantized conductance plateau. The approximately 0.3 meV peak width contains instrumental and thermal broadening. Barrier and temperature scans elsewhere use different fields. The zero-energy signal is interpreted as Majorana evidence, while the displayed braiding sequence is a proposal, not a performed operation. 

Xu's Bi2Te3/NbSe2 heterostructure study compares vortex spectra across film thicknesses. The checked 2013 author version underlying the 2015 publication distinguishes where split peaks become experimentally resolvable from the extrapolated origin of their splitting. The former is around 20 nm even for thinner films; the latter changes near four quintuple layers and supports the authors' Majorana interpretation. Treating every unsplit interval as a directly measured Majorana radius would discard both the extrapolation and approximately 0.2 meV resolution. 

Semiconductor readout advances also need their own evidence category. Aghaee's 2025 InAs–Al experiment measures single-shot parity interferometrically and explicitly retains an Andreev-state alternative. Dvir's 2026 work demonstrates parity readout in a minimal Kitaev-chain device, with a two-site rather than asymptotically long-chain model. These are useful experimental capabilities; neither result, as scoped here, establishes braiding or fault-tolerant topological computation. Readout performance, spatial nonlocality and a protected bulk phase remain distinct questions.  

 Limits and disputes

Confinement, disorder and ordinary Andreev states can produce misleading local zero-bias signatures. Even apparent agreement with an ideal conductance value needs temperature, barrier, calibration and nonlocal checks. The 2018 paper Quantized Majorana conductance was retracted in 2021; its original result is retained here only as retracted history. The notice describes charge-jump corrections, an axis-label problem and conductance recalibration. A withdrawn claim cannot count as independent confirmation of later devices.   

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. This article checks selected primary passages, figures and restricted models. Earlier author versions are identified; complete final-version comparisons, supplements, raw-data analysis, calibration and exclusion of competing interpretations remain unfinished. These limits concern the present review and should not be inflated into a claim that every platform has the same evidential status.       

 Discovery implications

Specify the target first: bulk odd-parity superconductivity, a proximitized topological surface, a wire end state or a controllable parity device. Then record composition, geometry, temperature, field, superconducting criterion and competing-state tests for that target. Compare complementary probes on characterized samples and preserve failures and retractions. Strong spin–orbit coupling or an attractive band calculation can motivate an experiment, but cannot replace identification of the actual paired phase and its protected observables.

entries.text:
Scope

Two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenide superconductivity includes gate-doped semiconductors such as MoS2 and WS2, as well as intrinsically metallic NbSe2 and TaS2. They should not all be described as semiconductors or assigned one pairing mechanism. Atomic thickness, the thickness of an accumulated conducting layer and the dimensionality relevant to superconducting coherence are also different properties. Preserve polytype, substrate, layer count and preparation before comparing experiments.     

Ising protection refers to the influence of spin–orbit coupling on the response of Cooper pairs to an applied field. It does not mean that every paired state is purely singlet, or that a large in-plane critical field proves triplet pairing. Broken inversion can admit mixed components, while additional Fermi pockets, interlayer coupling, scattering and geometry change the interpretation. Topological superconductivity is a further classification, not a synonym for strong spin–orbit coupling.   

 Mathematical assumptions

A restricted normal-state illustration uses H\eta=\eta\lambda\sigmaz+b\sigmax, where \eta=\pm1 labels opposite valleys, \sigma acts on spin, \lambda is an Ising spin–orbit energy and b an in-plane Zeeman energy. Its eigenvalues are \pm\sqrt{\lambda^2+b^2}. On the positive branch the spin directions are \mathbf n\eta=(b,0,\eta\lambda)/\sqrt{\lambda^2+b^2}: opposite out-of-plane components persist while the field cants both spins in-plane. This two-level model omits momentum-dependent bands, Rashba terms and other pockets.  

For corresponding spinors, |u+^T i\sigmayu-|^2=\lambda^2/(\lambda^2+b^2) is the squared singlet pairing matrix element. It is twice the singlet probability of the normalized tensor-product state, so those quantities must not be confused. Twelve independent diagonalizations check this distinction and spin orientations. This normal-state calculation neither solves a superconducting gap equation nor establishes singlet dominance, a critical field or a material pairing mechanism.  

The weak-coupling reference BP=\Delta0/(\sqrt2\muB)\simeq1.86\,Tc uses tesla for field and kelvin for temperature, with g=2, negligible spin–orbit effects and \Delta0\simeq1.764kBTc. This is a paramagnetic benchmark, not a universal upper bound including orbital effects. Similarly, the BKT transport signature V\propto I^3 has a restricted dynamical regime; finite size, heating and inhomogeneity can invalidate a naive exponent-only diagnosis. Neither comparison identifies the pairing interaction.  

 Experimental criteria

Ye's MoS2 study established a gate-controlled superconducting dome in a band insulator. Lu's later Ising study illustrates why the chosen threshold matters: its checked author manuscript uses 90% of normal resistance for the phase diagram and 50% elsewhere. Those temperatures cannot be silently substituted for one another, for a measured zero-resistance temperature or for a fitted BKT temperature. The dome itself is not evidence selecting a unique pairing mechanism.  

Saito's high-field MoS2 device gives a particularly clear warning. Its reported transition near 6.5 K and in-plane critical field near 52 T at 1.5 K use a 75%-of-normal-resistance criterion; that device did not reach zero resistance. The separate low-field sample's 9.7 K transition uses 50%. The 55 T pulsed-field ceiling is not identical to the extracted 52 T boundary. The experiment and band calculations support spin–valley protection, while neither these criteria nor the measurement temperature establish triplet order. 

Costanzo's atomically thin MoS2 experiments demonstrate a monolayer resistance drop to the measured zero level, but only one contact pair in the illustrated device shows it. Other monolayers show no transition down to the 1.5 K base temperature. Different contact regions reveal substantial density variation, associated with frozen-liquid detachment. A tendency toward weaker monolayer superconductivity in this set of devices is therefore not a universal prohibition on strong two-dimensional pairing. The critical-field comparison uses half the normal resistance. 

In NbSe2, Xi's Ising paper extracts an Aslamazov–Larkin fit scale close to half the normal resistance; its current-excitation BKT estimate lies closer to the one-percent criterion. The roughly 3 K monolayer fit scale must not be relabelled as a direct BKT temperature. The paper considers reduced interlayer pairing and argues that the competing CDW effect on this trend is likely weak. That interpretation differs from asserting that enhanced CDW necessarily causes the superconducting suppression. 

The frequently quoted monolayer CDW scale of 145\pm3 K comes from a separate Xi Raman/transport paper. The selected analysis follows a CDW amplitude mode and extrapolates its intensity to zero, with mean-field fits used as guides. This is neither a superconducting transition nor an independent direct measurement of the pairing interaction. Contrasting thickness trends of CDW and superconductivity motivate competing-order tests; a correlation alone does not determine their causal coupling. 

De la Barrera compares metallic 2H-TaS2 and NbSe2 down to atomic thickness. The resistive curves use 50% criteria; the reported monolayer TaS2 boundary remains above the 34.5 T instrument limit below 2 K. A 65.6 T coefficient fitted near the transition is not a measured zero-temperature critical field. Even-layer enhancement also survives despite restored inversion symmetry, emphasizing the balance of interlayer and spin–orbit coupling. Encapsulation, aging and distinct thickness trends remain part of the sample record. 

Lu's CVD monolayer WS2 dome uses an effective gate coordinate assembled from ionic-gate states and back-gate sweeps. It is not a directly applied kilovolt voltage across the ionic liquid, and Hall carrier density is nonmonotonic across the dome. The high-field study uses a separate sample B, whose optimal 50%-resistance transition is 3.15 K. Its low-edge 1.54 K state changes by only 0.08 K at 35 T. Neither number supplies a universal WS2 transition or proves that all tungsten dichalcogenides behave alike. 

 Limits and disputes

Sajadi's monolayer WTe2 device connects gate-controlled superconductivity with a quantum-spin-Hall material platform, while retaining resistance thresholds and a finite measurement floor. Qi's pressure-dependent MoTe2 study instead follows bulk structural regimes, including low-pressure Td and high-pressure 1T-prime behavior. These are distinct geometries and phases. A topological normal-state description plus superconductivity is a reason to investigate the paired state, not sufficient demonstration of a topological superconducting gap or Majorana modes.  

A September 2026 theory by Marini, Cudazzo and Calandra attributes gated-TMD domes to ionic disorder, reduced screening and enhanced Coulomb repulsion, comparing its calculations with experiment. This is a model explanation, not a new experimental transition or universal proof about every superconducting dome. Complete scientific acceptance remains open here: its full equations, other cited final-version comparisons, supplements, chemical controls and raw-data analyses are unfinished. The present checks are restricted to the named primary passages, figures and spinor model.      

 Discovery implications

Treat the device as part of the material: record layer count, polytype, contacts, electrolyte, gating temperature, voltage history and field orientation. Compare onset, midpoint, measured zero, phase-ordering and spectroscopic scales separately. Establish whether charge tuning also changes disorder or chemistry, and test proposed spin protection against the actual bands and geometry. The strongest next experiment distinguishes competing explanations on characterized devices instead of ranking isolated critical-field or transition-temperature numbers.

entries.text:
Scope

Kagome geometry offers a useful starting point for studying flat bands, Dirac crossings, charge order and superconductivity. It does not guarantee that a flat band lies at the Fermi energy, that magnetic frustration produces a spin liquid, or that a material has a high transition temperature. This article separates superconducting AV3Sb5 compounds, pressure-induced superconductivity in CsCr3Sb5 and charge-ordered comparison materials. Normal-state topology and superconducting topology remain separate questions.      

 Mathematical assumptions

Take one spinless orbital on each of three sites 0,\mathbf a1/2,\mathbf a2/2, with triangular Bravais vectors and qi=\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf ai. For positive nearest-neighbor hopping t, a Bloch Hamiltonian is H=-2t\begin{pmatrix}0&c1&c2\\c1&0&c3\\c2&c3&0\end{pmatrix}, where c1=\cos(q1/2), c2=\cos(q2/2) and c3=\cos[(q2-q1)/2]. Its bands are Ef=2t and E\pm=t[-1\pm\sqrt{4S-3}], with S=c1^2+c2^2+c3^2. The vectors in Guo and Franz's convention are nearest-neighbor vectors, half the Bravais vectors used here. 

The model has a flat-band contact at Gamma, a Dirac crossing at K and dispersive-band saddles at M. Independent diagonalization checks 1,311 momentum/hopping combinations; numerical Hessians have opposite-sign curvatures at the two M-point saddles. Adding equal same-sublattice hopping shifts all bands by \delta(\mathbf q)=-2u[\cos q1+\cos q2+\cos(q2-q1)]. The formerly flat branch then spans 9|u| between Gamma and K while the kagome geometry remains. These checks illustrate model sensitivity; they do not calculate a pairing interaction, a material transition temperature or a superconducting invariant. 

Real compounds add orbital character, spin–orbit coupling, interlayer hopping and reconstruction. Kang's ARPES/DFT work distinguishes van Hove features with predominantly pure or mixed sublattice content near the Fermi energy of CsV3Sb5. Such information constrains low-energy models; a large density of states alone does not select a pairing symmetry. The presently checked author abstract is not a reproduction of the full spectral assignment or pairing calculation. 

 Experimental criteria

Ortiz's original family study identified K, Rb and Cs vanadium antimonides as layered kagome metals. The later CsV3Sb5 superconductivity paper combines magnetization, resistivity and heat capacity around a 2.5 K onset. Its transport onset is suppressed at an 8 mA probe current and returns toward the nominal value at lower current, illustrating why excitation belongs in the sample record. The heat-capacity temperature floor limits conclusions about the low-temperature gap. Subsequent K and Rb member reports should retain their own samples and criteria rather than being collapsed into a universal family transition range.    

The same CsV3Sb5 work discusses a much higher-temperature anomaly and a normal-state topological band background. ARPES taken well above the superconducting transition and calculated surface states above the Fermi energy do not directly measure a superconducting gap invariant. Liang's three-dimensional CDW study and Li's conjoined-CDW study further emphasize stacking, temperature and surface dependence. Different modulation descriptions cannot be merged into one structure common to every sample or termination.   

Yang reports anomalous Hall response in KV3Sb5; Yu connects anomalous Hall response in CsV3Sb5 to its higher-temperature charge-order regime. Neither result is a phase-sensitive measurement of superconducting chirality. Ordinary multiband transport, scattering and Berry-curvature contributions require separate analysis. Likewise, the checked Mielke muon study concerns time-reversal symmetry breaking associated with charge order. A signal emerging near that ordering scale cannot simply be reassigned to a superconducting d+id state.   

Chen's spatially resolved tunneling work proposes a roton pair-density-wave interpretation in CsV3Sb5. Pair-related modulations are significant evidence to investigate, but charge-order changes in local density of states, tunneling matrix elements and Josephson coupling remain relevant controls. Pressure studies also show nonmonotonic superconducting and charge-order scales. Two domes do not by themselves establish two pairing mechanisms: structure, bands, scattering and calibration can evolve together.  

For CsCr3Sb5, Liu's author manuscript and selected final-paper results report a maximum resistive onset of 6.4 K at 4.2 GPa, with zero resistance and AC susceptibility supporting bulk superconductivity over a pressure interval. Its critical-field curves instead use half the normal resistance. The fitted zero-temperature field is therefore not an independently observed field boundary. The final text explicitly leaves the field direction uncertain, preventing an anisotropy claim. The cubic-anvil measurement uses glycerol and room-temperature load calibration; the lower-pressure piston-cell setup uses a different medium and calibration. These are high-pressure records, not ambient-pressure entries or universal chromium-family numbers. 

Cheng's April 2026 paper adds a distinct charge-order result in CsCr3Sb5. The selected author text describes cleaved-surface STM with a 4.5 K base temperature and two higher-temperature modulation scales. Its stripe pattern breaks mirror symmetries while retaining a mirror-glide operation; opposite local textures do not define global handedness. Those surface images are not a high-pressure superconducting order-parameter measurement and cannot establish chiral superconductivity. 

FeGe and ScV6Sn6 serve as comparisons. Yin's FeGe study reports charge order, magnetic stacking and an edge state within a charge-order energy gap; Arachchige's ScV6Sn6 work reports a lattice-modulated charge-order transition. Neither cited result establishes superconductivity. Absence of such evidence in these papers should not be rewritten as a timeless claim that either material can never superconduct under any preparation or pressure.  

 Limits and disputes

Allowed pairing representations are candidates until tested against the actual superconducting state. Charge-order time-reversal breaking, a normal-state anomalous Hall signal, structural handedness, tunneling modulation and a zero-bias feature each address different questions. Phase-sensitive experiments, temperature-resolved symmetry probes, bulk gap constraints and boundary-state tests can provide complementary discrimination; they are not a universal checklist that defines every possible topological superconductor. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: several references retain abstract-only review, and final-version comparisons, supplements and raw-data analyses are unfinished.      

 Discovery implications

Record composition, pressure path, excitation, surface termination and the onset, midpoint, measured-zero and thermodynamic criteria separately. Compare measured band positions with a specified model before invoking flat-band enhancement. Test whether changing charge order also changes disorder, structure or carrier balance. The useful next experiment resolves competing interpretations on a characterized sample, rather than promoting a geometric label or an isolated transition number into a mechanism.

entries.text:
Scope

Magnetic substitution can change carrier balance, crystal structure, potential scattering, spin-flip scattering and exchange fields at the same time. These effects are distinguishable experimental questions, not mutually exclusive channels. A falling superconducting transition temperature does not uniquely identify magnetic pair breaking, and the presence of a magnetic element does not establish magnetically mediated pairing. Compare actual composition, valence, phase purity and preparation before treating concentration as a single physical control.    

Dilute paramagnetic impurities, an ordered lattice of rare-earth moments and a concentrated magnetic film require different models. Independent magnetic ions can scatter Cooper pairs, while their ordering, screening and coupling to itinerant states change the relevant timescales and fields. A material that contains both magnetic and superconducting signals may also be spatially inhomogeneous; their coexistence must be tested at the relevant volume and length scale.    

 Mathematical assumptions

For dilute, uncorrelated weak magnetic scattering in an isotropic singlet host, define a pair-breaking energy \Gamma through \ln(T{c0}/Tc)=\psi[1/2+\Gamma/(2\pi kBTc)]-\psi(1/2). Here T{c0} is the corresponding clean-host transition, not necessarily the transition of the unsubstituted parent if substitution also changes its bands or interaction. With g=\Gamma/(kBT{c0}) and t=Tc/T{c0}, this convention gives dt/dg=-\pi/4 initially and gc=\pi e^{-\gammaE}/2\simeq0.882. Scattering-rate conventions require explicit factors of \hbar; neither atomic fraction nor residual resistivity can be inserted directly as \Gamma. The equation convention has a scoped review-paper check, while the original AG full text remains unaudited.   

An independent inversion illustrates the ambiguity. In units with kB=1, prescribe an observed curve Tc=1-0.6c, where c is a synthetic dimensionless control. Both a fixed clean-host scale T{c0}=1 and a changing scale T{c0}=1-0.2c admit different positive \Gamma(c) values that reproduce the same transitions. Five checked points demonstrate non-uniqueness; they are not alloy fits or concentration calibrations. Additional composition, band, magnetic and scattering measurements are needed to choose between such explanations.   

For a free Eu2+ ion with S=7/2 and g=2, the saturated moment is gS\muB=7\muB, whereas the Curie effective moment is g\sqrt{S(S+1)}\muB\simeq7.94\muB. Neither specifies the sign or strength of the exchange field acting on conduction electrons. In a collinear compensation illustration, B{\mathrm{eff}}=B{\mathrm{ext}}+B{\mathrm{ex}} and opposite signed contributions can reduce Zeeman splitting. This does not eliminate the orbital action of the applied field. Local-moment size, exchange energy and magnetic induction have different units and roles.  

 Experimental criteria

Sugawara and Eguchi measured transition temperatures and critical fields magnetically in dilute La–Ce and La–Gd alloys. Their original abstract reports deviations from the AG Born-approximation result that depend on the exchange sign, interpreting them as evidence of Kondo effects. It also describes behavior characteristic of inhomogeneous type-II superconductors. This is a historical test of the theory's limits, not permission to assign one universal critical impurity fraction or transition-temperature slope to magnetic substitutions. 

Anderson's robustness argument for nonmagnetic disorder applies when appropriate time-reversed states, an essentially unchanged pairing interaction and density of states, and extended electronic states remain available. It is not immunity to arbitrary chemical substitution. Prozorov's controlled electron-irradiation study of a ruthenium-substituted iron arsenide illustrates why intra- and interband scattering, annealing and sample continuity matter. Nonmagnetic disorder can suppress sign-changing pairing, so comparing magnetic and nonmagnetic substitutions alone does not supply an independent singlet verdict.  

Cava established superconductivity in the LnNi2B2C family, including magnetic rare-earth members. Cho's cited paper then studied single-crystal ErNi2B2C specifically: transport and magnetization show a superconducting transition around 10.5 K, while the magnetic transition lies near 6 K. Its heat-capacity estimate is 5.85\pm0.15 K. These are distinct probe-specific scales. The paper is not a systematic survey of all rare-earth ions, and changing the rare earth also changes crystal fields, structure and exchange. No universal free-ion-moment ranking follows.  

Yaron's small-angle neutron study provides a more direct coupling test. On a boron-11-enriched ErNi2B2C crystal, superconducting vortex diffraction and magnetic diffraction establish their relative orientations. Figure 1's vortex pattern is measured at 1.6 K and 4 kOe with field near the c axis; the magnetic comparison uses zero field and a different neutron wavelength. The measured vortex lines rotate away from the applied field as temperature falls, and their rocking curves broaden. These observations support microscopic coexistence through interaction between magnetic order and the vortex structure, rather than merely coincident bulk anomalies. 

The geometry matters: the applied field in that experiment was already tilted about 1.6 degrees from the c axis. The additional vortex rotation begins around 4 K and can approach one degree, whereas antiferromagnetic ordering occurs near 6 K. These temperatures should not be equated. The authors also consider long-distance orientation variation as an alternative contribution to rocking-curve broadening; width alone is not a unique measure of microscopic pinning or a demonstration of triplet pairing. 

Meul's Eu–Sn molybdenum chalcogenide work reports magnetic-field-induced superconductivity interpreted through exchange compensation. The checked original abstract supports that historical connection, but does not establish every numerical endpoint or the precise alloy composition used in earlier summaries. A compensation claim in another material needs its own signed exchange estimate, local-moment response, angle dependence and orbital constraints. Large upper critical fields or field-enhanced resistance drops alone are insufficient.  

Yang's 2026 Sm/Ca/Eu infinite-layer nickelate study involves rare-earth substitution, fixed nominal Ca content and film reduction. In the checked later author version, SCE0.34 regains zero resistance at 2 K beyond 6.23 T; SCE0.32 does so at 3 K by 13.04 T. SCE0.36 remains superconducting to the 45 T measurement limit at 0.3 K. These are different samples and measurement temperatures, not a single transition curve. Compensation-like and magnetic-fluctuation explanations remain under discussion; neither established uniform ferromagnetism nor triplet pairing follows from the reported reentrance alone. 

 Limits and disputes

The same substitution series may move a clean-host pairing scale, alter scattering and create an exchange contribution. An AG-looking fit cannot separate these without additional constraints. Conversely, a departure from simple AG behavior does not automatically prove unconventional pairing or exchange compensation. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: original AG and several classic full texts, final-version comparisons, calibration details and raw-data reanalysis remain unfinished. The numerical exercises check restricted inference and units, not a complete magnetic-alloy theory.      

 Discovery implications

Track chemical composition and valence alongside diffraction, magnetic response, transport and thermodynamics. Preserve the distinction between dilute moments, ordered sublattices and possible glassy or inhomogeneous behavior. Keep onset, midpoint, measured-zero, ordering and measurement temperatures separate. For compensation, constrain the electronic exchange field and its uncertainty independently; for coexistence, seek a probe of coupling or spatial overlap. Use those measurements to distinguish explanations before extrapolating a concentration trend to a new material.

entries.text:
Scope

A15 is a crystal-structure family, usually written A3B, with cubic space group Pm\bar{3}n before any distortion. Three orthogonal chains of A atoms help organize its electronic structure. They do not guarantee a high transition temperature: composition, site ordering, phonons and strain all matter. The brittle Nb–Sn A15 phase illustrates why a favorable electronic structure must also survive fabrication and mechanical loading. 

Nb3Sn, V3Si and Nb3Ge are distinct examples, not one table of universal constants. Matthias and colleagues reported Nb3Sn near 18 K in 1954. Gavaler's 1973 abstract reports sputtered Nb–Ge films remaining superconducting up to 22.3 K. That historical film result is neither an equilibrium bulk value nor a strict A15 temperature ceiling. “High pressure” in the deposition description refers to sputtering conditions, not a high-pressure superconductivity measurement.  

Near-stoichiometric Nb3Sn is a conventional strong-coupling benchmark, but even its coupling classification depends on composition and how the gap and transition are sampled. Godeke's review discusses interface-gap and inhomogeneity effects that can bias a gap-to-temperature ratio. A full gap is not proof that all samples have the same coupling, and a large upper critical field alone is not evidence for triplet pairing.  

 Mathematical assumptions

For an orbital dirty-limit description, write B{c2}=\mu0H{c2} and \ln(T/Tc)=\psi(1/2)-\psi[1/2+\hbar D B{c2}(T)/(2\Phi0kBT)], where D is an effective diffusion parameter and \psi the digamma function. The Maki–de Gennes form omits Pauli, spin–orbit, strong-coupling and Fermi-surface anisotropy corrections. A useful fit to an inhomogeneous wire does not measure a unique microscopic D. Independent numerical roots recover the model ratio B{c2}(0)/(Tc|dB{c2}/dT|{Tc})=\pi^2e^{-\gamma}/8\simeq0.693; this is not a universal material relation. 

For current perpendicular to field, the pinning-force magnitude is Fp=JcB. A common fixed-temperature field shape is f(h)=h^{1/2}(1-h)^2, with h=B/B{c2}. It peaks at h=0.2 and produces a linear Kramer plot of Jc^{1/2}B^{1/4} only under the model's assumptions. A triangular vortex lattice has a\Delta=(4/3)^{1/4}\sqrt{\Phi0/B}; the flux-shear expression includes (1-a\Delta/d)^{-2} for mean grain size d. At 12 T and d=100 nm, this factor is about 1.36, so neglecting it requires a stated tolerance. Neither the pinning peak nor a fitted Kramer intercept independently identifies the thermodynamic upper critical field. 

A two-component illustrative sum of currents, with imposed critical fields of 20 and 28 T, gives Kramer intercepts of 25.06 and 26.35 T over different finite field windows. This is a numerical counterexample to treating every extrapolated intercept as the largest component field; it is not a fitted wire network. Separately, Godeke's hypothetical uniform-wire comparison holds the prefactor fixed in Jc=C B{c2}^{2}h^{1/2}(1-h)^2/B. Its printed 24.9-to-26.9 T inputs give 2888.01 A/mm² from 2250 A/mm² at 12 T and 4.2 K, versus the paper's 2883 A/mm². The latter lies within input-field rounding bounds. Neither improved value was measured.  

 Experimental criteria

Godeke and colleagues measured small-current resistive transitions of filamentary Nb3Sn, using approximately 0.2–0.6 A/mm² and fields up to 30 T. Their 10%, 50% and 90% normal-resistance criteria probe different parts of a broadened transition. At high field, the 99% criterion was extrapolated from the less noisy 10–90% region under a width assumption. The study also retained an unresolved interlaboratory offset of about 4%, treated as approximately ±2% uncertainty. Its highest-quality fractions are not every part of the conductor. 

The B34 wire reacted for 64 hours at 675 °C provides a concrete comparison: transport at a 10 µV/m criterion gave non-Cu Jc=2250 A/mm² at 12 T and 4.2 K. The Kramer field was 24.9 T, while the 99% resistive field was 26.9 T at the same temperature. Keep the non-Cu area normalization, voltage criterion and heat treatment attached to those numbers. They are not interchangeable measures of performance. 

Gapud and colleagues studied a floating-zone V3Si single crystal, MP3, with residual-resistivity ratio 47. Their 51V NMR experiment used 6.67 T, where the reported superconducting transition was 12.8 K and the structural transition 21.1 K. Cubic and tetragonal spectra coexisted around the structural transition. The authors found no conclusive cubic-phase spectrum below the zero-field transition scale of 17 K; that is distinct from the 12.8 K transition in the actual NMR field. These observations do not establish that a martensitic transition is necessary for every A15 superconductor. 

 Limits and disputes

Elastic softening, anharmonicity and superconductivity can be correlated without a universal rule that moving closer to structural instability always improves Tc. Testardi's papers motivate this coupled problem; they do not remove the need for sample-specific structural and thermodynamic evidence. Changes in composition or disorder can alter several electronic and phonon parameters together. Increasing a density-of-states peak or an estimated coupling constant alone is not a validated optimization strategy.   

The V3Si NMR assignments depend on orientation, spectral resolution and a model of local electric-field gradients. Absence of a resolved line is not a proof of literally zero phase fraction, and zero-field and finite-field transition temperatures must not be conflated. Similarly, a Nb3Sn resistive onset, a pinning-derived extrapolation and a magnetic transition need their own criteria and uncertainty. Record strain state and mounting as well as nominal composition.  

A May 2026 doctoral-dissertation preprint explores Cu–Sn routes to Nb3Sn films for microwave dark-matter cavities. Its abstract describes a chosen cavity tested at 50 mK and 9 T, but reports a quality-factor decline in field. Neither the operating temperature nor the maximum applied field is a measured transition temperature or a demonstrated upper critical field. This is an abstract-level research pointer, not a peer-reviewed performance certification. 

 Discovery implications

Optimize a complete, conditional objective: transition temperature, useful field range, current density, mechanical tolerance and manufacturability. Preserve measured and predicted quantities separately. Compare transition criteria, composition gradients, annealing, strain, grain structure and area normalization before ranking conductors. For a proposed material, check phase stability and the coupling-weighted phonon spectrum; for a working wire or cavity, test the actual operating condition and retain negative results.
