entries.text:
Scope

Cuprates contain electronically important CuO2 planes, but layer count, oxygen coordination, charge reservoirs, disorder and doping differ across families. Many parent compounds are correlated antiferromagnetic insulators. Superconductivity, pseudogap behavior and competing orders do not define one universal phase diagram or establish a unique pairing interaction. A schematic dome organizes observations; its coordinates require a material-specific calibration. 

The discovery sequence also needs that specificity. Bednorz and Müller's 1986 original abstract describes three-phase Ba–La–Cu–O polycrystals with a current-dependent resistivity decrease in the 30 K range, interpreted as possible percolative superconductivity. It is not a complete bulk magnetic characterization of a modern, homogeneous composition. 

Wu and colleagues' 1987 discovery studied mixed-phase material with nominal composition Y1.2Ba0.8CuO4−y. It established a reproducible transition above liquid-nitrogen temperature using transport and magnetic measurements, while detailed phase identification remained open. The later Grant study of the principal YBa2Cu3Ox superconducting phase is a separate publication. Do not replace the original sample composition with a retrospectively assigned pure Y123 crystal.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Oxygen content is not automatically the hole density in a CuO2 plane. As an explicitly formal ionic exercise for YBa2Cu3O7−δ, assign Y charge +3, Ba +2, O −2, two plane Cu sites charge 2+p, and one chain site charge vc. Neutrality gives 2(2+p)+vc=7-2\delta, or p=(3-2\delta-vc)/2. Ten checked allocations show that the same oxygen count admits different plane/chain charge partitions. This exercise illustrates missing information; it does not measure actual orbital occupation or include ligand-hole covalency. 

Liang, Bonn and Hardy's author manuscript explicitly distinguishes chain oxygen ordering from total oxygen content. Its empirical dome, Tc/T{c,\max}=1-82.6(p-0.16)^2, has two inverse branches away from its peak. Five independent algebra controls confirm that a single transition temperature cannot choose underdoping versus overdoping. The authors also discuss deviations near one-eighth doping, so treating this relation as a universal carrier-density measurement is unjustified. 

The familiar square-lattice expression \Delta(\mathbf{k})\propto\cos kx-\cos ky illustrates a d-wave sign structure. Its symmetry does not supply a gap magnitude, a material's exact Fermi surface or a pairing mediator. Orthorhombicity, disorder and the measurement geometry must remain part of a material-specific interpretation. See the dedicated  and  pages for the model boundaries.  

 Experimental criteria

Wu's selected final text distinguishes a resistive deviation at 93 K, a sharp drop beginning at 92 K, zero resistance at 80 K and a diamagnetic onset at 91 K. The diamagnetic signal at 4.2 K was compared with a similarly sized lead sample; that relative signal is not an independently corrected superconducting volume fraction. Its 80–180 T upper-critical-field estimate is an extrapolation, whereas the reported field measurements reached 5.7 T. Preserve these criteria and scales separately. 

A later doping-calibration experiment used a different operational criterion: Liang and colleagues chose the midpoint of the field-cooled magnetic transition with 1 Oe along the c axis. Their lattice parameter was measured by room-temperature diffraction. Temperature, field direction, oxygen ordering and the selected calibration therefore belong with the inferred doping, rather than being discarded after assigning a number to a phase diagram. Only the named author-version passages and figure have been checked here. 

Phase-sensitive and magnitude-sensitive probes answer different questions. Tsuei and colleagues' original abstract reports scanning-SQUID measurements of tricrystal rings at 4.2 K, providing a phase-sensitive constraint. Hardy and colleagues' penetration-depth abstract describes a low-temperature linear term in YBa2Cu3O6.95, constraining low-energy excitations. Neither abstract alone verifies all junction assumptions, sample comparisons or raw traces; combine complementary evidence without turning a nodal observation into an unconditional mechanism verdict.  

 Pressure and recovered samples

Schilling's historical Hg-based report concerns superconductivity above 130 K at ambient pressure. Gao's original abstract reports resistive measurements under quasihydrostatic pressure up to 45 GPa and a maximum of 164 K for the three-layer member. The often-quoted 31 GPa point and its onset-versus-zero criterion have not been re-extracted from the full original in this review. The comparison record therefore leaves the exact pressure unknown; a study's maximum applied pressure is not the pressure of every reported transition.  

The 2026 pressure-quench report now has a selected primary-text and author-figure check inherited from the  page. Sample S4, released from 18.9 GPa at 4.2 K, showed an ambient-pressure resistive onset of 151 K on warming and 150 K on cooling. This is a reported onset in a recovered metastable sample, not a zero-resistance criterion or an equilibrium ambient-pressure phase. 

The magnetic onset near 140 K came from retrieved sample S2, not the S4 transport sample. The estimated shielding at 70 K, the separate cold-storage protocol, and an unreproduced broad 172 K anomaly are distinct observations. The latter has no accepted transition-temperature value in this catalogue. Complete final supplementary comparison, raw-data reanalysis and independent replication remain open. 

 Limits and disputes

A charge-density modulation does not alone establish a pair-density wave; a linear resistivity does not alone determine a scattering time. Pseudogap, magnetic and charge correlations constrain theories without selecting one unique glue. Oxygen rearrangement and pressure history can alter more than carrier concentration, so a changed transition temperature does not by itself identify the causal variable. Complete scientific acceptance remains open for this article and the associated materials.   

 Discovery implications

Compare matched compositions, preparation histories and criteria. Record what each probe measures, what a model infers and what alternative explanation survives. A mechanism proposal should connect an interaction to a symmetry prediction and a falsifiable material trend. For recovered samples, add decompression temperature, storage and subsequent measurement history before comparing them with equilibrium materials. The site preserves those conditions in searchable records and section exports.

entries.text:
Scope

Iron-based superconductors contain Fe–pnictogen or Fe–chalcogen layers in several structural families. Multiple Fe orbitals contribute to their low-energy electronic structure, and parent magnetic or structural transitions must be distinguished from superconductivity in a substituted sample. Kamihara and colleagues' fluorine-doped LaOFeAs discovery established a high-temperature 1111 platform. Its original abstract reports a transition near 26 K; the exact operational criterion remains unassigned in this review. 

A 122 arsenide, a binary 11 chalcogenide and a single-layer interface are different experimental systems. Rotter and colleagues studied K-substituted BaFe2As2, while Hsu and colleagues reported superconductivity in PbO-type FeSe. Neither result establishes that every related composition has the same gap, transition temperature or magnetic ground state. Starting mixture, refined phase composition and nominal formula should remain separately identifiable.  

 Mathematical assumptions

The coefficient y in \mathrm{BaFe}{2-y}\mathrm{Co}y\mathrm{As}2 and the site fraction x in \mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{Fe}{1-x}\mathrm{Co}x)2\mathrm{As}2 obey y=2x. Eleven exact atom-count checks verify this normalization. Likewise, nominal \mathrm{FeSe}{1-x} becomes \mathrm{Fe}{1+\delta}\mathrm{Se} with \delta=x/(1-x) when normalized to one Se. Five checks preserve the elemental ratio. These conversions do not measure crystal occupancy, mobile-carrier density or the location of a defect. 

Bulk fractions also have a precise but limited meaning. For superconducting and magnetic fractions fS and fM of the same volume, their overlap lies between \max(0,fS+fM-1) and \min(fS,fM). Two explicit arrangements with 95% and 90% fractions give 85% or 90% overlap. This set-theory bound neither establishes atomic-scale coexistence nor removes probe calibration and sample-matching requirements. A microscopic interpretation must use additional spatial, temporal and model evidence. 

A multiband gap \Deltai(\mathbf{k}) is defined on specified bands. Relative sign reversal can arise in a candidate s± pairing solution, but it does not follow simply from the presence of iron. Orbital weights, shallow bands and the accessible scattering channels affect the inference. The  and  articles state their model assumptions and preserve alternative interpretations.  

 Experimental criteria

The revised Rotter author manuscript gives a resistive midpoint of 38.1 K for Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2, a first deviation near 39 K and a reported zero-resistance point of 37.2 K. Figure 4 also labels 37.2 K as its 10% threshold, so the term zero retains an unresolved instrumental-threshold caveat. Its 90–10% width is 1.5 K. Quoting only the rounded 38 K headline loses distinctions that matter in a searchable record. 

The same revision measures magnetic cycles at 0.5 and 1 mT, replacing the earlier manuscript's 10 mT example. Diamagnetism begins near 38.3 K; shielding and field-cooled responses differ and depend on density and demagnetization assumptions. The powder contains a minor FeAs impurity. Selected revised-manuscript figures have been checked, but the final published methods and raw data have not been completely compared here. 

Hsu's final FeSe report identifies zero resistance near 8 K in a sample labelled by nominal FeSe0.88 composition. Magnetic susceptibility at 30 G and a broad heat-capacity anomaly provide complementary evidence. Its field-dependent transition uses 50% of normal resistance, with applied fields through 9 T; the roughly 16.3 T upper-critical-field value is a fit extrapolation. Nominal selenium deficiency and a fitted critical field must not be promoted to directly measured phase occupancy or field limits. 

McQueen and colleagues subsequently found nearly stoichiometric superconducting FeSe and strong preparation sensitivity. Their selected neutron-refinement analysis gives Fe1.01±0.02Se, with limited ability to distinguish tiny deviations. Nominal composition, oxygen contamination and annealing temperature vary across the comparison. A sample labelled Fe1.03Se showed no superconductivity down to 0.6 K; that lower measurement bound is not a superconducting transition. The proposed defect-site explanation remains a hypothesis. 

 Pressure and magnetism

Medvedev's author manuscript associates a resistive onset of 36.7 K with 8.9 GPa in Fe1.01Se. Broadened transitions and curve offsets require careful interpretation; at 15 GPa the authors report residual resistance associated with a second phase. Their resistance method uses a diamond-anvil cell, platinum contacts, a van der Pauw arrangement and ruby pressure measurements at low and room temperature. The silicone-oil medium specified for the Mössbauer experiment must not automatically be assigned to the separate resistance experiment. 

The earlier Mössbauer nondetection of static order is not a universal FeSe phase diagram. Bendele and colleagues later reported pressure-induced static magnetism using zero-field muon-spin rotation and AC susceptibility in nominal FeSe0.94 and FeSe0.98 samples. Their selected revised manuscript specifies Daphne 7373, pressure-cell background treatment and low-temperature pressure calibration. Its Figure 3 supports a pressure-dependent coexistence interpretation near and above 0.8 GPa, with model-dependent spatial conclusions. Different probes, samples and pressure environments must remain explicit.  

 Evidence for gap structure

Christianson's neutron experiment concerns K-doped Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2. Its superconductivity-related resonance and the relevant coherence-factor model constrain candidate signs, without directly determining every iron-based gap. Background, momentum, orbital matrix elements and independently measured gap scales remain necessary parts of that interpretation. A resonance measurement cannot be substituted for a family-wide phase verdict.  

At a FeSe/SrTiO3 interface, Lee's replica bands and mean-field gap-closing scale retain their spectroscopic labels. Faeth's later photon-energy comparison supports an intrinsic electron–phonon interpretation within its stated analysis, but does not determine all contributions to pairing enhancement. A gap-closing temperature is not interchangeable with zero resistance or a magnetic transition. These interface results remain linked to the detailed  discussion rather than silently entering a bulk Tc comparison.  

 Limits and disputes

Several orbitals, correlations, nematicity and magnetic proximity help organize the evidence without selecting one universal pairing mechanism. A mass renormalization is not automatically a larger pairing eigenvalue. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including final-version comparisons, full supplementary methods and raw-data analysis. Differences between a source's claim and this article's review scope are preserved in the references.    

 Discovery implications

Test a specific model with controlled composition, structure, pressure or disorder changes, and identify the confounding changes. Preserve actual measurement criteria and sample provenance when comparing results. For a proposed coexistence regime, report what each probe resolves and how sample fractions were calibrated. For a candidate pairing mediator, explain which alternative survives the same observation.

entries.text:
Scope

Nickelate superconductors include infinite-layer reduced films, bilayer Ruddlesden–Popper crystals and engineered layer sequences. The number of NiO2 layers, oxygen coordination and sample preparation distinguish these systems. An ambient-pressure epitaxial film and a compressed bulk crystal should retain separate records even when both contain lanthanum and nickel. Structural resemblance to cuprates motivates comparisons without establishing a shared pairing mechanism.  

The 2026 La2PrNi2O7 high-field transport study concerns a bilayer Ruddlesden–Popper film. The inherited draft incorrectly placed it in the infinite-layer family. Its field-induced normal state is also distinct from the Eu-substituted infinite-layer material exhibiting re-entrant resistance suppression. Family, composition and probe must accompany these interpretations.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Formal charge neutrality gives nickel valence v{\mathrm{Ni}}=1+x+2\delta for an idealized R{1-x}\mathrm{Sr}x\mathrm{NiO}{2+\delta} with trivalent R, divalent Sr and divalent oxygen. For R3\mathrm{Ni}2\mathrm{O}{7-\delta}, it gives v{\mathrm{Ni}}=2.5-\delta. Sixty-six exact bookkeeping checks preserve neutrality. These averages do not measure orbital occupancy, vacancy location, ligand holes or mobile carriers. In particular, an annealing-gas dose does not specify oxygen stoichiometry.  

Even the elementary two-carrier low-field Drude expression RH=(p\muh^2-n\mue^2)/[e(p\muh+n\mue)^2], with e>0, prevents a unique carrier count from Hall sign alone. Three explicit counterexamples give negative Hall coefficients with different electron–hole population orderings. This model illustrates nonuniqueness; it is not a fit to nickelate data. Both Li and Hsu discuss multiband limitations, so a negative Hall coefficient must not be silently converted to a single-band electron density.  

 Experimental criteria

For the representative Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 film in Li's 2019 discovery, the published text identifies a 14.9 K onset by maximum curvature, a 13.6 K midpoint and 9.1 K resistance indistinguishable from the noise floor. The final methods describe six-point electrical measurements, 9–11 nm precursor films and topotactic reduction. Two-coil mutual inductance supports a diamagnetic response, but the authors explicitly decline to extract a penetration depth because of finite-size, disorder and other uncertainties. These three temperatures describe different criteria on the selected sample. 

Sun's 2023 bilayer-crystal report gives an 80 K resistance onset at 18.5 GPa in run 1 without pressure medium. Run 2 uses KBr and reaches a 78 K onset at 18.9 GPa. Figure 3 distinguishes the 10 μA run-1 excitation from 300 μA in run 2. Its magnetic response near 77 K is measured separately at 25.2 GPa. Residual resistance and specimen differences prevent combining these observations into one zero-resistance or bulk-fraction record. 

 Oxygen, strain and transport

Bhatt's final strain study distinguishes nominal substrate mismatch from measured strain: the strongly compressed film is labelled approximately −1.6% measured strain, rather than the inherited draft's −1.8%. Growth method, oxygen treatment and substrate vary across comparisons. In-plane compression accompanied by out-of-plane expansion is not equivalent to hydrostatic compression. The  article retains the source-specific structural comparison and its confounding variables. 

Xiang's revised author manuscript demonstrates an oxygen-removal and ozone-annealing sequence that can recover degraded bilayer films. Repeating ozone treatment alone can instead damage the superconducting response. Its proposed phase diagram uses cumulative annealing-gas volume; oxygen concentration is not precisely measured, and unknown phases complicate interpretation. Figure 2 identifies a zero-resistance point near 5.5 K for sample S1049-4, far below its onset region. The recovery experiment constrains preparation sensitivity without establishing a calibrated carrier-density axis or a universal recycling recipe. 

Hsu's final La2PrNi2O7 study defines 41 K using 90% of a fitted normal-state resistivity. Pulsed-field measurements access a low-temperature normal state with approximately quadratic resistivity; an extrapolated zero-field normal-state curve is not directly observed below the transition. The film is about 5 nm thick, grown on SrLaAlO4 with a SrTiO3 cap and kept cold between measurements. The reported effective mass uses an empirical Kadowaki–Woods relation, not direct calorimetry. These results describe a strained bilayer specimen, not every nickelate. 

 Recent structures and membranes

Nie's publisher abstract, published in April 2026, reports ambient-pressure onset temperatures spanning 46–50 K in engineered 1212 and 2323 layer sequences, alongside a nonsuperconducting 1313 comparison. The exact operational criterion and lower nondetection bound have not been extracted here, so this range is not assigned to a precise searchable Tc record. Associated orbital and Fermi-surface observations constrain structure–electronic-state relationships; they do not independently prove a unique pairing interaction. 

Lee's April 2026 membrane preprint reports 74.2 K at 91.5 GPa using 99.5% of an extrapolated normal-state resistance. Extended Data Figure 1 gives 69.1 K with an intersection construction and 75.4 K with a second-derivative construction for the illustrated transition. These differences are criterion dependence, not separate superconducting phases. Zero resistance is defined by the noise floor and occurs lower. The preprint remains explicitly labelled and is not an ambient-pressure result. 

The same preprint measures six membranes and fits an onset increase near 0.65 K/GPa over its sampled range. It uses room-temperature ruby calibration below 50 GPa and diamond Raman calibration above that, with the latter measured adjacent to the specimen. Silicone-oil solidification and nonhydrostatic stress complicate broadening. Its 13 T field measurements and fitted coherence lengths should not be mistaken for direct measurements of a much larger zero-temperature critical field. Extrapolating the pressure trend beyond the measured range is not a demonstrated materials prediction. 

 Limits and disputes

Eu-substituted infinite-layer films show field-dependent resistance recovery in a specific sample and temperature window. Magnetic compensation and triplet pairing remain interpretations rather than conclusions forced by re-entrance alone. The  and  articles preserve field orientation, measurement temperature and alternative mechanisms. None of these observations establishes a universal nickelate gap symmetry. 

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected primary passages, figures and model checks have been reviewed, while full supplements, final-author version comparisons, independent reproduction and raw-data analysis remain incomplete. Onset, midpoint, noise-floor zero, spectroscopic gaps and normal-state measurement temperatures retain distinct meanings. Pressure and strain comparisons require matching phase and preparation rather than ordering headline temperatures.    

 Discovery implications

A useful comparison records layer sequence, oxygen history, nominal and measured composition, substrate, thickness, pressure calibration, probe and temperature criterion. Controlled oxygen cycles and structural contrasts are informative only with their phase and interface changes documented. A promising design hypothesis should specify which variable changes, which confounders remain and what observation would distinguish competing mechanisms.

entries.text:
Scope

Hydrogen-rich superconductors connect light nuclei, strong electron–phonon coupling and pressure-dependent chemistry. Ashcroft's metallic-hydrogen proposal and later hydrogen-dominant-alloy proposal motivate this route; neither established a recoverable ambient-pressure superconductor. H₃S and LaH₁₀ are important high-pressure experimental systems. Their formulae, pressure scales and sample histories must accompany any quoted transition temperature.    

“Chemical precompression” describes a design idea, not a guarantee of low operating pressure. A predicted metallic structure, a synthesized hydride and a superconducting phase are different achievements. Distinguish the starting H₂S reagent from its proposed H₃S product, and a clathrate-like hydrogen framework from directly measured hydrogen positions. The sulfur-hydride diffraction study supports the sulfur sublattice and coexistence with sulfur; its measured patterns cannot by themselves distinguish hydrogen arrangements with the same sulfur periodicity.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For a specified structure, a commonly used modified-McMillan estimate is Tc=(\omega{\log}/1.2)\exp[-1.04(1+\lambda)/(\lambda-\mu^(1+0.62\lambda))], with \omega{\log} expressed in kelvin here. Duan's harmonic calculations give \lambda=2.07, \omega{\log}=1125.1 K for R3m at 130 GPa and \lambda=2.19, \omega{\log}=1334.6 K for Im\bar{3}m at 200 GPa. Substitution with \mu^=0.13 and 0.10 gives approximately 155–166 K and 191–204 K, respectively. This reproduces the printed estimate convention, without additional strong-coupling or spectral-shape factors; it does not reproduce the underlying density-functional perturbation calculation. 

Hydrogen motion can invalidate a harmonic treatment. Errea and colleagues calculated a change from \lambda=2.64 to 1.84 for H₃S at 200 GPa when including anharmonicity. Their full isotropic Migdal–Eliashberg calculation with \mu^=0.16 changed the calculated transition from 250 to 194 K. That table is not obtained by simply substituting parameters into the preceding approximate formula. Zero-point contributions also alter the calculated decomposition landscape: both 3\mathrm{H2S}\rightarrow2\mathrm{H3S}+\mathrm{S} and 5\mathrm{H2S}\rightarrow3\mathrm{H3S}+\mathrm{HS2} conserve atoms, but atom balance alone does not establish stability or a reaction pathway. 

An isotope comparison uses \alpha=\ln(T{c,\mathrm H}/T{c,\mathrm D})/\ln2 only after checking structure, pressure and transition criteria. The final LaH₁₀ paper compares approximately 249 K and 180 K for fcc hydride and deuteride near 150 GPa; its Fig. 4 specifies 151 and 152 GPa. These rounded values give 0.468, while the paper states 0.46. The early author's 250/168 K comparison gives 0.573 and must not be silently substituted for the final result. Phase mixtures and different deuteride structures further limit interpretation. 

 Experimental criteria

For sulfur hydride, the 2015 report combined resistance, field response, isotope substitution and magnetization. Its author-version Fig. 4a reports a zero-field-cooled magnetic onset of 203(1) K at 155 GPa, with a 20 Oe field-cooled comparison. The plotted transport comparison is a different pressure, 145 GPa, and must not be treated as the identical specimen condition. Background subtraction and diamond-anvil-cell contributions require scrutiny; this scoped reading does not independently reproduce raw magnetization. The later simultaneous diffraction/transport experiment on deuteride at 173 GPa provides structural context, not a direct measurement of every hydrogen coordinate.  

The two early lanthanum-superhydride studies have different evidence scopes. Somayazulu's author v3 describes a large resistance drop around 260 K, with room-temperature pressure changing from 188 to 196 GPa across a thermal cycle; pressure at the actual transition was not measured in that run. The lowest four-probe resistance was about 20 μΩ, while pseudo-four-probe measurements carried contact-resistance limitations. This should not be rewritten as an independently established zero-resistance or magnetic-shielding result. The final journal abstract was checked, but the selected detailed methods here come from the identified author version. 

Drozdov's final 2019 LaH₁₀ paper reports zero resistance, isotope dependence and field suppression, with a maximum near 250–252 K around 170 GPa. Its transition criterion is the onset of deviation from normal metallic resistance. Measurements to 9 T support an extrapolated zero-temperature upper critical field of approximately 95–136 T; they are not direct measurements at 136 T. The authors explicitly state that their tiny samples were below the available SQUID sensitivity. Their H₂/D₂ vibron pressure estimates were often 10–30 GPa lower than diamond-edge estimates around 150 GPa, so pressure calibrations cannot be freely interchanged. 

 Limits and disputes

The 2020 carbonaceous-sulfur-hydride article was retracted on 26 September 2022. The corrected notice identifies concerns about non-standard, user-defined magnetic-background subtraction; all authors disagreed with the retraction. The 2023 nitrogen-doped lutetium-hydride article was retracted on 7 November 2023 following concerns including sample provenance, measurements and processing. These original papers remain linked as historical claims, accompanied by their notices. Their claimed temperatures are not usable experimental benchmarks in this catalogue. A retraction notice is not a substitute for an independent misconduct finding.    

An independent LuH₂±xNᵧ study reported no superconductivity above 2 K over 0.4–40.1 GPa in its transport measurements. That constrains its tested samples and synthesis route; it does not prove that every possible Lu–N–H composition is nonsuperconducting. The final published pressure range differs from an early preprint's narrower range. In particular, a blue-to-pink colour change is not a superconductivity measurement. 

 Discovery implications

A credible search must connect composition and structure to dynamical and thermodynamic stability, finite-temperature and nuclear-quantum effects, synthesis access and multiple superconductivity probes. A finite structure search can miss larger cells; absence of imaginary harmonic frequencies is a local dynamical check, not proof of global stability. Preserve decompression history, mixed phases, pressure standards and unsuccessful samples instead of ranking formulae by isolated temperature claims.   

A June 2026 study recovered Y₃Fe₄H₂₀ at ambient pressure after synthesis above about 60 GPa, with survival on the scale of tens of hours. This is useful progress in hydride recovery, but its reported SQUID test found no superconductivity down to 3 K in the tested recovered sample. Hydrogen positions were supported by structure searches, and the sample was small and not pure. Recovery, long-term stability and ambient-pressure superconductivity remain distinct questions. Full raw-data, convergence and cross-laboratory assessment remain open for this article.

entries.text:
Scope

Magnesium diboride, MgB₂, is a useful benchmark for electron–phonon superconductivity with different gap scales on different Fermi-surface sheets. Its 2001 discovery report combined magnetization and resistivity near 39 K in a simple hexagonal compound. This historical temperature is not a universal sample constant or an upper bound on phonon-mediated superconductivity.  

Boron honeycomb layers provide most of the electronic states near the Fermi level. The approximately cylindrical σ sheets derive mainly from in-plane boron orbitals; the π sheets have substantial out-of-plane character. Strong coupling of σ states to boron bond stretching helps explain the large gap. “Two gaps” is a useful reduction of a momentum-dependent problem: Choi's calculation at 4 K spans 6.4–7.2 meV on σ sheets and 1.2–3.7 meV on π sheets, with averages of 6.8 and 1.8 meV. These are calculated distributions, not two exactly constant measured gaps.  

 Mathematical assumptions

In an illustrative clean weak-coupling model with a shared cutoff, the linearized equations are \Deltai=L(T)\sumj\lambda{ij}\Deltaj. The largest positive eigenvalue of the pairing matrix determines the first instability. Off-diagonal pair-transfer terms can make both gap components nonzero at the same transition, even when their amplitudes differ. For the chosen toy matrix \lambda=\begin{pmatrix}0.40&0.08\\0.04&0.15\end{pmatrix}, the leading eigenvalue is approximately 0.4122 and \Delta2/\Delta1\approx0.1526 at onset. Setting both off-diagonal entries to zero removes the induced second component at the higher transition. These numbers illustrate coupled equations; they are not fitted MgB₂ parameters.  

Pair transfer and impurity interband scattering are different processes. An elastic scattering rate contains impurity matrix elements and connects single-particle states; it must not replace \lambda{ij} in the pairing equation. Mazin's analysis distinguishes weak σ–π impurity mixing from potentially large scattering within each band. Its normal-state conductivity adds parallel band contributions, so a single residual resistivity cannot uniquely determine the interband rate. Using its illustrated in-plane plasma weights and intraband rates, a simplified residual-conductivity calculation shifts the σ share from about 33% to 92% between the selected clean and dirty examples. This is a model illustration, not a resistivity measurement or a calculation of the full temperature dependence. 

For isotope substitutions, \alphai=-\Delta\ln Tc/\Delta\ln Mi is a partial coefficient. Bud'ko's rounded 40.2 K and 39.2 K values give \alpha{\mathrm B}\approx0.264 using masses 10 and 11, consistent with the reported 0.26\pm0.03. Hinks separately measured both elements and reported approximately \alpha{\mathrm B}=0.30(1) and \alpha{\mathrm{Mg}}=0.02(1). Their sum near 0.32 differs from the simplest harmonic single-scale expectation of 0.5. This does not uniquely isolate anharmonicity, Coulomb effects or multiband contributions.  

 Experimental criteria

The original discovery paper reported a resistive onset of 39 K and an endpoint of 38 K using four probes at zero applied field. Magnetization used zero-field-cooled and field-cooled protocols at 10 Oe; the authors estimated a 49% superconducting volume fraction at 5 K. Their 196 MPa argon pressure was used during hot isostatic synthesis at 973 K for ten hours. It is not the pressure of the superconductivity measurement. Onset, endpoint, magnetic response and synthesis conditions must remain separate fields. 

Bud'ko used a 2% diamagnetic-onset criterion on warming after zero-field cooling, with a 25 G measuring field. The isotopically enriched samples had narrow but different transition widths. Hinks used a 1 G field and compared extrapolated onset with a 10% criterion; natural and enriched Mg samples showed possible impurity differences that the authors could not quantify. The Mg contribution therefore belongs to the Hinks study, not to the earlier boron-only experiment. The six printed boron comparisons have been recalculated here, but the raw magnetization has not been refitted.  

Szabó's Cu–MgB₂ point contacts showed small and large gap scales around 2.8 and 7 meV. Their two-component BTK fits kept interface transparency and relative weight fixed across temperature; thermal smearing makes the two contributions harder to separate near the bulk transition. Fields up to 1 T preferentially suppressed the small-gap spectral contribution, helping reveal the large-gap features. This does not mean that 1 T is the bulk upper critical field, and these spectra alone do not determine the relative sign of the gaps. Using a transition temperature of 39 K, the low-temperature gap ratios are approximately 1.67 and 4.17, rather than a single weak-coupling BCS ratio. 

 Limits and disputes

The final Choi calculation uses the anisotropic Eliashberg framework and compares calculated thermodynamics with experiments. Its successful description does not turn a two-constant-gap approximation into an exact band-resolved result. Spectroscopic weights depend on geometry and matrix elements; fitting two components is strongest when checked against independent thermodynamic and field-dependent evidence. The original specific-heat datasets and full anisotropic numerical calculation have not been independently reproduced in this review.  

The Hinks author manuscript contains a version issue: Table 1 prints a Mg mass of 25.001 for a sample family, while the methods describe enriched ²⁶Mg. This discrepancy is retained as unresolved pending comparison with the final published table. No Mg-mass refit is presented. The boron ratios use the explicitly printed boron masses and temperatures. Likewise, the Mazin author PDF's generated date is not its submission date; the cited version is the arXiv submission of 1 April 2002.  

 Discovery implications

Materials development must connect gap physics to usable conductors. A 2026 study of square, 19-filament MgB₂ wire reports a 14.2% filling factor and an engineering-current benchmark at 4.2 K and 6.5 T. This reference is currently checked only through the publisher's indexed summary and the authors' publication record; the electric-field criterion, full methods and coil comparison require further review. Engineering current density uses the whole composite cross-section, unlike a current density normalized to superconducting material alone. Neither operating temperature nor a current-density benchmark should enter a transition-temperature ranking. 

Preserve processing, connectivity, field orientation, temperature and voltage criterion when comparing wires. Increasing intraband disorder, changing band filling and increasing interband impurity mixing are not interchangeable interventions. A useful candidate must satisfy its operating requirements as well as the microscopic pairing model; this article's scoped calculations do not certify a wire or magnet design.  

 Related topics

See , , ,  and .

entries.text:
Scope

Heavy-fermion superconductors pair electrons in a strongly renormalized metallic state. Their large low-temperature electronic heat capacity and magnetic response reflect interactions involving partially filled f shells, not unusually heavy atoms moving as Cooper pairs. CeCu₂Si₂ established this class in 1979; the discovery paper reported a transition near 0.5 K. Different compositions and probes need not reproduce that exact number. The family is a laboratory for competing correlations rather than a single pairing mechanism.  

Kondo screening, conduction-electron-mediated magnetic interactions, hybridization and valence changes provide useful organizing ideas. Doniach's competition between magnetic order and a compensated state is a model framework. Proximity to a magnetic boundary does not by itself identify the pairing interaction or predict a superconducting transition. Uranium compounds also require attention to itinerant 5f character and strong spin–orbit coupling; a label borrowed from a cerium compound is not a complete microscopic description.   

 Mathematical assumptions

In a Fermi-liquid regime, the electronic coefficient \gamma=\lim{T\to0}Ce/T is proportional to the renormalized density of states. A finite-temperature value of total C/T is not automatically that limit. Petrovic's CeCoIn₅ report gives about 290 mJ mol⁻¹ K⁻² above 2.5 K but a much larger low-temperature normal-state value under field. Thus its apparent \Delta C/(\gamma Tc)\approx4.5 cannot be converted mechanically into a coupling strength using a temperature-independent normal-state baseline. 

Kittaka's CeCu₂Si₂ analysis subtracts a nuclear term. With numerical field h in tesla and temperature t in kelvin, its empirical expression is Cn/T=(7.4h^2+0.1)t^{-3}\times10^{-6} J mol⁻¹ K⁻². At 60 mK it gives approximately 0.00046, 0.111 and 0.309 J mol⁻¹ K⁻² for 0, 1.8 and 3 T. These recalculations illustrate the size of the correction; they are not a new fit or evidence that any arbitrary subtraction is acceptable. 

Pang's simplified band-mixing model uses |\Delta(\varphi)|=\sqrt{a^2\cos^2(2\varphi)+b^2\sin^2(2\varphi)} at zero temperature. For nonzero amplitudes on the assumed cylinder, the minimum is \min(|a|,|b|); exchanging them preserves angular averages. The reported S-type fit uses a=2.5kBTc and b=0.58kBTc. This magnitude does not specify the full band matrix or its time-reversal properties. A scalar chiral gap can have the same magnitude; that algebraic coincidence does not equate the two physical states. 

 Experimental criteria

The CeCu₂Si₂ specific-heat study used a 13.8 mg S-type crystal, measurements down to 40 mK and a nuclear correction constrained by high-field normal-state data. It reported low-energy behavior consistent with full gaps and no detected in-plane angular oscillation within stated sensitivity. The result constrains quasiparticles weighted strongly by thermodynamics; it is not a universal exclusion of every possible small-band node. The author manuscript's February 2014 version must not be dated from its later PDF generation stamp. 

Pang's penetration-depth measurements reached 40 mK. Its S-type sample showed a specific-heat transition near 0.64 K; an A/S-type sample showed superconducting and antiferromagnetic anomalies near 0.53 and 0.7 K. These are different transitions. Nodeless low-temperature behavior motivates the proposed d+d description, but fitting these data does not uniquely settle the order parameter. Raw-data refitting and the complete supplement remain outside this scoped review. 

For CeCoIn₅, the discovery study combined zero resistance, magnetic shielding and a heat-capacity anomaly near 2.3 K. It also found substantially different upper critical fields parallel and perpendicular to the c axis. Later neutron work found magnetic order that disappears with superconductivity at the high-field boundary. A coupled magnetic Q phase therefore cannot be described as a clean demonstration of a standalone textbook FFLO state.  

 Limits and disputes

CeCu₂Si₂ should not be assigned an unqualified textbook nodal d-wave label. Full-gap thermodynamics, sign-sensitive interpretations and band structure must be reconciled. Its pressure response adds another question: Holmes measured resistivity and ac heat capacity above 6 GPa in helium and interpreted anomalies near 4.5 GPa through valence fluctuations. That interpretation is a proposed mechanism, not a direct measurement of a unique pairing interaction.   

UPt₃ has multiple superconducting phases and Kerr evidence constraining time-reversal symmetry. Heating, field training and the phase being probed matter. This does not uniquely select f-wave symmetry or establish a topological device. URhGe and UCoGe provide coexistence evidence for ferromagnetism and superconductivity, but their magnetic and superconducting transition temperatures are distinct. Their respective field responses cannot be exchanged between compounds.   

UTe₂ requires particularly careful qualifiers. Antiferromagnetic neutron fluctuations, transverse high-field fluctuations and sample-dependent Kerr results probe different conditions. The 2023 Kerr study found no spontaneous signal in the tested single-transition samples; it does not negate every other superconducting phase. No single large upper critical field, fluctuation spectrum or null Kerr observation determines spin structure and topology together.   

 Discovery implications

The 2025 UTe₂ halo study mapped transport boundaries with pulsed fields, generally near 0.63 K, using resistance and contactless proximity-detector measurements. Tilting away from the b axis revealed an extended high-field region. The experiment reached approximately 73 T; extrapolated persistence beyond that field is not a measured upper boundary. Its multicomponent triplet interpretation remains a model conclusion. Supplementary sample details, heating corrections and the deposited raw data have not been independently reanalyzed here. 

The 2026 transverse-fluctuation study measured the normal state at 4 K; superconducting phase boundaries at 300 mK were comparisons with earlier work. Neither temperature is a newly measured transition temperature in that experiment. Discovery records should retain the sample, pressure, field direction, probe and criterion, then compare mechanisms across compatible conditions. The goal is to identify informative constraints, not rank unrelated temperatures or convert candidate topology into an established engineering capability.

entries.text:
Scope

Alkali-doped fullerides join molecular vibrations, narrow electronic bands and strong local interactions in one material family. In ideal A₃C₆₀, three donated electrons half-fill the three molecular t₁ᵤ orbitals, whose spin capacity is six. Potassium, rubidium and cesium compounds must be identified by stoichiometry, crystal structure and preparation. Pressure-induced equilibrium superconductivity and light-driven responses are separate evidence classes.  

The 1991 potassium discovery already illustrates why one temperature is insufficient: the abstract reports a thin-film resistive onset near 16 K and essentially vanishing resistance by 5 K, while bulk magnetic and microwave measurements indicate an 18 K transition. The subsequent rubidium report gives a maximum of 28 K from bulk magnetic and microwave evidence. These abstract-level checks establish historical observations; they do not constitute a complete reassessment of the original specimens.  

 Mathematical assumptions

One influential model represents each molecule by three effective p-like orbitals with local terms HU=U(n-3)^2/2 and HJ=J[2\mathbf S^2+\mathbf L^2/2]+5J(n-3)^2/6. Angular momenta are dimensionless. In this convention ordinary Hund exchange has J=-JH<0; integrating out Jahn–Teller vibrations can instead give J=-JH+J{JT}>0. This static reduction requires the coherent electronic scale ZW to lie below the relevant phonon energy. It should not be applied across the whole bandwidth range without checking retardation. 

At exactly three electrons, the model multiplets ^4S, ^2D and ^2P have energies 15J/2, 9J/2 and 5J/2, with respective degeneracies 4, 10 and 6. They account for \binom{6}{3}=20 local states. Positive effective J favors the low-spin ^2P multiplet; negative J favors ^4S. This is an algebraic check of the effective local Hamiltonian, not a measured molecular spectrum or proof of superconducting order. 

The heuristic Cooper-channel amplitude A^\simeq ZU-10J/3 illustrates how correlations can reduce repulsion relative to an inverted exchange. For illustrative fixed ratios U/W=0.5 and J/W=0.05, its sign changes at Z=1/3. Simultaneously the coherent bandwidth is ZW: decreasing Z does not supply an unlimited transition-temperature gain. The published argument explicitly allows deviations near the Mott boundary; its underlying DMFT model uses an infinite-coordination Bethe lattice. No self-consistent DMFT calculation or measured transition follows from this toy sweep. 

 Experimental criteria

For fcc Cs₃C₆₀, Ganin and colleagues report a pressure-dependent magnetic onset: 25.6 K at 1.3 kbar has only about 0.1% shielding, whereas 29.7 K at 2.2 kbar has about 12%. The maximum is approximately 35 K near 7 kbar, equivalent to 0.7 GPa. Measurements use 20 Oe, zero-field-cooled/field-cooled protocols and a tin pressure reference. A15 Cs₃C₆₀ reaches a separately reported maximum near 38 K; its value must not be assigned to the fcc sample.  

The fcc study also separates magnetic ordering near 2.2 K from the A15 ordering scale near 46 K. Neither is a superconducting transition. Multiphase powders and small shielding fractions require particular care when locating the first superconducting signal. The magnetometry pressure range ends near 10.6 kbar; the separate diffraction measurements extend to much higher pressures. Combining those ranges would falsely imply that superconductivity was measured throughout the structural experiment. 

Published online on 9 June 2026, Shchukin and colleagues tune Rb uptake in nanostructured C₆₀ films. Figure 2f labels Rb₂.₇₁C₆₀ with T{\mathrm{onset}}=22.4 K and T{\mathrm{zero}}=7.0 K, and Rb₂.₉₈C₆₀ with 26.4 K and 14.5 K. The former criterion is a local resistivity maximum; the latter uses d\rho/dT<5\times10^{-4} mΩ cm K⁻¹ in the plotted low-temperature window. It is a stated operational criterion, not an instrument-independent definition of exact zero resistance. 

That experiment uses Raman analysis with relative scattering cross sections to estimate composition, and van der Pauw transport. The 10 μA intercalation current differs from the 1 μA resistance-probe current. Stoichiometry, grain connectivity, thickness and transition criterion must accompany any comparison with bulk rubidium fullerides. The supplement and underlying transport datasets have not been independently reanalyzed here. 

 Limits and disputes

Mitrano's optical study and Budden's longer-lived driven response concern pumped K₃C₆₀. A finite-frequency inductive response and suppressed transient resistance constrain the nonequilibrium state, but do not by themselves establish an equilibrium thermodynamic transition. Budden's 100 K operating condition is therefore recorded as a transient-response temperature with no equilibrium Tc. Its pulsed two-terminal readout and static four-terminal contact calibration are distinct measurement steps. Pulse conditions, delay, lifetime and alternative conductivity models remain essential.  

The historical hole-doped C₆₀ claim at 52 K was retracted on 6 March 2003. The original paper and its notice are retained together for traceability; the withdrawn value is excluded from experimental transition records. The notice identifies concerns about device-measurement data following an independent investigation. A citation in an older, otherwise valid paper does not restore the withdrawn claim.  

 Discovery implications

Fullerides motivate simultaneous control of bandwidth, local vibronic interactions, molecular valence and disorder. A superconducting dome near a Mott state is compatible with cooperation between phonons and correlations; it does not uniquely determine the pairing kernel. Neither a fully open gap nor proximity to a magnetic insulator proves that one interaction acts alone. Report model assumptions beside the experimental evidence used to constrain them.  

Current-driven intercalation offers a method for tuning samples rather than a new bulk temperature record. Reproducible optimization needs composition maps, measurement-current controls and comparable transition definitions. Keep pressure polymorphs and optically driven states separate when selecting targets: their conditions cannot be collapsed into a single family-wide Tc ranking.

entries.text:
Scope

Pressure changes interatomic distances, electronic bandwidths, lattice vibrations and phase stability. It can also change the material itself through structural conversion or chemical reaction. A diamond anvil cell identifies an apparatus; it does not establish a purely hydrostatic stress state at the sample. Pressure medium, temperature, loading history and sample geometry belong to every quantitative comparison.   

This article concerns measurements while pressure is applied. A state retained after rapid pressure release has a different thermodynamic and kinetic history. Deng's 2026 pressure-quench paper explicitly separates creating a phase under load, releasing pressure and characterizing the recovered state. Its reported 151 K scale must not be pooled with an in-situ pressure curve. Here only its abstract and introductory protocol are checked; the detailed transition criterion and recovery evidence require a separate review. 

 Mathematical assumptions

With tensile stress positive, define P=-\mathrm{tr}(\sigma)/3 and s{ij}=\sigma{ij}+P\delta{ij}. Then \sigma{ij}=-P\delta{ij}+s{ij} with \mathrm{tr}(s)=0. Hydrostatic stress has s=0; equal mean pressure does not imply equal deviatoric stress. For a symmetric stress tensor, \sqrt{3s{ij}s{ij}/2} is a rotationally invariant scalar measure of deviatoric magnitude. It summarizes stress anisotropy, but does not identify its orientation or predict superconductivity. These definitions and rotation identities were checked on illustrative tensors. 

A measured pressure dependence is a path through several changing variables. Within a differentiable single phase, dTc/dP=\suma(\partial Tc/\partial xa)(dxa/dP) is a chain rule, not evidence that any one variable causes pairing. Phase conversion, hysteresis or a changed resistance criterion can invalidate a single smooth derivative across the whole dataset. Even an ideal dome has different local slopes on opposite sides of its maximum.  

In the simplified weak-coupling expression Tc=A\omega\exp(-1/\lambda), holding A fixed gives d\ln Tc/dP=d\ln\omega/dP+\lambda^{-2}d\lambda/dP. A rising frequency can therefore compete with decreasing coupling. This illustration neglects the Coulomb term, strong-coupling corrections, multiple bands and structural changes; it is not a quantitative model for the hydrides or FeSe. Numerical differentiation checks the stated algebra only.  

 Experimental criteria

Torikachvili and colleagues used sample-resistance anomalies, cross-checked against manganin, to locate freezing-related changes in pressure media. Their room-temperature manganin calibration and low-temperature Pb manometer are distinct measurements. Between 300 and 90 K, pressure was estimated by interpolation; below 90 K it was assumed constant. Data used for the anomaly analysis came from slow warming near 0.35 K per minute. These details prevent the loading pressure from silently becoming the pressure at every temperature. The silicone-oil freezing points were not unambiguously determined. 

Medvedev's Fe1.01Se study reports an approximately 36.7 K resistive transition at 8.9 GPa and a decrease at higher pressures. At 15 GPa the roughly 25 K transition did not reach zero resistance, in a mixed-phase regime. The selected transport Methods describe DC van der Pauw measurements, ruby checks at both room and low temperature and a reported spatial pressure spread no greater than 0.05 GPa. Silicone oil is specified in the separate Mössbauer paragraph; this review does not assign that medium to transport without evidence. 

Gao's original abstract reports resistive measurements of mercury cuprates under quasihydrostatic pressures and a maximum of 164 K for the three-layer member. It does not, at this checked scope, establish a zero-resistance or thermodynamic criterion. The full 1994 methods remain inaccessible here, so no more precise criterion is manufactured for the material record. A family trend in that report is not a universal positive pressure coefficient for superconductors. 

The bilayer nickelate report combines resistance signatures with a separate magnetic experiment. Its checked methods use KBr and room-temperature ruby calibration; residual resistance and sample-specific onset criteria remain explicit. In sulfur and lanthanum hydrides, pressure also helps produce or stabilize the hydrogen-rich phases being measured. Pairing a transport curve with a proposed structure requires attention to synthesis history, phase fractions and the conditions of each probe.   

 Limits and disputes

A small spread in pressure inferred from calibrant readings does not reconstruct the full sample stress tensor. Conversely, a frozen medium need not produce the same shear stress in every geometry. Hydrostaticity is an experimental condition to assess, not a binary quality label inferred solely from the material name. The freezing study's calibration assumptions and unresolved oil anomalies should remain attached to any reuse of its data. 

Onset, midpoint, zero resistance and magnetic or thermodynamic signatures answer different questions. The high-pressure FeSe curves broaden and coexist with a structurally transformed fraction; a surviving conducting path is not a direct bulk-volume measurement. Likewise, a structural measurement at room temperature cannot by itself establish the complete structure at a low-temperature transition. This entry retains the historical report's conditions without generalizing its magnetic conclusions to every later FeSe experiment.  

 Discovery implications

Design a pressure series around explicit alternatives: distinguish an electronic crossover from a structural transformation, a pressure gradient from intrinsic broadening, and a reversible response from kinetic trapping. Combine loading and unloading curves with pressure calibration near the measurement temperature, and compare transport with structural or magnetic probes wherever feasible. Differences between probes are evidence to explain, not numbers to average away.   

For transferable discovery records, preserve composition, pressure interval, medium, calibrant, temperature, protocol and transition criterion. Quote a slope only over its stated phase and pressure interval. Keep ambient recovered states, in-situ high-pressure phases and theoretical estimates separately searchable. Pressure can expose useful physics without guaranteeing a recoverable ambient material or a technologically useful conductor.

entries.text:
Scope

Pressure quenching is a preparation path: establish a state under pressure, cool while maintaining load, release pressure at a chosen temperature, then measure the recovered specimen. Quench pressure and measurement pressure are different fields. A retained state may be metastable, and its properties depend on unloading, defects and subsequent temperature excursions. This topic concerns decompressed specimens; superconductivity measured under load belongs to pressure tuning. 

Schilling's 1993 discovery paper reports magnetic and resistive evidence around 133 K in Hg-based cuprates. Gao's 1994 study reports resistive superconductivity up to 164 K under quasihydrostatic pressure. Those publisher abstracts establish historical context here, not a verified pressure-specific zero-resistance criterion. They do not establish that the high-pressure state survives unloading.  

 Mathematical assumptions

An illustrative kinetic model assigns a retained fraction x a one-way escape rate \Gamma: \dot x=-\Gamma x, hence x(t)=x(0)\exp[-\int0^t\Gamma(P(t'),T(t'))dt']. A thermally activated approximation is \Gamma=\Gamma0\exp[-\Delta G^\ddagger/(kBT)]. The prefactor has units of inverse time; the integral is dimensionless. This assumes a single effective barrier and negligible repopulation. Kramers' classical escape analysis also makes the prefactor depend on damping; it does not justify ignoring tunneling, barrier distributions or transformations involving nucleation and growth. No Hg-1223 barrier or lifetime is extracted here. 

For the retrieved Hg-1223 specimen, the authors estimate a shielding fraction using a thin-disk geometry: f\simeq\pi|M|/(Hr^3) with their cgs moment/field convention. Taking |M|/H=1.9\times10^{-8} emu/Oe and effective radius r=42.5 micrometres gives f\approx0.778. This reproduces the reported arithmetic, not an independent volume measurement. Because f\propto r^{-3}, a hypothetical radius change of ±5% gives roughly 67–91%; that sensitivity interval is not a reported confidence interval. Thickness cancels only within the stated disk approximation. Background subtraction, irregular shape, penetration and flux pinning still matter. 

 Experimental criteria

Deng and colleagues' 2026 paper defines its quoted transition temperatures as resistive onsets using the temperature derivative. Author Figure 2 compares five quench experiments: S1 at 26.0 GPa/77 K retained 139 K; S1 at 28.4 GPa/4.2 K retained 147 K; S2 at 10.1 GPa/4.2 K retained 147 K; S3 at 10.9 GPa/4.2 K retained 149 K on warming and 148 K on cooling; S4 at 18.9 GPa/4.2 K retained 151 K on warming and 150 K on cooling. These are ambient-pressure measurements after quenching, with broad transitions. The highest onset is not a measured 151 K zero-resistance threshold. Multiple runs from this group are not independent laboratory replication. 

Magnetization was measured on retrieved S2 after its 10.1 GPa/4.2 K preparation and subsequent handling. Its magnetic transition was near 140 K in a 10 Oe field; the approximately 78% estimate applies at 70 K. It must not be transferred to S4 at 151 K. Author Figure S6 multiplies the post-quench curve by ten for display; its specimen photograph is approximately 104 by 66 micrometres. Comparing plotted amplitudes without the scale correction would give a misleading fraction. 

The stability experiment used S3, initially near 149 K: storage at 77 K for up to three days and excursions to 160–170 K caused a slight decrease. A separate S2 cycle to 293 K lowered its onset from about 147 K to 143 K. Cold-storage survival does not establish a room-temperature shelf life for the 151 K specimen. In S5 after a 29.7 GPa/4.2 K quench, a broad warming anomaly extended to about 172 K, disappeared on subsequent cooling after a 180–193 K excursion, and was not reproduced. This entry records 172 K as an unassigned anomaly, with no searchable superconducting transition temperature. 

The transport methods use van der Pauw contacts, a solid cubic-boron-nitride pressure medium and room-temperature ruby-fluorescence/diamond-Raman pressure calibration. Screws were released while cold. These details should accompany the preparation path; a generic label such as hydrostatic pressure is insufficient for the actual stress environment. The release rate has not been quantitatively reconstructed in this review. 

 Limits and disputes

The reported tetragonal structure persists in diffraction measurements up to 15 GPa, while recovered peaks broaden and lattice parameters change slightly. Those observations do not establish identical microscopic states before and after quenching. Calculated phonon stability in the tested model and a possible electronic Lifshitz feature are candidate explanations, not a measurement of the pairing cause or proof of global thermodynamic stability. No independent replication has been verified in this review; that is a review limitation, not proof that none exists. 

The journal article was published online on 9 March 2026; the checked author manuscript is arXiv v1 dated 12 March. Selected final PMC text was compared with author transport/magnetization methods and Figures 2, S2, S5 and S6. Final supplementary-file comparison, raw-data reanalysis and complete scientific acceptance remain open. The inherited bibliography names X. Deng; the published first author is Liangzi Deng. Gao and Schilling remain abstract-level checks here. Kramers supplies a simplified classical model, not a validated mechanism for this material.    

 Discovery implications

A useful follow-up tracks the same specimen before loading, under load and after release, combining transport, magnetism, composition and structure. Publish the complete pressure–temperature–time path, repeat cycles and failure cases, and measure retention versus temperature and time. Search records should distinguish preparation pressure from observation pressure and retain onset, zero-resistance, magnetic and unassigned-anomaly criteria separately. Applying this strategy to a different material is a proposal requiring new evidence; success in Hg-1223 does not guarantee a retained hydride or nickelate phase.

entries.text:
Scope

Chemical doping changes a material's composition; it does not supply a universal carrier counter. Distinguish the starting mixture, measured site occupancy, formal ionic charge and mobile carriers. Substitution can also change disorder, bond geometry and competing order. Oxygen removal or chain ordering adds another control variable. A superconducting dome is therefore a relationship among specified samples and criteria, not a recipe transferable between families.    

Notation matters even before measurement. Takagi's 1989 paper uses (\mathrm{La}{1-x}\mathrm{Sr}x)2\mathrm{CuO}4 and studies x\leq0.175. In the alternative formula \mathrm{La}{2-y}\mathrm{Sr}y\mathrm{CuO}4, the same composition has y=2x, reaching 0.35. The inherited draft attached 0.175 to the latter convention without converting it. This page corrects that factor-of-two mismatch; the original abstract, not its inaccessible full methods, was checked. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Charge neutrality is useful bookkeeping under explicit ionic assumptions. Taking La/Nd as 3+, Sr as 2+, Ce as 4+ and O as 2- gives formal average Cu valence 2+x+2\delta in \mathrm{La}{2-x}\mathrm{Sr}x\mathrm{CuO}{4+\delta}, and 2-x-2y in \mathrm{Nd}{2-x}\mathrm{Ce}x\mathrm{CuO}{4-y}. Stoichiometric infinite-layer \mathrm{Nd}{1-x}\mathrm{Sr}x\mathrm{NiO}2 gives formal Ni valence 1+x. These balances do not locate holes among orbitals or establish an itinerant carrier density. Oxygen deviations and compensating defects change the balance.  

Even the elementary weak-field two-band Drude model yields RH=(nh\muh^2-ne\mue^2)/[e(nh\muh+ne\mue)^2], with e>0. Mobilities weight the response. For compensation, ne=nh=n, this becomes (\muh-\mue)/[en(\muh+\mue)]; its sign can reverse at fixed density. This illustrative identity is not a fit to correlated transport. Kasahara explicitly discusses why that simple model fails for the magnitude of the observed Hall response. 

Liang's empirical YBCO calibration uses p=11.491u+5.17\times10^9u^6, u=1-c/c0, with c0=1.18447\,\mathrm{nm} and c measured at 22°C. It depends on chain-order assumptions and reference compositions. The relation Tc/T{c,\max}=1-82.6(p-0.16)^2 has two algebraic branches and fails near the material's suppressed one-eighth region. Neither expression is a universal oxygen-to-hole conversion; a fitted lattice parameter and a directly measured carrier density are different evidence. 

 Experimental criteria

Measure composition on the specimens whose transitions are compared. Ni's Co-substituted Ba122 series used wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy (WDS): actual Co fraction was about 0.74 times the nominal fraction for that growth series. A nominal 0.10 batch averaged approximately 0.074. Its phase diagram distinguishes resistance, magnetization and heat capacity. Resistive offset means maximum-slope extrapolation to zero, rather than an independently established instrumental zero. The reported maximum near 23 K spans measured fractions approximately 0.058–0.074. 

For YBCO, oxygen content alone omits chain configuration. Liang combined oxygen control, ordered-chain preparations and room-temperature lattice measurements; Tc was the midpoint of field-cooled magnetization in 1 Oe along the c axis. Fully oxygenated material's 85.3 K transition anchors the overdoped calibration through the empirical parabola. It is not a new direct measurement of p. Record thermal history, chain order, calibration assumptions and their uncertainty alongside oxygen stoichiometry. 

In the P-substituted Ba122 author manuscript, composition was measured by energy-dispersive X-ray analysis. Figure 2 separates onset and zero-resistivity temperatures. Version 3 reports zero resistance from x\geq0.20 and a maximum transition around 31 K, while observing a narrow transition at x=0.33. Do not turn “isovalent” into proof of unchanged Fermi surfaces, scattering or carrier populations. Nor does a similar phase diagram make chemical substitution physically identical to applied pressure. 

Li's nickelate study concerns 8–10 nm films on SrTiO3, capped and reduced from perovskite precursors. Its superconducting compositions lie inside 0.125<x<0.25. Figure 2 defines two temperatures at 10% and 90% of each sample's resistance at 20 K; symbols average multiple samples and error bars show extrema. The comparison cuprate curve instead uses 50%. These are unequal criteria. The 20 K normalization is not a superconducting transition, and the sign-changing Hall response is interpreted through multiple bands. 

 Limits and disputes

Changing composition and introducing pair-breaking disorder can occur together. Sidis's original abstract reports different neutron-resonance responses to Ni and Zn impurities in YBCO. That comparison does not justify a universal impurity ranking across pairing states or substitution sites. Separate scattering, magnetic moments, charge redistribution, structural effects and phase purity before inferring the origin of a Tc trend. Abstract-only evidence cannot support a detailed impurity-dose reconstruction. 

Version and specimen checks remain necessary. Ni's author manuscript mentions 0.078 in its specific-heat discussion while the phase-summary maximum uses 0.074; this page does not silently identify them as one specimen. Kasahara's earlier and later manuscripts differ in the composition range and reported zero-resistance boundary, and the later figure's color description conflicts with the displayed onset/zero labels. Use the labeled criteria, not color alone. Final journal comparisons and raw-data reproduction remain open.  

A dome does not establish a unique pairing mechanism, homogeneous microscopic coexistence or a universal optimal carrier concentration. The nickelate manuscript notes sample-to-sample resistivity variations associated with microstructure and does not establish the origin of its small dip within the dome. Preserve that uncertainty; numerical resemblance to a cuprate anomaly is not an ordering measurement. 

 Discovery implications

Store nominal and measured composition separately, including the chemical formula convention, analytical method, uncertainty and spatial variation. Link each transition to its specimen, phase, oxygen/reduction history, substrate or strain, measurement criterion and source version. Keep Hall-derived model parameters separate from valence arithmetic. Prioritize reproducible composition–structure–property relationships and independent magnetic or thermodynamic checks before ranking a tuning series. The calculations here verify notation and algebra, not an optimal synthesis or a carrier-density calibration.

entries.text:
Scope

Gating specifies an applied-voltage protocol, not its microscopic mechanism. A solid dielectric can accumulate interfacial charge; an electrolyte can also change oxygen content, drive redox or move ions. Whether a particular experiment is predominantly electrostatic requires evidence about the actual material, temperature, time and voltage history. Reversible resistance alone is insufficient: Jeong's VO2 study demonstrated reversible conductance switching associated with oxygen-vacancy formation. That experiment is a mechanism control, not a superconducting discovery. 

Keep the early platforms separate. Ueno's 2008 work concerned SrTiO3. The 15.2 K ZrNCl report was by Ye and colleagues, published online in November 2009 and in the February 2010 issue. The inherited draft conflated their attribution. This page corrects it while retaining the limited review scope: the ZrNCl institutional abstract supplies the reported temperature but not an independently checked onset, midpoint or zero-resistance definition.  

 Mathematical assumptions

For a uniform planar device with constant areal capacitance CA, an electron-accumulation convention gives \Delta n{2D}=CA\Delta V/e, where e>0. If the measured total differential capacitance C(V)=dQ/dV varies with voltage, use \Delta n{2D}=(Ae)^{-1}\int C(V)\,dV for gated area A. Multiplying the endpoint capacitance by the entire voltage interval is generally wrong. Caviglia explicitly integrated the nonlinear response of the SrTiO3 dielectric. 

In a simple positive-capacitance model, CA^{-1}=C{g,A}^{-1}+C{q,A}^{-1} accounts for geometric and quantum capacitances in series, with C{q,A}=e^2\partial n{2D}/\partial\mu. Traps, leakage, negative compressibility and spatially nonuniform channels require a richer treatment. For two gates, the ideal charge estimate is en{2D}=C{t,A}(Vt-V{t0})+C{b,A}(Vb-V{b0}). Offset voltages and dielectric calibration are assumptions to report, not quantities fixed by the formula.   

The distinction between induced charge and mobile carriers survives accurate capacitance arithmetic. Sajadi explicitly calls the gate-derived quantity a doping density rather than a carrier density; correlated insulating behavior and edge conduction complicate that interpretation. Likewise, integrating a gate current gives transferred charge, Q=\int Igdt, without proving how much enters the conducting channel or participates in chemistry. Local calculations here check units, integration and illustrative circuit identities; they do not measure charge transfer in a sample.  

 Experimental criteria

Caviglia's LaAlO3/SrTiO3 device used the substrate as a back-gate dielectric. Its capacitance depended on sweep history; conditioning at the highest positive voltage produced reproducible sweeps, and the resulting zero-voltage state was not the as-grown state. The superconducting dome used temperatures extracted from a BKT resistance model, reaching approximately 0.310 K. The 0.400 K normal-state resistance and 1.5 K capacitance measurements are separate observables. Preserve the fit model and preparation history when comparing this dome with other systems. 

Fatemi's monolayer WTe2 device 1 illustrates why one transition has several temperatures. At bottom/top gate voltages 4/5 V, resistance reached 90% of its normal value near 0.820 K, 50% near 0.580 K and zero near 0.350 K. Device 2 reached a midpoint near 0.950 K but retained residual resistance attributed to a device imperfection. The two devices and criteria must not be collapsed into “zero resistance at 1 K.” Their Hall and capacitance estimates broadly agreed, with low-density deviations discussed as possibly inhomogeneous transport. 

MoS2 provides a related criterion warning. Ye established a gate-controlled dome in a band insulator. In Lu's later author manuscript, the phase-diagram panel uses 90% of the normal resistance at 15 K, whereas the remaining analysis uses 50%. A corresponding low-temperature state is labeled 2.63 K by the former criterion and 2.37 K by the latter. Keep those labels distinct from BKT temperatures or high-field boundaries. The layer-localization and spin–orbit interpretation also depends on the device model and field orientation.  

Sajadi's WTe2 manuscript instead defines a characteristic temperature at half the resistance measured at 1 K. A reported noise floor around 0.3 ohm at 20 mK is an instrumental bound at a measurement temperature, not an exact superconducting transition. Record contact geometry, current distribution and residual resistance alongside nominal four-terminal measurements; a poorly known current path can affect the inferred sheet resistance. 

 Limits and disputes

Jeong's VO2 evidence went beyond reversible transport: conductance persisted after the ionic liquid was removed, vanadium core-level spectra changed, and reverse gating in oxygen-18 produced an isotope depth profile measured by secondary-ion mass spectrometry. Ungated regions receiving the same isotope exposure served as controls. These results support chemical modification in those devices; they do not prove that every ionic-liquid-gated superconductor follows the same mechanism. Full supplementary procedures and quantitative vacancy reconstruction remain outside this scoped review. 

A useful electrostatic interpretation therefore compares leakage and dwell-time behavior, sweep recovery, independent charge estimates, thickness dependence and before/after structural or chemical evidence. No single low-leakage threshold or unchanged spectrum proves the absence of all reactions. State the sensitivity and spatial sampling of each control. Conversely, hysteresis can arise from trapping in a dielectric and is not by itself proof of electrochemistry.  

A gate-induced dome does not uniquely identify a pairing mechanism or a quantum critical point. Strong in-plane critical fields require analysis of orbital geometry, spin–orbit coupling and the chosen resistive threshold; they do not automatically establish triplet pairing. Switching a quantum spin Hall material into a superconducting regime creates an opportunity to investigate topology, but does not by itself demonstrate a topological superconducting gap or Majorana modes.    

 Discovery implications

Treat the device and voltage history as part of the material record: dielectric or electrolyte, thickness, gate geometry, charging temperature, dwell time, leakage, reset protocol and independent carrier estimate. Separate superconducting onset, midpoint, measured zero and model-extracted BKT temperatures. Use chemistry-sensitive controls to decide whether a changed state belongs under electrostatic tuning or compositional modification. The source-linked records below preserve reported observations and explicit unknowns; they are not a ranking of intrinsic material performance.
