entries.text:
Scope

Strain is a directional deformation relative to a stated reference structure. A uniaxially loaded crystal, a clamped epitaxial film and a hydrostatically compressed sample follow different mechanical paths. Applied displacement is not necessarily sample strain: mounting adhesive, thermal contraction, bending and fracture can all intervene. The useful control variable is the calibrated deformation in the region probed, together with its uncertainty and history.  

Separate the early Sr2RuO4 experiments. Hicks's 2014 Science study reported different responses for loading along the crystallographic ⟨100⟩ and ⟨110⟩ directions, within an approximately 0.23% accessible range. The later Steppke study reached the much larger compressive strain associated with a transition near 3.4 K. These are distinct measurements, not interchangeable references for one apparatus or peak. The earlier result is checked here only through the authors' institutional abstract.  

 Mathematical assumptions

For a lattice parameter relative to a relaxed reference, engineering strain is \epsilon=(a-a0)/a0. Nominal epitaxial mismatch uses f=(a{\rm sub}-a{\rm ref})/a{\rm ref} instead. Neither a substrate name nor this calculation establishes the strain remaining after relaxation. Report reference composition, phase, temperature and orientation; compare actual film lattice parameters with that same reference. 

In small-deformation elasticity, \epsilon{ij}=(\partiali uj+\partialj ui)/2 and \sigma{ij}=C{ijkl}\epsilon{kl}. As an explicitly isotropic illustration, a film with equal in-plane strains \epsilon{xx}=\epsilon{yy}=f and a traction-free surface has \epsilon{zz}=-2\nu f/(1-\nu). Positive Poisson ratio therefore permits out-of-plane expansion under in-plane compression. This illustration is not an anisotropic nickelate fit, and it does not convert epitaxial mismatch into an equivalent hydrostatic pressure.  

Hicks's simplified adhesive model gives a load-transfer length \lambda=\sqrt{Etd/(nGe)}, with sample Young's modulus E, sample thickness t, adhesive thickness d, adhesive shear modulus Ge, and one or two bonded faces n. For symmetric ends, displacement is distributed over approximately L+2\lambda, not just the exposed length L. The stated illustrative parameters give about 90 micrometres. Rigid plates, a much softer adhesive and uniform sample strain across its section are assumptions; finite-element bending and real adhesive failure require additional treatment. 

 Experimental criteria

Steppke measured magnetic transitions using mutual inductance, with approximately 0.2 Oe excitation at 1–20 kHz, and used a capacitive displacement sensor. Figure 4 defines the plotted transition temperatures at 50% of the magnetic response; the 20% and 80% levels show transition width. The reported peak strain is approximately −0.60% with a ±0.06 percentage-point uncertainty from four samples, while individual strain calibration was estimated to have roughly 20% uncertainty. These are different uncertainty statements. 

The often-quoted 3.4 K scale is not a universal sample maximum: sample 5 reached approximately 3.5 K. Resistive transitions in the two contacted specimens did not exceed the highest magnetic transition by more than 0.08 K. That comparison does not redefine a magnetic midpoint as zero resistance. A flat feature near zero strain in sample 1 arose after the sample broke during cooling and needed compression to re-engage; it should not be fitted as an intrinsic phase boundary. 

Bhatt's final Figure 1 labels nominal/measured mismatch pairs, respectively, as SLAO −2.0%/−1.6%, LAO −1.2%/−0.9%, NGO +0.7%/+0.6% and STO +1.9%/+1.8%. These final labels replace several different measured values in the inherited chapter. The SLAO film has a broad resistive transition, with onset near 42 K and zero near 2 K; those endpoints cannot be merged into a 42 K zero-resistance claim. 

Ko's original thin-film report also distinguishes onset and zero resistance. Its March 2026 correction fixes resistivity-axis units to mΩ cm and the Figure 3d horizontal label to temperature T, not Tc. The correction was read in full; the original paper's detailed methods were not retrieved here. The source-linked temperature records below therefore cite Bhatt's checked final passage, rather than implying a complete reanalysis of Ko's experiment.   

 Limits and disputes

Bhatt's films on SLAO used pulsed-laser deposition, whereas the other substrate films used molecular-beam epitaxy. Oxygen annealing and uncertain oxygen occupancy remain relevant covariates. Figure 3 supports out-of-plane expansion under in-plane compression, contrasting with hydrostatic contraction. It does not support the inherited universal superlative that the SLAO film has the largest c-axis: the plotted LAO values are comparable or higher. Avoid turning a qualitative structural contrast into an unsupported ranking. 

A peak near a calculated Lifshitz transition constrains possible models without uniquely identifying pairing symmetry. Steppke's electronic-structure and order-parameter calculations are model-dependent; their discussion should not be read as a present-day determination of Sr2RuO4's order parameter. This scoped review checked selected experimental passages and a figure, not the full multiband calculation, all supplements or experimental raw data. 

 Discovery implications

Design a strain study around a measured mechanical path and a defined superconducting criterion. Retain loading direction, reference state, adhesive or substrate constraints, thermal history and reversibility. Check whether a broadened transition tracks strain inhomogeneity or a changed specimen, and compare transport with magnetic or thermodynamic evidence where feasible. Local arithmetic here verifies mismatch, ideal elastic identities and the adhesive model; it neither predicts a superconducting transition nor establishes a unique strain mechanism.

entries.text:
Scope

Magnetic field is both a control parameter and a probe of superconductivity. Orbital currents, Zeeman splitting, vortex motion and changes in the magnetic background can produce different boundaries. A resistive onset, loss of zero resistance, heat-capacity anomaly and magnetic transition need not coincide. Retain temperature, crystal orientation, sample history, sweep direction and pulse conditions when comparing field scales.   

This article uses B in tesla for the field scale; experimental papers often label that axis H while reporting tesla, meaning an applied \mu0H scale. Converting an applied field to local induction requires the magnetization and demagnetizing geometry. Neither an unusually large upper critical field nor field-induced superconductivity alone identifies a pairing symmetry.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For a weak-coupling singlet reference with Zeeman levels shifted by \pm g\muB B/2, zero residual superconducting spin susceptibility and no orbital cost, condensation-energy balance gives BP=\sqrt{2}\Delta0/(g\muB). Using \Delta0=\pi e^{-\gammaE}kBTc and g=2 gives about 1.86\,Tc tesla when Tc is in kelvin. This is a conditional reference, not a universal upper bound. Spin-orbit coupling, anisotropic spin response and strong coupling change the comparison. Clogston's historical identity is retained; its complete original derivation was not retrieved here.  

A second restricted reference is the dirty, single-band, purely orbital result B{c2}^{\rm orb}(0)\simeq0.693\,Tc|dB{c2}/dT|{Tc}. Gurevich's final paper recovers it when the two diffusivities are equal. Its Eq. (31) defines U(x)=\psi(1/2+x)-\psi(1/2), satisfying U(0)=0. The early author v1 prints a plus sign at that location; use the final definition. Unequal diffusivities produce different curves. This check does not validate a full WHH fit with Zeeman and spin-orbit terms, or a multiband fit to a particular material.  

The Maki parameter compares those reference scales, \alphaM=\sqrt{2}B{c2}^{\rm orb}(0)/BP; it is not by itself an FFLO detection criterion. In a parabolic band with small splitting, the Fermi-wavevector mismatch is \delta k\simeq g\muB B/(\hbar vF). The inherited expression contains an extra factor of two under the stated Zeeman convention. This kinematic estimate does not solve for the optimum finite-momentum pair wavevector or establish the stability of a Fulde–Ferrell–Larkin–Ovchinnikov state. Disorder, orbital effects, dimensionality and competing orders matter.  

 Experimental criteria

Petrovic's discovery report describes zero resistance and full diamagnetic shielding at approximately 2.3 K in CeCoIn5. Its field–temperature paragraph compares specific heat with zero resistance for field along the c-axis. That zero-field transition is distinct from lower-temperature anomalies inside the superconducting phase. 

Bianchi's selected author-manuscript passages describe heat-pulse and temperature-decay calorimetry, including subtraction of the In/Co nuclear Schottky contribution. Figure 1 uses different vertical quantities in its panels: (C-C{\rm Sch})/T and C, with a C/T inset. Equal-entropy construction concerns the integral of C/T, not equal areas under an unconverted C curve. At high in-plane fields the report finds a first-order upper boundary and an internal anomaly around 0.3 K. These are not new zero-field transition temperatures. Its final title explicitly says “Possible” FFLO state; calorimetry does not directly measure pair momentum. 

The later Kenzelmann neutron-scattering report finds magnetic order coupled to superconductivity in this high-field region. Its symmetry interpretation suggests a modulated superconducting state, while the observed magnetic order does not alone reconstruct the spatial pair field. This article checked that paper's original abstract, not its complete neutron methods or supplementary analysis. 

Lewin's UTe2 experiments combine pulsed-field resistance and proximity-detector-oscillator measurements. Typical pulses reached 60 T or, in a different magnet, 73 T; the common measurement temperature was about 0.63 K. The high-field zero-resistance region depends strongly on both field angles. The oscillator frequency is a conductivity-sensitive proxy, and a comparison at 2.09 K without the superconducting feature is a normal-state measurement, not a 2.09 K transition determination. A measured field extent is not necessarily an observed upper critical field. 

Zambra's April 2026 study measures magnetotropic response at 4 K, where the superconducting phases are suppressed. Its Figure 1 separately reproduces a 300 mK superconducting phase diagram and 1.4 K magnetization from earlier work. These temperatures must not be merged into a claim of superconductivity at 4 K. “Transverse” refers to response perpendicular to the static field, not automatically an off-diagonal susceptibility element. The final article number is 3742, correcting the inherited 3814. 

 Limits and disputes

Magnetotropic susceptibility, an angular derivative of torque measured through a cantilever frequency shift, probes a different response from longitudinal magnetization. Zambra's long-wavelength result supports an inference of enhanced transverse ferromagnetic fluctuations; it does not measure a complete frequency-dependent pairing interaction. Values below 15 T in one normalized color map were set to zero to suppress amplified noise, rather than demonstrating a physically vanishing susceptibility. Alignment and calibration details remain relevant to comparisons with phase boundaries. 

Keep measured phenomena separate from candidate explanations. A heat-capacity anomaly, magnetic Q phase and proposed FFLO modulation are distinct statements. Likewise, the multicomponent triplet model discussed for the UTe2 field-angle halo is an interpretation, not a direct determination of topology. Selected original passages and figures were checked here; remaining final-version comparisons, full supplements, raw-data reproduction and complete scientific acceptance remain open.   

 Discovery implications

Construct a field–temperature–angle map with explicit criteria and uncertainties. Compare transport with thermodynamic or magnetic probes where possible, retain pulsed-field heating and alignment controls, and distinguish re-entrant regions from a simple monotonic critical field. The local equation checks verify declared Zeeman conventions, an orbital asymptote and an illustrative entropy construction. They do not establish a new superconducting phase, fit an experimental boundary or certify a universal pairing mechanism.

entries.text:
Scope

Light can change carrier populations, excite lattice motion and alter collective electronic response. Persistent photodoping, a transient pump–probe state and a periodically driven model are different protocols. Specify wavelength, polarization, pulse duration, fluence, repetition rate, base temperature and probe delay. A temperature at which a driven response is observed is not automatically an equilibrium superconducting transition temperature.    

The evidence now extends beyond optical conductivity. Electrical measurements in K3C60, transient magnetic measurements in YBa2Cu3O6.48 and a later sensitivity-limited magnetic experiment on K3C60 ask different questions. Preserve the specimen, geometry and measured observable rather than combining them into one universal light-induced transition.    

 Mathematical assumptions

With the e^{-i\omega t} convention, a normal Drude response is \sigma(\omega)=D/(\Gamma-i\omega), where D is the Drude weight and \Gamma>0 the relaxation rate. Thus \sigma2=D\omega/(\Gamma^2+\omega^2)\approx D/\omega when the measured frequencies greatly exceed \Gamma, although the DC conductivity D/\Gamma remains finite. A finite-band inductive trend alone cannot distinguish this limit from a condensate. This elementary counterexample is not a fit to, or refutation of, any particular experiment.  

Depth reconstruction also matters. For Dodge's illustrative saturating profile, \Delta\sigma(z)=\Delta\sigma{\rm sat}f e^{-z/\Lambda}/(1+f e^{-z/\Lambda}), with f=F/F{\rm sat}, integration gives sheet photoconductance \Delta G=\Delta\sigma{\rm sat}\Lambda\ln(1+f). The effective thickness grows with fluence even while the surface response saturates. Assuming a fixed exponential profile can therefore bias the inferred surface conductivity. This integral checks the stated profile, not a full electromagnetic inversion; the experimental interpretation is disputed below.  

Kennes's minimal quadratic electron–phonon model gives oscillator frequency \omega(n)=\omega0\sqrt{1+2gn} for site occupation n=0,1,2, requiring g>-1/4. At fixed phonon occupation nB, its induced interaction is \Delta U=(nB+1/2)\hbar\omega0[\sqrt{1+4g}+1-2\sqrt{1+2g}]. Concavity makes this nonpositive for either sign of stable g, with leading term -(nB+1/2)\hbar\omega0g^2. The author manuscript sets Planck's constant to one; it is restored here. This is a model mechanism, not a measured coupling or proof of a stable superconducting phase. 

 Experimental criteria

Fausti studied stripe-ordered La1.675Eu0.2Sr0.125CuO4 at a 10 K base temperature. The reported signal is a transient c-axis plasma edge and optical response interpreted as restored interlayer coherence. Figures 2–3 specify a 16 micrometre pump, approximately 1 mJ/cm² fluence and a 5 ps delay for the transient spectrum. The pump excites roughly 200 nm in depth, while the THz probe samples about 10 micrometres; the transformed-layer reconstruction is essential. A near-infrared plateau observed to 100 ps does not directly measure a many-nanosecond lifetime. 

Hu's YBa2Cu3O6.5 specimen has an equilibrium transition near 50 K. Its approximately 300 fs, 15 micrometre pump modifies both inter- and intra-bilayer optical response. The effective-medium analysis separates transformed and untransformed regions; screened plasma-edge positions are not the same as fitted unscreened plasma frequencies. Broadband data at 60 K and narrower-band measurements at 100 and 300 K have different information content. Mankowsky's associated structural study combines diffraction with calculations to connect driven distortions with electronic changes; structural response does not uniquely identify pairing.  

Mitrano's K3C60 report compares a transient optical response above the roughly 20 K equilibrium transition with the low-temperature spectrum. Its title deliberately says “Possible”. The reported optical-gap fit and enhanced carrier mobility are not a direct DC resistance or magnetic measurement. Temperature, pump–probe delay and model-dependent gap extraction must remain attached to that evidence. 

Budden extended the response using longer pulses. Figure 4 compares optical extrapolation with electrical measurements at a 100 K base temperature and about 25 mJ/cm² fluence. The optical and transport pump durations are 200 ps and 75 ps, respectively. The electrical experiment is transient two-terminal transport with contact contributions calibrated from static four-terminal measurements; it is not a direct transient four-terminal measurement. Resistance compatible with zero within that calibration and recovery over tens of nanoseconds strengthen the authors' metastable interpretation without establishing a pump-free equilibrium transition at 100 K. 

Adelinia's 2025 thin-film study uses a quasi-DC bias, 300 fs pulses at 7 micrometres and photoconductive switches to resolve voltage dynamics. Granular-film and powder results are not interchangeable. The above-transition voltage response changes sign at 80 K; at 100 K it is positive and linear across the measured current range. Fitted superfluid fractions and weak-link phase-slip dynamics depend on the granular two-fluid model. A 100 K measurement in this paper must not become a 100 K superconducting-transition record. 

Fava's 2024 YBa2Cu3O6.48 experiment detects a transient magnetic-field enhancement near the excited region's edge using Faraday rotation in a nearby GaP detector. Signals at 100 and 300 K last about 1 ps. The inferred diamagnetic susceptibility of order −0.3 depends on geometry and the magnetic-response model; the paper itself cautions that a quasi-static estimate is not fully justified for this dynamics. This provides a complementary magnetic observable, while remaining distinct from a persistent equilibrium Meissner state. 

De Vecchi's December 2025 K3C60 study reports no statistically significant photo-induced field signal above roughly 50 nT out to 1 ns in its protocol. Its model-based bound is \chiv>-0.1. The authors explicitly conclude that their resolution does not decide whether Meissner diamagnetism is present or absent. Granularity and a small expected response matter: this null result neither establishes superconductivity nor universally rules it out. 

 Limits and disputes

Dodge and colleagues argue that saturation-dependent excitation depth can create misleading superconducting-like reconstructed spectra. Buzzi and colleagues' March 2023 preprint response disputes that interpretation, arguing that the inductive signature survives their alternative reconstructions. The local profile and Drude checks above do not resolve this dispute. Compare raw reflected fields, depth assumptions, spectral bandwidth and independent transport or magnetic evidence rather than treating a fitted gap as a unique diagnosis.  

Long-lived after a short pulse does not mean thermodynamic equilibrium. Quantify absorbed energy, depth gradients, carrier and lattice temperatures, relaxation and repetition-rate heating. Selective excitation of a phonon does not establish that equilibrium pairing is phonon-mediated. The present review covers selected original passages and figures; full supplements, remaining version comparisons, experimental raw-data reproduction and complete scientific acceptance remain open.    

 Discovery implications

Use synchronized optical, electrical and magnetic probes with explicit controls and uncertainty. Report signal duration separately from formation time and instrumental resolution. Keep equilibrium transition records separate from driven base temperatures and model estimates in databases and search filters. Theory should predict observables under the actual drive protocol, including relaxation, rather than equating an attractive model interaction with an experimentally established superconducting phase.

entries.text:
Scope

Disorder is not one adjustable number. Elastic scattering, magnetic pair breaking, local bound states, localization, vortex pinning and poor grain connectivity affect different observables. Record defect chemistry, irradiation particle and energy, dose, temperature, annealing history and sample geometry. A larger residual resistivity does not by itself specify the pair-breaking rate or prove a change of carrier density.   

Anderson's time-reversed-state argument explains the robustness of an isotropic, sign-preserving superconducting state to nonmagnetic elastic scattering under restricted assumptions. The participating states must remain extended and the averaged pairing interaction and density of states must not change substantially. It is not immunity to arbitrary chemical substitution, localization, magnetic scattering or spatial granularity. Constant Tc alone does not uniquely determine pairing symmetry.  

 Mathematical assumptions

In the dilute, uncorrelated, weak magnetic-scattering model for an isotropic singlet state, define the pair-breaking energy \Gamma by \ln(T{c0}/Tc)=\psi(1/2+\Gamma/(2\pi kBTc))-\psi(1/2), where \psi is the digamma function. With g=\Gamma/(kBT{c0}) and t=Tc/T{c0}, the initial slope is dt/dg=-\pi/4, and Tc vanishes at gc=\pi e^{-\gammaE}/2\approx0.882. Rate conventions differ; do not substitute a transport lifetime without deriving its relation to this \Gamma. Local numerical checks compare the equation with independently bounded Matsubara sums. The original AG paper remains a bibliographic anchor, not a completed original-text audit.   

For one classical magnetic scattering channel in a particle–hole-symmetric, isotropic host with a fixed gap, use exchange J\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf s, \mathbf s=\boldsymbol\sigma/2, and normal density of states per spin N0. Defining \alpha=\pi N0JS/2 and potential strength \beta=\pi N0V, one signed Yu–Shiba–Rusinov branch is E/\Delta=(1+\beta^2-\alpha^2)/\sqrt{(1+\beta^2-\alpha^2)^2+4\alpha^2}; its particle–hole partner has opposite energy. At V=0, this reduces to (1-\alpha^2)/(1+\alpha^2). A zero crossing requires \alpha^2=1+\beta^2 in this model. These conventions and phase-shift checks do not solve quantum Kondo screening, multiple orbital channels or self-consistent gap suppression.    

Dose is a separate quantity: an electron charge dose of 1 C/cm² corresponds to approximately 6.24\times10^{18} incident electrons/cm². The 3.4 C/cm² exposure in Prozorov's protocol is about 2.12\times10^{19} electrons/cm². Neither number is the surviving defect concentration; displacement cross sections, recombination and annealing enter that conversion. 

 Experimental criteria

Prozorov studied Ba(Fe1−xRux)2As2 with WDS composition x=0.24 using 2.5 MeV electrons. Irradiation and in-situ resistivity measurements took place near 22 K; the initial superconducting transition is reported as 17.8 K in the methods and 17.85 K in the transport figure. Warming to room temperature between runs partially annealed the damage, by up to about 30%. The same contacts were retained. Increased resistivity and suppressed Tc were compatible with the authors' multiband sign-changing scenario, whose interband/intraband scattering ratio matters. The 22 K irradiation temperature is not Tc, and no unverified onset, midpoint or zero-resistance label is assigned here. 

Mizukami's BaFe2(As1−xPx)2 crystals had x=0.33–0.36 and initial transitions of 28, 29 or 30 K. The 28/29 K batches were tracked by tunnel-diode-oscillator frequency shifts; the 30 K crystal also supplied the resistivity series. Following 2.5 MeV irradiation, low-temperature penetration-depth curves evolved from nodal behavior to an activated regime, then back to gapless behavior with further disorder. The authors interpreted that sequence with accidental nodes and sign-changing multiband pairing. Here “topological change” concerns the gap's nodal structure; it does not establish a Majorana-carrying topological superconductor. The 80 mK measurement floor and 20–22 K irradiation bath remain separate from transition records. 

Hatter measured manganese phthalocyanine on Pb(111) at 1.2 K with a superconducting Pb tip. The resolved Shiba triplets have 50–100 microelectronvolt widths and separations up to 400 microelectronvolts. The measured conductance includes the tip density of states: near-zero sample excitation energy appears near the tip-gap bias, not necessarily at zero measured bias. The authors numerically deconvolved the spectra and used relative spectral weights to distinguish impurity ground states and magnetic-anisotropy effects. This is local spectroscopy, not a 1.2 K transition measurement or a standalone Majorana demonstration. 

 Limits and disputes

A suppression curve alone is not a unique symmetry test. Separate changes in pairing interaction, band filling, magnetic moments and defect morphology from elastic scattering; distinguish intra- and interband processes. Gapless superconductivity is also different from destruction of superconducting order. The classical single-impurity formula cannot establish the quantum impurity parity change on its own; spectroscopy, tip calibration, spatial structure and the appropriate many-body model are needed.     

Defects can help current transport by pinning vortices while harming other properties. BaZrO3-containing YBCO films illustrate an in-field current improvement that must be evaluated at specified temperature, field and orientation, rather than equated with higher Tc. Dirty two-gap theory also permits enhanced orbital upper critical fields under particular diffusivity and coupling conditions. Neither result implies monotonic improvement with damage, a universal type-I to type-II conversion, or an enhanced Pauli limit.  

The present article has selected original-paper and equation checks. The original AG full text and Shiba full derivation have not been read; Yu's original abstract and opening discussion were checked from scans. The detailed AG/YSR equation convention was cross-checked in the Balatsky author manuscript, with final-version comparison still open. Full supplements, raw-data reanalysis and complete scientific acceptance remain unfinished.    

 Discovery implications

Use controlled defect series with repeat measurements before irradiation, after irradiation and after annealing. Compare Tc, gap spectra, residual resistivity, magnetic response, H{c2} and Jc under matched conditions. Preserve sample identifiers and probe-specific transition criteria in machine-readable records; never merge irradiation temperatures, spectroscopy temperatures and superconducting transitions into a single temperature ranking.

entries.text:
Scope

Dimensionality compares geometry with physical length scales. A layered crystal, a two-dimensional electronic band and a superconducting film with a nearly uniform order parameter through its thickness are different descriptions. Compare thickness with the perpendicular coherence length, wire transverse dimensions with coherence lengths, and lateral size with magnetic screening lengths. Interlayer coupling, substrate, disorder and carrier density can change when layers are removed. Reduced thickness alone does not establish an ideal two-dimensional phase transition.  

For a short-range two-dimensional phase model, vortex–antivortex unbinding separates quasi-long-range order from a disordered phase. The relevant stiffness is renormalized by fluctuations. In a charged film, magnetic screening changes the vortex interaction at long distance: Kosterlitz and Thouless explicitly identified this limitation in their original paper. BKT-like behavior requires an appropriate range of length, current and temperature scales; do not transfer the neutral infinite-system limit to every finite superconducting sheet.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Define the sheet phase stiffness J in energy units by F\theta=(J/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2. A single vortex has logarithmic energy \pi J\ln(L/a) and positional entropy 2kB\ln(L/a) within this model, where a is a core cutoff. The universal jump is JR(T{\rm BKT}^-)=2kBT{\rm BKT}/\pi, with the long-distance renormalized stiffness JR. The elementary energy–entropy balance explains the scale; it is not a replacement for the renormalization calculation. For a local sheet inductance Lk per square, the corresponding stiffness convention is J=\hbar^2/(4e^2Lk). Frequency, vortex response and finite size matter when comparing a measured inductance with the static jump.  

In a uniform narrow wire near its mean-field transition, the zero-current Ginzburg–Landau saddle gives \Delta F0=(8\sqrt2/3)uc A\xi, where uc=Bc^2/(2\mu0) is the SI condensation-energy density and A is cross-sectional area. A local check integrates the normalized saddle f(y)=\tanh(y/\sqrt2), y=x/\xi, in \int[(1-f^2)^2+2(df/dy)^2]dy. This checks the barrier factor under those assumptions, not a finite-current barrier, quantum tunneling action or the full LAMH prefactor. The original Langer–Ambegaokar and McCumber–Halperin full derivations have not been retrieved for this review.  

For rare independent thermal phase slips, define r0 explicitly as the zero-bias rate per direction. With \Phi0=h/(2e), detailed balance gives r\pm=r0\exp[\pm I\Phi0/(2kBT)] to leading small-bias barrier tilt, V=\Phi0(r+-r-) and R{I\to0}=\Phi0^2r0/(kBT). The thermal activation factor belongs inside r0; this definition avoids confusing a total event rate with a directional one. Low-temperature resistance saturation alone does not identify coherent quantum phase slips.   

 Experimental criteria

Xi's encapsulated NbSe2 devices distinguish several transition definitions. In the checked author manuscript, the monolayer Aslamazov–Larkin fit gives T{c0}\approx3.0 K, close to the 50% normal-resistance criterion; the inferred BKT transition lies near the 1% criterion. Those are separate quantities. Normal resistance was taken at 8 K. The four-terminal field series used a 50% criterion, while a separate two-terminal monolayer device used a rapid-resistance-drop criterion. The 0.3 K measurement floor is not another transition. Large in-plane critical fields support the authors' Ising-pairing interpretation under their model, rather than proving triplet pairing by themselves. The journal issue is from 2016; online publication was 9 November 2015. 

Bezryadin's nanotube-templated amorphous Mo79Ge21 wires were approximately 10 nm or less in diameter and 95–185 nm long. The resistance drop near 5.5 K belongs to the electrodes, after which the wire resistance could be isolated. In the studied series, samples on opposite sides of a normal-resistance scale near RQ=h/(4e^2)\approx6.45 kilohms showed decreasing or increasing resistance on cooling. One superconducting sample was checked down to 50 mK. These are sample-specific transport observations and a quantum-fluctuation interpretation, not a universal wire transition temperature or universal critical resistance for all geometries and environments. 

Astafiev's InOx loop experiment used microwave spectroscopy to investigate coherent coupling between flux states. The checked author version describes a 35 nm film, a narrow segment about 40 nm wide and 400 nm long, and measurements at 40 mK. A two-state fit gave ES/h=4.9 GHz and persistent current 24 nA for the illustrated device; resonator features distorted portions of the spectrum. The film's separately reported 2.7 K transition is distinct from the loop spectroscopy temperature. Coherent coupling evidence is stronger and different in kind from fitting a dissipative resistance tail; the selected readings do not reproduce the complete supplementary analysis. 

For aluminum nanoparticles, Black, Ralph and Tinkham reported even/odd differences in tunneling excitation thresholds and field suppression of a spectroscopic gap in sufficiently large particles, with radius roughly 5 nm or greater in their abstract. Radius is not diameter. Discrete levels, charging and parity enter the interpretation. Local pairing signatures do not demonstrate zero resistance across an isolated grain or global phase coherence in an array. This entry currently relies on the original publisher abstract, without a complete original-text audit. 

 Limits and disputes

Use several diagnostics for a BKT interpretation: nonlinear current–voltage behavior, stiffness and resistance scaling over justified windows, together with finite-size, heating and inhomogeneity checks. A convenient fit does not establish its asymptotic assumptions. Likewise, Giordano's early indium-wire work reported low-temperature deviations from thermal-activation predictions consistent with quantum tunneling; it should not be generalized into a rule that every residual resistance tail proves quantum phase slips. Weak links, contacts, normal regions and electromagnetic environment need independent controls.     

Selected original KT passages, NK journal text and author-version experimental sections have been checked. The NK equations were read from extracted publisher text, not a visually verified scan. The original LA, McCumber–Halperin, Giordano and nanoparticle full texts remain unreviewed; final-version comparisons for Xi, Bezryadin and Astafiev and complete supplements/raw-data analyses also remain open. Local algebra checks and successful software tests do not complete scientific acceptance.         

 Discovery implications

Build thickness and width series with documented oxidation protection, substrate, contacts and disorder. Store pairing-fit, phase-coherence, resistance and local-spectroscopy criteria separately, retaining the actual sample and measurement temperature. A route that strengthens pairing can simultaneously reduce phase stiffness; dimensional reduction is a tuning parameter, not a guarantee of a higher usable superconducting transition.    

 Related topics

Compare ,  and .

entries.title: Twist angle: moiré geometry, bandwidth and sample variation
entries.summary: Connect twist angle to moiré filling and interlayer coupling while preserving device-specific transition criteria, pressure history and stiffness-model limits.

entries.text:
Scope

A twist angle controls the relative orientation of two layers, changing the moiré pattern and the coupled electronic Hamiltonian. It does not independently specify carrier filling, interlayer tunneling, disorder, pairing interaction or superconducting topology. The original continuum model explains narrow bands and suppressed Dirac velocity at particular parameter values; observing a moiré pattern alone does not demonstrate a flat band or superconductivity. 

Magic-angle graphene supplies experimentally accessible correlated phases, but an adjacent insulating state does not uniquely identify a one-band Mott mechanism or a common pairing mediator. The 2018 correlated-insulator and superconductivity papers are distinct sources, with different questions and evidence. Pressure-dependent superconductivity further shows why nominal angle cannot be treated as the only tuning parameter.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For two matched, unstrained hexagonal lattices, define a=0.246 nm as graphene's lattice constant, not its carbon–carbon bond length. Then Lm=a/[2\sin(\theta/2)], Am=\sqrt3Lm^2/2 and Lm\approx a/\theta for a small angle expressed in radians. Bistritzer–MacDonald's manuscript instead calls the bond length a, so its numerator is \sqrt3a: these conventions are equivalent. Using the bond length in the lattice-constant formula would underestimate the period by \sqrt3 and overestimate the inferred full-filling density by a factor of three.  

With four spin–valley states per moiré band, define the full-band density ns=4/Am and filling \nu=nAm=4n/ns, measured relative to charge neutrality. At 1.10°, the ideal geometry gives Lm\approx12.81 nm and ns\approx2.81\times10^{12} cm⁻². This is a calculated reference, not a measured device value. The small-angle sensitivity is \delta ns/ns\approx2\delta\theta/\theta; the exact logarithmic derivative is d\ln ns/d\theta=\cot(\theta/2). A contact-averaged filling estimate cannot resolve a local twist/strain map, and broken-symmetry states need not retain fourfold degeneracy.  

Let k\theta=2K\sin(\theta/2), K=4\pi/(3a), and \alpha=w/(\hbar vFk\theta), using wavevector units for k\theta. In the first-shell approximation with the small layer-rotation correction neglected, v/vF=(1-3\alpha^2)/(1+6\alpha^2). Its zero at \alpha=1/\sqrt3 illustrates velocity cancellation, not an exact experimental magic angle. Tunneling, lattice relaxation and strain affect a realistic calculation. Our local check covers reciprocal geometry, density conversion and the stated algebraic zero; it does not diagonalize the complete continuum Hamiltonian or calculate a superconducting transition.  

 Experimental criteria

Cao's published superconductivity paper labels M1 at 1.16° and M2 at 1.05°. Figure 2 assigns maximum half-normal-resistance transition temperatures of about 0.5 K to M1 and 1.7 K to M2; the figure and caption resolve the device assignment. Both reached the reported zero-resistance state at the 70 mK measurement floor. A separate tentative cubic current–voltage fit for M2 at n=-1.44\times10^{12} cm⁻² gave T{\rm BKT}\approx1.0 K. The midpoint, inferred BKT scale and measurement floor must remain separate records. 

Yankowitz's nominal 1.27° device D2 developed superconducting transport under hydrostatic pressure. The published pressure plot defines Tc by the intersection of low- and high-temperature linear fits, and the reported resistance falls to a roughly 10-ohm noise floor. The author supplement lists approximately 3.1 K at 1.33 GPa and 1.7 K at 2.21 GPa; the 300 mK base temperature is separate. These fitted transition temperatures should not be relabeled as exact zero-resistance or half-resistance thresholds. The same supplement reports removal, solvent cleaning and reloading between these pressures, which adds a possible disorder change to the pressure comparison. 

The same study's ambient-pressure D1, at approximately 1.14°, had fitted transition scales near 0.4 K for holes and 0.25 K for electrons, with a 10 mK base temperature. Different contacts showed different full-filling densities; the final text reports moiré unit-cell-area variations up to roughly 30% within a device. The authors used full-filling features and quantum-oscillation extrapolations to estimate angle. They did not establish a uniform angle at every point merely by quoting two decimal places. 

Tanaka and colleagues' 2025 paper combines microwave kinetic inductance and transport to study superfluid stiffness. The checked earlier manuscript uses a parallel proximitized-edge circuit model and an assumed active-region aspect ratio to convert inductance into sheet stiffness. It distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK device temperature and uses a half-normal-resistance transition scale near 1 K over much of the dome. Its comparison supports a quantum-geometric contribution and anisotropic gap interpretation without extracting a model-independent geometric fraction or uniquely determining the pairing mediator. 

 Limits and disputes

Compare local geometry, filling calibration, contacts and thermal history before interpreting differences between devices. Pressure-dependent transition curves, a nearby insulator or a broadened dome are not unique fingerprints of a pairing mechanism. Distinguish measured resistance, nonlinear response and stiffness from a proposed microscopic explanation. Likewise, normal-state band topology does not alone fix the topology of the superconducting quasiparticles. Transferring graphene conclusions to a lattice-mismatched semiconductor stack requires a new model and platform-specific evidence.     

This review checks selected BM author equations, Cao final figures, Yankowitz final pressure passages plus selected author supplementary methods, and Tanaka author-version circuit/temperature definitions. The inherited source attributed the 2025 stiffness paper to Randeria; the publisher identifies Tanaka and colleagues. The BM and Tanaka final-version comparisons and complete supplementary/raw-data audits remain open. The correlated-insulator paper is used at publisher-abstract scope here, not as a completed microscopic-mechanism audit.     

 Discovery implications

Optimize angle together with tunneling, strain, filling and phase stiffness. Store each transition under its device, carrier branch, pressure and criterion; keep measurement floors separate. Use local imaging and contact-resolved transport to test uniformity. A useful design can combine favorable pairing and adequate phase coherence, but narrow bandwidth alone is not a sufficient target or a universal guarantee of higher Tc.   

 Related topics

Compare , , ,  and .

entries.title: Quantum metric: state distance, conventions and response limits
entries.summary: Define Bloch-state geometry with explicit normalization, distinguish metric from topology, and keep geometric response models separate from measured total stiffness.

materialCases.temperatureNote: Approximately40mK effective device temperature, distinct from20mKbase andnear1Khalf-resistance scale; no Tc assigned here.

entries.text:
Scope

The quantum metric measures how a normalized quantum state changes with parameters after removing its unobservable overall phase. For Bloch bands, those parameters can be crystal momentum. It describes wavefunctions rather than only energy dispersion. A flat band can therefore have nonzero metric, while a large metric alone neither supplies an attractive interaction nor establishes superconductivity. Provost and Vallée developed a general state-manifold construction; later multiband superconductivity work connected band geometry to current response under specified assumptions.   

This page uses a single isolated band or a specified smooth band subspace. It does not identify a single-particle Bloch metric with every many-body fidelity susceptibility. Keep the Hilbert space, parameter coordinates, orbital basis and selected subspace explicit. A geometric quantity can vary continuously without becoming a quantized topological invariant.  

 Mathematical assumptions

For a normalized state |u\rangle, let P=|u\rangle\langle u| and Q{ij}=\langle\partiali u|(1-P)|\partialj u\rangle. We define g{ij}=\mathrm{Re}\,Q{ij} and \Omega{ij}=-2\mathrm{Im}\,Q{ij}, consistent with Ai=i\langle u|\partiali u\rangle. Thus Q{ij}=g{ij}-i\Omega{ij}/2. The nearby-state fidelity obeys 1-|\langle u(\mathbf k)|u(\mathbf k+d\mathbf k)\rangle|^2=g{ij}dki dkj+O(|d\mathbf k|^3). With physical wavevectors, the metric components have units of length squared; dimensionless lattice coordinates change those units.  

For a rank-one projector, Q{ij}=\mathrm{Tr}[P(\partialiP)(\partialjP)] and g{ij}=\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}[(\partialiP)(\partialjP)]. The projector is unchanged by |u\rangle\rightarrow e^{i\phi(\mathbf k)}|u\rangle, so this construction removes phase-gauge artifacts. For an isolated group of touching bands, use the smooth subspace projector and state the trace convention. A chosen individual eigenvector can become singular or ambiguous at a degeneracy. Phase-gauge invariance within a fixed orbital representation is not permission to ignore a momentum-dependent change of the underlying basis.  

Positivity of the two-coordinate matrix Q gives \det g\geq\Omega{xy}^2/4 and g{xx}+g{yy}\geq|\Omega{xy}|. The trace statement refers to the selected common coordinate convention. For the spinor u=(\cos(\theta/2),e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)), our convention gives g{\theta\theta}=1/4, g{\varphi\varphi}=\sin^2\theta/4 and \Omega{\theta\varphi}=-\sin\theta/2. This two-level example saturates the determinant inequality; a three-level family can satisfy it strictly. These are model checks, not measurements of a material. 

Normalization must be translated before comparing formulas. Liang's checked manuscript defines \mathcal R{ij}=2\mathrm{Tr}[P(\partialiP)(\partialjP)] and calls its real part the metric. Consequently g^{\rm Liang}=2g in this page's convention, and that paper writes the fidelity distance with an extra factor of one half. Its curvature sign must likewise be translated consistently. This is a convention difference, not a contradiction or a factor-of-two enhancement of a physical stiffness. 

As a counterexample to equating metric with topology, take u=(\cos(kx/2),\sin(kx/2)), independent of ky. The projector is periodic on a 2\pi torus, g{xx}=1/4, and the Berry curvature vanishes. The Hamiltonian H=E0(2P-I) has flat eigenvalues \pm E0 for positive constant E0. It has nonzero metric and zero Chern number without introducing pairing. Our finite-difference checks compare projector derivatives, phase-transformed states and symmetric fidelity curvature; they do not calculate a superconducting response. 

 Experimental criteria

An experimental response may constrain band geometry through a model and matrix elements; it need not uniquely reconstruct every metric component. For superconductivity, distinguish the measured total stiffness from a decomposition into conventional and geometric terms. Report carrier filling, band window, temperature, units and the response-to-metric conversion. A successful fit does not by itself identify a unique microscopic pairing mechanism.  

Tanaka and colleagues' 2025 MATBG study combines microwave kinetic inductance and transport. The checked author version includes a parallel edge-proximity circuit and an assumed active-region aspect ratio. It distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK wired-device temperature, and a half-normal-resistance transition near 1 K across much of the gate range. These are different quantities. Its comparison supports a connection to quantum geometry without directly isolating a model-independent geometric fraction. This page stores the 40 mK value only as a measurement condition. 

 Limits and disputes

Peotta–Törmä's flat-band result assumes an interaction window between the bandwidth and separating band gaps, together with an appropriate uniform-pairing construction. Liang extends the response analysis, but the isolated-band expression retains time-reversal, orbital-uniform pairing and band-separation assumptions. Huhtinen and colleagues subsequently identify missing order-parameter-response terms in earlier formulas and connect isolated-flat-band stiffness to a minimal quantum metric. Therefore an arbitrary raw metric integral should not be presented as an automatically complete quantitative stiffness prediction.   

The review covers selected Peotta published passages, Liang author-version equations and Tanaka author methods; it does not complete their raw-data, full supplementary or final-version audits. Provost's original is checked at publisher-abstract scope. Huhtinen's published introduction and selected response derivation, pages 1–4, were checked; its full minimal-metric proof and band-touching analysis were not reproduced. The inherited F1 bibliography misattributes the MATBG paper to Randeria; the published authors are Tanaka and colleagues. Complete scientific acceptance remains open.     

 Discovery implications

Calculate geometry with a reproducible orbital convention and subspace, check mesh convergence and preserve normalization factors. Test pairing and total phase stiffness separately. A topological lower bound can be useful under its assumptions, but zero Chern number does not exclude useful geometry, and nonzero metric does not guarantee superconductivity. Geometry is one constraint in a material-specific calculation, alongside interactions, filling, disorder and phase coherence.   

 Related topics

Compare , ,  and .

entries.title: Wilson loops: gauge covariance, phase conventions and topological tests
entries.summary: Read closed-loop eigenphases with consistent signs, isolated subspaces and converged meshes; distinguish Chern flow, time-reversal topology and physical polarization.
entries.text:
Scope

A Wilson loop describes transport around a closed path within a specified band subspace. Its eigenvalues survive unitary changes of basis inside that subspace; individual matrix entries do not. Use a fixed-rank, isolated projector and a consistent boundary identification. An insulator's occupied bands and a fully gapped Bogoliubov Hamiltonian's negative-energy bands are different physical constructions. A computed phase spectrum alone does not demonstrate superconductivity, a measured bulk gap or Majorana modes.  

The loop can organize Chern winding, time-reversal topology and hybrid Wannier centers. Those interpretations require additional assumptions. A closed-loop phase is not generally quantized, and an attractive crossing pattern is not sufficient evidence for a topological invariant. Zak's original abstract emphasizes symmetry-dependent quantization; the complete original derivation has not been reviewed here.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Let the columns of Uj form an orthonormal frame. Define \mathcal A=iU^\dagger dU and forward overlaps Mj=Uj^\dagger U{j+1}. In a periodic model basis, close the final link with UN=U0 and order W=M0M1\cdots M{N-1} from left to right along the path. Since Mj=I-i\mathcal Aj\Delta k+O(\Delta k^2), the corresponding ordered exponential has -i\mathcal A, not +i\mathcal A. For one band, \arg W=-\gamma modulo 2\pi, where \gamma=\oint\mathcal A. The inverse-loop convention is also valid if every phase and orientation is translated consistently. 

Under Uj\mapsto UjGj, with unitary Gj, each link becomes Gj^\dagger MjG{j+1} and the closed product becomes G0^\dagger WG0. Interior factors cancel. This algebra explains both spectral gauge invariance and the need for closure. Actual Bloch bases can require a reciprocal-lattice sewing operator and orbital-position information instead of a naive endpoint identification. A different orbital embedding is not automatically a harmless gauge rotation within the same physical projector.  

Finite-step overlaps are generally not unitary. For Mj=Vj\Sigmaj Zj^\dagger, use its polar unitary factor Qj=VjZj^\dagger when the overlap is nonsingular. This construction preserves gauge covariance and yields a unitary discrete product. Record the smallest singular values, subspace dimension, direct gap and mesh convergence. Polar projection cannot repair a singular overlap, an incorrectly selected subspace or an unresolved band touching.  

An independent rank-two example combines spinors (\cos(\vartheta/2),e^{iwt}\sin(\vartheta/2)) in separate two-dimensional blocks. Their analytic forward phases are 2\pi w\sin^2(\vartheta/2) modulo 2\pi. Meshes of 32, 64 and 128 points approach these phases while raw-product eigenvalue magnitudes remain below one. Random U(2) frame rotations, shifted basepoints and reversed paths pass the covariance and conjugation checks. Omitting the closing link deliberately breaks spectral gauge invariance. These are synthetic checks, not a material calculation.  

For an increasing-kx loop and positive (kx,ky) orientation, the continuously unwrapped phase \Theta(ky)=\arg\det W(ky) winds by 2\pi C as ky traverses its period in this convention. Four lower-band examples of h=(\sin kx,\sin ky,m+\cos kx+\cos ky)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma give C=0,+1,-1,0 at m=-3,-1,+1,+3. Three meshes agree with separate analytic-curvature quadratures, and reversing the loop reverses the sign. The critical masses -2,0,2 have explicit gap zeros and are rejected. Integer output alone is not a convergence certificate. 

 Experimental criteria

In a two-dimensional band insulator with time reversal satisfying \mathcal T^2=-1, the parity of Kramers-partner exchange over half the transverse Brillouin zone diagnoses the \mathbb Z2 class. Preserve the complete occupied projector, the bulk gap and symmetry constraints. Sorting principal phases independently at every point can invent discontinuities at a branch cut; follow spectral connectivity or a validated gap-tracking procedure. The local checks above do not implement or certify a general \mathbb Z2 classifier.  

For a single band with the stated Bloch convention, a hybrid center satisfies \bar x/a=\gamma/(2\pi)=-\arg W/(2\pi) modulo one. In multiple bands, Wilson eigenphases correspond to centers in the appropriate parallel-transport or maximally localized hybrid construction, not arbitrary individual Wannier functions. Physical electronic polarization also needs electron charge, occupations, cell volume and a consistent origin; total polarization includes ionic contributions. Insulating adiabatic changes can be meaningful while an absolute branch remains ambiguous by a polarization quantum. A BdG phase spectrum cannot simply be substituted into the ordinary electron-polarization formula.   

An experimental comparison needs an explicit map from the measured observable to the modeled projector, including sample state, orbital basis, energy window and relevant symmetry. Band inversion, a calculated loop or an isolated boundary feature does not by itself verify the full pairing state. No experimental transition temperature or material certification is assigned to the synthetic examples on this page.  

 Limits and disputes

An isolated band manifold can have a well-defined Wilson loop even when a material is metallic. Its invariant is then not automatically the invariant of all physically occupied states: a Fermi surface makes that projector change rank. Likewise, band disentanglement selects a model subspace whose validity needs separate evidence. For BdG systems, respect particle-hole and time-reversal constraints and avoid interpreting Nambu duplication as independent electron occupations. Strong interactions, disorder and nodal systems can require different formulations.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected author and published passages, two original polarization pages and independent numerical examples have been checked. The full Yu equivalence proof, full Zak derivation, final-version comparisons, realistic orbital sewing, material fits and a general time-reversal classifier have not been reproduced. The numerical checks certify only the stated bounded constructions.    

 Discovery implications

Archive the Hamiltonian or projector, basis and embedding, symmetry operators, loop orientation, sewing rule and phase convention with every topology claim. Keep raw singular values and mesh history alongside the plotted spectrum. Compare a simple limit with an independent curvature or symmetry calculation before interpreting a complicated model. This makes a Wilson-loop result a reproducible hypothesis about a specified system rather than an unsupported label attached to a candidate superconductor.    

 Related topics

, , , and .

entries.title: Berry curvature: phases, Hall response and topology
entries.summary: Track geometric phase and Hall conventions while separating local curvature, occupied-band topology and evidence for superconducting chirality.

materialCases.sample: Mielke aligned crystal mosaic, charge-order-associated muon response
materialCases.temperatureNote: Approximate charge-order scale, not superconducting Tc; zero-field-only ambiguity and field controls retained.
materialCases.probe: Muon spin relaxation with longitudinal- and higher-field controls

entries.text:
Scope

Berry curvature describes local geometric twisting of a quantum-state family in parameter space. In a crystal, momentum-space curvature can contribute to electronic transport, but curvature, anomalous Hall conductivity and superconducting chirality are different objects. Specify whether the states belong to a normal-state Hamiltonian, a Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonian or a selected degenerate subspace before drawing a topological conclusion. Berry's original construction separates geometric and dynamical phases during adiabatic evolution.  

The inherited chapter includes the Xiao–Chang–Niu and Nagaosa reviews as broader reading. Here the defining phase equations are checked against Berry's original paper, semiclassical motion against Sundaram–Niu, and the metallic Hall interpretation against Haldane. Review citations are not substitutes for a completed audit of every underlying experiment.     

 Mathematical assumptions

For an isolated normalized Bloch state, use Ai=i\langle u|\partiali u\rangle and \Omega{ij}=\partialiAj-\partialjAi=-2\mathrm{Im}\,Q{ij}. Under u\rightarrow e^{i\phi}u, the connection changes as Ai\rightarrow Ai-\partiali\phi, while curvature is unchanged. The closed-loop phase \gamma=\oint Ai dki is defined modulo 2\pi. In a smooth patch, Stokes' theorem relates it to the curvature flux. Nontrivial bundles can require multiple patches and transition functions; a globally smooth eigenvector should not be assumed.  

For a nondegenerate eigenstate of H, differentiating the eigenvalue equation gives \langle m|\partiali n\rangle=\langle m|\partialiH|n\rangle/(En-Em) for m\ne n. Consequently \Omega{n,ij}=-2\mathrm{Im}\sum{m\ne n}\langle n|\partialiH|m\rangle\langle m|\partialjH|n\rangle/(En-Em)^2. Small denominators require resolving the neighboring bands and the validity of the isolated-band approximation. Exactly degenerate states require a subspace treatment, not arbitrary assignments to individual eigenvectors. Wilczek–Zee supplies the historical non-Abelian extension; its full derivation is not audited here.  

With electron charge -e, e>0, and zero magnetic field, the weak-field semiclassical equations are \hbar\dot{\mathbf k}=-e\mathbf E and \dot{\mathbf r}=\hbar^{-1}\nabla{\mathbf k}\epsilon-\dot{\mathbf k}\times\boldsymbol\Omega. For the clean intrinsic response, \sigma{xy}^{\rm int}=-(e^2/\hbar)\sumn\int d^dk\,fn\Omega{n,xy}/(2\pi)^d, with jx=\sigma{xy}Ey. The two-dimensional quantity is a sheet conductance; in three dimensions it has conductivity units. Haldane's checked manuscript uses the opposite connection sign, so its curvature and displayed Hall sign must be translated together.  

For a gapped two-dimensional occupied subspace, C=(2\pi)^{-1}\int{\rm BZ}\mathrm{Tr}\,\Omega{xy}\,d^2k is an integer under the stated orientation. The corresponding clean filled-band result in this convention is \sigma{xy}=-Ce^2/h. A metal can still contain an isolated band with an integer band Chern number; its partially occupied curvature integral is generally not that integer. Haldane expresses the nonquantized metallic contribution through Fermi-surface Berry phases, retaining a quantized ambiguity and Brillouin-zone boundary terms. It is not a license to discard all filled-band contributions. 

As a bounded check, the spinor u=(\cos(\theta/2),e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2)) taken around increasing \varphi at fixed \theta gives \gamma=-\pi(1-\cos\theta) modulo 2\pi. We compare cyclic overlap products with an independently integrated curvature flux, reverse the loop orientation and apply phase changes at every point. The energy-denominator formula and Hall-current sign are checked separately. These calculations validate conventions in a model, not a material's measured topology.  

 Experimental criteria

An anomalous Hall measurement is not a unique image of a curvature hotspot. Onoda and colleagues' original impurity-transport study distinguishes skew-scattering and intrinsic regimes within its dilute-impurity approximation; that is not a universal material-independent scaling law. Separate magnetic state, occupation, disorder and the conductivity-to-resistivity conversion before fitting a mechanism. A finite normal-state Hall signal does not determine the topology of a superconducting gap.  

Mielke and colleagues studied KV₃Sb₅ using muon spin relaxation. The checked author manuscript finds enhanced relaxation around the approximately 80 K charge-order scale, while the selected zero-field relaxation stays approximately constant through the separate superconducting transition. It explicitly notes that zero-field results alone cannot establish the time-reversal-breaking interpretation because charge order can modify nuclear electric-field gradients. Longitudinal-field and higher-field controls form part of the argument. This is evidence about the charge-ordered material, not a direct reconstruction of Berry curvature or a demonstration of chiral superconductivity. The 80 K record is excluded from superconducting-temperature search. 

 Limits and disputes

Time reversal relates the curvature of symmetry-partner states with opposite sign at opposite momenta; inversion relates the corresponding curvature with the same sign. For spinful systems with both symmetries, treat the Kramers subspace appropriately. Cancellation of charge Hall response does not imply that all spin, valley or non-Abelian structure is trivial. Likewise, broken time reversal alone does not guarantee a nonzero measured Hall component: other symmetries or cancellations can forbid it.   

This review visually checks Berry's original pages 46–47 and Haldane author v5 page 1, and reads selected Haldane, Sundaram–Niu and Mielke passages. The Haldane author copy prints an apparent repeated-momentum typo in its time-reversal equation; the transformation stated here follows the consistent symmetry argument rather than that literal expression. Full journal comparisons, non-Abelian derivations, disorder calculations and raw-data review remain open. Complete scientific acceptance has not been reached.      

 Discovery implications

Use curvature maps together with band gaps, occupation and symmetry, and test response predictions against independent measurements. For superconducting topology, calculate the appropriate gapped BdG subspace and compare relevant boundary or thermal probes. Keep a charge-order signal, normal-state anomalous Hall effect and a new symmetry change below the superconducting transition as separate claims. A promising normal-state band structure is an input to this analysis, not its conclusion.  

 Related topics

Compare , ,  and .

entries.title: Chern number: gapped subspaces and superconducting topology
entries.summary: Define the selected quantum subspace, test numerical convergence, and distinguish normal-state Hall response from a superconducting BdG invariant.
entries.text:
Scope

A Chern number characterizes a smooth, isolated family of quantum subspaces over a closed two-dimensional parameter surface. In a periodic crystal that surface can be the Brillouin-zone torus. The normal-state occupied-electron subspace and the negative-energy Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) subspace are different constructions: calculate and label them separately. Local Berry curvature, an integer band invariant and an observed transport coefficient should not be used interchangeably.   

The TKNN work connects a gap in a two-dimensional electron problem to quantized Hall conductance. Haldane's later lattice model shows that Landau levels are not required for a nonzero quantized Hall response. These are foundational model results, not evidence that a normal-state Chern band necessarily becomes a topological superconductor. Here their original publisher abstracts establish this historical context; complete original-paper audits remain open.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Use the convention of the : \mathcal Ai=i\Psi^\dagger\partiali\Psi for an orthonormal frame of the selected subspace, \mathcal F{xy}=\partialx\mathcal Ay-\partialy\mathcal Ax-i[\mathcal Ax,\mathcal Ay], and C=(2\pi)^{-1}\int{\rm BZ}\mathrm{Tr}\,\mathcal F{xy}\,d^2k. The subspace must remain separated from its complement throughout the Brillouin zone. Degeneracies inside the selected multiplet do not invalidate its total invariant, but arbitrary individual-band assignments at those degeneracies can fail. 

A nonzero invariant obstructs a single globally smooth periodic frame. One uses compatible local frames or a gauge-invariant discrete construction. For a continuous deformation that preserves the subspace gap and the closed integration surface, the integer cannot change. This is a statement about the quantum-state bundle, not an identification of momentum-space Berry curvature with the Gaussian curvature of a physical surface. 

For the clean, zero-temperature filled-electron-band response, with electron charge -e, e>0, positive (kx,ky) orientation and jx=\sigma{xy}Ey, the convention used here gives \sigma{xy}=-Ce^2/h. This sign follows the anomalous velocity and charge current used in F2; reversing orientation or the curvature definition changes the displayed relation. A partially occupied metallic band need not give an integer Hall response even when its complete band has an integer Chern number. Do not apply this electron charge-transport formula to a BdG integer without deriving the appropriate physical response.    

For a bounded numerical example, take H=\sin kx\,\sigmax+\sin ky\,\sigmay+(m+\cos kx+\cos ky)\sigmaz, with dimensionless momenta and a fixed energy unit. The lower-band curvature is \Omega{xy}=\mathbf d\cdot(\partialx\mathbf d\times\partialy\mathbf d)/(2|\mathbf d|^3) in our convention. Analytic gap zeros occur only at m=-2,0,2. The lower-band values at m=-3,-1,1,3 are respectively 0,1,-1,0. These are illustrative Hamiltonian results, not measured material properties.  

We compare normalized-overlap lattice sums on 12^2, 24^2 and 48^2 meshes against an independently integrated analytic curvature on 64^2 and 128^2 meshes. Pointwise phase changes leave the result unchanged; reversing one momentum direction reverses its sign. We also reject the analytically identified gap-closing points. A positive gap sampled on a finite grid alone would not exclude an unsampled closing in a general Hamiltonian. 

 Experimental criteria

For a normal-state Hall interpretation, identify the carrier subspace, occupation, bulk gap and response convention. Hatsugai's original work relates the bulk TKNN integer to edge-state winding for a square-lattice quantum Hall model. The measured presence of an edge signal is not by itself a complete reconstruction of that model's invariant; boundary conditions, additional states and the probe must be addressed. The full edge-state proof is not reproduced here.  

For superconductivity, specify the Nambu basis, negative-energy projector and a bulk quasiparticle gap. Read and Green distinguish weak and strong pairing in a spinless continuum chiral p-wave model: positive and negative chemical potential give distinct phases, separated at zero chemical potential under their assumptions. Their weak-pairing phase is connected to weak coupling, but the two phrases are not synonymous. Their selected edge calculation uses a prescribed gap function and a domain wall between the phases to obtain a chiral Majorana branch; it does not solve a material-specific self-consistent edge. 

A time-reversal-breaking signal does not establish a full quasiparticle gap or a nonzero BdG Chern number. A zero-bias feature likewise does not supply the negative-energy projector or identify a chiral boundary mode. Charge Hall response is especially delicate: Read and Green explicitly discuss collective response and the order of limits, rather than equating it to the paired-state topological integer. No sample-specific transition-temperature records are assigned to this theoretical article. 

 Limits and disputes

In the Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki method, normalized overlaps define links and a principal-branch logarithm defines plaquette flux. Overlaps must not vanish. The finite-grid integer is gauge invariant, but agreement with the continuum requires adequate resolution and an isolated subspace. The multiplet version uses the determinant of the overlap matrix. In our +i connection convention, the curvature flux is minus the oriented overlap-product phase; translate the original paper's imaginary-connection convention explicitly. 

Selected author pages and a visual check of the discrete equations support this account. Full final-version comparisons, the TKNN and Hatsugai derivations, interacting/disordered invariants, edge-spectrum computations and material data remain outside the completed checks. Complete scientific acceptance has not been reached. A lattice-model regression is neither an experimental replication nor proof that every proposed topological superconductor is correctly classified.    

 Discovery implications

A useful report names the Hamiltonian, selected projector, orientation, gap criterion, mesh sequence and independent checks before giving an integer. For superconducting candidates, repeat the analysis for the actual pairing structure and compare appropriate boundary or response predictions with measurements. Preserve the distinction between a promising normal band, a model BdG phase and an established property of a specimen.
