entries.title: Time-reversal-invariant topological superconductivity: class DIII
entries.summary: Distinguish binary and integer invariants, test antiunitary symmetries, and state the limits of odd-parity and boundary-state arguments.
entries.text:
Scope

Class DIII describes a gapped Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian with time-reversal and particle–hole symmetries whose single-particle antiunitary operators square to -1 and +1, respectively. It is a symmetry class, not a pairing mechanism or a certificate that a particular material is topological. Dimension, the bulk gap and the allowed perturbations must be specified before assigning an invariant. 

For the stable, noninteracting strong classification, DIII has \mathbb Z2 sectors in one and two spatial dimensions and an integer \mathbb Z classification in three. By comparison, class D has \mathbb Z2, \mathbb Z and a trivial strong classification in dimensions one, two and three. Extra crystalline or translation symmetries can introduce further distinctions; the simple table does not enumerate those. In particular, “2D DIII is trivial” and “3D DIII has only a binary invariant” are incorrect statements of this free-fermion classification. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Write T=UTK and C=UCK, where K is complex conjugation. The requirements are UTH(\mathbf k)^UT^\dagger=H(-\mathbf k), UCH(\mathbf k)^UC^\dagger=-H(-\mathbf k), UTUT^=-I and UCUC^=I. A suitably phased product of the two antiunitary operations gives a unitary chiral symmetry that anticommutes with H. Merely checking the ordinary matrix squares UT^2 and UC^2 would miss the conjugation in the antiunitary operation. 

An explicit illustrative lattice model in the basis (c\uparrow,c\downarrow,c\uparrow^\dagger,c\downarrow^\dagger) is H=\xi\tauz\otimes I+\sin kx\,\taux\otimes\sigmaz+\sin ky\,\tauy\otimes I, with \xi=m+\cos kx+\cos ky. Here UT=I\otimes i\sigmay, UC=\taux\otimes I, and a Hermitian chiral operator is \taux\otimes\sigmay. Its squared spectrum is E^2=\xi^2+\sin^2kx+\sin^2ky. Sixteen selected parameter/momentum points pass Hermiticity, both antiunitary relations, chiral anticommutation and this spectral identity. These checks establish the stated model relations, not a general classification proof or a material realization.  

The boundary distinction can be seen in a Majorana edge basis. For one helical pair, take h(k)=vk\sigmaz, T=i\sigmayK and C=K. A constant mass me\sigmay anticommutes with the velocity and preserves particle–hole symmetry but is time-reversal odd. For two copies, h=vk\sigmaz\otimes I admits the time-reversal-even mass me\sigmax\otimes\rhoy, where \rho acts on the copies; its spectrum obeys E^2=v^2k^2+me^2. This bounded calculation illustrates an even–odd distinction. It does not cover arbitrary interactions or a self-consistent microscopic edge. 

In three dimensions the free-fermion invariant is an integer winding number. The odd-parity criterion of Fu and Berg instead determines its parity, \nu=n\bmod2. Their sufficient criterion assumes a fully gapped, time-reversal-invariant, centrosymmetric odd-parity superconductor. The simple Fermi-surface reduction is made in a weak-pairing setting with normal bands at time-reversal-invariant momenta separated from the Fermi energy. An odd enclosed count establishes odd parity under those assumptions; an even count does not establish that the integer is zero.  

 Experimental criteria

The Balian–Werthamer description of superfluid helium-3 B is a three-dimensional DIII prototype with unit winding in the convention of the checked classification paper. It is an atomic superfluid, not a solid superconducting device. A surface-state model and a particular experimental signal are different levels of evidence; this article does not independently review helium-3 surface spectroscopy or assign a pressure-independent transition temperature.  

Fu and Berg's application to copper-intercalated Bi₂Se₃ is a two-orbital pairing model and a proposed route to test odd parity. It does not by itself settle a specimen's pairing symmetry, gap or topology. For any solid candidate, establish time-reversal behavior and the bulk quasiparticle gap, evaluate a justified invariant or sufficient criterion, and compare the predicted boundary response with measurements that address competing explanations. A zero-bias feature alone does not complete this sequence. 

Qi and colleagues' paired Majorana defect construction concerns a time-reversal-invariant defect: in their equal-spin example, a vortex in one component coincides with an antivortex in the other. Do not transfer that conclusion automatically to an ordinary magnetic vortex, which breaks time reversal. The paper's boundary construction and protected Kramers structure also should not be read as experimental evidence of braiding or of a completed topological qubit. 

 Limits and disputes

The free-fermion table and an interacting many-body classification are distinct. Fidkowski, Chen and Vishwanath discuss symmetric gapped surfaces with topological order. The later Metlitski and colleagues preprint explicitly analyzes the interaction reduction to \mathbb Z{16}, focusing on even-index surfaces. That is not a replacement of the three-dimensional free-fermion integer by a universal \mathbb Z2 label. In the many-body discussion time reversal squares to fermion parity; the single-particle T^2=-1 statement must be interpreted at the appropriate level.  

We visually checked the DIII classification row, read selected original author passages on helical boundaries and odd-parity conditions, and performed explicit small-matrix checks. Full journal-version comparisons, the interacting surface construction and material-specific evidence audits remain open. Complete scientific acceptance has not been reached. The 2014 interaction source is labelled as a preprint; its presence in the bibliography is not a claim that its full proof has been reproduced.    

 Discovery implications

Use DIII as a conditional classification after identifying the physical symmetries and a gapped BdG description. State whether a result is a full integer, its parity or a boundary-model prediction. Report what changes when time reversal is broken, when the gap closes, or when additional symmetries or strong interactions are included. This keeps a useful theoretical criterion separate from an experimentally established material property.   

 Related topics

Compare , ,  and .

entries.title: Majorana zero modes: models, parity readout and evidence
entries.summary: Distinguish Majorana algebra, finite-chain modes, experimental parity readout and topological protection, with explicit source and retraction boundaries.
entries.text:
Scope

A Majorana operator is self-adjoint. A Majorana zero mode additionally represents a zero-energy degree of freedom of a specified Hamiltonian, localized at an end, boundary or defect in an appropriate setting. Decomposing an ordinary fermion into two self-adjoint operators is always possible; that algebra alone establishes neither spatial separation nor topological protection. Here the ideal chain, experimental readout and claims about fault-tolerant computation are treated separately. 

Chiral two-dimensional pairing and one-dimensional superconducting chains provide distinct theoretical settings. Read and Green connect the weak-pairing spinless chiral state to non-Abelian quasiholes; its weak-pairing terminology is not a synonym for weak interaction strength. A proposed Hamiltonian or boundary solution does not establish the pairing state or topology of a measured solid. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Fix the normalization \{\gammai,\gammaj\}=2\delta{ij} and \gammai^\dagger=\gammai. Then c=(\gamma1+i\gamma2)/2, n=c^\dagger c=(1+i\gamma1\gamma2)/2 and the occupation parity is P=(-1)^n=1-2n=-i\gamma1\gamma2. Papers may normalize the operators or label parity signs differently. Mixing a factor 1/\sqrt2 from another convention into these equations would spoil the fermionic anticommutator.  

For a uniform spinless chain, use hopping t, chemical potential \mu, real pairing \Delta, lattice spacing one and open ends. The bulk excitation spectrum satisfies E(k)^2=(2t\cos k+\mu)^2+4\Delta^2\sin^2k. The gapped topological domain is |\mu|<2|t| with \Delta\ne0; |\mu|=2|t| closes the gap. At \mu=0 and t=\Delta>0, the ideal finite chain has exactly unpaired endpoint operators. More general finite chains can have overlap splitting: exponential localization does not imply exactly zero energy at every length. 

Our bounded calculation checks the Majorana algebra, compares eight small-chain many-body spectra with independently constructed BdG spectra, verifies exact endpoint commutators at the special point, and follows decreasing overlap splitting for one sequence of increasing chain lengths. These are model checks. They do not fit a device, establish a universal prefactor or exclude oscillatory splitting at other parameters. 

The minimal two-site model makes a useful distinction explicit. With \delta=(\muL+\muR)/2 and \epsilon=(\muL-\muR)/2, its even and odd energies are Ee^\pm=-\delta\pm\sqrt{\delta^2+\Delta^2} and Eo^\pm=-\delta\pm\sqrt{\epsilon^2+t^2}. At t=\Delta and zero onsite energies the ground states coincide. Detuning one site leaves this ideal degeneracy intact, whereas common detuning gives a quadratic splitting and changing t-\Delta gives a linear one. Direct four-state diagonalization checks these relations; they explain why a two-site sweet spot is not equivalent to generic long-chain protection. 

 Experimental criteria

In the ideal grounded-superconductor tunneling setup analyzed by Law, Lee and Ng, a Majorana resonance can produce conductance 2e^2/h. Interpreting a measured peak requires the actual coupling, resolution, temperature and competing states. Pan and Das Sarma model trivial low-energy peaks from mechanisms including confinement and disorder, and discuss limitations of end-to-end correlations in short wires. Their theoretical alternatives are reasons to test a signal, not a diagnosis of every later experiment.  

Aghaee and colleagues, published on 19 February 2025, report interferometric single-shot fermion-parity readout. Their selected results include millisecond-scale parity dwell times and approximately 1% assignment error at an optimized measurement time. The paper explicitly states that the measurements do not uniquely distinguish topological Majorana modes from suitably tuned low-energy Andreev states. It also constrains the alternatives through support at both wire ends and weak coupling to other low-energy states. Preserve both the achieved readout and that unresolved interpretation. 

Van Loo and colleagues, published online on 11 February 2026, read out the parity of a minimal InSb–Al quantum-dot chain through quantum capacitance. The selected author text reports lifetimes exceeding a millisecond and contrasts the readout with a local charge sensor unable to distinguish parity at the sweet spot. The authors explicitly describe limited protection in this two-site device. The accepted-author version was uploaded on 6 October 2026; that upload is not the experiment's publication date. 

Spectroscopy, parity lifetime, readout fidelity, robustness, fusion and exchange probe different properties. Report the measured observable and the alternatives addressed by that particular protocol. A parity readout result alone does not demonstrate a non-Abelian exchange operation or a fault-tolerant processor. There is no platform-independent checklist in which every local zero-bias feature automatically advances toward a universal confirmation threshold.   

 Limits and disputes

The 2018 article “Quantized Majorana conductance” was retracted on 8 March 2021. The authors' notice describes undisclosed charge-jump corrections, a mislabeled axis and recalibration shifting plateau values above the claimed quantized conductance. The withdrawn positive claim is retained only as a historical record with its retraction notice. It cannot validate a device, and its retraction does not itself settle every other Majorana proposal.  

This review checks selected original chain and readout passages, two-site energy equations, the author-institution retraction text and bounded calculations. The transport alternatives remain at original-abstract scope here; full device datasets, supplementary analyses, final-version comparisons and platform-by-platform fusion or braiding audits remain open. Complete scientific acceptance has not been reached. Neither commercial terminology nor a manuscript upload date closes those gaps.     

 Discovery implications

Keep the operator convention, physical geometry, bulk-gap assumptions and measurement protocol attached to each claim. Search for a reproducible combination of localization, controlled perturbations and protocol-specific evidence, while reporting failed or ambiguous tests. Separate a useful quantum-device component from a verified topological phase and from a demonstrated computational operation. This article does not make a worldwide priority claim or certify a material family from a single resonance.    

 Related topics

Continue with , , ,  and .

entries.title: Flat-band superconductivity: pairing and phase coherence
entries.summary: Compare pairing scales with phase stiffness, test finite-bandwidth limits, and retain the internal-field relaxation needed for a reliable geometric response.

materialCases.temperatureNote: Approximately40mK effective device temperature, distinct from20mKbase andnear1Khalf-resistance scale; no Tc assigned here.

entries.text:
Scope

Flat-band superconductivity involves two distinct questions: whether electrons develop a pairing amplitude, and whether the resulting state resists a spatial phase twist. A narrow dispersion can favor pairing while suppressing the usual velocity contribution to current. Neither a large density of states nor a large mean-field gap establishes a high measured transition temperature.  

This article focuses on the scale hierarchy and response calculation. The isolated-band reduction of Peotta and Törmä assumes a bandwidth small compared with the attraction, itself small compared with the separation to other bands, together with an appropriate uniform pairing field. Those are conditions for that reduction, not necessary conditions for every superconducting flat-band system. Huhtinen and colleagues also analyze situations where a touching dispersive band can help within their mean-field treatment.  

 Mathematical assumptions

As an independent pairing illustration, take one state per spin per cell, half filling, a rectangular density of states \rho(\xi)=1/W over -W/2\lt\xi\lt W/2, and an effective attraction G>0. Absorb the Hartree shift into the chemical potential. The zero-temperature reduced mean-field gap is \Delta0=W/[2\sinh(W/G)]. Its linearized pairing onset obeys 1=(G/W)\int0^{W/2}\tanh[\xi/(2kBT{\rm pair})]\,d\xi/\xi. State counting and the projected interaction are fixed here; G is not automatically a multiorbital lattice's bare onsite attraction.  

In this illustration, W/G\to0 gives \Delta0\to G/2 and kBT{\rm pair}\to G/4. Seven bandwidth ratios were checked using an independent zero-temperature quadrature and numerical roots of the onset equation. The gap-to-pairing-scale ratio approaches two in the flat limit and approximately 1.764 in the broad-band weak-coupling regime. This density-of-states model specifies no Bloch eigenvectors, current operator or phase stiffness. Its pairing onset must not be relabelled an experimental Tc.  

For the multiband response, a conventional/geometric split is useful only with its precise definitions. An isolated flat band can have zero conventional contribution while its wavefunctions support a geometric contribution. The corrected response includes how the orbital pairing fields change under the applied twist. In the time-reversal-symmetric isolated-flat-band setting with uniform pairing, Huhtinen and colleagues connect the response to the minimal integrated quantum metric, rather than an arbitrary orbital representation's unrelaxed metric expression.   

A separate scalar example shows why relaxation matters. Let a free-energy density be f(Q,\eta)=D0Q^2/2+bQ\eta+a\eta^2/2, with a>0, an imposed phase gradient Q and a relaxable internal coordinate \eta. Minimization gives \eta=-bQ/a and D{\rm relaxed}=D0-b^2/a. A stable example with D0=a=b=1 has positive frozen curvature but zero relaxed curvature. Four parameter sets and twelve coordinate changes \eta'=\eta+cQ reproduce the same relaxed response while the frozen curvature can change. This illustrates a chain-rule correction, not a full superconducting lattice calculation. 

Quantum-metric normalization also matters. In this Wiki, g{ij}=\operatorname{Re}\langle\partiali u|(1-|u\rangle\langle u|)|\partialj u\rangle. Liang and colleagues use a metric with twice this normalization in the checked author equations. Copying a response prefactor without translating conventions can introduce a factor-of-two error. A nonzero Chern number provides particular geometric bounds under additional assumptions; the Chern-trivial Lieb-lattice example shows why it is not necessary for all geometric superfluid response.  

 Experimental criteria

Cao and colleagues established gate-tunable superconducting transport in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. The published paper documents four-probe measurements with non-superconducting Cr/Au contacts. It establishes a platform for narrow-band superconductivity, while leaving the relative roles of lattice vibrations, electronic correlations and quantum geometry to further tests. A twist angle or band label alone does not identify the pairing interaction. 

Tanaka and colleagues, published on 5 February 2025, infer sheet stiffness through microwave kinetic inductance alongside transport. The reviewed author manuscript distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base temperature from an approximately 40 mK wired-device temperature. Its roughly 1 K resistive scale uses half the normal-state resistance. Those three quantities have different meanings; the measurement temperatures are excluded from transition-temperature searches here. 

Their circuit analysis includes a parallel electrode-proximitized edge and assumes the active region has the device aspect ratio when converting inductance to sheet stiffness. The comparison with a conventional Fermi-liquid estimate supports a quantum-geometric interpretation within the analysis, but does not experimentally isolate a model-independent geometric fraction or demonstrate that geometry supplies the attraction. Keep total measured response, inferred parameters and theory comparisons separate. 

 Limits and disputes

The response correction identified in 2022 can alter more than a numerical prefactor: freezing the internal pairing response can yield a nonzero stiffness even when the relaxed result vanishes. Time reversal and equal pairing at zero twist do not by themselves remove that issue. Conversely, failure of an isolated-band approximation does not prove that a touching or nearby band suppresses superconductivity; it requires a calculation that retains the relevant bands. 

Selected original passages, two visual equation checks and reduced calculations have been reviewed. Complete scientific acceptance has not been reached. Full published-version comparisons for the author manuscripts, multiorbital self-consistent response, raw microwave data and a complete material survey remain open. A kagome lattice or a flat photoemission feature is not, by itself, a measurement of geometric superfluid weight.    

 Discovery implications

Compare bandwidth, interband separation, filling and interaction projection before choosing a flat-band approximation. Evaluate pairing and phase response independently, retaining the response of internal fields. For a real sample, compare spectroscopy, resistive criteria and inductive measurements with their temperature, geometry and fitting assumptions attached. Favor a reproducible combination of pairing and coherence over a ranking based solely on band flatness.    

 Related topics

Compare , , ,  and .

entries.title: Geometric superfluid weight
entries.summary: Relate interband response to quantum geometry while preserving units, internal-field relaxation and the limits of extracting a geometric fraction from experiment.

materialCases.temperatureNote: Approximately40mK effective device temperature, distinct from20mKbase andnear1Khalf-resistance scale; no Tc assigned here.

entries.text:
Scope

Superfluid weight is a current or phase-twist response defined with a particular thermodynamic and electromagnetic convention. In a multiband superconductor, its conventional part is associated with intraband dispersion, while geometric terms involve the wavefunctions and interband matrix elements. These are parts of a specified response calculation, not two experimentally separated streams of Cooper pairs.  

A response kernel also depends on how frequency and wavevector approach zero. Scalapino, White and Zhang discuss distinct limiting procedures for diagnosing insulating, metallic and superconducting lattice states. A clean metal's ideal transport response should not be identified with the equilibrium Meissner response merely because both are called a stiffness. This entry checks that paper's original abstract; its full correlation-function derivation remains open. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For an isotropic superconducting sheet, define the phase-energy density by f=\rhos|\nabla\theta-(2e/\hbar)\mathbf A|^2/2, with \rhos in joules. The sheet electromagnetic kernel is K\square=4e^2\rhos/\hbar^2=1/L\square, where L\square is sheet kinetic inductance. Peotta and Törmä instead define a mass-normalized weight through f=Ds ps^2/8, with ps=\hbar\nabla\theta in zero field. Thus their convention gives \rhos=\hbar^2Ds/4 and K\square=e^2Ds. These quantities have different units even when each is called superfluid weight.  

A pair phase written as \theta=2\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r introduces another factor: the curvature with respect to \mathbf q is four times the curvature with respect to \nabla\theta. For a hypothetical L\square=10 nH, the sheet convention above gives \rhos/kB\approx0.7845 K. Three illustrative inductances were checked with SI charge, Planck and Boltzmann constants. These are conversion examples, not measured superconducting transition temperatures.  

In a fixed orbital basis, differentiating H|m\rangle=\varepsilonm|m\rangle gives \langle n|\partialiH|m\rangle=\delta{nm}\partiali\varepsilonm+(\varepsilonm-\varepsilonn)\langle n|\partiali m\rangle. Flat eigenvalues set the diagonal velocity to zero without forcing the interband matrix elements to vanish. Fifteen checks in an illustrative two-band model reproduce this identity and g{kk}=1/4 for a rotating eigenvector; multiplying either eigenvector by a smooth phase leaves the metric unchanged. This checks a band identity, not superconductivity or a self-consistent current response.  

The familiar isolated-band expression D{s,ij}^{\rm geom}\propto\sum{\mathbf k}(|\Delta|^2/E{\mathbf k})\tanh[E{\mathbf k}/(2kBT)]g{ij}(\mathbf k) displays a geometric structure, not a convention-free numerical formula. It requires stated pairing, band-isolation and symmetry assumptions, a wavevector integration measure and charge factors. The metric used in the checked Liang manuscript is twice the Wiki convention g{ij}=\operatorname{Re}\langle\partiali u|(1-|u\rangle\langle u|)|\partialj u\rangle. Translate that normalization before comparing prefactors.  

The internal pairing fields must also respond to the twist. Under the time-reversal and equilibrium-minimum assumptions studied by Huhtinen and colleagues, the total free-energy curvature contains a negative-semidefinite relaxation correction to the frozen-field result. In their isolated flat-band uniform-pairing setting, the relevant integrated metric has minimal trace with respect to orbital positions. Equal pairing at zero twist does not justify freezing all relative phases at nonzero twist. A nonzero unrelaxed result can even become zero after relaxation. The scalar illustration in the flat-band article shows this possibility without claiming to reproduce the complete lattice response. 

 Experimental criteria

Measure and report the total response with its units, dimensionality, frequency, geometry and fitting model. Tanaka and colleagues obtain stiffness through microwave kinetic inductance with a parallel electrode-proximitized edge in the circuit model. Their conversion uses an assumed active-region aspect ratio equal to the device aspect ratio; their reported Ds=l/(wL{\rm total}) corresponds to inverse sheet inductance. A comparison with a conventional estimate can support a geometric interpretation without constituting a model-independent measurement of its fraction. 

The selected author manuscript distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK wired-device temperature. Its roughly 1 K resistive scale uses half the normal-state resistance. Neither the measurement temperature nor that resistive criterion should automatically be labelled a BKT transition. Full published-version and raw-data comparisons remain open. 

For an effective isotropic two-dimensional BKT description, the jump involves the renormalized total sheet phase stiffness: kBT{\rm BKT}=\pi\rhos(T{\rm BKT}^-)/2. It does not determine a separate geometric component. Substituting a zero-temperature stiffness gives only an upper estimate if the stiffness at the transition does not exceed that zero-temperature value. With the hypothetical 10 nH example this estimate is about 1.232 K; it is neither a measured transition nor evidence that the BKT assumptions hold in a particular device.  

 Limits and disputes

A nonzero Chern number can provide a geometric lower bound in specified models, but it is not necessary for every geometric contribution. The Chern-trivial Lieb-lattice example has a finite flat-band response under its interaction assumptions. A bound on an integrated metric is not automatically a numerical bound on a dimensionful measured stiffness: filling, interaction, normalization and the complete response matter.   

Selected original passages and equations, the band-current identity and unit conversions have been checked. Complete scientific acceptance has not been reached. Full current-correlation and BKT derivations, self-consistent multiband response, remote-band convergence and experimental data audits remain open. Disorder, finite frequency, sample inhomogeneity and phase fluctuations can affect the comparison between a theoretical weight and a measured response.     

 Discovery implications

Report conventional, geometric and total response using a common convention, including internal-field relaxation. Check a band model's current operator and geometry before applying a flat-band formula, and retain the uncertainty of the experimental baseline. Geometry can constrain transport by pairs; it does not automatically supply the attraction, determine gap symmetry or ensure macroscopic phase coherence.   

 Related topics

Continue with , , ,  and .

entries.title: BKT transition: phase coherence and experimental diagnostics
entries.summary: Connect vortex unbinding and renormalized stiffness with transport criteria, finite-size limits and explicit tests of misleading fits.

materialCases.temperatureNote: Approximate fit temperature from author Figure2; not the distinct BKT or zero-resistance criterion.
Measurement floor only; not the AL-fit, BKT or zero-resistance temperature.
Reference temperature for Rn; not Tc.

entries.text:
Scope

The Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless (BKT) framework describes vortex–antivortex unbinding in an appropriate two-dimensional phase system. The ideal short-range XY model has algebraically decaying correlations below the transition, rather than ordinary finite-temperature long-range order. Above it, free vortices destroy that quasi-long-range order. A resistance drop in a thin film does not by itself establish this mechanism.  

Charged superconducting films require a further qualification: magnetic screening changes the vortex interaction at sufficiently long distance. Kosterlitz and Thouless explicitly identified this limitation in their original paper. Effective BKT behavior can be relevant over experimentally accessible scales, but finite size, screening, interlayer coupling and spatial inhomogeneity must be assessed before transferring the infinite neutral-system result.   

 Mathematical assumptions

Define the sheet phase stiffness in energy units by F\theta=(\rhos/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2. The universal jump uses the long-distance renormalized total stiffness, \rhos^R(T{\rm BKT}^-)=2kBT{\rm BKT}/\pi. A bare pairing calculation or finite-frequency inductive response is not automatically this quantity. In the local sheet convention, \rhos=\hbar^2/(4e^2L\square); frequency, vortex dynamics and geometry enter its experimental interpretation. The jump does not separate conventional and geometric contributions.   

For dimensionless K=\rhos/(kBT) and dilute vortex fugacity y, one convention gives dK/d\ell=-4\pi^3K^2y^2 and dy/d\ell=(2-\pi K)y. The Benfatto manuscript instead uses K{\rm B}=\pi K and g=2\pi y; its stiffness is expressed in temperature units. Keeping these factors prevents a spurious disagreement between equations. Two illustrative flows from K0=0.5,0.8 and y0=0.01 were checked at three step sizes, stopping at \ell=4 while y\lt0.1. They illustrate proliferation versus suppression within a dilute approximation; they do not determine a material transition or justify continuation to strong fugacity.  

On the disordered side, an asymptotic resistance form is R=R0\exp[-b/\sqrt{t}], with t=T/T{\rm BKT}-1\gt0 and nonuniversal R0,b. This is the near-transition limit, not the full Halperin–Nelson interpolation into the Gaussian fluctuation regime. If those parameters are temperature independent over the fit window, [d\ln R/dT]^{-2/3}=(2T{\rm BKT}/b)^{2/3}(T/T{\rm BKT}-1). Its linear extrapolation is a consistency test under those assumptions. Derivatives amplify measurement noise, and a temperature-dependent background changes the result.  

 Experimental criteria

Compare the jump, nonlinear transport and resistance tail on the same sample and temperature scale, using independent observables where available. Report the measurement frequency, current interval, contact configuration, geometry and uncertainty. Agreement across probes strengthens a BKT interpretation; it is not a universal requirement that every experiment resolve all three ideal signatures. A broadened or unobserved jump needs a quantitative account of resolution, finite scales and inhomogeneity.   

In the commonly used homogeneous vortex-transport regime, V\propto I^{a(T)} with a=1+\pi\rhos^R/(kBT) gives a=3 at the ideal jump. This is a dynamical response relation with an applicable current window. Finite samples can recover an ohmic low-current response; heating and contact effects need separate checks. As a logical counterexample, dimensionless v=i+i^3 has a finite zero-current resistance but an apparent log–log slope of approximately 2.996 between i=10 and 100. No phase transition is encoded in that example. 

A second synthetic example tests the resistance diagnostic. For dimensionless temperature x, the positive function R/R0=\exp(-4/x) has no finite-temperature transition. Yet [d\ln R/dx]^{-2/3} is nearly linear on x=3.96–4.04: a local fit has R^2\gt0.999999 and extrapolates to approximately x=1. A visually impressive line over a narrow interval therefore does not identify a transition. This constructed example is not a diagnosis of any cited device. Fit-window stability and physically consistent parameters matter. 

Xi and colleagues illustrate why temperature criteria must remain distinct. Their NbSe₂ author manuscript takes normal resistance at 8 K; the Aslamazov–Larkin fit temperature is close to the half-resistance temperature, while a BKT temperature inferred from current excitation is close to the one-percent-resistance criterion. The approximate 3 K monolayer AL-fit value must not be relabelled as a measured BKT temperature. The final supplement and raw nonlinear traces have not been audited here. Ye's gate-tuned MoS₂ dome provides another material context, but its checked institutional abstract alone does not verify BKT behavior.  

 Limits and disputes

Pair formation, gap closing, resistive onset, phase coherence and an instrumental zero-resistance threshold can differ. A BKT interpretation addresses phase ordering and vortex physics; it does not identify the pairing interaction or gap symmetry. The accessible range of logarithmic vortex interactions and the crossover into amplitude fluctuations constrain how far a BKT fit can be extrapolated. Spatially varying stiffness and percolative transport deserve sample-specific comparison rather than automatic assignment to one mechanism.   

This review covers selected original KT/NK passages, selected Benfatto and Xi author passages, and bounded local calculations. The original Halperin–Nelson full derivation, full author-to-journal comparisons, supplements and raw experimental data remain open. The selected Nelson–Kosterlitz text was not visually checked. Mathematical counterexamples and passing software tests do not complete scientific acceptance.      

 Discovery implications

For thin-film screening, preserve the sample, density, thickness, field, current and frequency alongside each fitted or measured temperature. Compare stiffness with pairing indicators and test size or frequency dependence when possible. Improving a pairing scale need not improve phase coherence; conversely, a small stiffness does not by itself prove a BKT transition. Keep alternative interpretations and source-access limits visible in exported records.

entries.text:
Scope

A superconducting vortex is a defect of the real-space order parameter. For a single complex component that stays nonzero on a closed contour C, its phase winding is n=(2\pi)^{-1}\ointC\nabla\phi\cdot d\mathbf l\in\mathbb Z. The contour must avoid cores and other zeros. Reversing its orientation reverses the sign; enclosing several defects gives their net winding. This integer is distinct from the momentum-space Chern number of a band or Bogoliubov Hamiltonian. 

Winding, fluxoid and measured magnetic flux answer different questions. Fluxoid combines magnetic flux with supercurrent circulation. A detector measures a geometry-dependent magnetic response, which need not equal the fluxoid around a chosen contour. Junction phase shifts and multicomponent textures require additional constraints; a fractional magnetic signal alone does not specify a new bulk condensate charge, Chern number or Majorana mode.   

 Mathematical assumptions

Use the explicit positive-charge phase convention q=2e, with e\gt0, and the local London relation \mu0\lambdaL^2\mathbf js=(\hbar/q)\nabla\phi-\mathbf A. For constant \lambdaL on the contour, integration gives \Phi+\mu0\lambdaL^2\ointC\mathbf js\cdot d\mathbf l=n\Phi0, where \Phi0=h/(2e)\approx2.0678\times10^{-15} Wb. With a negatively charged pair-field convention, the associated phase winding reverses sign. These are equivalent conventions when used consistently. The simple constant-\lambdaL expression assumes a local, uniform condensate response away from the core.  

Only when the circulation term is negligible does magnetic flux itself approach n\Phi0. A lumped uniform ring makes the distinction explicit: I=(n\Phi0-\Phi{\rm ext})/(Lg+Lk), \Phi=\Phi{\rm ext}+LgI, and \Phi+LkI=n\Phi0. Here Lg and Lk are geometric and kinetic inductance. At zero applied flux with n=1 and Lk=9Lg, the magnetic flux is only 0.1\Phi0 although the fluxoid is one quantum. Twelve illustrative branches check this identity and the energy (n\Phi0-\Phi{\rm ext})^2/[2(Lg+Lk)]; they do not model phase-slip switching or an experimental device.  

Twenty-four discrete phase-loop checks compare enclosed defect charges, contour reversal and smooth single-valued gauge changes at two resolutions. A contour intersecting a zero is rejected. These checks establish the numerical examples under the stated complex-field construction, not a classification of every superconducting order-parameter manifold. Singular gauge choices require separate treatment and were not tested. 

For an ideal triangular array with one flux quantum per cell, B(\sqrt3 a^2/2)=\Phi0 gives a=\sqrt{2\Phi0/(\sqrt3 B)}. At mean induction B=1 T this is approximately 48.9 nm. Four geometric checks verify the cell area; they do not establish that a particular sample has a triangular lattice. Use mean induction B, not applied field H without a stated magnetization approximation. The later Abrikosov lecture favors the triangular array in the isotropic model but allows crystal-dependent alternatives; its result should not be attributed uncritically to the different early numerical estimate in the 1957 paper.  

 Experimental criteria

Deaver and Fairbank reported discrete trapped flux in tin cylinders consistent with hc/2e in Gaussian units, including a first-step uncertainty of approximately 20 percent and explicit geometric corrections. Doll and Näbauer independently observed steps in lead-tube measurements, but their original report compared approximately 0.2 Oe spacing with 0.5 Oe predicted using hc/e and left that discrepancy unresolved. Preserve the observations and uncertainties of each paper instead of rewriting both reports as identical precision determinations. The SI flux quantum has no factor of c.  

Tsuei and colleagues reported spontaneous half-quantum flux in a three-junction YBCO tricrystal ring, absent in the two-junction controls, consistent with d-wave pairing. Their 4.2 K value is the scanning SQUID measurement temperature. Interpreting such a result requires the junction geometry and phase constraints, trapped-flux controls and a calibrated magnetic response; it is not an observation of an isolated half vortex in every ordinary single-component superconductor. The original abstract has been checked here, not the complete flux-map analysis. 

Bauer and colleagues used niobium loops with PdNi ferromagnetic junctions and conventional-loop controls. Their final paper describes 2 K field sweeps, cooling-field reversal and subtraction of the Hall probe's temperature-dependent background; the low-temperature spontaneous flux approaches half a quantum. The final Figure 4 onset near 5 K replaces the author manuscript's approximate 5.5 K value. This is a device spontaneous-current scale, not a new bulk Nb transition temperature. Neither that onset nor the 2 K measurement is entered as experimental Tc. 

Finite inductance matters even in a simple sinusoidal single-π-junction model. At zero applied field and negligible ring kinetic inductance, set x=2\pi\Phi/\Phi0, \betaL=2\pi LgIc/\Phi0 with Ic\gt0, and normalized energy u=x^2/2+\betaL\cos x. The stable nonzero solutions obey x=\betaL\sin x for \betaL\gt1. Illustrative values \betaL=2,10,100 give positive fluxes approximately 0.302,0.454,0.495 quanta; at 0.5 the minimum is zero. The half-quantum limit is approached with large \betaL, not imposed exactly at every inductance. This independently checked model is distinct from the paper's gamma notation and from a multijunction tricrystal.  

 Limits and disputes

Current-driven vortex motion can produce an electric field and dissipative transport. The checked Bardeen–Stephen abstract supports this result in a local vortex-motion model. Its full viscosity and Hall-response calculation has not been reproduced here. 

The full Byers–Yang proof, complete 1994 tricrystal analysis, multicomponent fractional-vortex energetics and experimental raw-data audits remain open. Selected original scans, the later Abrikosov lecture and the published Bauer passages support the bounded discussion above. The local winding and ring calculations are illustrative checks. They do not complete scientific acceptance or establish a material's topological superconductivity.      

 Discovery implications

Store the contour, phase convention, inductive terms, field history, probe calibration and sample state alongside a vortex claim. Separate cell flux inferred from average induction, local sensor flux, fluxoid and momentum-space invariants. For a proposed fractional defect, identify the order-parameter or Josephson constraint and test competing trapped-flux explanations. These distinctions make a magnetic signal useful for comparing hypotheses without treating it as a complete pairing or topology diagnosis.

entries.text:
Scope

Antiferromagnetism and superconductivity can be adjacent in a phase diagram, compete within a sample, or coexist microscopically. These statements require different evidence. A nearby superconducting dome does not locate both orders in the same volume. A magnetic anomaly below a superconducting transition shows an interaction only after alternative structural, volume-fraction and instrumental explanations are considered. Static magnetic order is also distinct from the dynamic spin fluctuations proposed to mediate pairing.   

Microscopic coexistence means that superconducting and magnetic order occupy overlapping regions on the length and time scales resolved by the probes. Combine local magnetic information with evidence for bulk superconductivity, report detection limits, and identify whether measurements used the same specimen, a crystal mosaic or different crystals from one batch. A resistance drop and a magnetic transition alone cannot exclude minority phases or pressure and composition gradients.  

 Mathematical assumptions

A homogeneous Landau example uses x=M^2\geq0, y=|\Delta|^2\geq0 and F=amx+bmx^2+asy+bsy^2+gxy, with bm,bs\gt0. Here g\gt0 penalizes simultaneous amplitudes; it does not automatically exclude them. An interior minimum requires D=4bmbs-g^2\gt0 and positive solutions x=(-2bsam+gas)/D, y=(-2bmas+gam)/D. These coefficient definitions differ from papers that put factors of two or four in the free energy. 

For dimensionless am=as=-2 and bm=bs=1, competitive coupling g=1 gives x=y=2/3 and F=-4/3, below either pure-order energy -1. At g=3, the interior stationary point is a saddle and the two pure minima tie. At g=2, a continuum x+y=1 is degenerate and higher-order terms can select the state. Strong negative coupling g\lt-2\sqrt{bmbs} makes this quartic theory unbounded in the physical quadrant. Twelve constrained examples were checked against an independent dense grid; they are not material fits. 

Inside a coexistence branch, M^2=-am/(2bm)-g|\Delta|^2/(2bm). Thus positive coupling suppresses the moment relative to its continuation without superconductivity. It need not make the moment decrease as temperature falls: the bare magnetic growth can dominate. Two independent linear-temperature examples verify both cooling slopes with the same positive coupling. A decrease below Tc is useful evidence, but its absence does not establish that the orders cooperate. 

For fixed scattering geometry, an illustrative magnetic intensity scales as I\propto fmM^2, where fm is magnetic volume fraction. A uniform moment reduced to 0.8 of its reference and an unchanged moment in 0.64 of the volume both give the same normalized intensity 0.64. This simple nonuniqueness is why local-field distributions and amplitudes add information to diffraction. Real refinements also need magnetic structure factors, domains and instrumental corrections.  

 Experimental criteria

Vaknin and colleagues' neutron result establishes magnetic order in undoped La2CuO4-y; it does not establish static antiferromagnetism inside an optimally doped superconducting sample. Huang and colleagues' BaFe2As2 diffraction study anchors the parent magnetic and structural transition. Neither parent result supplies a universal superconducting coexistence interval. Preserve family, stoichiometry and sample conditions instead of transferring a magnetic transition temperature into a superconducting Tc table.  

Pratt and colleagues' final abstract reports structural and antiferromagnetic transitions near 60 K and 47 K in Ba(Fe0.953Co0.047)2As2, with superconductivity below 17 K, reduced static magnetic order and redistributed low-energy excitations. The sole author manuscript instead gives 15 K and a 4 meV gap. Its methods describe diffraction crystals grown under conditions matching the bulk-measurement specimens. Use the final abstract's 17 K as a reported transition, retain the version difference, and do not claim that every measurement used the identical crystal. The complete final methods remain unchecked. 

Marsik and colleagues provide complementary local-probe evidence in BaFe1.89Co0.11As2. Their 21.7 K value is the midpoint of the zero-field-cooled susceptibility transition. Transverse-field muon measurements imply a magnetic volume exceeding 90 percent, with essentially unchanged signal fractions but reduced relaxation below Tc. A field-pinning experiment supports bulk superconductivity; infrared spectra from crystals in the same growth batch support condensate formation. The authors infer coexistence on nanometer scales, not atomic uniformity at every site. Their composition corresponds to x=0.055 in Ba(Fe1-xCox)2As2, not x=0.11. 

Mito and colleagues report CeRhIn5 at 1.75 GPa: NQR splitting appears below TN=2.5 K, while in-situ coil susceptibility has a superconducting onset near 2.0 K. The comparable diamagnetic response at higher pressures supports bulk superconductivity. Their crushed grains and estimated pressure spread of approximately 0.05 GPa are part of the evidence conditions. The retrieved author PDF includes captions but omits the actual spectra and susceptibility figures, so this review verifies the reported interpretation and methods without claiming visual confirmation of those plots. 

Park and colleagues use pressure- and field-dependent specific heat in CeRhIn5 to infer a magnetic transition line inside the superconducting state. Their low-temperature phase diagram is an extrapolation from finite temperatures. The supplementary method measures relative ac heat capacity and calibrates pressure with a tin transition; these details matter when interpreting anomalies. Calorimetry supports thermodynamic boundaries but does not alone determine a magnetic ordering wavevector or the spatial arrangement of coexisting orders. 

 Limits and disputes

The Landau model organizes homogeneous amplitudes near transitions. It omits magnetic texture, superconducting phase coherence, disorder and gradients; a strong-coupling first-order boundary does not calculate the resulting domain structure. Fernandes and Schmalian's pairing inference additionally assumes itinerant electrons contributing to both orders and a system near particle-hole symmetry. Coexistence by itself is not a universal proof of sign-changing pairing or of a unique magnetic pairing interaction. 

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected original abstracts, author methods and available figures have been checked, alongside bounded numerical examples. Missing Mito figures, complete final-version comparisons, absolute volume calibration and experimental raw-data audits remain unresolved. Cross-probe agreement is evidence whose spatial, temporal and sample limits should remain visible, not a reason to remove those limits.    

 Discovery implications

Record magnetic wavevector or local-field evidence, superconducting criterion, probe timescale, volume fractions, batch identity, pressure distribution and composition convention together. Compare the magnetic response above and below Tc against its normal-state continuation. Separate a proposed fluctuation mechanism from evidence for static coexistence, and prefer quantitative competing explanations over a single label such as magnetic superconductor.

entries.text:
Scope

Intrinsic ferromagnetism and superconductivity coexist in the uranium compounds UGe2, URhGe and UCoGe under specific conditions. Establishing two orders in one material, establishing their spatial overlap, and determining the pairing wavefunction are separate tasks. This page concerns bulk materials; superconducting correlations induced across an engineered ferromagnet interface are a different problem. Pressure, composition, field direction and the experimental transition criterion belong with each result.    

Ferromagnetic fluctuations can provide an equal-spin pairing interaction in a model. Fay and Appel's longitudinal-fluctuation calculation predicts a nonmonotonic superconducting transition as the ferromagnetic boundary is approached. It does not imply that increasing magnetization always improves superconductivity. Static ordered moment, dynamic magnetic susceptibility and the electronic exchange splitting are different quantities. Their abstract supplies model motivation, not a measured pairing interaction for every uranium compound. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Consider an inversion-symmetric spin model with normal Hamiltonian H0=\xi{\mathbf k}I-h\sigmaz. Here h is an energy, not a magnetic field in tesla. With an imposed singlet gap \Delta0, the four Bogoliubov energies are \pm\sqrt{\xi{\mathbf k}^2+|\Delta0|^2}\pm h. The gap held fixed closes spectrally at |h|=|\Delta0| when \xi{\mathbf k}=0. This spectral condition does not locate the thermodynamic transition of a self-consistent superconductor. 

At zero temperature, a separate weak-coupling comparison with constant single-spin density of states N(0) gives Fs-Fn=N(0)(-\Delta0^2/2+h^2). Its energy crossing occurs at |h|=\Delta0/\sqrt2, before that fixed-gap spectral closure. This reference assumes a homogeneous singlet state and a spin-only field. Orbital effects, finite-momentum pairing, strong coupling and spin-orbit coupling are outside it. The original Clogston paper's identity is verified; this explicit energy example is independently checked. 

For diagonal equal-spin gaps, the positive branches instead read E\uparrow=\sqrt{(\xi-h)^2+|\Delta\uparrow|^2} and E\downarrow=\sqrt{(\xi+h)^2+|\Delta\downarrow|^2}. The imposed gaps pair states within their respective spin bands. Their spectra do not establish immunity to magnetic fields: the band populations, interaction, orbital motion and gap amplitudes can change. All 150 singlet and equal-spin matrix examples satisfy Hermiticity, the analytic spectra and particle-hole symmetry between opposite momenta. The triplet momentum factor is odd.  

Write \Delta=(\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)i\sigmay. Then \Delta\Delta^\dagger=|\mathbf d|^2I+\mathbf q\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma, with \mathbf q=i\mathbf d\times\mathbf d^. A unitary gap has \mathbf q=0. Equal-spin pairing can be unitary: \mathbf d=(0,-i,0) gives \Delta=I at the selected momentum. By contrast, \mathbf d=(-1/2,-i/2,0) gives \Delta=\mathrm{diag}(1,0), a nonunitary example with one ungapped spin band. One hundred complex-vector checks verify the identity and nonnegative squared gaps. This spin-basis illustration is not a determination of total sample magnetization or a realistic spin-orbit-coupled band structure. 

 Experimental criteria

Saxena and colleagues' UGe2 discovery uses resistivity and ac susceptibility under pressure. The published phase-diagram caption defines the superconducting temperature by a 50-percent resistivity drop; it scales that axis by ten for display. Its susceptibility caption uses approximately 1.3 GPa for the main magnetic curve and 1.5 GPa for the superconducting inset. These are distinct conditions. The paper reports magnetic survival below the superconducting transition, but defers the detailed neutron analysis. Selected methods and captions are checked here; the original plots are not visually audited. 

Aoki and colleagues' URhGe discovery adds a thermodynamic superconducting signature at ambient pressure. Its abstract explicitly leaves the pairing symmetry and dominant mechanism unidentified. Levy and colleagues subsequently report a second superconducting field pocket around a spin reorientation near 12 T for a field along the crystal b axis, above the field that suppresses the first pocket. This ties superconductivity to magnetic evolution without uniquely identifying a gap symmetry. The complete discovery curves and reentrant phase boundaries remain outside this selected review.  

For Huy and colleagues' UCoGe sample 3, the resistive onset is 0.82 K, while heat capacity and thermal expansion begin their broad anomalies near 0.66 K. An idealized equal-entropy construction places a sharp transition near 0.45 K. Those values represent different criteria, not three competing measurements of one exact universal constant. The approximately 3 K Curie temperature is magnetic and must not populate a superconducting-temperature filter. The thermodynamic anomalies support bulk superconductivity; the suggested triplet mechanism remains an inference. 

Ohta and colleagues' separate polycrystalline UCoGe sample has a susceptibility onset near 0.7 K and midpoint near 0.55 K. At 95 mK, similar nuclear recovery at peaks with and without internal magnetic fields supports superconducting response in both regions. The slow relaxation component accounts for about 30 percent of the measured recovery, not a demonstrated uniform superconducting response at every site. Pulse-condition sensitivity and model assumptions matter. A self-induced vortex state is proposed to explain the components; this is not a direct vortex image. 

 Limits and disputes

UTe2 should not be inserted into the established ambient-pressure ferromagnetic-coexistence list simply because its discovery paper invokes nearly ferromagnetic fluctuations. That paper provides superconductivity and unconventional-pairing clues, without establishing static long-range ferromagnetism. Later neutron work reports antiferromagnetic fluctuations and a resonance; its absence of detected ferromagnetic scattering is restricted to the measured window. Neither result by itself fixes the full pairing interaction.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected source passages, local-probe figures and independent matrix checks support the discussion. Detailed magnetic and superconducting volume calibration, raw-data analysis, complete version comparisons and material-specific spin-orbit models remain unresolved. A large critical field, a small net moment or coexistence alone cannot replace a consistent set of spin, thermodynamic and phase-sensitive constraints.    

 Discovery implications

Keep magnetic ordering temperature separate from superconducting onset, midpoint and bulk-anomaly criteria. Preserve specimen identity, field orientation and pressure for every observation. Test whether a pairing model accounts jointly for the measured magnetic response and superconducting evidence; do not turn one suggestive signature into a unique pairing assignment.

entries.text:
Scope

A large upper critical field means superconductivity survives a strong field; it does not establish that the field creates superconductivity. At fixed temperature, a field-induced state appears from a zero-field normal state. Field reentrance means a low-field superconducting regime is lost and subsequently recovered. Field enhancement means a specified observable improves over an interval. These distinctions require the same specimen, temperature, orientation and operational criterion throughout the comparison.  

A resistive decrease can indicate reduced dissipation without demonstrating a new bulk phase. Zero resistance establishes a conducting path; diamagnetic screening or a thermodynamic anomaly provides complementary information. Record whether an intermediate state is demonstrably normal or simply dissipative. A field sweep and a temperature sweep trace different paths through a phase diagram, and must not be joined as though every point belongs to one isotherm.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Jaccarino–Peter compensation concerns an exchange contribution opposing the applied field in the electron spin sector. An illustrative effective Zeeman field is b{\rm eff}=B-BJ(B,T), with every term expressed in tesla and positive BJ defined to oppose positive applied B. The exchange term does not automatically cancel orbital coupling to the physical field. The original 1962 paper's identity is verified here; the following threshold example is independently calculated, rather than presented as its complete theory.  

At a fixed temperature, impose the artificial conditions |b{\rm eff}|\lt BP and 0\le B\lt B{\rm orb}. With a constant saturated exchange field J, the permitted interval is the intersection of (J-BP,J+BP) with the nonnegative orbital window. Its width is \max[0,\min(B{\rm orb},J+BP)-\max(0,J-BP)]. For J=8 T and BP=2 T, an orbital ceiling of 7 T leaves only 6\lt B\lt7 T; a ceiling of 5 T leaves no interval. A universal width of 2BP therefore fails even in this simplified model. 

A constant saturated exchange field is unsuitable near zero field if the moments are unpolarized there. For an explicitly synthetic alternative, take BJ=J\tanh(B/Bs). With J=10 T, Bs=BP=1 T and B{\rm orb}=15 T, the threshold model has a low-field interval ending near 0.112 T and a second interval approximately between 9 and 11 T. Reducing the orbital ceiling to 7 T removes the second interval. Reversing the exchange sign removes the compensation pocket. Root finding on monotonic segments agrees with 120,006 independent grid checks across six parameter sets. This is neither a material fit nor a self-consistent gap or free-energy calculation.  

 Experimental criteria

Meul and colleagues reported magnetic-field-induced superconductivity in Eu-Sn molybdenum chalcogenides in 1984. Their original abstract interprets the phase-diagram shape through compensation. The detailed composition, measurement protocol and complete curves have not been checked in this review, so an exact stoichiometry or numerical field window is not assigned from that abstract alone. 

URhGe supplies a distinct magnetic setting. Its ambient-pressure discovery includes thermodynamic superconducting evidence; Levy and colleagues subsequently identify a second field pocket near the roughly 12 T spin reorientation for a field along the b axis. Gourgout and colleagues connect this region to transport and thermoelectric anomalies, a first-order magnetic transition and Fermi-surface changes. These observations constrain the mechanism without establishing a simple continuous quantum critical point or a unique pairing interaction. The original discovery abstracts and selected later author text support this limited comparison.   

Yang and colleagues' Sm0.95−xCa0.05EuxNiO2 study reports reentrance in Eu-rich films. For the 54-unit-cell x=0.34 specimen, resistance returns to zero above approximately 6.23 T at 2 K; mutual inductance on that specimen shows screening at 9 and 12 T, absent at 3 T. For x=0.32, the 13.04 T recovery is measured at 3 K, while persistence above 32 T refers to 1.7 K. Neither measurement temperature is a transition temperature for database filtering. 

Varbaro and colleagues investigate a separate Nd0.7Eu0.3NiO2 system. Their final Figure 3 combines two specimens using 20-percent and 50-percent normal-resistivity criteria; open and filled markers distinguish measurement facilities and specimens. These boundaries are not zero-resistance contours. The low-temperature Hall analysis uses a non-superconducting film on NdGaO3, whereas the superconducting transport uses LSAT-grown films. Their proposed competing Eu and Nd paramagnetic contributions should not be silently substituted for the magnetic interpretation of the Sm/Ca/Eu material. 

 Limits and disputes

The Sm/Ca/Eu author's revised manuscript does not establish the long-range magnetic structure. Its angular reentrance extends nearly in-plane for some dopings, and the compared angular maps use different temperatures. The 50-percent resistance contours and phenomenological compensation fits do not prove triplet pairing. These qualifications replace stronger statements in the fixed planning source. 

The public Sm/Ca/Eu dataset predates the checked manuscript revision. A read-only check of its Fig2 workbook preserves small negative baseline readings instead of clipping them to zero. Missing unit labels and an unverified noise floor prevent assigning an independently validated zero-resistance threshold from the spreadsheet alone. Complete correspondence between dataset and revised figures remains open. Separately, the URhGe author manuscript gives 12.75 T in its abstract but 11.75 T in its body; the published abstract gives 12.75 T. The discrepancy remains unresolved here.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Full historical methods, selected final-version comparisons, absolute screening calibration, supplementary-data checks and independent material-specific model fits remain outstanding. Distinguish evidence supporting a superconducting state from evidence selecting its mechanism, and a measured high-field survival point from a measured upper critical field.    

 Discovery implications

Compare full field paths with matched criteria, preserve field direction and specimen identity, and test temperature control and sweep dependence. Evaluate compensation against magnetic response and orbital limitations; evaluate magnetic reorientation against relevant magnetic and electronic probes. Retain disagreements rather than averaging incompatible definitions. A useful candidate explains several measurements under their actual conditions, not merely a high-field resistance drop.

entries.text:
Scope

Reentrance describes a path through a phase diagram. Specify which phase returns, which parameter is swept, its direction, and what is held fixed. A field scan can produce superconducting, dissipative, and superconducting regimes in sequence. The historical term reentrant superconductor also covers a different sequence on cooling: normal, superconducting, then normal ferromagnetic. A pair of maxima in a transition-temperature curve does not by itself establish disconnected superconducting regions.   

Use superconducting and normal labels only to the extent supported by the probes. A resistive intermediate regime may retain pairing or superconducting correlations, while zero resistance may follow a connected minority path. The same plotted boundary can have different meanings when it represents onset, a resistance fraction, a magnetic response or a thermodynamic anomaly. Paths assembled from different samples need explicit specimen labels.   

 Mathematical assumptions

An independent dimensionless example separates path geometry from mechanism. Define an imposed transition curve Tc(x)=\max[0,1+v-(x^2-1)^2], and label a point superconducting when 0\lt T\lt Tc(x). The variable x is a control coordinate, not an assigned pressure in GPa. With v=0.2, both peaks reach 1.2 and the valley remains at 0.2. A horizontal scan at T=0.6 crosses two superconducting intervals; at T=0.1 it crosses one connected interval. The two higher-temperature pockets therefore belong to one connected region in the full positive-temperature plane.  

For v=-0.2, the imposed curve has a zero-temperature gap between two lobes. At T=0.1, its superconducting intervals run approximately from -1.355 to -0.404 and from 0.404 to 1.355. The analytic endpoints follow from (x^2-1)^2=1+v-T. Six cases, including scans above both peaks, agree with 120,000 independent grid evaluations. This construction demonstrates a logical distinction; it does not infer a second order parameter, pairing symmetry or microscopic interaction from the number of lobes. 

A separate homogeneous example represents the historical temperature sequence. Let f=a(T)s^2+s^4/2, where s\ge0 and a(T)=(T-1)(T-3) in dimensionless units. Its global minimum has s^2=\max[0,-a(T)]. Cooling through T=4,2,0.5 gives normal, superconducting and normal states. Only one superconducting interval exists. The model has continuous boundaries and no domains or hysteresis, so it cannot reproduce the observed history dependence of ErRh4B4. It illustrates which state reenters, not that material's magnetic mechanism.  

 Experimental criteria

Sinha and colleagues' 1982 ErRh4B4 study combines neutron diffraction and resistivity. Its abstract reports an intermediate region below 1.2 K with ferromagnetic and modulated magnetic structures, followed below 0.71 K by disappearance of the modulation and superconductivity into a normal ferromagnetic state. The proposed coexistence of ferromagnetic and superconducting domains is an interpretation of these measurements, not proof of uniform coexistence at every microscopic position. The full historical methods remain unchecked here. 

Prozorov and colleagues later resolve directional and historical differences using dynamic susceptibility. Their approximately 10 MHz probe uses a small excitation field, and their Figure 3 compares multiple temperature-ramp rates. Warming from the ferromagnetic state produces steps; cooling is more gradual. The reported rate insensitivity covers the tested ramps, not every possible relaxation timescale. Superconducting screening can conceal remaining ferromagnetic regions. Minor temperature loops also differ from the initial warming path, so sweep direction alone does not completely specify sample history. 

Crespo and colleagues add local tunneling spectroscopy with a superconducting Pb tip. Their analysis deconvolves the tip response to infer the sample density of states. They select about twenty suitable surface locations; many other areas have suppressed or absent superconducting features. The representative heating and cooling transitions differ by about 90 mK. At 0.3 K the measured superconducting features come from the tip, while the inferred sample spectrum is featureless. This is a local, surface-sensitive absence within the measured conditions, not a complete volume census. The author manuscript identifies the crystal as the one previously used in the neutron and transport study. 

Yuan and colleagues' original 2003 abstract reports disconnected pressure domes in partially Ge-substituted CeCu2Si2. Their later institutional report distinguishes the continuous region of the pure compound from the separated domes near substitution x=0.1. The comparison uses relative pressure \Delta p=p-p{c1}(x); the reference pressure depends on composition. Ge substitution changes both disorder and lattice volume. The report also combines comparison curves from different probes and uses distinct pressure-cell techniques across its range. These conditions prevent a universal pressure window from being assigned to every CeCu2(Si,Ge)2 sample.  

URhGe and Eu-rich Sm/Ca/Eu nickelates provide field-scan examples, with different magnetic settings. The former has a second pocket near a b-axis spin reorientation; the latter combines selected high-field zero-resistance and screening observations. Keep these examples distinct from the normal-state reentrance on cooling in ErRh4B4. Similar phase-diagram shapes do not establish a shared microscopic mechanism. The sample-specific field and temperature conditions are treated in the linked field-induced-superconductivity page.   

 Limits and disputes

A lowest measured temperature is a detection boundary, not proof that the true transition temperature vanishes. The institutional pressure report describes measurements extending down to 50 mK; its absence of observed superconductivity cannot establish an exact zero-temperature interval without further evidence. Likewise, its discussion of a possible volume collapse cites diffraction on CeCu2Ge2 rather than a direct structural measurement on every specimen in its superconducting phase diagram. Magnetic and valence-mediated pairing remain interpretations to test against additional measurements. 

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The original Sinha and Science pressure papers have only abstract-level checks here; other selected passages and figures have more detailed review. Raw spectra, absolute magnetic calibration, complete final-version comparisons and historical field boundaries remain incomplete. Local gaplessness, resistance, screening and global phase coherence must not be treated as interchangeable observations. The independent examples verify their stated assumptions only.    

 Discovery implications

Record the full path, sample history, parameter uncertainties, measurement floor and transition criterion with each reported pocket. Compare warming, cooling and partial loops before assigning an equilibrium boundary. Separate a new region in a measured slice from a distinct phase in the full diagram, then use magnetic, structural and spectroscopic measurements to test the proposed mechanism. Preserve unresolved differences instead of averaging incompatible temperatures or pressure origins.

entries.text:
Scope

The Jaccarino–Peter effect is compensation of the spin-splitting field experienced by conduction electrons. An exchange contribution opposite to the applied field can reduce Zeeman pair breaking near a finite field. It does not cancel the applied field everywhere in space or remove orbital coupling. A large critical field, a second superconducting pocket or the presence of magnetic ions alone does not establish this mechanism. The original proposal dates to 1962; its identity is verified here, but its full derivation has not been reread.  

Meul and colleagues' 1984 work reports field-induced superconductivity in a Eu–Sn molybdenum chalcogenide system and interprets it through compensation. The original abstract supports that historical connection. Exact composition, numerical field endpoints and complete measurement methods have not been verified here, so they are not promoted to universal material parameters. A classical example cannot supply the missing exchange measurement for a different compound. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Choose the positive direction along the applied field and define the signed effective field as B{\mathrm{eff}}=B{\mathrm{ext}}+B{\mathrm{ex}}. Compensation requires B{\mathrm{ex}}\lt0 in this convention. In the collinear single-band illustration, spin energies are E\pm=\pm h, with h=g\muB B{\mathrm{eff}}/2 and positive g. Their full separation is 2|h|=g\muB|B{\mathrm{eff}}|. A source using another sign for its exchange constant must first be translated into this convention; the sign of a symbol called J is not transferable without its Hamiltonian.  

An independent synthetic example isolates an inference used in shift measurements. Suppose corrected frequency shifts obey y=m(B-B), with nonzero, field-independent slope and a saturated exchange contribution. A fitted line y=mB+c gives B=-c/m. Four imposed fields, 14.5, 21, 26 and 28 T, recover six noiseless examples with target intercepts of 20, 32 and 40 T and both slope signs. The latter two targets are extrapolations outside this measurement interval. These calculations reproduce the algebra, not published spectra. 

A residual constant correction d moves the inferred intercept by -d/m. In the synthetic examples, a 0.06 MHz offset shifts it by +2 T for a slope of -0.03 MHz/T, or by -1.2 T for +0.05 MHz/T. A zero slope leaves the intercept unidentifiable. Nine separate spin-energy checks verify the distinction between half splitting and full splitting, including negative effective fields. Neither exercise contains orbital coupling, spin-flip scattering or a gap equation, so neither demonstrates a superconducting transition.  

 Experimental criteria

Balicas and colleagues measured four-terminal transport in lambda-(BETS)2FeCl4 with field near the conducting plane. Their phase diagram distinguishes resistive midpoints from resistance below instrumental sensitivity; the broad 18–41 T field-induced region is not uniformly a zero-resistance region. Below 2 K, resistance reaches the experimental zero near 33 T. Tilting introduces a transverse component that suppresses the state. Figure 3's pairing-state curves are theoretical fits, not direct imaging of a modulated order parameter. These results support a compensation interpretation while retaining orbital and measurement limits. 

Hiraki and colleagues provide a different probe: corrected 77Se NMR shifts in the metallic state at 1.5 K and fields up to 28 T. They infer an exchange-field magnitude of 32 ± 2 T by extrapolating a field-dependent shift. This is not an observed zero crossing at 32 T. Chemical, dipolar and demagnetization corrections enter the analysis; demagnetization dominates their stated uncertainty. The interpretation assumes sufficiently saturated local moments and suitable field-independent electronic response. The transport specimen discussed alongside the NMR came from the same batch, not necessarily the identical crystal. 

Wu and colleagues instead infer an exchange field of -32.7 ± 1.5 T from a 9 T, 5 K angular-shift experiment. Their author manuscript uses a hyperfine calibration partly informed by the nonmagnetic Ga analogue, and explicitly excludes an unknown uncertainty in its axial Knight-shift coefficient. Its predicted value at 33 T is a further model adjustment. Keep the applied field, temperature, inferred exchange field and uncertainty scope separate; the quoted exchange magnitude is not the applied field at which these spectra were taken. 

For a new material, the evidence should connect a measured local-moment response to a signed electronic exchange contribution, then test whether its field and angle dependence account for the superconducting observations. Compare transport with independent magnetic or thermodynamic evidence where available. Different samples, transition criteria, pressure conditions and temperatures must remain identifiable. A numerical similarity between a resistance minimum and an inferred exchange field is supporting evidence, not a replacement for calibration or alternative-mechanism tests.   

 Limits and disputes

The selected Wu author manuscript has a convention issue requiring further review: the signed angular-difference formula and the subsequent printed numerical input do not match under direct substitution. The final publisher abstract confirms the reported exchange value, but the full final calibration has not been compared. This page therefore attributes the value to the authors and does not claim to reproduce it independently. The discrepancy is an unresolved source-version issue, not evidence that the experimental phenomenon is false. Complete scientific acceptance remains open. 

The 2026 Eu-rich Sm/Ca/Eu nickelate study reports reentrance and discusses exchange compensation alongside other magnetic physics. Its selected later author version leaves the magnetic order unresolved and includes sample-dependent angular behavior. It does not justify a universal claim of established ferromagnetism or triplet pairing. A separate Nd/Eu nickelate study develops a paramagnetic-compensation interpretation using different material and substrate conditions. Their similarities motivate tests; they do not make the two systems interchangeable or establish one uniquely complete mechanism.  

 Discovery implications

Store the exchange-field estimate with its sign convention, probe, applied field, temperature, correction model and uncertainty coverage. Record whether compensation was measured directly, extrapolated or assumed in fitting a phase boundary. Separate those records from superconducting transition temperatures. For multiband systems, test whether one effective exchange field is adequate rather than assuming every band has the same coupling. Preserve the independently measured orbital constraints when evaluating candidate compensation windows.
