entries.text:
Scope

The Pauli paramagnetic limit compares the energy gained by a spin-polarized normal state with the condensation energy of a specified superconducting state. It is a model-dependent reference, not a universal upper bound on every superconductor. Exceeding a weak-coupling, g = 2 estimate signals that its assumptions need examination. It does not by itself establish triplet pairing, a spatially modulated state or a topological phase. Chandrasekhar and Clogston's 1962 publication identities are checked here; the following explicit calculation is independent rather than a claimed reproduction of their complete original papers.  

Suppressing orbital depairing in a very thin film can expose spin depairing that would otherwise be hidden. Geometry alone does not remove the spin-energy cost. Spin–orbit coupling, an altered gap scale, anisotropic response, exchange compensation and multiband physics require distinct models. Keep the applied field, internal exchange field and spin–orbit energy scale separate when interpreting an apparently large critical field.   

 Mathematical assumptions

Use B in tesla and dimensionless SI volume susceptibilities. With positive zero-field condensation-energy density Uc, constant spin susceptibilities and no orbital contribution, the free-energy difference is Fs-Fn=-Uc+(\chin-\chis)B^2/(2\mu0). For \chin\gt\chis, its crossing occurs at BP=\sqrt{2\mu0Uc/(\chin-\chis)}. If the susceptibilities vary strongly with field, this quadratic expression must be replaced by the appropriate magnetization integral. Equal susceptibilities remove this particular quadratic penalty, not every physical limit on superconductivity. 

For a simple uniform, fully gapped spin-singlet state at zero temperature, set \chis=0. Let n be the single-spin density of states per unit energy and volume. Taking Uc=n\Delta0^2/2 and \chin=\mu0n(g\muB)^2/2 yields BP=\sqrt{2}\Delta0/(g\muB). At g=2 and \Delta0=1.764kBTc, the numerical coefficient is about 1.857 T/K. The familiar approximate 1.84–1.86 T/K benchmark is meaningful only with its gap and response assumptions. It is a zero-temperature reference, not a measured transition curve at arbitrary temperature.   

An independent calculation checks eighteen combinations of transition temperature, g factor and gap ratio, and verifies the free-energy sign on both sides of each crossing. Holding the other assumptions fixed, halving g doubles the reference field; increasing the gap ratio from 1.764 to 2.2 multiplies it by about 1.247. A synthetic Tc=3 K, g = 2 example gives approximately 5.571 T with the first gap ratio. These parameter changes demonstrate sensitivity, not fitted explanations for a named material.  

A further controlled example fixes Uc and \chin while assigning r=\chis/\chin. The crossing grows by 1/\sqrt{1-r}: r = 0, 0.25 and 0.75 give factors 1, approximately 1.155 and 2. This scaling cannot be carried unchanged into a system where spin–orbit coupling also changes the normal susceptibility or condensation energy. The finite checks verify the stated energy comparison; they do not solve a self-consistent gap equation or select the stable pairing state. 

 Experimental criteria

For Xi and colleagues' monolayer NbSe2 study, the approximately 35 T zero-temperature scale comes from fitting a spin–orbit-protected pair-breaking model. An independent contact-conductance measurement extends to 31.5 T and finds a strongly diminished Andreev-related feature. The author text gives 0.3 K, while its Figure 4 caption specifies 0.36 K for the inset; those labels are preserved here. The fitted effective spin–orbit scale near 660 T is not an applied laboratory field. Field-transition criteria and two-terminal versus four-terminal devices must also remain distinct. 

De la Barrera and colleagues report that monolayer TaS2's parallel-field transition remains above their 34.5 T measurement ceiling below 2 K. Their quoted 65.6 T is a near-transition square-root fit parameter, not a directly measured critical field. They define phase-boundary points using half the normal-state resistance, which is distinct from zero resistance. Alignment is optimized at fixed temperature and field by minimizing resistance; maintaining alignment during a temperature sweep is harder. Their 25 mK/12 T and 300 mK/34.5 T apparatus limits must not be combined into one unperformed measurement. 

Calorimetry provides another kind of evidence. Bianchi and colleagues observe a high-field, low-temperature anomaly in CeCoIn5 and interpret it as a possible finite-momentum superconducting state. The final publication explicitly retains “Possible” in its title. Subsequent neutron evidence establishes coupled magnetic order in the high-field superconducting phase. An extra phase boundary therefore requires assessment of competing or coexisting order; it is not an automatic image of a spatially modulated superconducting gap. The older calorimetry and later magnetic observations have different review depths here.  

 Limits and disputes

The orbital field in a Maki ratio must come from an orbital model or suitable independent estimate: \alphaM=\sqrt{2}B{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}/BP. Inserting an already Pauli-limited measured field into its numerator changes the meaning. The dirty, single-band orbital estimate involving 0.693 times Tc and the magnitude of the near-transition slope has restricted assumptions. Unequal band diffusivities can change the extrapolation. A large ratio motivates further investigation; it does not certify a finite-momentum state or determine a universal onset threshold.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected TMD methods and figures have been checked, but raw transport, full supplementary calibration, complete final-version comparisons and material-specific susceptibility reconstructions remain incomplete. A fitted spin–orbit parameter, a resistance midpoint and a bulk thermodynamic boundary are different quantities. Even when a spin-sensitive probe agrees with a proposed interpretation, compare alternative states under the same field direction, temperature and experimental conditions before assigning pairing symmetry.    

 Discovery implications

Record the measured field range and any censoring or extrapolation, the superconducting criterion, field direction, sample thickness and transition temperature used in the reference ratio. Report the chosen g factor, gap ratio, susceptibility assumptions and orbital model separately. Use departures from the simple benchmark to design discriminating measurements, not to rank triplet content by the size of a critical-field ratio. A future model must explain both the enhanced direction and the directions in which superconductivity is more easily destroyed.

entries.text:
Scope

A quantum spin liquid is not identified simply by an absence of detected magnetic order. A candidate material must be tested against valence-bond order, disorder, freezing and the finite temperature and time windows of the measurements. A spin gap can occur in different states; its observation alone does not identify topological order or fractionalized excitations. Here the organic Mott insulator κ-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3 illustrates how interpretations change when additional probes become available.   

RVB, or resonating valence bond, describes a family of theoretical constructions built from superpositions of singlet configurations. Anderson's cuprate proposal connects this idea to superconductivity in a doped correlated insulator; the abstract is a historical proposal, not a material-level proof of a spin-liquid parent. The allowed coverings, amplitudes and constraints must be specified. A generic U(1) construction is not automatically a Dirac state, and BCS mean-field language does not imply a phonon-only pairing interaction. 

 Mathematical assumptions

An independent finite example makes one logical limitation explicit. Consider an isolated singlet of energy zero and three triplet states with energies \Delta-h, \Delta and \Delta+h. Use units kB=g\muB=1, so temperatures, gaps and the field variable h are expressed in compatible energy units; the response below is not an SI molar susceptibility. The partition function is Z=1+e^{-\Delta/T}[1+2\cosh(h/T)]. Differentiating the mean moment at zero field gives \chi0=2e^{-\Delta/T}/\{T[1+3e^{-\Delta/T}]\}. This illustrative model addresses an inference problem raised by the magnetic measurements, rather than fitting those experiments.  

The model has a gap and a nonmagnetic singlet ground state, yet an isolated dimer has neither bulk topological order nor mobile charge. Adding a synthetic Curie contribution gives \chi{\mathrm{obs}}=\chi0+c/T. With an illustrative gap of 6 K, c = 0.001 and T = 0.1 K, the background exceeds 99.9999% of the total response even though the intrinsic response is exponentially suppressed. The chosen 6 K is a model parameter, not the measured anomaly temperature or a fitted material gap. An inverse-temperature tail cannot by itself establish a gapless intrinsic state. 

Five finite-difference derivatives agree with the analytic response, and fifteen temperature/background combinations check this counterexample. Its Curie term assumes independent, unsaturated moments; interactions, anisotropy and finite-field saturation are excluded. Singlet correlations in an insulating model also do not demonstrate charge coherence or superconductivity. The separate  examines wavefunction normalization and charge-response assumptions. These finite calculations are not a simulation of a bulk quantum spin liquid.  

 Experimental criteria

Shimizu and colleagues' lowest-temperature proton NMR measurements used a single crystal at 2.2 T perpendicular to the conducting planes, reaching 32 mK. That temperature floor is not a zero-field result. Their higher-temperature polycrystalline NMR used 3.9 T, and susceptibility measurements used 0.32 T. No resolved splitting or major broadening was observed at low temperature, but the small-moment estimate relies on calibration against a different chloride salt. The absence of a resolved signal therefore has a probe- and model-dependent bound. 

Below approximately 0.4 K, the reported recovery needs two exponential components, with roughly linear and quadratic temperature dependences of their relaxation rates. The authors discuss spatial inhomogeneity and possible disorder-related explanations. Combining these components into one universal power law would discard relevant evidence. The approximately 250 K exchange scale obtained from the susceptibility analysis is neither the 32 mK measurement floor nor a superconducting transition temperature. 

Miksch and colleagues separate a decreasing main ESR contribution below the approximately 6 K anomaly from narrow defect-related components. Their author manuscript uses conventional 9.5 GHz measurements near 340 mT down to 1.9 K, alongside separate low-frequency measurements near 40 mT reaching 25 mK. These are different protocols, not one continuous zero-field measurement. Samples from four laboratories show different defect signals. The proposed microscopic defect origin remains an interpretation; the final abstract describes a gapped ground state consistent with a valence-bond solid. 

 Limits and disputes

Gap values require their observable and fitting model. Miksch's author supplement compares a simple activated fit giving 7.3 K with a chain-based fit giving 12.1 K. Its main text and figure legend include an inverse-temperature prefactor that the displayed supplementary expression omits; no unreported correction or independent reproduction of that fit is claimed here. Pustogow's final paper explicitly distinguishes its transport scale Eg=2\Delta\approx30–50 K from the approximately 12 K ESR spin gap. These numbers are not interchangeable measurements of one quantity, nor evidence by themselves of a manuscript-version error.  

The strain-transport study favors a valence-bond-solid interpretation but leaves a gapped chiral spin liquid possible. Its hydrostatic-equivalent pressure is inferred for a substrate-coupled crystal; it is not a directly applied hydrostatic pressure. Kurosaki's pressure phase diagram establishes neighboring electronic phases and superconductivity, but proximity does not identify the pairing mediator. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: final-version comparisons, raw-data analysis, full calibration and discrimination among microscopic states are incomplete. Reference labels identify which selected methods, figures or abstracts were actually checked.   

 Discovery implications

Record the sample, magnetic field, frequency or time window, temperature floor, background subtraction and fitting assumptions for each proposed spin-liquid signature. Compare magnetic, structural, thermodynamic and charge-coherence observations under compatible conditions. A useful mechanism proposal must predict observations that distinguish alternatives across the transition, including the behavior of defects. Superconductivity next to a candidate insulating state motivates such tests; it does not establish fractionalization-mediated pairing.

entries.text:
Scope

Spin–orbit coupling links electronic motion to spin and changes the normal-state band structure and magnetic response. It does not, by itself, specify the attractive interaction responsible for superconductivity. In a nonmagnetic system without inversion symmetry, antisymmetric spin–orbit coupling can split bands and allow pairing components that inversion would separate. Permission by symmetry is not a measurement of their relative weights. Gor'kov and Rashba's two-dimensional model explicitly leaves the pairing mechanism unspecified and assumes its spin–orbit splitting remains small compared with the Fermi energy.  

In an ideal Rashba model, the spin texture lies in the plane and winds perpendicular to momentum. In the Ising description used for monolayer NbSe2, opposite valleys have predominantly opposite out-of-plane spin orientations. These are different textures and give different directional responses. A spin–orbit energy expressed as an equivalent field is not an applied laboratory field. Strong spin–orbit coupling and a large upper critical field do not independently certify triplet pairing or topological superconductivity.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For a two-spin effective model, write h(\mathbf k)=\xi(\mathbf k)I+\mathbf g(\mathbf k)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma, with even \xi and odd \mathbf g under momentum reversal. Its normal energies are \xi\pm|\mathbf g|. An even-frequency gap may be written \widehat\Delta=[\psi+\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]i\sigmay, with even singlet component \psi and odd triplet vector \mathbf d. The chosen spin or pseudospin basis matters; this two-component model is not a complete multiorbital classification. Neither the normal splitting nor the algebraic gap decomposition determines a self-consistent interaction.  

An independent calculation imposes a real, purely singlet gap \widehat\Delta=\psi i\sigmay. Its Bogoliubov excitation energies are E\pm=\sqrt{(\xi\pm g)^2+\psi^2}, where g=|\mathbf g|. For a nonzero Matsubara frequency, define f\pm=-\psi/(\omega^2+E\pm^2). The anomalous propagator decomposes as F=[fs+\mathbf ft\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]i\sigmay, with fs=(f++f-)/2 and \mathbf ft=(f+-f-)\hat{\mathbf g}/2. Thus a momentum-resolved triplet pair amplitude can be nonzero although the imposed gap has no triplet component. These quantities should not both be labeled an experimental “triplet fraction.” 

One hundred independently assembled matrices reproduce the spectra and fermionic relation F(\mathbf k,i\omega)=-F^T(-\mathbf k,-i\omega); one hundred decompositions match the analytic amplitudes. Three controls check cancellation at zero spin–orbit coupling or at \xi=0, and a nonzero amplitude at generic parameters. The result distinguishes a propagator from a gap interaction. It does not compute a momentum-integrated mixing ratio, susceptibility, transition temperature or topological invariant. 

Frigeri and colleagues' weak-coupling treatment neglects small particle-hole-asymmetry mixing terms and studies pairing channels separately. Alignment of \mathbf d with \mathbf g avoids a leading suppression term; it does not select the stable material state. Their erratum adds an omitted linear contribution to the MnSi spin–orbit vector and rescales the original Figure 2 parameter by dividing by \sqrt{3/2}. Claims about which p-wave component is suppressed therefore require the corrected vector and its relative coefficients.  

 Experimental criteria

Nishiyama and colleagues report a nearly unchanged Knight shift and approximately cubic temperature dependence of the relaxation rate in Li2Pt3B, interpreted as evidence for triplet pairing with nodes. Their crushed polycrystalline sample has a zero-field susceptibility transition at 2.68 K. For boron NMR, 0.26 T gives a transition near 2.1 K, while 0.35 T gives approximately 1.8 K. The 0.1 K spectrum is a measurement temperature, not a transition. The Li2Pd3B comparison uses a different field, 1.46 T, and the Knight-shift interpretation includes an orbital contribution and a fitted gap model. 

Häfliger and colleagues instead find low-temperature saturation in μSR-derived penetration depth and activated specific heat in Li2Pt3B, favoring a fully gapped interpretation. Their final text nevertheless notes that a simple single-gap fit to the penetration-depth data is unsatisfactory and that triplet states cannot be excluded. The low-field temperature scans extend to 30 mK, while the field-dependent comparison is made at 1 K; calorimetry reaches 0.1 K and uses a 4 T normal-state reference. These different probes and protocols must remain separately identifiable. 

Ising-protected superconductivity provides another route to an enhanced field scale. In the NbSe2 study, the approximately 35 T scale is fitted, whereas contact-conductance data extend to 31.5 T. In the TaS2 study, 34.5 T is an experimental ceiling and 65.6 T is a fit parameter. Orbital geometry, alignment, gap scale and the resistance criterion accompany any comparison with a weak-coupling Pauli estimate. A larger ratio alone does not determine the spin structure of the gap.  

 Limits and disputes

The Li2Pt3B disagreement cannot be settled by labeling one result “bulk” and another “surface”: NMR also probes bulk material. The μSR/calorimetry paper discusses sample inhomogeneity and metallic inclusions, but those possibilities are not independently demonstrated explanations for every contrasting measurement. Retain both experimental interpretations and their assumptions. Absence of a coherence peak is not, by itself, a unique nodal or triplet diagnostic. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including raw-data comparisons, final-version checks and the wider subsequent literature.  

A topological assignment requires a specified superconducting Hamiltonian, symmetry class and appropriate invariant, together with evidence that the physical system realizes the assumed state. Normal-state spin splitting, absence of inversion and a superconducting transition do not supply those steps. Likewise, a crystal's effective spin–orbit texture cannot be inferred quantitatively from a simple atomic-number scaling rule. Use a material-specific band model and experimentally constrained parameters before proposing a pairing mechanism or device advantage.  

 Discovery implications

Separate normal-state texture, superconducting gap, pair correlations and measured magnetic response in both language and data records. Compare field directions and sample conditions; retain corrections to theoretical papers and competing experimental interpretations. Useful spin–orbit engineering should predict an observable change under controlled gating, thickness or symmetry changes, then test it against alternatives such as orbital depairing and multiband response. An adjustable model parameter is a research hypothesis until the same model explains independent observations.

entries.text:
Scope

Altermagnetism describes compensated collinear magnetic order whose opposite-spin sectors are related by crystal operations such as rotations. It can produce momentum-dependent spin splitting without requiring spin–orbit coupling. Cancellation of the total magnetic moment does not imply degeneracy of opposite spins at every momentum. Nor does the absence of a uniform moment remove every constraint on superconducting pairing. The magnetic symmetry, the occupied bands and the proposed superconducting state must be specified separately.  

Three questions should remain distinct: whether a specimen has altermagnetic order, whether it becomes intrinsically superconducting, and whether superconducting electrodes induce correlations in a hybrid device. Evidence for one does not establish the others. A 2026 In–CrSb–In experiment provides a concrete proximity platform, so a blanket statement that experimental altermagnet–superconductor systems do not exist is outdated. That device does not establish intrinsic bulk superconductivity in CrSb.  

 Mathematical assumptions

A useful symmetry relation is E\uparrow(\mathbf k)=E\downarrow(R\mathbf k) for an appropriate crystal operation R. It need not imply E\uparrow(\mathbf k)=E\downarrow(\mathbf k). In a simple even-parity texture, \delta(\mathbf k)=d(\cos kx-\cos ky) changes sign under a right-angle rotation and vanishes along diagonal directions. This illustrates a possible angular pattern, rather than identifying a material or determining its superconducting gap.  

The Chakraborty–Black-Schaffer construction retains two low-energy states with opposite spins on different sublattices. Its onsite singlet restriction depends on those projected states: opposite spins on the same site are absent from that retained space. A two-component band Hamiltonian must therefore preserve what its components represent. Reading its Pauli matrices as ordinary spin while discarding sublattice information changes the pairing problem. The result should not be promoted to an unconditional ban covering every multiband or strongly hybridized material. 

An independent local calculation illustrates the projection explicitly. For spin \sigma=\pm1, take h\sigma=(\delta+\sigma M)\tauz+t\taux, with M>0, real hybridization t and sublattice Pauli matrices \tau. Let u\sigma be the normalized lower-band eigenvector. An imposed unit onsite singlet has projected magnitude P=|u\uparrow^T u\downarrow|. When t=0 and |\delta|<M, the two vectors occupy opposite sublattices and P=0. At \delta=0, direct diagonalization gives P=|t|/\sqrt{M^2+t^2}. Thus finite mixing changes the projection even when the imposed interaction is unchanged. 

Forty-five parameter cases verify these limits and the exchange of spin branches under \delta\rightarrow-\delta. This is an algebraic illustration, not a reproduction of the paper's full lattice calculation. It computes neither a stable superconducting phase nor a transition temperature. A nonzero projected matrix element does not establish that pairing wins over competing states; a zero matrix element in a truncated space does not by itself exclude higher-band processes. Self-consistency, available states and interaction structure remain additional questions. 

 Experimental criteria

Long and colleagues map CrSb's bulk angular electronic structure using magnetic quantum oscillations. Measurements use a 41.5 T magnet and include 0.4 K traces. Figure 3 compares angular oscillation branches with a g-wave interpretation; its displayed map is symmetrized. The comparison uses adjusted electronic bands, including a −0.11 eV shift for one pocket family and a compensating +0.015 eV shift for another. Oscillation frequencies constrain extremal orbit areas; assigning an order-parameter structure involves symmetry and band modeling. This is magnetic evidence, not a superconducting transition measurement. 

Esin and colleagues use superconducting indium contacts separated by 2 μm beneath CrSb flakes thicker than 1 μm. At 30 mK, the device shows a zero-resistance current interval; a 1.2 K trace shows suppression. They compare directional switching currents and average ten sweeps. Keep switching and return currents separate, and compare opposite current directions at the same field when assessing a diode effect. A relation involving simultaneous current and field reversal is a different test. The lowest measurement temperature is not a bulk CrSb transition temperature. 

 Limits and disputes

The CrSb device authors interpret transport asymmetries using surface and bulk spin structure and discuss finite-momentum pairing. Such interpretations are not a direct image of pair momentum or a unique measurement of triplet content. Interface transparency, field history, geometry and alternative transport mechanisms still matter. The angular quantum-oscillation result and the proximity experiment also concern different specimens and observables; they should not be combined into a single specimen-level proof of a superconducting mechanism.  

RuO2 illustrates why candidate labels require evidence dates and methods. Liu and colleagues report spin-resolved photoemission inconsistent with the proposed altermagnetic splitting in their investigated films and crystals. This challenges the assignment; it does not authorize transferring either a positive or a negative result to every strained film or interface. A superconducting transport report in a candidate material cannot establish magnetic coexistence without magnetic evidence for the relevant state. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including broader competing literature, final-version comparisons and specimen-specific verification. 

 Discovery implications

Use experiments that can distinguish mechanisms: establish the magnetic symmetry, state the interface orientation, compare current and field reversals separately, and retain the orbital or sublattice content of the model. Proposed finite-momentum or topological states require their own discriminating observations. An altermagnetic label is a starting point for a testable pairing problem, not a shortcut from zero net moment to a confirmed superconducting device mechanism.

entries.text:
Scope

A strange metal is identified through unusual normal-state behavior, often including resistivity approximately proportional to temperature after superconductivity is suppressed. It is an observational category, not a uniquely established microscopic phase or order parameter. The early Bi-based transport work and later overdoped-cuprate experiments concern particular specimens and temperature ranges. Their results do not provide a universal slope for all superconductors. Ordinary high-temperature electron–phonon transport can also be linear, so a room-temperature straight line alone is insufficient.   

This article focuses on how observations constrain explanations. Linear resistivity, a transport relaxation rate near a thermal quantum scale, proximity to a quantum critical point and a high superconducting transition temperature are separate propositions. Each requires additional evidence. Even the identity of a relevant lifetime matters: a single-particle linewidth and a current-relaxation rate need not weight scattering processes in the same way.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For a fitted normal-state curve, write \rho(T)=\rho0+AT+BT^2. This is an empirical decomposition over a stated interval; its terms do not automatically identify independent microscopic mechanisms. Define a local exponent relative to a trial residual \rhor by n{\mathrm{eff}}=d\ln(\rho-\rhor)/d\ln T, wherever the logarithm is defined. Derivatives amplify noise and depend on the residual subtraction. An exponent should therefore accompany its temperature window, uncertainty and treatment of the superconducting region.  

An independent illustration uses exactly quadratic data, \rho=\rho0+BT^2. If the trial residual differs by \epsilon=\rhor-\rho0, then n{\mathrm{eff}}=2BT^2/(BT^2-\epsilon). One hundred and eight finite-difference checks verify this relation. With the correct residual, a positive mixture of linear and quadratic terms gives n{\mathrm{eff}}=(A+2BT)/(A+BT), continuously between one and two; nine parameter cases confirm that limit. No abrupt phase boundary is required by this smooth crossover. These are synthetic checks, not fits to a paper's measurements. 

Two additional synthetic fits use \rho=10+0.1T^2 in arbitrary consistent units. A best straight line over 9\leq T\leq11 has maximum deviation below 0.4% of the mean resistivity; extending the interval to 1\leq T\leq20 raises it above 20%. Thus apparent linearity over a narrow interval can hide curvature. These percentages depend on the chosen example and are not universal acceptance thresholds. Real analysis needs residual plots, independent temperature calibration and a measurement-specific noise model. 

For parallel conducting channels, conductivities add: \sigma{\mathrm{dc}}=\sigma0+S/\Gamma in a specified Drude convention. If S and \sigma0 are constant and \Gamma\propto T, the resulting resistivity is \rho=1/(a+b/T), which is generally nonlinear. Adding channel resistivities would describe a different circuit. Temperature-dependent spectral weight and finite frequency coverage must also be tested before assigning a lifetime from the total d.c. curve. 

 Experimental criteria

Grissonnanche and colleagues measured angle-dependent magnetoresistance in Nd-LSCO at hole concentration p=0.24\pm0.005. The sample's zero-resistance transition is 11 K; the transport measurements use 45 T at 6, 12, 20 and 25 K. At the two lower temperatures, some field orientations still enter a superconducting region. A high field alone therefore does not certify that every angular data point is normal-state transport. 

Their fit separates a temperature-independent anisotropic contribution from an isotropic temperature-dependent rate, giving \alpha=1.2\pm0.4 in \hbar/\tau{\mathrm{inel}}=\alpha kBT. Total scattering is not isotropic. The analysis uses a bandwidth scale 160\pm30 meV constrained by specific heat and omits a low-temperature correction that could change it by about 20% at 6 K. Temperature stability of ±1 mK differs from absolute uncertainty of approximately ±1 K at 6 and 12 K. These qualifications belong with the extracted coefficient. 

Romero and colleagues resolve a narrower Drude channel and a broad background in two FeTe1−xSex films. The final abstract associates most condensate spectral weight with the narrower channel. In the checked author version, the scattering-rate fits use 20–40 K, and linewidths below the approximately 0.2 THz measurement limit cannot be resolved directly. Its frequency variable uses cycles per second, so h appears in \Gamma=\Gamma0+\alpha kBT/h; an angular-frequency rate instead uses \hbar. A fitted spectral decomposition is stronger evidence than assigning a lifetime from total resistance alone, but it does not uniquely determine the pairing interaction. 

Cooper and colleagues report that a low-temperature linear contribution extends over a range of LSCO dopings and tracks superconductivity. The checked abstract supports that association, not a reanalysis of its numerical curves. Magic-angle graphene measurements provide another material setting with nearly linear transport; a similar temperature exponent across systems does not prove identical scattering or pairing mechanisms. Material geometry, filling and fit assumptions must accompany cross-system comparisons.  

 Limits and disputes

The marginal-Fermi-liquid proposal organizes anomalies using an assumed charge- and spin-response spectrum. Its phenomenological success would not identify a unique microscopic origin. The original article has an erratum; this review records the correction's identity but has not independently read its contents, and therefore does not reproduce a supposedly corrected derivation. Quantum critical, incoherent-metal and phonon-based explanations require separate discriminating evidence rather than a choice made from one resistivity exponent.   

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected final passages and figures have been checked, but full version comparisons and raw-data fits remain incomplete. A slope correlation with superconductivity does not establish causation, and a channel contributing to the condensate does not identify the interaction binding its electrons. Retain alternative explanations and distinguish an experimental observable from quantities inferred through a model.  

 Discovery implications

Compare transport, spectroscopy and superconducting response on well-characterized samples, with field, geometry and temperature windows recorded. Use independent changes in disorder, pressure or filling to test whether a proposed scattering process also controls pairing. A useful discovery claim predicts an observable change and survives alternative fits; simply finding another straight resistivity curve adds a candidate observation, not a complete microscopic explanation.

entries.text:
Scope

A quantum spin liquid is a quantum magnetic state with correlations and excitations beyond a conventional ordered magnet. Absence of static magnetic order alone is not a definition that identifies it experimentally: a trivial singlet state, disorder or a finite measurement window can also suppress the expected signal. Candidate materials require positive evidence and tests of alternatives. Chiral spin liquids can break time-reversal symmetry, so preserving every conventional symmetry is not a universal requirement.   

The connection to superconductivity is a research route, not an automatic consequence. Anderson's RVB proposal motivates doping a correlated singlet state, but undoped La2CuO4 has antiferromagnetic order. A spin-only Hamiltonian has no mobile electrical charge or superconducting stiffness. Emergent neutral Majorana fermions in such a model do not make its material a topological superconductor. A specific charge sector and gauge-invariant superconducting response must be established separately.    

 Mathematical assumptions

An explicit counterexample clarifies the diagnostic problem. A product of disconnected spin singlets has \langle\mathbf Si\rangle=0 and vanishing correlations between different dimers, yet is not thereby a long-range-entangled spin liquid. For two spin-one-half singlets, direct matrix evaluation gives \langle\mathbf S1\cdot\mathbf S2\rangle=-3/4 and \langle\mathbf S1\cdot\mathbf S3\rangle=0. These finite-state checks disprove the inference from zero local moments alone; they do not classify an interacting bulk material.  

Use the honeycomb convention H=-\sum{\langle ij\rangle\alpha}J\alpha\sigmai^\alpha\sigmaj^\alpha, with Pauli matrices \sigma=2S. A Hamiltonian written with spin operators requires couplings K\alpha=4J\alpha for the same energy. The vortex-free zero-field matter spectrum has zeros when the three |J\alpha| satisfy triangle inequalities. Kitaev calls this the gapless B region, including isotropy; the dominant-coupling A regions are gapped. The source draft had these labels reversed. 

Near isotropy, a weak field with all three spin-axis components nonzero generates a time-reversal-breaking term scaling as hxhyhz/J^2 at third order. This perturbative result is not exact solvability at arbitrary field. For an ideal equilibrated chiral Majorana edge above a gapped bulk, \kappa{xy}^{2D}/T=c-\pi^2kB^2/(3h) with c-=\pm1/2. This is thermal conductance per layer, not three-dimensional conductivity or electrical Hall conductance. Independent checks verify the phase-boundary algebra, spin normalization and positive-energy thermal integral. 

For a gapped two-dimensional topologically ordered ground state and a sufficiently large smooth region, S=\alpha L-\gamma+\cdots with \gamma=\ln\mathcal D and \mathcal D=\sqrt{\suma da^2}. The Abelian Z2 example gives \gamma=\ln2. This expression is not a universal entropy formula for every gapless spin liquid, and a single entropy constant does not fully specify anyon statistics. Finite geometry, boundaries and correlation length matter before identifying a universal term. 

 Experimental criteria

Shimizu's organic candidate kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3 shows no proton-NMR signature of long-range magnetic order down to 32 mK. The single-crystal experiment applied 2.2 T perpendicular to the conducting planes; the susceptibility-derived exchange scale around 250 K came from a separate fit. Neither number is a superconducting transition temperature, and the experiment does not directly observe the zero-field, zero-temperature ground state. Kurosaki's pressure phase diagram separately connects the correlated insulator with metallic and superconducting regions; it does not identify a unique pairing mechanism.  

Pustogow's 2023 strain-transport study instead favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic material's 6 K anomaly. Its hydrostatic-equivalent pressure is inferred from comparison with transport data, rather than directly applied hydrostatic pressure. The paper retains a gapped chiral-spin-liquid alternative and discusses mounting-related microcracks. Thus a revised interpretation must preserve both the measured anomaly and the remaining discrimination problem. 

Han's neutron study used deuterated herbertsmithite, ZnCu3(OD)6Cl2, at 1.6 K. Broad momentum-energy scattering supports the authors' fractionalization interpretation, but the measured low-energy signal can include interlayer Cu defects. The apparent absence of a gap down to the measured energy limit does not establish a universally gapless intrinsic kagome state. A later primary study explicitly analyzes correlated impurity contributions. Preserve isotope, background subtraction, resolution and momentum window before comparing these results with a theoretical continuum.  

In alpha-RuCl3, zero-field magnetic order and candidate field-induced behavior must be separated. Xing's 2025 ultraclean-crystal study reports a narrower near-half-quantized thermal Hall plateau and weakened oscillation-like features. It discusses sample-dependent magnetic boundaries, possible stacking faults and phonon-edge coupling. The 5.0 K Hall measurement used heat current along b and field along a; the comparison crystal was measured at 4.3 K. These are not identical conditions or a universal material threshold. 

Shragai's 2026 ultrasound study measures acoustic Faraday rotation and infers a phonon Hall-viscosity contribution. Its conversion to thermal transport requires assumptions about frequency, phonon branches and viscosity components; the directly measured single-component estimate does not independently measure every thermal carrier. One displayed comparison also combines 2 K, 55-degree-tilted ultrasound with 4.9 K, 45-degree-tilted thermal data. This supplies substantive phonon evidence without making every field geometry or claimed quantized plateau equivalent. 

 Limits and disputes

A continuum, a low-temperature heat-capacity term, absent NMR splitting and a thermal Hall signal test different observables. Their interpretation depends on defects, phonons, magnetic order, probe time scales and sample history. Do not turn one positive signal into a sufficient spin-liquid criterion, or one disputed material interpretation into a claim about every possible quantum spin liquid. Broad statements that all materials are settled or that none can ever be established would exceed this review.     

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The present check covers selected primary passages, figures and restricted independent models. Several references retain abstract-only or earlier manuscript scopes; complete final-version comparisons, defect subtraction, thermal calibration and raw-data reproduction remain unfinished. The exact-model results and experimental interpretations are therefore presented at different evidence levels.        

 Discovery implications

Track the insulating magnetic state, tuning parameter and superconducting response independently. For a pressure or doping trajectory, distinguish structural changes and disorder from changed bandwidth or filling. Compare several probes on characterized samples and ask what would exclude a trivial singlet, ordered or disordered alternative. A successful spin-liquid model provides testable mechanisms and excitations; establishing superconductivity additionally requires mobile charge, phase coherence and the corresponding experimental criteria.

entries.text:
Scope

A Planckian-scale claim compares a defined relaxation rate with kBT/\hbar. It must identify the observable, residual subtraction and uncertainty. Charge transport, optical response, single-particle decay and quantum scrambling need not share one lifetime. An approximate coefficient near unity is an empirical observation within a model, not a universal theorem obtained from a straight resistivity curve. 

The evidence has several levels: measured conductivity, an extracted rate, a cross-material scaling relation, and a proposed bound. Moving between them adds assumptions. Bruin's transport comparison, Legros's cuprate analysis, angular magnetoresistance and frequency-resolved film measurements test different parts of this chain. A useful comparison retains each experiment's conditions instead of pooling every quoted coefficient.    

 Mathematical assumptions

Write \gamma{\mathrm{tr}}=\gamma0+\alpha{\mathrm{inel}}kBT/\hbar. Then \alpha{\mathrm{tot}}=\hbar\gamma{\mathrm{tr}}/(kBT)=\alpha{\mathrm{inel}}+\hbar\gamma0/(kBT). A constant residual rate makes the total ratio temperature dependent even when the inelastic slope is fixed. Twenty-seven independent synthetic parameter checks verify this algebra; they do not justify additive scattering in a material. 

With temperature-independent density and mass in a single-band Drude model, \rho=m^\ast\gamma{\mathrm{tr}}/(ne^2) gives \alpha{\mathrm{inel}}=(\hbar ne^2/kBm^\ast)d\rho/dT. A two-dimensional, spin-degenerate parabolic band instead uses sheet slope A1^\square, areal density n{2D} and TF=\pi\hbar^2n{2D}/(m^\ast kB), yielding A1^\square TF=\alpha{\mathrm{inel}}h/(2e^2). The geometric conversion and mass estimate are essential inputs, not outputs of a resistivity slope. Noncircular or multiple Fermi surfaces require additional analysis. 

An independent angular-scattering illustration makes the lifetime distinction explicit. On a circular Fermi line, define an elastic event kernel W(\theta)=\gamma[1+a\cos\theta]/(2\pi) with |a|\leq1. The event rate is \int0^{2\pi}W\,d\theta=\gamma, whereas current relaxation weights changes of direction: \int0^{2\pi}W(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta=\gamma(1-a/2). Fifteen numerical quadratures verify both integrals. Forward-weighted events therefore relax current less efficiently in this specified model. The event rate is explicitly defined; it is not silently identified with a spectral half-width. This elastic Boltzmann example proves neither a quantum bound nor a superconducting mechanism. 

For a fitted Drude denominator \Gamma-i\nu, both variables use cycles per second. The corresponding decay rate is \gamma=2\pi\Gamma, so \Gamma=\alpha kBT/h and \gamma=\alpha kBT/\hbar have the same dimensionless coefficient after conversion. Mixing the conventions without converting the fitted width changes the apparent coefficient by 2\pi. Parallel channels add conductivities, further limiting inference from total resistance. 

 Experimental criteria

Bruin and colleagues report linear resistivity in Sr3Ru2O7 at 7.9 T and use independently characterized Fermi-surface inputs to estimate scattering. The retrieved opening page describes a 1.5–400 K transport study and a field-induced nematic region below 1.2 K near that field. Those boundaries matter: the available page does not justify extending the measured law through the intervening phase or verify every cross-material fit. The remaining article pages and supplementary tables are outside this check. 

Legros's author manuscript compares sheet-resistance slopes with Fermi-temperature estimates. Its electron-doped comparison gives \alpha=1.0\pm0.3; the hole-doped estimates require more approximate geometry and specific-heat masses, with temperature-dependent mass an explicit complication in Nd-LSCO. The displayed \alpha=1 prediction is a tested assumption, not an independent lifetime measurement. This article uses selected author-version passages; a complete comparison with the final publication remains open. 

Grissonnanche's final Nd-LSCO analysis separates an isotropic temperature-dependent component from anisotropic elastic scattering and reports \alpha=1.2\pm0.4. The band-energy scale is constrained by specific heat, and the quoted uncertainty includes fitting and sample-geometry contributions. Measurements at 45 T include superconducting angular sectors at the lower temperatures; those sectors are excluded. Neither a large applied field nor the isotropic inelastic term makes every datum normal-state or the total scattering isotropic. 

Romero's author manuscript fits two FeTe1−xSex films over 20–40 K using a narrow Drude contribution plus a broad background. It reports cycle-frequency coefficients 3.02 for x=0.45 and 2.42 for x=0.35, with widths below 0.2 THz unresolved in its spectral window. These are author-version fit values, not newly reproduced final-paper estimates. The published abstract confirms a parallel-channel interpretation; complete version comparison and fitting covariance remain open. A linear narrow-channel width can coexist with nonlinear total resistivity. 

 Limits and disputes

The conditional chaos result \lambdaL\leq2\pi kBT/\hbar bounds exponential growth of a suitable regularized out-of-time-order correlator. Its argument requires thermal-strip analyticity and boundedness, controlled factorization errors and separated dissipation and scrambling scales. This is not a measured charge-transport rate; identifying the exponent with one requires another, model-specific argument. The theorem alone neither fixes a transport coefficient to one nor verifies a material's inferred mass.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected primary passages, figures and independent model checks do not constitute raw-data reproduction. Distinguish published results from the author's interpretation of universality; preserve unresolved frequency coverage, final-version and calibration limits. Spectral weight entering a condensate also does not identify the pairing mediator.   

 Discovery implications

Compare rates only after aligning channel definitions, sample conditions and frequency units. Test whether alternative band weights or a temperature-dependent mass can explain the same measured curve. Then seek independent optical or angle-dependent constraints. A connection between normal-state relaxation and superconductivity is a research hypothesis to test; faster scattering does not, by itself, predict a higher transition temperature.

entries.text:
Scope

A pseudogap denotes suppressed low-energy spectral weight without requiring a fully gapped insulator or coherent superconductivity. In cuprates the term connects observations from nuclear magnetic resonance, photoemission, tunnelling and transport, but those probes interrogate different responses. A reported T^ must retain its material, doping, observable and onset criterion. It need not be one universal transition temperature shared by every probe.   

The central question is which microscopic processes produce these changes and how they relate to superconductivity. Pairing, charge or magnetic order and strong-correlation scenarios remain distinguishable explanations. Observing a gap above Tc, a charge modulation or a Hall anomaly does not independently identify a unique origin. The original source chapter is retained, but its misattribution of Wise's STM sample to Na-CCOC is corrected here to Pb/La-substituted Bi2201.     

 Mathematical assumptions

A useful non-uniqueness example is the two-level matrix H=\begin{pmatrix}\xi&\Delta\\\Delta&-\xi\end{pmatrix} with real \Delta. Its diagonal retarded resolvent is G{11}(z)=(z+\xi)/(z^2-\xi^2-\Delta^2), where z=\omega+i\eta and \eta>0. The spectral function is A{11}=-\operatorname{Im}G{11}/\pi. Its poles lie at E\pm=\pm\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}, with positive weights (1\pm\xi/\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2})/2. Three hundred fifteen numerical comparisons verify the resolvent against this pole decomposition; four finite-window integrations recover almost all spectral weight, with small Lorentzian tails outside the window.  

In a perfectly nested density-wave illustration, the matrix acts on two electron momenta; in a BCS illustration it acts on a particle–hole Nambu basis. The same diagonal spectrum can therefore accompany physically different off-diagonal correlations. This independently checked example does not model an actual cuprate, establish nesting or calculate phase stiffness. It shows why a spectral gap alone cannot select the broken symmetry. Additional momentum, spin, phase-sensitive and thermodynamic information must constrain the interpretation.  

For the Hall comparison, nH=V/(eRH) expresses a number per chosen structural unit when V is the corresponding volume. Its interpretation as carrier density requires transport assumptions; multiple bands, mobility imbalance, Fermi-surface reconstruction and scattering anisotropy can alter RH. The high-field inference is consequently stronger when accompanied by magnetoresistance and specimen calibration, and it cannot be transferred unchanged to zero-field spectra. 

 Experimental criteria

Warren's YBa2Cu3O6.7 study reports a decrease of planar Cu nuclear relaxation below about 100 K, above its bulk superconducting transition. The authors discuss spin pairing as a possibility; the abstract does not establish Cooper-pair phase coherence. Alloul's 89Y NMR work separately constrains spin susceptibility through shifts and relaxation. Ding's underdoped Bi2212 ARPES reports an anisotropic normal-state pseudogap evolving into the superconducting gap. These historical results are checked at primary-abstract scope here, without reproducing their lineshape or calibration analyses.   

Wise's final paper measures Pb/La-substituted Bi2201. Its Figures 1–2 compare conductance maps at 6 K: specimens labelled by Tc=35,32,25 K have modulation periods approximately 6.2,5.1,4.5a0, respectively. The wavelength varies with doping, while the reported modulation is nondispersive over the investigated bias window. That supports the authors' charge-order interpretation within these measurements; it neither proves a universal pseudogap mechanism nor assigns their data to Ca2−xNaxCuO2Cl2, which appears as cited earlier work. The 6 K mapping temperature is not a transition. 

Rullier-Albenque's YBCO analysis uses pulsed fields up to 55–60 T along the c axis and a normal-state magnetoresistance background to extract excess conductivity. The author v2 defines a fluctuation-onset threshold of 10^3\,(\Omega\,\mathrm{m})^{-1}; the earlier v1 prints 10^{-3} at that location, so version choice matters. Figure 8 shows distinct doping trends for the fluctuation onset and pseudogap scale. This constrains the identification of the entire pseudogap region with superconducting fluctuations. The threshold is an operational sensitivity criterion, not a universal thermodynamic boundary. 

Badoux's Hall measurements reach 88 T. The author Figure 4 compares YBCO samples at 50 K using values measured or extrapolated to 80 T, with about 15% uncertainty in the absolute Hall coefficient. The inferred change near p^=0.19\pm0.01 is separated from the charge-reconstruction endpoint near p=0.16. Those values belong to this material analysis. The two highest dopings use Ca substitution, and the figure also incorporates comparison data from other cuprates; it must not be presented as one homogeneous specimen series or an unconditional carrier count. 

 Limits and disputes

Sordi's calculation obtains a pseudogap and a nearby Widom crossover in a square-lattice Hubbard model using a 2 × 2 plaquette CDMFT approximation at U=6.2t. Spectral, spin and singlet-probability criteria approach the compressibility crossover near the model's critical endpoint. Competing broken symmetries are unnecessary for that calculation to produce a pseudogap, but this does not exclude their role in real materials. The plotted conversion using t=0.35 eV is a model choice, not a universal experimental temperature calibration. 

Magnetic interpretations also remain contested. Fauqué reports translation-preserving polarized-neutron magnetic order; Croft reports no corresponding order in two underdoped YBCO specimens. Croft's upper bound depends on the assumed current pattern and experimental sensitivity. The linked 2018 Comment and Reply are recorded as identities, not as a dispute resolved by this review. Neither one positive signal nor one null result establishes the origin of every pseudogap observation.    

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Historical abstracts, selected figures and toy spectra do not replace full final-version comparisons, raw-data reproduction or a comprehensive competing-literature assessment. Maintain separate definitions for a gap magnitude, crossover onset, charge modulation and superconducting transition.   

 Discovery implications

Seek predictions that discriminate between explanations on characterized specimens. Compare the same doping and field conditions across spectroscopy, transport and symmetry probes; test whether disorder or controlled tuning separates pairing fluctuations from the larger spectral suppression. A promising theory should explain both supporting observations and boundary cases instead of treating every normal-state anomaly as its confirmation.

entries.text:
Scope

A charge-density wave (CDW) modulates the electronic density at a finite wave vector, often together with atomic displacements. Cuprates and kagome compounds exhibit several distinct charge-order patterns. Their coexistence or competition with superconductivity depends on composition, temperature, field, pressure and the probe's spatial and temporal resolution. Neither a density modulation nor a nearby superconducting dome identifies the pairing interaction.    

This page addresses observations and their interpretation. Pair-density waves instead modulate the superconducting pair field; spin-density waves modulate magnetization. Charge order, structural chirality, broken time-reversal symmetry and superconducting chirality are different claims. The retained source chapter's citation of Stahl for the conjoined-CDW paper is corrected: that paper is by Li and colleagues; Stahl's temperature-dependent stacking study has a different DOI.    

 Mathematical assumptions

A single-component modulation can be written as \rho(\mathbf r)=\rho0+\operatorname{Re}[\rho{\mathbf Q}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}]. Peak position identifies periodicity, while width constrains correlations under a stated line-shape model. For the illustrative lattice correlation C(n)=r^{|n|}, with r=e^{-1/\xi} and \xi in lattice spacings, the Fourier sum is S(q)=(1-r^2)/(1+r^2-2r\cos q). Here q is dimensionless radians per spacing, measured from the ordering wave vector. Finite \xi produces a finite-width peak; observing that peak does not establish infinite-range order. This is an independent correlation model, not a fit to the cited specimens.  

Correlation lengths also depend on resolution and conventions. If both intrinsic and instrumental profiles are Gaussian, \sigma{\rm obs}^2=\sigma{\rm int}^2+\sigmaR^2. The convention \xi=1/\sigma{\rm int} then requires momentum widths in inverse-length units. Reciprocal-lattice widths need the appropriate lattice conversion. Uncorrected 1/\sigma{\rm obs} is a lower bound within this model. Gaussian standard deviations, Lorentzian half-widths and full widths are not interchangeable; a resolution-limited peak yields a bound rather than a precisely measured divergence.  

A phenomenological free energy F=as|\Delta|^2+bs|\Delta|^4+ac|\rho{\mathbf Q}|^2+bc|\rho{\mathbf Q}|^4+g|\Delta|^2|\rho{\mathbf Q}|^2 illustrates static competition when g>0. With positive quartic coefficients, a stable interior coexistence minimum additionally requires 4bsbc-g^2>0 and positive equilibrium squared amplitudes. Competition alone neither guarantees coexistence nor determines the frequency-dependent pairing kernel. Charge fluctuations could contribute to an effective interaction in a specified microscopic model without making every observed CDW a pairing mechanism.  

 Experimental criteria

Tranquada's historical neutron result concerns Nd-substituted La1.6−xNd0.4SrxCuO4 at x=0.12. Its static stripe evidence and suppressed superconductivity should not be assigned indiscriminately to every one-eighth-doped cuprate. Ghiringhelli's resonant X-ray study adds an element-sensitive charge response in underdoped YBCO. The selected author text uses 130 meV instrumental resolution and argues for a much smaller energy bound; that bound is not a separately resolved sharp collective mode.  

Chang's 2012 experiment on detwinned ortho-VIII YBa2Cu3O6.67 finds charge-order intensity suppressed on entering the superconducting regime and enhanced by magnetic field below it. Those controlled changes support competition in this specimen. They do not isolate every field-induced change in vortices or electronic structure, and do not identify a unique microscopic interaction. 

Gerber's high-field diffraction shows additional interlayer-correlated order developing above about 15 T at 10 K. The author Figure 3 separates peaks near integer and half-integer out-of-plane coordinates and extracts Gaussian widths. Its reported lengths are explicitly uncorrected for resolution. Chang's 2016 study instead reports resolution-corrected widths: for YBCO6.67, the c-axis scale reaches about four lattice periods within the measured field range. Finite three-dimensional correlations must remain distinct from unlimited long-range coherence. These analyses cannot be combined by silently treating corrected and uncorrected widths as equivalent.  

Kagome studies probe different structures and surfaces. Liang's STM step-edge phase shift suggests 2\times2\times2 order. Stahl's bulk diffraction reports a low-temperature 2\times2\times2 structure changing to 2\times2\times4 near 60 K on warming; its null response to fields up to 10 T does not rule out broken time-reversal symmetry. Li's separate CsV3Sb5 study resolves conjoined 2\times2\times1 and 2\times2\times2 charge-order responses, with distinct resonant behavior and a roughly 4 K onset separation at 1 GPa. That separation concerns charge order, not two superconducting transitions.   

 Limits and disputes

A scattering superlattice peak needs electronic, structural and instrumental interpretation; it is not by itself proof of an exclusively electronic instability. STM conductance modulations must be compared across bias, surface termination and bulk probes. Li's surface modulation and bulk-null comparison illustrates why a surface pattern cannot automatically be promoted to a universal bulk phase. The present review does not independently reproduce those sensitivity limits or resolve every reported stacking structure.  

Mielke's accepted-manuscript abstract reports enhanced internal-field widths in KV3Sb5 below charge ordering, interpreted as time-reversal symmetry breaking. This is a normal-state charge-order claim, not a direct determination of chiral superconducting pairing. Chen's spatially modulated tunnelling signatures motivate a kagome PDW interpretation, but interpretation of the pair field requires additional evidence beyond ordinary charge contrast. Material identity, probe coupling and the superconducting transition must remain explicit.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected methods and figures, historical abstracts and independent line-shape checks do not replace full source-version comparisons, raw diffraction reproduction, all supplementary calibrations or competing-structure assessment. A Hall anomaly, a Fermi-surface pocket or a charge onset below a pseudogap scale cannot alone specify which charge structure causes reconstruction or whether it mediates pairing.   

 Discovery implications

Preserve the measured wave vector and reciprocal units, sample composition, oxygen order, field direction, pressure medium, line shape and resolution treatment. Compare competing-order amplitudes on characterized specimens and distinguish a static order parameter from dynamic spectral weight. Useful predictions should connect a particular charge structure to a testable electronic reconstruction and superconducting response, including results that could falsify the proposed connection.

entries.text:
Scope

A spin-density wave (SDW) is a spatial modulation of magnetization. Static order, fluctuating magnetism and superconductivity are distinct observations. Chromium, iron arsenides and cuprate stripes supply different examples; their microscopic interactions need not be identical. A spin order parameter can couple to charge and lattice distortions. Calling a state magnetic does not imply that the lattice is uninvolved.   

Overhauser demonstrated an instability of the uniform electron gas within Hartree–Fock theory, near twice the Fermi wave vector. This is a foundational model result, not an exact solution for all interacting metals. Similarly, a spin-fluctuation calculation that favors a sign-changing superconducting gap establishes a candidate mechanism under its assumptions, not a measurement of the pairing phase.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Write \mathbf M(\mathbf r)=\operatorname{Re}[\mathbf M{\mathbf Q}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}]. A complex vector amplitude describes either collinear or rotating magnetization. In a continuum single-harmonic example, the Fourier coefficient of |\mathbf M(\mathbf r)|^2 at +2\mathbf Q is (\mathbf M{\mathbf Q}\cdot\mathbf M{\mathbf Q})/4. This dot product has no complex conjugation. For \mathbf M{\mathbf Q}=m e^{i\phi}(1,i\epsilon,0) it is proportional to 1-\epsilon^2: a collinear wave has a scalar second harmonic, while a circular helix has constant magnitude. These independent algebraic examples illustrate possible couplings, not fits to chromium data. 

For the illustrative free energy F=\kappa|\rho{2\mathbf Q}|^2+\lambda[\rho{2\mathbf Q}^{}(\mathbf M{\mathbf Q}\cdot\mathbf M{\mathbf Q})+\mathrm{c.c.}], with \kappa>0 and real \lambda, minimization gives \rho{2\mathbf Q}=-\lambda(\mathbf M{\mathbf Q}\cdot\mathbf M{\mathbf Q})/\kappa. The coupling absorbs normalization conventions. Vanishing of this particular scalar coupling for a circular helix does not exclude other spin–orbit or lattice responses. Commensurate harmonics that coincide modulo a reciprocal vector require a separate treatment. 

Wave-vector notation is part of an experimental claim. Lumsden uses a tetragonal in-plane lattice spacing a, while the Fe square lattice has \tilde a=a/\sqrt 2 and rotated axes. Its tetragonal (1/2,1/2) corresponds to square-lattice (1/2,0) in reciprocal-lattice units, or (\pi/\tilde a,0) in inverse-length coordinates. Huang's crystallographic (101) and Wang's orthorhombic (1,0,0) must retain their own basis and out-of-plane convention. Identical-looking tuples need not identify identical momenta.   

 Experimental criteria

Rotter's parent BaFe2As2 study reports a magnetic/structural anomaly near 140 K. Its 5.2 T Mössbauer hyperfine field at 77 K is a local internal field, not an applied-field threshold for superconductivity. Huang's neutron abstract reports a 0.87(3)\,\muB ordered moment per Fe along the longer orthorhombic axis. These parent studies must remain separate from Rotter's K-doped superconducting discovery.  

In de la Cruz's LaOFeAs parent specimen, the structural transition near 155 K precedes magnetic ordering at 137(3) K. Nuclear-normalized neutron intensities give 0.36(5)\,\muB per Fe at 8 K. The fluorinated superconducting specimen is separate. The paper's constrained structural refinement admits an orthorhombic description under specified atomic coordinates; its in-plane moment direction is not resolved. These qualifications prevent a structural label or moment direction from being transferred uncritically between compounds. 

Lumsden's BaFe1.84Co0.16As2 exhibits a superconducting-state resonance at 8.6\pm0.5 meV, compared at 10 K and 30 K, without detected long-range antiferromagnetic order. The dynamical peak is not a static magnetic Bragg peak. The composition is Ba(Fe0.92Co0.08)2As2: Co fractions in these two formula conventions differ by a factor of two. An intensity-onset fit is not an independently established bulk superconducting transition criterion. 

FeSe makes the probe distinction concrete. Böhmer's low-frequency NMR relaxation increases below the structural transition; the authors argue against a magnetic driver of nematicity. Wang's later neutron study observes finite-energy stripe fluctuations already above that transition and enhanced below it. Its neutron spectra use orthorhombic coordinates and a different energy window from NMR. The results must be compared through probe sensitivity, not reduced to “magnetism absent” versus “magnetism present.” Wang interprets the enhancement as supporting spin-driven proposals; it does not uniquely prove causation.  

 Limits and disputes

The absence of conventional static magnetic order in ambient-pressure FeSe does not exclude magnetic fluctuations or imply the same behavior under pressure. Conversely, a magnetic resonance supports particular coherence-factor interpretations only with a specified gap structure, continuum and susceptibility model. It does not uniquely establish the pairing interaction. This page makes no blanket claim that an entire materials family lacks phase-sensitive experiments.   

Coexisting magnetic and superconducting signals require spatial and sample controls. Pratt's experiments and Fernandes's model address competition and coexistence under particular conditions; neither makes a bulk-average signal a universal microscopic-coexistence proof. Pratt's author manuscript and final abstract give different transition numbers, so this page imports no transition record from that unresolved comparison.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Chromium is checked here at review-abstract scope; several historical sources remain abstract-only. Selected author manuscripts still require final-version comparisons. Wang's PDF states that it was corrected online, and an erratum is identified, but its exact changes have not been independently compared. The de la Cruz figure-label discrepancy also remains recorded. These limitations must travel with exported claims.     

 Discovery implications

Keep composition, coordinate basis, resolution, energy transfer, temperature, field direction and sample identity attached to each measurement. Compare static order and dynamical spectral weight separately while testing superconducting responses on characterized samples. A useful mechanism prediction should distinguish alternatives under controlled tuning, rather than infer a pairing interaction solely from neighboring magnetic and superconducting regions.

entries.text:
Scope

Electronic nematic order makes symmetry-related directions inequivalent without requiring a new translation period. For a tetragonal crystal, a common example is spontaneous fourfold-to-twofold symmetry reduction. Resistivity anisotropy is a possible response, not a universal definition of the order parameter: external strain, pre-existing orthorhombicity and domain populations can also make transport anisotropic. Establishing spontaneous order requires identifying the symmetry-breaking field and its zero-field limit.   

Electronic and lattice degrees of freedom with the same symmetry couple. Evidence for an electronic instability does not make the lattice irrelevant, and the small size of a distortion alone does not prove which subsystem drives the transition. Orbital polarization, unequal fluctuations at two magnetic wave vectors and structural strain are candidate coupled variables; their appearance together is not a causal ranking.  

 Mathematical assumptions

A uniform illustrative free energy is F=a\phi^2/2+b\phi^4/4+C0\epsilon^2/2-\lambda\phi\epsilon-\sigma\epsilon, with nematic variable \phi, symmetry-matched strain \epsilon and stress \sigma. In the stable symmetric regime, the relaxed modulus is C=C0-\lambda^2/a. At fixed strain, \partial\phi/\partial\epsilon=\lambda/a; stress control instead allows the lattice to relax. For a=A(T-T0), a continuous mean-field coupled instability occurs at Ts=T0+\lambda^2/(AC0). The extrapolated bare scale T0 is neither automatically the measured transition nor a superconducting temperature. Positive quartic stabilization and explicit strain conventions are required.  

Band splitting also needs a symmetry test. At a symmetry point, the independent two-orbital illustration H=\lambda{\rm so}\tauy\sigmaz+\phi\tauz has energies E\pm=\pm\sqrt{\lambda{\rm so}^2+\phi^2}, each twice degenerate. Pauli matrices \tau and \sigma act on orbital and spin space. The spin–orbit term can preserve fourfold and time-reversal symmetries even when the bands are split; the nematic term reverses sign under a quarter rotation. Thus an observed splitting alone is not a symmetry-breaking diagnosis. This minimal model omits realistic dispersions and is not a fit to FeSe. 

For pre-existing nematic order, symmetry can permit \phi(\Deltas^\Deltad+\mathrm{c.c.}) when the chosen d-wave component transforms like \phi. In the illustrative quadratic matrix with diagonal entries as(T-T{s0}), ad(T-T{d0}) and real off-diagonal h=g\phi, the highest instability is Tc=(T{s0}+T{d0})/2+\sqrt{(T{s0}-T{d0})^2/4+h^2/(asad)}, for positive slopes. The mixed gap has a common onset; anisotropic gap magnitude or critical fields do not imply separate a-axis and b-axis thermodynamic transition temperatures. Quartic terms can permit additional lower-temperature phases, which this calculation does not solve. 

 Experimental criteria

Chu's detwinned Co-substituted Ba122 crystals show larger resistivity along the shorter orthorhombic b axis. Above the structural transition, applied uniaxial stress already induces anisotropy, consistent with a substantial susceptibility. That induced response must not be relabelled spontaneous high-temperature order. Differential elastoresistance adds a strain-response measurement, with geometric backgrounds, strain transfer and residual bias requiring control.  

Böhmer's three-point bending experiment measures a normalized Young modulus along tetragonal [110]. Inferring the shear modulus uses an approximation, a noncritical background and normalization choices. Its thermodynamic treatment cannot by itself distinguish spin-driven from orbital-driven order. The Co- and K-substituted series show different Curie–Weiss behavior; the study does not establish an identical quantum critical point beneath every superconducting dome. 

Shimojima's FeSe ARPES assigns a roughly 50 meV zone-corner separation to orbital order in detwinned samples. The experiment uses different photon energies and resolutions for zone-center, zone-corner and detwinned measurements; these are not interchangeable spectra. Watson's later zone-center study resolves a spin–orbit contribution above the structural transition and additional splitting below it. Its constrained peak fits have larger uncertainty for a band partly above the Fermi cutoff. Momentum location, orbital assignment and fitting assumptions must accompany each energy scale.  

FeSe also separates static magnetism from dynamical evidence. Böhmer's NMR interpretation and Wang's later finite-energy neutron results sample different frequency windows. The absence of conventional ambient-pressure magnetic order does not exclude spin fluctuations or settle the microscopic nematic driver. Neither a structural onset nor an ARPES measurement temperature is a superconducting transition record.  

Cuprates require their own controls. Ando reports anisotropic transport in untwinned crystals and interprets it in terms of conducting stripes. Lawler analyzes intra-unit-cell STM contrast near the pseudogap energy, with oxygen-site differences and precise lattice registration. This is not an ARPES image of Fermi arcs. Existing lattice anisotropy, chain contributions where present, spatial inhomogeneity and charge modulation must be assessed before inferring a distinct bulk nematic transition from any one signal.  

 Limits and disputes

A susceptibility enhancement or extrapolated Curie–Weiss scale supports a proposed instability within its analysis model; it is not direct observation of an uncovered zero-temperature critical point. A superconducting dome near that scale does not establish the pairing interaction. Controlled theories of nematic fluctuation enhancement remain distinct from a unique material-level mechanism, and composition-dependent deviations must stay visible.   

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Chu's correction text still needs primary verification. Selected author manuscripts require final-version comparisons, including Watson's abstract/body difference in the quoted splitting increase and Shimojima's transition labels. Full strain calibration, ARPES fitting and STM registration have not been independently reproduced. No precise transition record is extracted from unresolved version differences.    

 Discovery implications

Combine symmetry-resolved strain response with structural, magnetic and momentum-resolved measurements on documented samples. Track domain history, mechanical boundary conditions, energy resolution and the reference axes used for symmetry-channel names. Predictions should specify which measurement distinguishes a primary instability from a coupled response, and whether the proposed tuning changes static order, fluctuations or both. Keep proposed pairing benefits separate from demonstrated superconducting transition shifts.

entries.title: Nonlinear Hall effect: response order, symmetry and hysteresis
entries.summary: Distinguish second-order Hall transport from ordinary field nonlinearity, anomalous Hall response, hysteresis and superconducting diode signals.
