entries.text:
Scope

A nonlinear Hall effect is a transverse response beyond first order in the driving electric field. A curved Hall-resistivity trace versus magnetic field can instead arise within ordinary linear-response transport. An anomalous Hall effect, a second-order Hall response, magnetic hysteresis and a superconducting diode signal therefore require separate measurement definitions. The second-order effect can appear in time-reversal-symmetric conductors; a zero-field linear Hall conductivity requires the relevant time-reversal symmetry to be broken.   

The familiar empirical separation into ordinary Hall and a term proportional to magnetization is not a universal definition of anomalous Hall physics. Noncollinear Mn3Sn provides a counterexample to requiring a large net ferromagnetic moment. Its magnetic symmetry matters even though the net moment is small. A hysteresis loop alone establishes history dependence, not the microscopic origin of a Hall signal.  

 Mathematical assumptions

In a fixed laboratory frame, write ja=\sigma{ab}Eb+\chi{abc}EbEc+\cdots, summing repeated indices. The spatially uniform electric-dipole second-order tensor vanishes when inversion symmetry is present. Breaking inversion is necessary for this contribution but does not guarantee an allowed nonzero component. Boundaries, finite-wave-vector effects and other response mechanisms require separate treatment. 

For the illustrative voltage law Vy=\alpha I+\beta I^2 and peak-amplitude drive I=I0\cos\omega t, the quadratic contribution is \beta I0^2[1+\cos(2\omega t)]/2. A controlled quadratic DC measurement can also establish second-order transport; detecting 2\omega is not an exclusive definition. Conversely, a thermal voltage proportional to dissipated power has the same harmonic structure, so a second harmonic is not sufficient evidence for a Berry-curvature mechanism. Phase and peak-versus-RMS conventions must be reported.  

In the two-dimensional semiclassical constant-relaxation-time model, Da=\sumn\int d^2k/(2\pi)^2\,f{n0}\partial{ka}\Omega{n,z} has dimensions of length. Time reversal makes Berry curvature odd in momentum, allowing its occupied-state integral to vanish while its dipole remains finite. The model gives a second-harmonic current proportional to (\mathbf{D}\cdot\mathcal{E}). Here \mathcal{E} is a complex field amplitude; omitted charge and Planck-constant factors must be restored consistently before numerical comparison. This is a model contribution, not the complete measured nonlinear conductivity.  

In this two-dimensional setting, a surviving mirror permits a dipole perpendicular to the mirror line, whereas an in-plane twofold rotation forces it to vanish. Thus fourfold-to-twofold nematic symmetry reduction alone does not establish a finite dipole, even before checking inversion. These two-dimensional vector rules should not be transferred unchanged to the three-dimensional dipole tensor. 

 Experimental criteria

Ma's bilayer WTe2 experiment measures transverse second-harmonic voltages while independently tuning two gates. Figure 2d compares transverse and longitudinal contacts at 50 K and 177.77 Hz; Figure 2e uses 100 K, and the systematic Figure 3 gate maps use 10 K. Those temperatures describe different measurements, not superconducting transitions. The methods test several low frequencies and specify a sine-reference phase convention. The gate-dependent hysteresis associated with ferroelectric switching is not a magnetic-field hysteresis measurement. 

Kang's few-layer WTe2 work combines Hall bars with circular devices for angular measurements. Its five-layer example is measured at 1.8 K and 137 Hz, while an eight-layer disk maps the angular response. Longitudinal and transverse first-harmonic signals help identify geometric mixing, and the disk analysis antisymmetrizes opposing injection angles. Temperature-dependent scaling suggests both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions; layer number, scattering and device geometry prevent assigning one universal nonlinear coefficient to all WTe2 samples. 

A credible identification records raw longitudinal and transverse channels, amplitude and frequency dependence, contact permutations, crystal axes, thermal stability and sweep history. Quadratic current scaling and allowed angular symmetry are necessary consistency checks for the proposed second-order contribution, but they do not alone eliminate heating or separate every scattering mechanism. Keep fixed-axis current reversal distinct from rotating the injection and voltage-measurement frame; the latter can change a reported transverse component's sign without changing the quadratic field law.   

 Limits and disputes

The superconducting diode effect concerns unequal positive- and negative-direction critical-current magnitudes. Ando's Nb/V/Ta superlattice demonstrates this through DC resistance–current measurements, rather than a transverse Hall channel. A zero-resistance window in one direction does not make the whole switching cycle lossless. Later conventional-film work identifies asymmetric vortex barriers and screening currents as possible diode mechanisms, so nonreciprocity alone does not establish exotic pairing.  

Romero's longitudinal terahertz/DC study and Yang's high-field re-entrant nickelate measurements do not supply nonlinear Hall evidence in the portions checked here. A scattering rate, nematic motivation or re-entrant zero-resistance field must not be relabelled a Hall coefficient or Hall switching field. Magnetic history can motivate additional measurements but cannot fill a missing transverse dataset.  

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected Ma final figures and methods, Kang author-manuscript methods and figures, and Sodemann's theory were checked; full artifact controls, final-version comparisons and raw-data reproduction remain incomplete. Kang's current-reversal wording additionally requires complete wiring and reference-frame reconciliation before a sign rule is exported. Ando, Nakatsuji and Hou are used at primary-abstract scope.      

 Discovery implications

Design a discrimination experiment before assigning a mechanism: state which response order is measured, which symmetry allows it, and which contact or thermal control could falsify the interpretation. When magnetic or superconducting states coexist, compare magnetization, longitudinal resistance, transverse harmonics and field history on the same documented device. Preserve two-dimensional versus bulk units and distinguish a calculated Berry-curvature dipole from the total experimental response.

entries.title: Parallel conduction channels: multiband transport and identifiability
entries.summary: Distinguish parallel conductivities from additive scattering rates, test model identifiability, and track superconducting spectral weight with explicit conventions.

materialCases.temperatureNote: 10K lowest reflectance temperature in reported series; not Tc.

entries.text:
Scope

Two bands, two Drude components, two scattering processes and two pairing channels are different claims. Independent channels experiencing the same electric field add their conductivities. Scattering events within one channel instead enter a collision problem and can add as rates only under appropriate approximations. A good fit to DC resistivity alone rarely identifies which microscopic description is correct. MgB2 illustrates why band-resolved superconducting gaps must also be distinguished from independently conducting subsystems.    

This entry concerns transport decomposition and spectral-weight accounting. A fitted component can represent a band, an orbital sector, a spatial layer or an effective relaxation scale; the label must be justified with additional evidence. Identifying carriers that contribute to the condensate does not by itself identify the interaction responsible for pairing.  

 Mathematical assumptions

For independent isotropic channels, use angular frequency \omega and the convention e^{-i\omega t}: \sigma(\omega)=\sumj Sj/(\Gammaj-i\omega), where Sj=nje^2/mj and \Gammaj>0 in the elementary Drude model. At zero field, \rho{\rm DC}=1/\sumj(Sj/\Gammaj), not the sum of channel resistivities. A broad component has \sigmaj\simeq Sj/\Gammaj only within a window where \omega\ll\Gammaj; its constant approximation cannot be integrated to infinite frequency. 

Even exact DC data admit infinitely many positive pairs with the same total conductivity. Frequency information helps, but if two linewidths are identical, their sum is exactly a single Drude peak with weight S1+S2 at every frequency. A finite frequency window can also leave a very broad component's weight and linewidth strongly correlated. Report uncertainty and competing models, not just a residual sum of squares.  

Independent scattering contributions can approximately give \Gamma=\Gamma{\rm imp}+\Gamma{\rm ph}+\cdots within one relaxation model. This Matthiessen approximation is not a prescription for adding the resistivities of parallel bands. Interchannel momentum exchange generally couples their kinetic equations: an illustrative positive relaxation matrix has diagonals \gamma1+g,\gamma2+g and off-diagonals -g. In normalized equal-density units its conductivity is \mathbf{1}^{T}C^{-1}\mathbf{1}, reducing to 1/\gamma1+1/\gamma2 at g=0. This toy model exposes the independence assumption; it is not a material fit. 

Normalization matters in spectral-weight sums. For one Drude term, \int0^\infty\sigma1(\omega)d\omega=\pi S/2. With condensate response \sigma{2,s}=Ss/\omega, the positive-frequency missing area is \pi Ss/2, provided the relevant total optical weight is conserved and backgrounds are treated consistently. Thus Ss=(2/\pi)\int0^\infty[\sigma{1,N}-\sigma{1,S}^{\rm reg}]d\omega in this convention. Cyclic frequency \nu=\omega/(2\pi) requires \Gamma\nu=\Gamma/(2\pi) and S\nu=S/(2\pi) in the same Drude form. Delta-function boundary conventions must also be stated. The numerical checks establish these model identities, not the complete historical derivation or experimental sum-rule saturation.   

 Experimental criteria

Romero's FeTe1−xSex study uses complex terahertz conductivity with a DC constraint to distinguish a narrow response from a broad background. The checked author version covers two films, x=0.45 and x=0.35, over 0.2–3 THz. The broad component is not resolved as a second complete peak, so assigning it a unique scattering rate or a second Planckian coefficient would exceed the measurement. Its displayed rate uses cycle frequency and a thermal scale proportional to kBT/h; substituting \hbar without conversion changes the convention. 

The same study compares a fitted superconducting term, a low-frequency extrapolation of \nu\sigma2, and a missing-area analysis. These are useful consistency comparisons but share measured spectra and modeling assumptions; they are not three independent experimental replications. Near the transition, a finite-width low-frequency response complicates extrapolation to zero frequency. The normal reference temperature, unmeasured low-frequency region and residual background must remain part of any condensate-weight claim. 

Qazilbash's LaFePO experiment combines in-plane reflectance with ellipsometry and Kramers–Kronig-compatible optical extraction. The final paper analyzes a low-frequency Drude response, higher-energy interband transitions and an extended-Drude scattering rate. Its comparison of integrated optical weight with band theory supports a correlation interpretation under that analysis; it does not establish exactly two independent Drude carriers throughout the iron-based family. The reported kinetic-energy ratio has extraction bounds, rather than being an exact universal one-half. 

MgB2 supplies a complementary comparison. Liu and Choi calculate band-dependent electron–phonon pairing, while Souma resolves different superconducting gaps on sigma and pi bands by photoemission. Choi's coupled calculation has a common transition. These results do not authorize treating the bands as two unrelated superconductors with separately assigned transition temperatures, or translating gap values into Drude scattering rates. Surface-sensitive spectroscopy and bulk optical transport retain different measurement conditions.   

 Limits and disputes

A spectral decomposition is not unique simply because it is causal or fits both real and imaginary conductivity. Independent Fermi-surface, mass, Hall and magnetoresistance constraints can narrow possibilities, while interband optical transitions and coupled scattering can invalidate a simple channel interpretation. Optical spectral weight, a transport lifetime and a superconducting gap are different quantities; no universal cross-material conversion is justified here.    

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The Romero author manuscript's printed missing-area prefactor differs from the normalization implied by its Drude numerator; the final paper and calibration must be compared before importing precise condensate fractions. The LaFePO supplement and complete historical sum-rule derivations have not been checked. Independent model integrations do not resolve those source-version questions or reproduce the experimental data.    

 Discovery implications

First specify what would distinguish two physical channels from an effective two-component fit. Extend the measurement window where possible, constrain the DC limit, document tensor geometry, and test whether fitted weights and rates remain stable when backgrounds or cutoffs change. For superconducting spectral transfer, compare a justified normal-state reference with the regular superconducting response and quantify missing bandwidth. A successful transport decomposition constrains candidate mechanisms; it does not identify a unique pairing interaction.

entries.title: Hall-coefficient sign reversal: carriers, mobility and evidence
entries.summary: Separate a Hall sign change from a Hall-number inference, account for multiband mobility and anomalous terms, and retain each experiment's normal-state boundary.

materialCases.sample: Tsukada epitaxial LSCO films on SrTiO3; room-temperature doping series
materialCases.temperatureNote: Hall measurement temperature, not a superconducting transition temperature.
Hall measurement temperature, not a superconducting transition temperature.

entries.text:
Scope

A Hall-coefficient sign reversal is a change in the sign of the transverse response under a declared wiring and field convention. It is distinct from a change in Hall magnitude, a peak, or an inferred Hall number. Electron and hole contributions can exchange transport weight without either Fermi-surface pocket disappearing. Neither a sign change nor a Hall anomaly by itself proves superconductivity, a Lifshitz transition or a particular pairing mechanism.    

Here Ey=RHJxBz defines the sign. The elementary single-band Drude values are RH=-1/(ne e) for electrons and RH=1/(nh e) for holes, with e>0. These density interpretations require restrictive assumptions. Even a single crystalline band can have a complicated Hall response because Fermi-surface curvature and a momentum-dependent mean free path affect the weak-field conductivity. A temperature-dependent Hall coefficient is therefore not sufficient evidence for multiple bands. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For independent isotropic electron and hole Drude channels with positive mobilities and \mui B\ll1, RH=(nh\muh^2-ne\mue^2)/[e(nh\muh+ne\mue)^2]. The sign changes when the mobility-squared weights cross. Fixed carrier densities can therefore produce a reversal as the mobility ratio varies. At zero field \sigma0=e(nh\muh+ne\mue); even simultaneous values of \sigma0 and weak-field RH do not uniquely determine four density/mobility parameters. Independent tensor-inversion checks illustrate this degeneracy without fitting a material.  

Beyond weak field, add conductivity tensors and invert the sum. In the same classical model, when both \muiB\gg1 and nh\ne ne, the asymptotic slope is \rho{yx}/B\to1/[e(nh-ne)]. Exact compensation is a different limit: for nh=ne=n, \rho{yx}/B=(\muh-\mue)/[en(\muh+\mue)] at all fields in this model. A large laboratory field alone establishes neither of these asymptotic conditions. Quantum effects, coupled scattering and reconstructed bands may require a different model.  

Ordinary and anomalous contributions must also be distinguished. A schematic \rho{yx}=R0B+\rho{yx}^{A} is not a universal fit, and an anomalous term need not be proportional to magnetization with a constant coefficient. Intrinsic Berry curvature, skew scattering and side jump are distinct mechanisms. Field antisymmetrization, [\rho{yx}(B)-\rho{yx}(-B)]/2, removes even longitudinal contact leakage but retains an odd anomalous Hall contribution. It does not isolate ordinary Hall transport by itself. 

 Experimental criteria

Tsukada and Ono studied epitaxial La2−xSrxCuO4 films on SrTiO3 with residual tensile strain. Their room-temperature Hall coefficient changes from positive to negative between x=0.28 and x=0.32. The heavily overdoped samples used field sweeps to ±6 T. This is a sample-series result at 300 K, not a universal cuprate doping boundary. The x=0.32 film lacks zero resistance but has a reported resistive onset, which the authors discuss in relation to possible oxygen inhomogeneity. Describing it simply as having no superconducting evidence would erase that distinction. 

Brouet's Ba(Fe0.65Ru0.35)2As2 study reports a temperature-dependent Hall sign together with electron and hole pockets. The checked primary abstract supports that limited statement; complete transport methods and a precise reversal temperature remain unreviewed here. Mun's Co- and Cu-substituted BaFe2As2 crystals provide a separate comparison: thermopower and Hall changes occur at comparable added-electron counts, but the Cu comparison does not show the corresponding resistive superconductivity. These Hall anomalies are not a superconductivity criterion or a universal sign-change threshold.  

Mun's experiment measured composition by wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy and applied the Hall field along the crystal c axis, reversing field polarity to reduce contact offsets. Its 25 K comparison is a measurement temperature, not a transition temperature. Sample exfoliation can alter geometric factors, so normalized trends and absolute Hall magnitudes carry different uncertainties. Co/Cu substitution fraction and inferred added-electron count are also different horizontal axes. 

Iida's strained Ba(Fe1−xCox)2As2 films used MgO and CaF2 substrates and Hall measurements at 9 T. Their effective Hall number nH=V/(4e|RH|), with unit-cell volume V, is positive by construction and expressed per Fe. It discards the Hall sign and is not a direct count of all mobile carriers in a multiband metal. The reported phase-diagram alignment concerns the studied strained films and selected bulk comparisons. The superconducting temperature uses a resistive onset criterion, rather than silently substituting zero resistance or magnetic shielding. 

Badoux's YBa2Cu3Oy experiment distinguishes a charge-order reconstruction endpoint near p=0.16 from a pseudogap endpoint near p=0.19. The Hall-number interpretation changes from approximately 1+p toward p; this is not evidence for a mandatory Hall-sign reversal at the latter point. Pulsed fields reached 88 T, with a 50 K, 80 T cross-sample comparison. The author manuscript establishes normal-state access down to at least 40 K and explicitly leaves the lower-temperature p=0.16 behavior unresolved. Its vortex-melting field is not automatically the upper critical field. 

 Limits and disputes

Normal-state extraction needs more than a high-field label. Retain temperature, current, field direction, hysteresis branch and the independently justified superconducting boundary; vortex motion and magnetic contributions can contaminate a transverse signal. Yang's field-induced superconductivity study is a boundary example, not a source of an ordinary-Hall reversal field. Its superconducting phase-diagram scales must not be relabeled as Hall or anomalous-Hall thresholds.   

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Most experimental checks here cover selected author-manuscript methods, results and figures, not complete final articles or raw-data reproduction. Brouet remains abstract-scoped; Ong's full geometric derivation and the anomalous-Hall review remain incompletely read. Apparent numeric typographical inconsistencies in the Mun and Iida author versions require final-version comparison; those uncertain composition values are not adopted. The independent Drude checks establish model algebra, not a unique interpretation of any experimental Hall curve.       

 Discovery implications

Treat a sign change as a prompt to test competing transport explanations. Combine field-dependent longitudinal and transverse resistivity, magnetoresistance, magnetic characterization and independent Fermi-surface information. Compare constrained models and retain geometry, strain, oxygen content and uncertainty. A mobility crossover, reconstructed Fermi surface and anomalous contribution can produce different predictions beyond a single Hall slope; a defensible conclusion specifies which alternatives the measurements actually exclude.     

 Related topics

entries.title: Experimental methods for superconductivity
entries.summary: A practical evidence guide to fifteen probes and preparation methods: what each measures, which assumptions it needs, and what it cannot establish alone.
aliases: ARPES STM STS INS RIXS NMR muSR TDTS IR DAC MBE PLD XRD
entries.text:
Scope

Choose a probe by the observable it measures and the inference that is needed. A spectral gap, a resistance drop, a magnetic response and a thermodynamic anomaly answer different questions. This handbook connects fifteen experimental methods to concrete original studies and their limitations. It is a guide to interpreting evidence, not a universal instrument operating procedure or a catalogue of confirmed transition temperatures. The fixed I1–I15 identifiers preserve the approved reference structure.    

 Mathematical assumptions

Every inversion needs a forward model: the measured signal is affected by sample response, instrument resolution and background. Parameters are identifiable only if different allowed parameter sets produce distinguishable signals within uncertainty. The independent calculations accompanying this handbook check a triangular London-limit lattice sum, a Gaussian field-distribution transform and additive broadening. They do not reproduce an interacting material or calibrate an instrument. See I6 for the physical assumptions behind the example.  

 I1 — ARPES and synchrotron photoemission

Angle-resolved photoemission maps the energy and emission direction of electrons leaving a surface. Relating those counts to an electronic spectral function requires occupation factors, matrix elements, energy and angular resolution, and a specified momentum conversion. Photon energy and polarization can change which bands are visible; a weak feature is not automatically an absent band. Record surface preparation, sample temperature, energy reference and the fitting or symmetrization procedure alongside an extracted gap. Synchrotron access does not itself establish bulk sensitivity or remove these assumptions. 

The selected single-layer FeSe study illustrates the inference boundary. He and colleagues tracked annealing-dependent spectra and fitted the temperature dependence of symmetrized energy-distribution curves. The reported high temperature scale is a spectroscopic indication; it is not a simultaneous demonstration of zero resistance or magnetic screening in that measured layer. Band counting also used a degeneracy assumption. Compare the same preparation and carrier state across probes before identifying a superconducting transition or a causal effect of annealing. 

 I2 — Scanning tunnelling microscopy and spectroscopy

STM resolves a surface through a tunnelling junction, while STS measures its differential conductance versus bias. Interpreting that conductance as a local density of states assumes an adequately characterized tip, tunnelling matrix element and junction regime. Temperature, modulation broadening, setpoint and drift affect the apparent gap or spatial contrast. Preserve the topographic channel and acquisition conditions rather than treating every conductance feature as an intrinsic bulk excitation. A Fourier peak also needs its energy dependence and relation to the atomic lattice. 

Wise and colleagues' selected final figures concern Pb/La-substituted Bi2201; Na-CCOC appears as earlier work, not their specimen. Their spatial maps provide an example of separating a checkerboard modulation from a dispersing quasiparticle-interference interpretation. Such an assignment requires competing explanations and energy-dependent controls, rather than one visually striking image. A local gap or zero-bias peak alone does not establish bulk superconductivity, a unique gap phase or a Majorana state. Surface termination and reproducibility across fields of view belong in the evidence record. 

 I3 — Inelastic neutron scattering

INS resolves energy and momentum transferred between neutrons and a sample. Extracting a magnetic spectrum requires resolution, normalization, background and the distinction between magnetic, phonon and nuclear scattering. Single crystals preserve directional information; a powder measurement averages orientations. A resonance at a superconducting transition can constrain a model of the gap and magnetic susceptibility, but the assignment depends on coherence factors, band structure and competing explanations. The measured peak is not by itself a unique identification of the pairing interaction. 

Christianson and colleagues studied polycrystalline Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2, not a Co-substituted sample. The selected methods specify the MERLIN time-of-flight instrument, several incident energies and vanadium normalization. Their below/above-transition comparison used 7 K and 50 K. Energy and momentum integration windows, the elastic-scattering cutoff and a possible small phonon contribution matter when interpreting the resonant excess. A background-subtracted excess fading near the transition must not be described as every count or all magnetic scattering disappearing. Full detector-data reanalysis remains outside this handbook's review. 

 I4 — Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering

RIXS measures the energy and momentum lost by resonantly scattered photons. The chosen absorption edge, incoming and outgoing polarization, scattering geometry and intermediate-state dynamics determine which excitations contribute. Elastic, orbital and magnetic channels must be separated with the actual resolution and model. A measured magnetic dispersion can inform a pairing theory, but does not alone prove that the observed excitation is the pairing mediator. Small-volume sensitivity also does not eliminate surface, self-absorption or normalization questions. 

Ament and colleagues' local tetragonal Cu model makes the selection rule concrete: a direct spin flip forbidden for a moment along the orbital normal can become allowed for an in-plane moment at the L or M edge. That result cannot be transferred unqualified to the K edge. Their collective example uses an ultrashort-core-hole expansion and a Heisenberg spin-wave model. The accessible momentum range at the M edge is much smaller than at L3. Preserve these conditions when comparing intensities or calling a missing peak evidence against magnetism. 

 I5 — NMR and Knight shift

NMR probes nuclei through resonance shifts and relaxation. A Knight-shift interpretation must separate spin, orbital and diamagnetic contributions and specify the field direction, site and hyperfine coupling. The spin susceptibility inferred in an applied field is not automatically the zero-field response of an unperturbed condensate. Relaxation and shift provide complementary information; neither can be replaced by a single pairing-symmetry label without its model and control measurements. Temperature calibration is especially important when the excitation pulse itself can heat a small sample. 

Pustogow and colleagues' selected oxygen-17 Sr2RuO4 manuscript explicitly examines radio-frequency pulse energy and heating. Its zero-strain and strained measurements use different fields, so those datasets cannot be merged as though strain were the only changed variable. A reduced spin contribution constrains candidate states under the stated field and spin-orbit conditions; it does not uniquely determine every orbital, band or parity component. Report which nucleus, spectral line, strain state, field and reference were compared, and retain the author's pulse-control qualification. 

 I6 — Muon spin rotation and relaxation

Muon polarization samples an internal-field distribution. Transverse-field vortex measurements can constrain penetration depth through a field-profile model; zero-field relaxation and a muon Knight shift address different questions. Brandt's ideal triangular London limit gives \langle\delta B^2\rangle\simeq0.00371\Phi0^2/\lambda^4 only in its restricted field and large-\kappa regime. An independent reciprocal-lattice sum converges to 0.0037107353. This does not validate the approximation near either critical field or for a strongly disordered lattice. The paper's variance symbol must not be mistaken for a relaxation rate.  

For a Gaussian field distribution, P(t)=\exp[-(\gamma\mu\Delta B\,t)^2/2] in a rotating frame, with angular gyromagnetic ratio. A convention without the one-half changes the named rate. Independent numerical integration checks this normalization. Sonier and colleagues show why magnetism and vortex disorder can change the inferred penetration depth and its temperature dependence; their competing fits are not a unique gap assignment. Under an illustrative independent-Gaussian model, unassigned extra broadening would bias an inferred penetration depth downward. Real non-Gaussian or correlated contributions require a fuller model. 

 I7 — Time-domain terahertz spectroscopy

TDTS records an electric-field waveform, giving amplitude and phase over a finite frequency window. Recovering complex conductivity requires a sample/reference comparison and a justified optical model for the film, substrate and interfaces. Thickness, time-window choices, multiple reflections and calibration can affect the inversion. The real and imaginary parts must be fitted consistently; a narrow unresolved channel can resemble a different low-frequency response. Keep angular frequency and ordinary frequency distinct when comparing a fitted scattering rate with a temperature scale. 

Romero and colleagues' selected author manuscript describes MBE-grown FeTe1−xSex films and a conductivity model constrained by DC transport. It separates a narrow channel from a broader response. The stated rate convention uses ordinary frequency, hence a comparison with kBT/h, rather than silently substituting kBT/\hbar. The reviewed manuscript's spectral-weight normalization needs a final-version/calibration comparison; this handbook therefore does not adopt an exact condensate fraction. A finite-frequency inductive response must also be distinguished from a demonstrated equilibrium zero-resistance transition. 

 I8 — Infrared spectroscopy

Infrared measurements constrain charge dynamics through reflectance, transmission or ellipsometry. Converting them to conductivity requires an optical model and, for reflectance-only reconstruction, justified extrapolations outside the measured range. Intraband response, interband transitions, phonons and substrate contributions may overlap. State the frequency convention, integration limits and reference spectrum before comparing a spectral weight or an apparent missing area. An absorption feature is not automatically a superconducting gap, and extracting an effective bosonic spectrum is a model-dependent inverse problem. 

Qazilbash and colleagues' LaFePO study combines reflectance and ellipsometry with a Kramers–Kronig and extended-Drude analysis. Its experimental-to-band kinetic-energy comparison depends on the chosen intraband window and band reference. It is not a universal two-Drude prescription for every iron compound. Reproducing the plotted ratio requires the actual integration and subtraction, rather than copying a material-independent correlation factor. Compare temperature, composition, polarization and spectral windows before combining results from separate crystals. Complete raw-spectrum and supplementary checks remain open in the present source review. 

 I9 — Andreev and tunnelling spectroscopy

A normal-metal/superconductor contact probes conversion between electron and hole excitations as well as ordinary transmission. Barrier transparency, mode mixing, temperature and bias determine whether an ideal Andreev-scattering model applies. In a tunnelling limit, spectral weighting and broadening still matter. Contact heating, nonuniform current paths and multiple channels can change a conductance curve without implying a different pairing symmetry. A peak or a fitted gap should be reported with junction geometry, normalization and alternative fits, not just its preferred interpretation. 

Beenakker's selected lecture derivation treats a two-terminal conductance in the zero-temperature, zero-voltage and zero-field limit, with separately modeled normal and Andreev scattering. That domain explains why a successful ideal-channel formula is not a general finite-bias fitting routine. Preserve whether transmission probabilities refer to the normal region or to the full superconducting junction. A measured gap scale does not supply phase information automatically; sign changes and surface-bound-state interpretations require additional interface assumptions or independent phase-sensitive evidence. The full review and all microscopic contact effects have not been audited here. 

 I10 — Diamond-anvil pressure cells

A DAC changes pressure while confining a small sample, pressure medium, contacts and calibrant. The reported scalar pressure is only part of the state: gradients, deviatoric stress, thermal history and loading path can matter. Record when and where the pressure was calibrated, its uncertainty, the medium and any transition or freezing of that medium. Structural, magnetic and transport measurements performed in different cells are complementary evidence, not automatically simultaneous observations of one identical phase and sample.  

The selected pressure-medium study distinguishes solidification from loss of hydrostaticity and uses a specified warming/calibration protocol. Its thresholds should not be transplanted to another medium or cell without qualification. In Sun and colleagues' high-pressure nickelate report, the reviewed transport methods use KBr and room-temperature ruby calibration; the magnetic experiment is separate. Resistive onset and residual resistance must remain distinct. Establishing a high-pressure superconducting phase requires checking contacts, sample structure and alternative transitions, while reserving temperature records for their actual measurement criterion.  

 I11 — MBE and pulsed-laser film growth

MBE and PLD prepare films through different deposition processes; neither guarantees a desired superconducting state merely because nominal layer counts or target compositions agree. Substrate termination, oxygen history, strain, interdiffusion, thickness and subsequent annealing can change the conducting region. Treat growth diagnostics and structural characterization as evidence about the prepared object, then connect that object to transport, spectroscopy or screening. A nominally one-unit-cell film and an electronically confined interface are different descriptions that require their own support.  

The selected oxide examples illustrate this distinction. Gozar and colleagues' MBE cuprate bilayers depend on stacking order and oxygen treatment; their magnetic screening setup has a stated frequency. Reyren and colleagues' PLD LaAlO3/SrTiO3 samples combine structural preparation with low-temperature transport and separate transition analyses. These observations do not license a universal recipe for interface superconductivity or identify charge transfer as the sole cause. Compare layer order and the full preparation history before pooling samples, and preserve the difference between observed conduction, superconducting screening and an inferred thickness of the active region.  

 I12 — High magnetic fields

High-field experiments test anisotropy, depairing and field-induced phases, but the maximum available field is not itself a measured critical field. Pulsed and steady fields impose different time scales and thermal constraints. Record field orientation, sweep direction, pulse profile, sample thermometry and the observable's threshold. Resistive onset, midpoint, zero resistance and an inductive anomaly need not coincide. An extrapolation beyond the measured range must be identified as such, with the model and uncertainty retained. 

The selected UTe2 high-field study combines resistance and proximity-detector-oscillator responses in carefully specified angular geometries. Its typical 60/73 T pulse capabilities, low-temperature measurement and warmer normal reference are separate quantities. A restricted angular halo is not a generic statement about every orientation or a direct reconstruction of the order parameter. Compare warming, pulse history and background response before interpreting a new feature as reentrant superconductivity. Full supplementary pulse/calibration analysis remains open; no magnet's rated field is entered here as an experimental transition record. 

 I13 — Heat capacity

Heat capacity tests the thermodynamic response of the sample and can reveal a superconducting anomaly that complements transport. Extracting an electronic contribution requires addenda, lattice and possible magnetic-background treatment, a mass or molar normalization and a justified normal reference. A field used to suppress superconductivity can also alter other contributions. Residual terms, broad transitions and a small superconducting volume fraction can complicate gap fits. Quote the transition construction and uncertainty rather than equating every peak temperature with a resistive criterion. 

Johnston's alpha-model analysis makes model assumptions explicit. In its specified setting, an entropy comparison uses \int0^{Tc}(Cs-Cn)\,dT/T, with consistent reference states and extrapolations. A single-band phenomenological gap rescaling does not become a self-consistent multiband calculation simply by summing fitted curves. A normalized jump or low-temperature power law is consequently a constraint, not a unique coupling-strength or gap-symmetry determination. Check entropy balance, background sensitivity and competing gap models; the selected source review does not reproduce every experimental dataset or its full final version. 

 I14 — Electrical transport and Hall measurements

Transport measures a voltage response in a particular current path. Four-terminal geometry removes some lead contributions but not all problems from inhomogeneity, heating, finite voltage resolution or misplaced contacts. Specify current, field and temperature protocol, sample dimensions and the criterion for a transition. For Hall measurements, reversing the field helps isolate the odd transverse component; reversible conditions are needed, and genuine hysteresis must be retained rather than averaged away. A Hall sign is not a direct count of carrier type in a general multiband system.  

The selected Co/Cu-substituted Ba122 methods use field reversal and a defined crystal orientation, while their sample geometry contributes uncertainty. Badoux and colleagues' high-field cuprate work states temperature and field ranges over which a normal-state interpretation is available; its vortex-melting field is not automatically the upper critical field. Do not infer a zero-temperature carrier density from an inaccessible normal state. Absolute geometry error and relative temperature-dependent uncertainty are distinct, and apparently precise carrier counts require a transport model in addition to a measured Hall slope.  

 I15 — Synchrotron X-ray diffraction

Diffraction constrains periodic structure through reciprocal-space positions, intensities and widths. Lattice constants, atomic positions, occupancies, domains and modulation order involve different fitting assumptions. State photon energy, scattering geometry, reciprocal-lattice convention, temperature, field and instrument resolution. A weak superlattice peak may indicate a structural or charge modulation, but is not a direct measurement of the superconducting gap or phase stiffness. Distinguish structural refinement from evidence for a field-dependent ordering correlation length.  

The selected YBa2Cu3O6+x studies show why peak-width conventions matter. Chang and colleagues use resolution-corrected Gaussian widths, whereas the reviewed Gerber author manuscript reports uncorrected widths and corresponding lower bounds on correlation lengths. These numbers cannot be pooled as though their resolution treatment were identical. A reciprocal-space width becomes a real-space length only after specifying the line shape and units; Gaussian and Lorentzian formulas are not interchangeable. Field-induced enhancement or three-dimensional stacking constrains competing-order physics, while causal claims about superconductivity require the separate temperature and field evidence.  

 Experimental criteria

Match the probe, specimen and preparation before combining observations. A report should preserve the raw observable, reduction model, calibration, uncertainty, transition criterion and any failed controls. Distinguish a sample temperature from a gap-closing scale, a maximum applied field from a fitted critical field, and a resolution-limited width from a deconvolved correlation length. This handbook points to examples; it creates no new sample-specific Tc records.   

 Limits and disputes

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Each method has a named selected primary-source review; some use author manuscripts whose final versions and supplements have not been fully compared. Reused checks retain their original dates and limitations. The independent model calculations test stated algebra and conventions, not instrument performance or the correctness of every interpretation in a cited paper. A good fit, a successful build and agreement between summaries are not independent experimental replication.   

 Discovery implications

Design complementary tests around an explicit competing explanation. Pair local spectroscopy with a macroscopic response when the question is bulk superconductivity; combine structural and transport controls when pressure or growth can change phase identity. Preserve disagreements rather than selecting one favorable probe. A useful next experiment should distinguish hypotheses within its actual resolution, sample and calibration limits.   

 Related topics

entries.title: Theoretical tools for superconductivity
entries.summary: Twelve theoretical and computational approaches, with their inputs, convergence checks, physical assumptions and limits on predicting superconductivity.
aliases: BCS Eliashberg Allen Dynes DFT DFPT QMC DMRG DMFT RPA FLEX Wannier RG BdG
entries.text:
Scope

Theoretical tools answer different questions: whether a model has a pairing instability, how a sample responds, or which approximation is defensible. This handbook connects twelve approved topics to their inputs, outputs and limitations. A solver result is conditional on the Hamiltonian, numerical convergence and physical approximations; it is not an experimental transition record. The J1–J12 identifiers remain stable even where an old planning label needed scientific correction.   

 Mathematical assumptions

State the degrees of freedom, interactions, energy and length units, boundary conditions and limit being taken before comparing calculations. Distinguish an exact identity within a model from an approximation to a real material. The accompanying independent checks cover mass weighting, a four-state atomic Green function, Fourier interpolation, a scalar Cooper-channel flow and complex Bogoliubov matrices. They do not run a material DFT calculation, an interacting impurity solver or a full multichannel renormalization group.    

 J1 — BCS mean-field theory

BCS theory constructs a coherent many-electron paired state and a self-consistent gap. In the elementary isotropic model, the quasiparticle energy is Ek=\sqrt{\xik^2+|\Delta|^2}, with energies measured relative to the chemical potential. The familiar exponential transition scale assumes a weak attractive interaction, an energy shell and a sufficiently smooth density of states. Specify whether that density counts one spin or both; changing the convention without changing the coupling produces a different exponent. 

The Cooper problem instead places two added electrons above an inert Fermi sea. Its instability motivates pairing but does not replace the many-body gap and number equations. A BCS gap solution describes pair formation within the approximation; phase fluctuations, spatial inhomogeneity and competing order can alter the observed transition. A material's similar gap ratio is therefore a consistency check, not unique proof of a phonon mechanism. Use the full band and symmetry assumptions when extending the elementary model.  

 J2 — Eliashberg theory

Eliashberg theory retains the frequency dependence of the interaction and electronic self-energy. A phonon-mediated calculation needs an electron–phonon spectral function, a treatment of the effective Coulomb interaction and an explicitly chosen isotropic, anisotropic or multiband approximation. The gap and mass-renormalization functions are coupled. A converged solution on a Matsubara grid also needs frequency-cutoff and temperature checks; numerical precision alone does not justify neglecting vertex corrections or changes in the phonon system. 

The selected Marsiglio review provides a simple Einstein-spectrum benchmark, while Choi and colleagues' MgB2 calculation illustrates why band-dependent interactions and gaps can matter. Neither example licenses using one averaged coupling for every material. A Matsubara gap value is not automatically the measured tunnelling gap: real-frequency continuation and spectral features require care. Preserve how the Coulomb parameter was chosen and which electronic and phonon inputs were computed, fitted or assumed. The reviewed examples are scoped checks, not independent reproduction of every numerical result.  

 J3 — McMillan and Allen–Dynes estimates

Compact transition-temperature estimates summarize solutions of a specified electron–phonon theory; they do not replace its inputs. Allen and Dynes use a logarithmic phonon-frequency scale and introduce strong-coupling and spectral-shape corrections. An implementation should name which version it evaluates, preserve the effective Coulomb parameter, and state whether its frequency input is an energy, angular frequency or temperature. A number copied between these conventions without conversion can be wrong even when the expression looks familiar. 

The original abstract describes the accuracy of the modified McMillan estimate for the materials known at that time and its failure at larger coupling. That historical comparison is not a universal modern applicability boundary. Report sensitivity to the spectrum and Coulomb input, and compare a compact estimate with a suitably converged Eliashberg solution when justified. Here the original abstract was checked; the inaccessible original fit derivation and dataset are not claimed as fully reviewed. No fitted or hypothetical estimate is entered into the experimental Tc filter.  

 J4 — DFT and density-functional perturbation theory

DFT and DFPT connect an electronic-structure approximation to forces, harmonic phonons and response functions. The mass-weighted force-constant matrix D=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2} has eigenvalues \omega^2, where K is the energy Hessian. Its eigenvalues are not superconducting transition temperatures. An independent two-mass calculation checks the translational zero mode and shows that negative curvature produces a negative squared frequency; removing that sign would conceal an instability. 

Baroni and colleagues' selected formulation requires self-consistent induced charge and potential. Metallic calculations couple momentum sampling to the smearing treatment; arbitrary numerical smearing is not a physical electronic temperature. The electron–phonon spectral function also differs from the transport-weighted spectrum. Specify structure, exchange-correlation approximation, basis, sampling and response convergence before interpreting a prediction. Harmonic stability alone neither establishes superconductivity nor tests anharmonic effects, strong correlations or every competing structure. The independent checks here verify elementary mechanics, not a full first-principles workflow. 

 J5 — Hubbard-model QMC and DMRG

Quantum Monte Carlo and density-matrix renormalization group methods address interacting lattice models across different coupling regimes; they are not collectively weak-correlation methods. LeBlanc and colleagues compare several algorithms for specified two-dimensional Hubbard parameters. Agreement must be assessed observable by observable and after the relevant finite-size, temperature and algorithmic extrapolations. Agreement in ground-state energy alone does not establish a particular pairing state or a finite superconducting transition temperature. 

In the reviewed auxiliary-field formulation, particle-hole symmetry protects the half-filled model with zero next-nearest hopping from the sign problem. Away from that setting, a constrained-path calculation adds trial-state-dependent systematic error and is not generally variational. DMRG requires checks of retained states or bond dimension, truncation error, cylinder length and width, boundary conditions and competing metastable patterns. Taking cylinder length to infinity does not take its width to the two-dimensional thermodynamic limit. Historical computational sizes in a 2015 benchmark are not current hardware limits. 

 J6 — Dynamical mean-field theory

Single-site DMFT replaces a lattice environment by a self-consistent quantum impurity bath. It retains local temporal fluctuations through a frequency-dependent self-energy; it is not simply static Hartree-Fock theory. For the specified local-interaction models, its large-coordination limit becomes exact with the appropriate hopping scaling. Applied in finite dimensions, the single-site construction omits nonlocal self-energy components, so spatial correlations may require extensions or independent checks. 

The impurity Green function must equal the local lattice Green function after self-consistency. The Weiss propagator describing the bath is not generally the bare local lattice propagator. An independent four-state thermal calculation verifies the atomic-limit spectral weights and Green function, but does not validate a finite-hopping DMFT solution. State the impurity solver, bath or frequency discretization, interaction convention and convergence criteria. Two lattices with the same noninteracting density of states need not have identical magnetic response or ordered phases; local single-particle agreement is a narrower result. 

 J7 — RPA, fluctuation exchange and pairing kernels

Random-phase and fluctuation-exchange approaches organize selected interaction diagrams into response and pairing approximations. Their names do not specify the entire calculation: identify the bare or dressed propagators, orbital interaction matrix, retained channels and self-consistency. Bickers, Scalapino and White's original abstract describes self-consistent conserving approximations for two-particle correlations. Conservation properties are useful constraints, but do not make an approximation exact for arbitrary coupling or establish a measured material's pairing mechanism. 

Scalapino's selected review passages discuss a DCA vertex decomposition and a particle-particle Bethe–Salpeter eigenproblem. They illustrate how a momentum-dependent interaction and dressed propagators enter pairing analysis; those particular results must not be relabelled as an RPA or FLEX benchmark. An eigenvalue reaching the stated instability condition is conditional on the kernel and approximation. Check competing channels, resolution and the treatment of fluctuations before equating its temperature scale with a bulk experimental Tc. The full original conserving-functional derivation remains outside the reviewed scope.  

 J8 — Tight-binding and Wannier models

Wannier functions provide a localized representation of a chosen Bloch subspace. Unitary rotations within an isolated manifold preserve its projector but change the orbital shapes and hopping representation. With entangled bands, selecting the subspace and selecting its gauge are distinct tasks. The frozen inner energy window constrains which states are retained; outside it, projected bands can differ from the original calculation. A compact model therefore needs its orbital basis and energy windows, not just an attractive band plot. 

Interpolation relies on localization, a sufficient momentum mesh and adequate real-space hopping range. Independent Fourier recovery of a known finite-range model succeeds, while an undersampled distant hopping aliases into a different term despite perfect agreement on the sampled grid. Validate intermediate momenta and relevant observables. Nonzero Chern invariants can obstruct an exponentially localized representation of the isolated manifold; a different subspace or hybrid construction must be described explicitly. This check is not a material wannierization or proof that an empirical tight-binding fit is unique. 

 J9 — Renormalization group

Renormalization group methods track how an effective description changes as higher-energy modes are removed. The retained channels, cutoff, self-energy treatment and truncation determine what a flow can establish. In Shankar's stated Fermi-surface setting, angular Cooper channels decouple at one loop. With the normalization g=Vl/(4\pi) and \ell=\ln(\Lambda0/\Lambda), the selected equation gives dg/d\ell=-g^2. Negative coupling is attractive in this convention. 

Independent numerical integration agrees with g(\ell)=g0/(1+g0\ell) before its pole: attraction grows and repulsion decreases in this restricted flow. The divergence marks an instability and loss of perturbative control, not a measured Tc or a solved ordered state. The source explicitly warns that otherwise irrelevant terms can generate an attractive channel through the Kohn–Luttinger mechanism. Thus the simple positive-channel flow does not prove that every repulsive system remains a stable normal metal. Nested surfaces and additional channels require their own analysis. 

 J10 — Quantum geometry and Berry methods

Band eigenvectors carry geometric information beyond the dispersion. A quantum metric and Berry curvature can be constructed from the projector onto a specified band or subspace, with carefully stated normalization and gauge conventions. The selected Liang manuscript uses a metric normalization twice the convention used in the linked Wiki geometry article. Comparing numerical coefficients without reconciling that factor would produce a false disagreement. Degenerate or touching bands also require a suitable subspace treatment rather than unstable single-band derivatives. 

Geometric quantities can enter superfluid response, but a nonzero metric alone does not prove superconductivity. Peotta and Törmä's flat-band result has explicit interaction, isolation and pairing assumptions. Huhtinen and colleagues further show why order-parameter relaxation and representation dependence matter when differentiating the free energy. State what is held fixed and what is reoptimized before calling a curvature a physical stiffness. A frozen-field derivative and a relaxed response are not interchangeable; the full multiband response calculation remains a separate task.  

 J11 — Ginzburg–Landau theory

Ginzburg–Landau theory organizes a free-energy expansion in a complex order parameter and its spatial gradients. Its coefficients and applicable temperature range must be specified; in its conventional derivation it is controlled near the transition. A homogeneous minimum, a linearized upper-critical-field calculation and a vortex-lattice solution are different problems. The type-I/type-II boundary of the elementary isotropic model should not be transferred without qualification to every anisotropic or multicomponent material. 

Brandt's ideal vortex-lattice calculation illustrates how field, the Ginzburg–Landau parameter and lattice structure affect magnetic observables. Its assumptions exclude arbitrary disorder and pinning, and the commonly used London-limit variance is valid only in a restricted regime. Solving a phenomenological equation with chosen coefficients does not identify a microscopic pairing mechanism. Report boundary conditions, gauge, mesh and free-energy comparisons when several solutions exist; numerical convergence to one stationary configuration alone does not establish that it is the global equilibrium state. 

 J12 — Bogoliubov–de Gennes equations

Bogoliubov–de Gennes theory writes a quadratic paired Hamiltonian in a particle-and-hole basis. For a complete finite fermionic basis, Hermitian normal block h and antisymmetric pairing matrix \Delta, one convention is \mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta\\\Delta^\dagger&-h^T\end{pmatrix}. The doubled description has particle-hole redundancy, not twice as many independent physical states. Independent complex-matrix checks verify Hermiticity and paired eigenvalues in this convention; a reduced spin block can use different notation. 

Specify whether the pairing field is imposed or determined self-consistently, together with density, boundaries and the physical basis. Kitaev's selected chain model provides a controlled example of bulk and boundary structure, but a near-zero eigenvalue by itself does not prove a protected experimental Majorana mode. Finite-size splitting, competing localized states and model perturbations must be considered. A self-consistent mean-field solution also does not include every collective or correlation effect. Numerical particle-hole symmetry is a necessary algebra check, not a topological classification or material validation. 

 Experimental criteria

Compare calculated and measured quantities with matching sample conditions and definitions. A pairing eigenvalue, a harmonic phonon, a local spectral gap and an experimental zero-resistance criterion are different observables. Keep model temperatures out of the measured-Tc catalogue. Predictions should specify independent tests that could reject the assumed mechanism, structure or parameter set.   

 Limits and disputes

Each of the twelve sections has a named review scope. Some references were checked only at abstract level; others use selected author-manuscript passages with final-version comparisons still open. Independent small-model checks verify the stated algebra and counterexamples, not all numerical methods or every cited material. Complete scientific acceptance, full derivations, supplementary datasets and material-level reproduction remain open.    

 Discovery implications

Choose the simplest defensible model that can distinguish the proposed explanation from a concrete alternative. Carry its uncertainty into any material ranking. A useful workflow moves between structural evidence, electronic and interaction models, numerical convergence and experimentally testable observables; agreement at one stage does not remove assumptions at the next. Retain failed fits and competing states rather than reporting only the most favorable transition estimate.

entries.title: Superconducting applications: devices, conditions and evidence
entries.summary: Ten applications from cables and magnets to sensors, qubits and energy storage, with dated examples, operating conditions and limits on performance claims.
aliases: MRI SQUID SNSPD transmon maglev microwave flywheel
entries.text:
Scope

Superconducting applications combine materials with cryogenics, mechanical support, electronics and protection. This handbook connects ten approved topics to the physical function that superconductivity provides and the conditions required to assess a device. Historical demonstrations, design specifications and current operator explanations are identified separately. A material's transition temperature is not an equipment operating temperature, and a successful component does not establish the performance of an entire installation.   

 Mathematical assumptions

Compare like quantities: magnetic field at a named location, current with a stated criterion, power versus stored energy, and sensor efficiency referenced to a defined input. Independent calculations here test an ideal two-junction interference model, a finite charge-basis qubit Hamiltonian and a hypothetical rotating annulus. They do not certify a magnet, reproduce a detector calibration or establish service life. Engineering margins and uncertainty must accompany device-level claims.   

 K1 — Power transmission cables

Superconducting cables aim to carry large currents in a compact conductor, but the conductor choice is project-specific. The 2019 manufacturer-authored Bi-2223 review identifies copper-reinforced, spliced Bi-2223 wire in the AmpaCity three-phase coaxial cable and dates its long-term grid trial from 2014. It must not be relabelled as a REBCO installation merely because the planning outline named REBCO long wires. The two conductor families require separate manufacturing and qualification evidence. 

Assess usable current under the cable's field, temperature, strain and joint conditions, with the voltage criterion and area convention retained. Adding mechanical reinforcement can improve strength while reducing engineering current density when the entire conductor cross-section is counted. Low resistance in the superconducting path does not eliminate cryogenic loads, joint heating or alternating-current losses. Compare a complete installation over its load cycle, including cooling and fault response, before claiming an energy or cost advantage. The reviewed passage supports the conductor identification and historical deployment context; it does not independently quantify AmpaCity's total operating losses or long-term reliability. 

 K2 — MRI magnets

The selected MRI review describes conventional whole-body systems using liquid-helium-cooled NbTi coils, commonly operating near 4.2 K. That temperature is a cooling condition, not the material's transition temperature. The main magnet must provide a field with suitable spatial uniformity and stability across the intended imaging region. A larger central field alone does not specify image quality or make two scanners equivalent. Geometry, gradients, radio-frequency hardware and reconstruction also matter. 

Shorter magnets and wider bores change the balance between conductor quantity, peak field, field uniformity and accessibility. Reduced-helium and conduction-cooled designs can change installation requirements, but they still need refrigeration, thermal margins and protection against local heating. The source's product examples describe the state considered in its 2022 manuscript; they are not a current market ranking. The engineering discussion here does not provide clinical advice or assert that every magnet of a named material has the same operating limits. Detailed scanner qualification, final review-version comparison and the underlying device datasets remain separate checks. 

 K3 — Accelerator magnets

Accelerator dipoles bend charged-particle trajectories; quadrupoles focus the beam. Their field profiles, apertures and operating cycles impose different requirements. CERN's 5 December 2023 report describes a 7.2 m Nb3Sn quadrupole prototype for the High-Luminosity LHC, following earlier LHC use of NbTi. The reported third full-length prototype reached 16.53 kA in tests at both 1.9 K and 4.5 K, while planned operation was at 1.9 K. These are distinct test conditions, not interchangeable operating specifications. 

The same report links improved performance to changes in support-shell dimensions, assembly stress and production procedures after earlier prototypes were limited at 4.5 K. A useful comparison therefore includes conductor properties, mechanical loading, cooling and the specific magnet test, rather than attributing every improvement to chemical composition. Reaching a current target is an important milestone but does not independently establish beam performance, complete series-production acceptance or current fleet readiness. The Wiki records this as a dated prototype result; further system qualification requires its own evidence. 

 K4 — Fusion magnets

Magnetic-confinement fusion devices use different coils for different field functions. ITER's technical overview describes Nb3Sn in its toroidal-field and central-solenoid systems, and NbTi in the four largest poloidal-field coils. Its quoted peak fields refer to named parts of the magnet system: the toroidal-coil maximum and the central-solenoid maximum are not the same measurement location. Cooling near liquid-helium temperatures is also distinct from the plasma temperature. 

Coils, structural supports, cable jackets, cooling circuits and feeders form an engineered system. High-temperature superconducting current leads in a feeder should not be confused with the material used throughout the main winding. Nor are all ITER coils superconducting: the overview identifies copper conductors for in-vessel vertical-stability and edge-localized-mode coils. Treat the page's design capabilities and intended operation as design information. A magnet specification does not demonstrate a completed fusion campaign, sustained net electricity generation or commercial reactor availability. Those outcomes require separately dated operational evidence. 

 K5 — SQUID sensors and readout

A superconducting quantum interference device converts flux-dependent Josephson interference into an electrical signal. For an ideal loop with two identical sinusoidal junctions and negligible self-inductance, maximizing their summed currents gives I{\max}=2I0|\cos(\pi\Phi/\Phi0)|. This independently checked limit explains periodicity; unequal junctions leave a nonzero minimum at half a flux quantum. It is not a complete sensor-noise calculation. Tesche and Clarke's original abstract explicitly includes inductance, junction asymmetry, resistive shunts and noise when assessing performance. 

Practical sensitivity depends on the pickup geometry, flux-to-voltage transfer, bandwidth and noise environment. A noise density must carry its frequency normalization and refer to the correct input quantity. NIST's detector-readout project illustrates SQUID ammeters and multiplexing used to read cryogenic sensor arrays, together with room-temperature electronics. The SQUID readout and the sensor that absorbs a photon are distinct components. Neither an ideal interference curve nor the presence of a SQUID establishes the final instrument's energy resolution. The complete original noise derivation and device-specific calibration remain outside this scoped check.  

 K6 — Superconducting nanowire photon detectors

An SNSPD uses a biased superconducting nanowire and readout circuit to register photon-induced detection events. Efficiency, timing jitter, dark counts, recovery and maximum usable rate are separate metrics. Reddy and colleagues' 2020 experiment reported 98.0 ± 0.5% system detection efficiency at 1550 nm using MoSi, not WSi or NbN. Its definition refers to photons entering the fiber pigtail outside the cryostat, so the reported system efficiency must not be replaced by an internal absorption or conversion efficiency. 

The selected final-paper passages describe operation at 720–780 mK with optimized polarization. For the 50 μm device, series resistance in the readout changed pulse behavior and suppressed problems that otherwise affected operation. These conditions belong with the headline value. Do not combine this efficiency with another paper's best timing or dark-count result as though one device achieved them together. This is a dated experimental example, not an assertion of a current world record. The full calibration supplement, uncertainty reconstruction and raw detection traces have not yet been independently reviewed. 

 K7 — Superconducting qubits

Josephson circuits supply a nonlinear quantum element whose lowest levels can encode a qubit. The transmon model uses H=4EC(\hat n-ng)^2-EJ\cos\hat\varphi, where EC=e^2/(2C\Sigma) and \hat n counts Cooper pairs. Koch and colleagues show that increasing EJ/EC strongly suppresses sensitivity to offset charge, while reducing relative anharmonicity more slowly. The latter must remain sufficient to distinguish the intended transition from leakage to higher levels. 

Independent diagonalization in the charge basis checks this tradeoff across six energy ratios and verifies convergence under an increased charge cutoff. Absolute anharmonicity approaches a scale of order EC; confusing it with relative anharmonicity would misstate the result. The calculation does not include fabricated junction defects, all environmental noise, driven gates or measurement electronics. A stable transition in this model is not a measured coherence time, gate fidelity or fault-tolerant processor. The original 2007 design paper supplies a foundational model, not a benchmark for present-day hardware. 

 K8 — Magnetic levitation

Magnetic levitation is a family of systems, not a single superconducting material. JR Central's operator explanation describes liquid-helium-cooled NbTi magnets onboard SCMAGLEV vehicles. Propulsion uses powered guideway coils, while motion relative to other guideway coils generates levitation and guidance forces. This architecture must not be described simply as a YBCO bulk floating over permanent magnets. A low-loss superconducting magnet also does not imply a train that consumes no electrical energy. 

Bulk-superconductor demonstrations provide a different example. The publisher-indexed abstract and excerpt of Wang and colleagues' 2002 paper describe a YBaCuO-bulk test vehicle over an NdFeB guideway and date the first reported test to 31 December 2000. That limited source access does not establish all load, speed or stability claims. Distinguish the demonstrated configuration from a transport service: propulsion, guidance, cooling, emergency support and operating reliability must be assessed for the actual system. This handbook preserves both examples and their evidence boundaries without declaring every maglev system superconducting or every prototype commercially deployed.  

 K9 — Microwave resonators and filters

Superconducting films can reduce conductor loss in microwave structures, but zero direct-current resistance does not imply zero microwave surface resistance. Resonator measurements must distinguish loaded from unloaded quality factor and account for coupling, dielectric loss, packaging and heating. Xin and colleagues compared unpatterned YBCO wafers with patterned stripline structures using different current distributions. Their selected methods include thermal control and a change of measurement method at high input power. 

The observed absence of patterning-induced degradation applied to the tested films and procedures; it is not a theorem about every fabrication process. Some comparisons also rescaled between frequencies using an assumed frequency-squared resistance dependence. Retain that assumption when interpreting agreement. Nonlinear response can limit power handling and generate unwanted frequencies even where small-signal loss is low. For a filter, quote frequency, temperature, bandwidth, insertion loss and power conditions together. The reviewed resonator experiment motivates these checks but does not establish the performance or current deployment of a particular communications filter. 

 K10 — Flywheel energy storage

A superconducting flywheel stores kinetic energy in a rotating mass; its superconducting bearing reduces contact friction. This differs from storing energy directly in a magnetic field. RTRI's 15 April 2015 system description reports a four-ton rotor supported by a bearing cooled to 50 K, with a yttrium-containing superconducting coil and a superconducting bulk on the shaft. It lists 300 kW output, 100 kWh storage and a maximum speed of 6,000 rpm; grid-connection tests were still planned in that document. 

Rotational energy is E=I\omega^2/2. Usable energy between two speeds depends on their squared difference, not just the maximum speed. Dividing the stated 100 kWh by 300 kW gives an ideal 20 minutes, not a measured discharge duration or round-trip efficiency. An independent uniform-annulus calculation illustrates why mass distribution matters; it does not reconstruct the actual layered rotor. Vacuum equipment, cooling, motor-generator losses, containment and maintenance remain part of system assessment. The source's historical capacity claim is preserved without repeating an absolute promise of unlimited lifetime or zero total loss. 

 Experimental criteria

For each device, retain material, geometry, cooling, measurement reference, date and operating conditions. Identify whether the cited result is a model, component test, integrated demonstration or operational report. Reliability and efficiency need a stated duration and system boundary. Current or field targets, detector efficiency and storage capacity cannot be merged into a generic measure of superconducting quality.   

 Limits and disputes

The ten sections have individual review records. Some use selected final-paper passages; others use author manuscripts, institutional engineering reports, reviews or explicitly limited abstract access. Full scientific acceptance remains open, including supplementary calibration, final-version comparisons and complete device records. The historical examples establish neither present-day records nor universal superiority over alternative technologies.    

 Discovery implications

Select materials against the application: usable current and mechanical margin for a cable, field quality for a magnet, noise and coupling for a sensor, or losses and control for a quantum circuit. A higher transition temperature can change cooling options but does not settle every engineering constraint. A useful development claim specifies which independently measurable system property should improve and which tradeoffs may worsen.
