entries.title: A history of superconductivity: milestones and evidence
entries.summary: Eighteen milestones from mercury to recent research, with original-source links, corrected chronology and the conditions behind reported temperatures.
entries.text:
Scope

The history of superconductivity includes discoveries, theories, material families and changing standards of evidence. These eighteen milestones connect major developments to their dates, measurement conditions and original evidence. A later author's recollection, an original discovery report and a modern reanalysis answer different historical questions. The cited review scope tells the reader which was checked.   

 Mathematical assumptions

There is no single mathematical curve that makes all reported transition temperatures directly comparable. A resistance onset, a midpoint, a noise-floor zero and a magnetic response can occur at different temperatures, even in one specimen. Pressure, composition, sample history and measurement field must remain attached to any point. The linked material articles preserve detailed records; this history does not create duplicate experimental Tc entries from narrative summaries.   

 L1 — 1911: mercury and the resistance transition

Onnes's 1911 mercury work opened the study of superconductivity. His 1913 Nobel lecture provides a firsthand account of the abrupt resistance decrease near 4.2 K and the limits of the electrical measurement. Resistance too small to resolve is an experimental statement; mathematical exactness is not read directly from an instrument. The lecture also discusses a current threshold above which a voltage appeared, anticipating the need to specify measuring current. 

The checked scan contains later notes, including a 1914 addendum. Those observations must not all be assigned to the original 1911 discovery. Nor should the initial resistance experiment be described as already establishing the later Meissner effect or a complete microscopic theory. The original 1911 communication itself remains outside the directly reviewed material; the author lecture is identified as the historical source used here. 

 L2 — 1933: the Meissner–Ochsenfeld effect

Meissner and Ochsenfeld's 1933 work added magnetic behavior to the definition of the superconducting state. The selected original reproduction describes field redistribution around tin and lead as the samples became superconducting. This changed the question from whether a conductor can sustain current without detectable resistance to which magnetic state it reaches. An ideal conductor's history-dependent trapped field does not by itself supply the same equilibrium magnetic condition. 

Geometry remains essential to reading the experiment. The original report also discusses retained field in a lead-tube cavity; a cavity is not the same region as the superconducting material. A simplified statement that every field everywhere becomes zero would erase this distinction. The historical paper's apparatus, uncertainty and complete translation have not been independently reconstructed here. The milestone records the new magnetic evidence while retaining the limits of the selected primary reproduction. 

 L3 — 1935: London electrodynamics

The London brothers' 1935 paper supplied an electromagnetic description of superconductors that accommodates magnetic screening. The selected original pages distinguish the consequence of perfect conductivity from an additional condition selecting the superconducting magnetic state. An integration constant associated with the initial field is therefore not a trivial detail: dropping it without stating the physical postulate would conceal what the theory adds. 

The London description links current and electromagnetic fields under its stated local assumptions. It does not determine a material's microscopic pairing interaction or explain every spatially nonuniform state. Modern equations often use SI units and different notation from the original scan; a historical formula should not be copied into a modern calculation without checking those conventions. This milestone concerns a phenomenological advance in electrodynamics, not an experimental discovery of a new transition-temperature record. 

 L4 — 1950: Ginzburg–Landau theory

Ginzburg and Landau introduced a complex order parameter and a free-energy description of superconductivity in 1950. Ginzburg's later firsthand lecture explains the motivation to extend the London treatment, including spatial variation and interfaces. The resulting framework connects electromagnetic response to the amplitude and phase of an order parameter and provides a basis for studying boundaries and competing configurations near a transition. 

The history is not identical to today's textbook presentation. Ginzburg recounts that the effective charge was not correctly settled at twice the electron charge in the original work; the later microscopic interpretation clarified that point. Their early analysis also focused on what are now called type-I superconductors. Avoid projecting every subsequent vortex result or the complete BCS interpretation back into 1950. The checked source is the 2004 retrospective, with its original-paper citation, rather than a full direct audit of the 1950 article. 

 L5 — 1957: the BCS microscopic theory

Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer's 1957 theory constructed a coherent paired many-electron state and related its excitation spectrum to superconducting observables. It moved beyond identifying macroscopic signatures by providing a microscopic explanation within a specified interaction model. The energy gap and thermodynamic behavior arise together in that framework, rather than being independent empirical labels attached to a zero-resistance state. 

The achievement should not be turned into a claim that one elementary approximation describes every later material. The familiar isotropic weak-coupling results assume a particular pairing structure and energy-scale hierarchy. Strong coupling, multiple bands, unconventional symmetry and substantial fluctuations require further treatment. A historical timeline should distinguish the theory's established role from a material-specific mechanism assignment. Agreement with one BCS-like ratio is a consistency check, not proof that a newly observed superconductor has the same microscopic interaction. 

 L6 — 1962: tunnelling supercurrents and field compensation

Josephson's 1962 paper predicted new tunnelling effects between superconductors. His 1973 lecture distinguishes the theoretical prediction from the later experiments that convincingly attributed observed supercurrents to tunnelling. Earlier zero-voltage currents could instead have involved metallic shorts, and unsuccessful measurements were part of the development. Phase-dependent response, magnetic interference and microwave-induced voltage steps provided more specific tests than a zero-voltage branch alone.  

Another development in 1962 was Jaccarino and Peter's proposal of ultra-high-field superconductivity through compensation of an external field by an internal exchange effect. This is a separate idea, not part of Josephson tunnelling. Its original bibliographic identity is checked here; the full original derivation is not. Later field-induced experiments and their limits are discussed in the linked exchange-compensation article. Keeping the two contributions distinct prevents a shared calendar year from becoming a misleading shared mechanism. 

 L7 — 1973: Nb–Ge films above 22 K

Gavaler's 1973 report describes superconductivity in sputtered Nb–Ge films above 22 K. The checked original abstract reports 22.3 K. The often-quoted 23.2 K value is not the value reported in this specific discovery abstract. A later optimized result, if added, needs its own citation, sample description and date rather than being silently attached to the earlier report. 

Processing is central to the historical interpretation: the source describes high-pressure sputtering, which is a deposition condition, not evidence that the superconducting transition was measured under high external pressure. Film composition, phase formation and preparation affect the result. Neither the reported temperature nor the A15 label defines a universal transition for all Nb–Ge samples or a strict ceiling for the entire structural family. Full methods and the exact operational transition criterion remain unreviewed at this abstract-level scope. 

 L8 — 1979: CeCu2Si2 and heavy fermions

The 1979 CeCu2Si2 report established a superconducting state in a system with strong Pauli paramagnetism and an unusually large electronic response. Its original abstract gives a transition scale around 0.5 K. The historical importance lies in opening a strongly correlated setting for superconductivity, not in raising the maximum known transition temperature. Different measures of progress therefore belong in a scientific timeline. 

This original observation should be separated from later debates over gap structure, magnetic coexistence and sample classification. Modern CeCu2Si2 experiments distinguish crystals and transitions that cannot be reduced to a universal 0.5 K constant. The presence of a heavy-electron normal state also does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction from the discovery abstract alone. The original full measurements have not been reconstructed in this review; the linked heavy-fermion article follows the subsequent evidence and its competing interpretations. 

 L9 — 1986: the Ba–La–Cu–O discovery

Bednorz and Müller's 1986 paper deliberately used the title “Possible high Tc superconductivity” for its Ba–La–Cu–O result. The publisher's original abstract describes multiphase polycrystals and a current-dependent, percolative resistive onset in the 30 K range. That is the evidence actually checked here. This abstract does not establish a precise bulk magnetic transition at 35 K. 

The milestone initiated a new materials direction, but the discovery report's sample and uncertainty deserve to remain visible. A connected superconducting path can strongly affect resistance without establishing that the whole sample occupies one superconducting phase. Later synthesis, phase identification and complementary measurements must retain their own citations. The original abstract and publication record were checked; the complete figures, apparatus and raw measurements remain outside this review scope. Historical significance does not remove the need to distinguish an initial report from later confirmation. 

 L10 — 1987: Y–Ba–Cu–O above liquid-nitrogen temperature

Wu and colleagues reported a transition above liquid-nitrogen temperature in mixed-phase Y–Ba–Cu–O material. The selected final paper distinguishes a resistance deviation at 93 K, a sharp drop beginning near 92 K, zero resistance at 80 K and a magnetic onset near 91 K. These values describe different criteria in the reported experiment; the 93 K headline is not a 93 K zero-resistance result. 

The original nominal sample composition was not a phase-pure YBa2Cu3O7 crystal. A subsequent structural, transport and magnetic study identified the principal YBa2Cu3Ox phase. Combining those papers is useful only when their roles remain distinct. Likewise, a low-temperature diamagnetic signal compared with lead is not automatically an independently corrected volume fraction. This milestone records both the striking temperature advance and the continuing work needed to establish the responsible phase and quantitative superconducting properties.  

 L11 — 1993: mercury-based cuprates above 130 K

Schilling and colleagues' 1993 report describes superconductivity above 130 K in the Hg–Ba–Ca–Cu–O system, with magnetic and resistive evidence summarized near 133 K. The commonly cited 135 K value should not replace the approximately 133 K result in this specific original report. Oxygen content, phase composition and the experimental criterion matter when later samples yield somewhat different quoted temperatures. 

Gao and colleagues' 1994 pressure study is a separate milestone in the development of this material family. Its abstract reports resistive superconductivity up to 164 K under quasihydrostatic pressure. That high-pressure result is neither an ambient-pressure value nor evidence that the state survives unloading. The exact pressure of the maximum and its onset-versus-zero criterion have not been re-extracted here. A plot that joins these numbers without marking conditions would confuse distinct experiments; the linked cuprate and pressure-quench pages preserve those boundaries.  

 L12 — 2001: MgB2 at 39 K

Nagamatsu and colleagues' 2001 MgB2 paper showed that a chemically simple binary compound could superconduct at a surprisingly high temperature for that class of material. In the selected final report, resistance begins to fall at 39 K and reaches its endpoint near 38 K; a separate low-field magnetization measurement supports the interpretation. The two criteria should not be merged into one exact temperature independent of the measurement. 

The synthesis pressure quoted in the methods is a preparation condition, not the pressure at which the reported transition was measured. The discovery also precedes the detailed body of isotope, spectroscopy and anisotropic electron–phonon work that established MgB2 as a multigap benchmark. Those later results do not all belong to the original discovery paper. Its role in the timeline is the 2001 observation with the sample and probes actually described, while the linked material article develops the subsequent microscopic evidence. 

 L13 — 2008: the iron-arsenide expansion

The 2008 fluorine-substituted LaOFeAs report brought a transition near 26 K to the iron-pnictide field. The publisher record distinguishes its February online publication from the later journal issue. The selected original abstract supports the composition range and reported temperature, but the detailed operational transition criterion remains unassigned at this review scope. Do not infer that criterion from the title alone. 

This was not the first superconducting iron-containing compound or even the first reported layered iron pnictide: the same research group's LaOFeP paper appeared in 2006. That earlier source is retained to avoid compressing the family history into an incorrect first-discovery claim. The 2008 advance instead marks the higher-temperature arsenide platform and the beginning of rapid diversification into related systems. Iron-based materials subsequently require separate structural, magnetic and pairing analyses; the presence of iron does not fix a universal gap symmetry.  

 L14 — 2015: sulfur hydride near 203 K

The 2015 sulfur-hydride report extended superconducting temperatures into a much higher range under extreme pressure. The selected author passages and published captions distinguish resistance measurements from the magnetic response, including a reported onset near 203 K at 155 GPa for the magnetic specimen. The pressure and measurement definition belong with the number; the result is not an ambient-pressure material property. 

The superconducting phase assignment also developed through further structural work. A sulfur-hydride starting composition is not by itself proof of the final high-pressure stoichiometry, and the later diffraction study must remain separately cited when discussing H3S. The selected scientific review did not independently reconstruct magnetization background subtraction or all raw transport data. This milestone records the reported evidence and the pressure-enabled material setting without treating the historical headline as a complete audit of every experimental inference.  

 L15 — 2019: lanthanum hydride and infinite-layer nickelates

Two distinct materials developments occurred in 2019. The lanthanum-hydride experiment reported a resistive transition around 250 K near 170 GPa. The selected final paper includes resistance, isotope comparison and field suppression, but no SQUID measurement. Applied magnetic fields and extrapolated upper-critical-field estimates are different quantities. This high-pressure result should not be plotted as an ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor. 

In a different materials setting, Li and colleagues reported superconductivity in reduced, Sr-substituted infinite-layer nickelate films. A representative Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 sample has separately defined onset, midpoint and noise-floor zero values of 14.9, 13.6 and 9.1 K. The result must not be relabelled as superconductivity in undoped bulk NdNiO2. Epitaxy, reduction, capping and sample preparation are part of the observation. The common year links these discoveries chronologically, not through an established common mechanism. 

 L16 — 2018: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

Cao and colleagues' superconductivity report appeared in 2018, not 2022. The discovery year should remain separate from the dates of later studies. In the selected final paper, two devices with different nominal twist angles have different transition scales: approximately 0.5 K and 1.7 K under the stated half-normal-resistance criterion. A device label, carrier density and transport definition belong with each number. 

The paper's tentative BKT analysis supplies another temperature scale, while a 70 mK measurement floor is not a transition temperature. These distinctions prevent one figure from becoming several apparently interchangeable records. The broader advance is geometric control of electronic bands and interactions through a moiré structure; it does not establish that every magic-angle device has the same phase diagram or that a flat band alone guarantees superconductivity. The chronological guide places this discovery before the 2019 hydride and nickelate results. 

 L17 — 2023: bilayer nickelate signatures near 80 K

The 2023 La3Ni2O7 paper reported signatures near 80 K under pressure. For the selected run, the resistance onset occurs near 18.5 GPa, with nonzero residual resistance. A separate magnetic measurement is part of the broader paper, but its sample and pressure must not be silently attached to that particular resistance record. The wording “signatures” and the operational criterion are scientifically meaningful. 

The checked passages also distinguish applied fields from an upper-critical-field extrapolation and retain pressure calibration and measurement-current conditions. A later zero-resistance result, thin-film experiment or structurally modified nickelate would be a separate entry with its own evidence. The historical milestone therefore establishes the reported pressure-induced phenomenon and the questions it raised, rather than declaring an independently reproduced 80 K bulk transition for every bilayer nickelate. Full raw-data and replication review remains open. 

 L18 — 2026: recovered cuprates, re-entrance and transport

Three recent papers illustrate different research directions; their dates and observables must remain separate. Deng and colleagues' pressure-quench article appeared online on 9 March 2026. Its highest retained ambient-pressure value, 151 K, is a resistive onset after a specific pressure-and-temperature preparation. A magnetic result on a different retrieved sample and cold-storage tests cannot be reassigned to that highest-onset specimen. 

The Eu-substituted infinite-layer nickelate paper and the iron-chalcogenide Planckian-scattering paper were published on 23 April 2026. The first concerns field-dependent re-entrance under specified conditions; the second analyzes normal-state transport with parallel conduction channels. A model-dependent scattering rate is not a new Tc record or proof of a universal pairing mechanism. These studies are recent research directions with scoped checks, not one combined discovery or a completed independent replication programme.  

 Chronological guide

Follow the links to the evidence for each milestone. The graphene discovery appears in 2018, before the 2019 hydride and nickelate results. Temperatures in the detailed sections are conditional reported values, not a uniform record-ranking dataset.

| Period | Milestones |
| --- | --- |
| 1911–1935 | , ,  |
| 1950–1962 | , ,  |
| 1973–1987 | , , ,  |
| 1993–2015 | , , ,  |
| 2018–2023 | , ,  |
| 2026 |  |

 Experimental criteria

A reported milestone is not a standardized material benchmark. Preserve the experimental criterion and distinguish the year of observation, first public report, journal publication and later author account. An accurate timeline can include a theory, a measurement or a material platform without assigning each one a transition-temperature point. Links to primary evidence make the interpretation inspectable.    

 Limits and disputes

Some early sources remain checked only at abstract or bibliographic level; other entries reuse selected original-paper reviews from the linked core articles. Those limitations remain attached rather than being upgraded by appearing in a history handbook. Later recollections help explain reasoning but are not the original laboratory record. Complete scientific acceptance, full final-version comparisons, supplementary data and independent replication remain open where stated.    

 Discovery implications

Progress has come from new materials, better preparation, more discriminating probes and theories that make testable predictions. A higher reported onset is only one kind of advance. The historical examples encourage a workflow that separates initial observations from phase identification, reproducibility and mechanism tests, preserving negative results and corrections instead of rewriting them out of the story.    

 Related topics

Continue with , , , , , , , , and .

entries.title: Research methods: data, prediction and verification
entries.summary: A practical guide to superconductivity databases, machine learning, computational screening and evidence-based reading, with explicit validation limits.
entries.text:
Scope

Reliable superconductivity research connects a question to a traceable dataset, a suitable method and an observation that could disprove the proposed answer. This handbook follows six parts of that process: finding data, predicting transitions, screening with calculations, checking claims, reviewing interpretations and reading papers closely. The aim is a reproducible chain of evidence, with the limits of each step visible.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For a binary classifier, TP and TN count correct positive and negative predictions; FP and FN count the corresponding errors. With a fixed positive-class definition and test set,


\mathrm{accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN},\qquad
\mathrm{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad
\mathrm{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}.


These are dimensionless fractions, not transition temperatures or discovery rates. Precision is undefined if no positive prediction exists; recall is undefined if the test set contains no positives. An original teaching example with 34 positive and 966 negative labels gives 96.6% accuracy and zero positive recall when every label is predicted negative. Its precision is undefined. This arithmetic illustrates class imbalance; it is not a fitted superconductivity model. 

 M1 — Databases, structures and provenance

NIMS is the institution that publishes SuperCon; the two names should not be counted as independent confirmations. The MDR SuperCon datasheet provides a versioned release with a DOI and a stated reuse license. Record the release identifier and original literature reference when extracting a value. A database row is a route to evidence, not a substitute for checking how the reported transition was measured. The checked Ver.220808 release is an explicit snapshot, not a claim to be today's latest dataset. 

ICSD serves a different purpose: inorganic crystal structures support structural identification and calculation inputs, but a structure match does not establish superconductivity. Its access and reuse terms differ from an openly licensed SuperCon release. Check the applicable license before redistributing records. In SCLib, use the  and  to follow retrieved results back to their publications. Preserve the query, returned identifier and retrieval date so another researcher can repeat the search.  

Keep composition, phase, sample treatment, pressure, magnetic field and transition criterion together. Separate records can share a formula while describing different experiments. Conversely, copies of the same measurement across databases are not independent evidence. For model evaluation, related compositions may need to share a train/test group even though their experimental records remain separate; this prevents data organization from silently becoming a claim of independent validation.  

 M2 — Machine learning for transition temperatures

Composition descriptors and neural representations can help prioritize experiments, but the target and validation design determine what a score means. Stanev and colleagues used random forests for classification and regression; their methods explicitly discuss inconsistent records and missing pressure information. Their proposed materials remain candidates. Predicting a threshold class is a different task from predicting a numerical Tc, and neither guarantees successful synthesis. 

Pogue and colleagues tested a neural-network approach with both uniform and leave-one-cluster-out validation. The latter exposed much poorer generalization. Their experimental loop combined model suggestions with expert filtering and new measurements. The reported counts are five successes among 190 suggestions and five among 65 after filtering. The printed second percentage is 7.5%; arithmetic from its stated count gives approximately 7.69%. These overlapping selections are not independent randomized trial arms, and the result should not be attributed to the model alone. 

In the recommended evaluation workflow, declare the candidate space, grouping rule, held-out data, selection threshold and error metric before inspecting the test results. Report unsuccessful synthesis separately from a successfully prepared sample with no transition in the measured range. Compare against a simple baseline, and retain uncertainty and known family limits when ranking new candidates. The majority-class counterexample above shows why accuracy alone can hide complete failure to identify the desired class. 

 M3 — High-throughput first-principles screening

A phonon-mediated screening workflow first specifies composition, crystal structure and pressure, then checks electronic structure, phonons and electron–phonon coupling under stated approximations. A calculated Eliashberg spectral function can inform an estimated transition temperature within that model. It is not a universal treatment of every unconventional pairing mechanism, nor a measurement of a synthesized material. 

Gibson and colleagues report 818 retained calculated spectra after screening and numerical quality checks. Their methods specify commensurate electronic and phonon meshes, smearing, pseudopotentials and numerical cutoffs. They also discuss imaginary modes caused by numerical issues or a mismatch between ideal stoichiometry and experimental composition. Thus, a calculation that converges is not automatically physically valid, while an imaginary mode requires diagnosis before drawing a materials conclusion. Their high-pressure extrapolation remains unvalidated. 

For a new candidate, save the input structure, code and pseudopotential versions, convergence evidence and failed calculations as well as successful outputs. Recheck finalists with tighter settings and the relevant stability assumptions. Report a predicted Tc with its model parameters and pressure rather than adding it to a table of experimental transitions. These workflow recommendations extend the documented calculation controls; they do not certify a new calculation or reproduce the published training run. 

 M4 — Preventing unsupported claims

A DOI helps identify a research object. It does not prove that the linked paper contains the proposed claim, that the claim concerns the right material, or that later work confirmed it. Check the title and authors, then locate the relevant passage, equation, figure or dataset. Crossmark can expose registered corrections and retractions; the service itself states that its presence is not a guarantee. Missing update metadata should not be treated as a certificate of validity. 

For each factual statement, retain the source version, location, sample identity, observable, conditions and review scope. Distinguish a publisher abstract from selected full text and a complete supplementary-data review. If a source has no DOI, preserve its official URL, title, version or date and, where appropriate, a local file checksum; inventing a DOI would weaken traceability. Versioned data and institutional documentation illustrate why the identifier must fit the source type.  

Resolve contradictions at the level of the underlying evidence. For example, onset and zero resistance should not be averaged into one transition, and a calculated field limit must not be relabelled as the highest applied field. Mark an unresolved difference explicitly, revise downstream summaries when evidence changes, and keep a correction history. This is an editorial verification workflow, not a guarantee that every indexed claim has already passed it.  

 M5 — Peer review and assisted critique

Scientific criticism should test a specific inference. Ask which alternative explanation fits the same measurement, whether a numerical result changes under a reasonable control, and whether the cited source actually supports the wording. A useful review records the disputed claim, supporting evidence and a concrete way to resolve it. COPE guidance emphasizes relevant expertise, declared conflicts, clear scope and constructive feedback rather than personal accusations. 

Model-generated critiques can suggest missing checks, but agreement among several models is not independent peer review or experimental replication. They may repeat the same source error or overlook the same missing condition. Treat each objection as a hypothesis to inspect against primary evidence, and document who performed the substantive verification. A journal's peer-review decision and a wiki's editorial check are distinct events and should be labelled separately.  

Follow the actual publisher's confidentiality and AI-use policy when reviewing a submitted manuscript. Nature Portfolio's checked policy retains human scholarly accountability and distinguishes assistance from delegating evaluative judgment. These publisher-specific rules do not establish a universal policy for every venue. For public scientific discussion, preserve the same practical discipline: make the critique inspectable, state its limitations and change the conclusion when a counterexample survives checking. 

 M6 — Close reading and PDF extraction

Begin with the question the paper claims to answer, its publication version and any linked correction. Read the methods needed to interpret the central observable before summarizing the headline. Build a small evidence record containing the sample label, control conditions, definition of each reported quantity, figure location and remaining uncertainty. Compare the conclusion with the actual result rather than assuming that a familiar title supplies the necessary details. COPE's review guidance also distinguishes reading the manuscript and ancillary material from a specifically commissioned raw-data audit. 

OpenDataLoader PDF is one tool for converting a paper into structured text with reading order and element coordinates. Its documentation describes extraction capabilities; that description does not validate any particular extracted equation or table. Inspect the original page when columns interleave, symbols disappear, subscripts move or a legend changes the interpretation. Keep the original file and extraction version, and link a quoted or summarized finding to its page or bounding box. A parser output is a navigation aid, not the final authority on the paper. 

Record unavailable supplements and unresolved version differences as specific missing evidence. A practical reading note separates the author's conclusion, the observation supporting it and the reader's remaining objection. Keep the public summary within the material actually reviewed; if a figure has not been inspected, do not describe its contents from a citation title alone. 

 Experimental criteria

A null observation is bounded by the prepared sample, measurement range and sensitivity. A failed synthesis is not the same result as no superconducting transition in a well-characterized specimen. Complementary transport, magnetic and thermodynamic probes address different possibilities; retain their separate conditions and uncertainty. These distinctions matter both when curating training labels and when deciding whether a model suggestion became an experimental discovery.  

 Limits and disputes

Selected original methods, figures and official documentation were checked for this handbook. The independent arithmetic examples test definitions and denominators only. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: the published machine-learning models, full supplemental datasets, first-principles convergence and laboratory results were not independently reproduced. Policies and software documentation can change, so their checked date and source must remain visible.    

 Discovery implications

A productive research loop records both useful predictions and informative failures, then updates the next experiment without erasing provenance. Separate the question “does the method rank this test set well?” from “does it identify a new, reproducible superconducting phase?” The answer to the second question requires evidence about the material itself.

entries.title: What limits Tc in flat-band superconductors?
entries.summary: Separate pairing from phase coherence, optical upper bounds from geometric lower bounds, and controlled models from experimental transition temperatures.
aliases: 平坦带超导 Tc 上限
entries.text:
Scope

There is no single numerical temperature ceiling supplied by the phrase “flat band.” A meaningful limit specifies the Hamiltonian, density, dimensionality, interaction and current response. A bound is also different from a predicted transition: satisfying an upper bound does not establish that superconductivity occurs. This question concerns constraints on phase coherence and their relation to pair formation.  

A narrow dispersion can enhance pairing while suppressing ordinary band transport. In a multiorbital system, however, the wavefunctions and interband matrix elements can support a geometric contribution to superfluid weight. Flattening the eigenvalues alone does not determine that contribution. The relevant question is whether a particular interacting system can develop a robust total phase stiffness, with the required electromagnetic and thermodynamic limits.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Define the two-dimensional phase stiffness Ds by F=(Ds/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2. Hazra and colleagues bound it by the optical spectral weight, Ds(T)\leq\widetilde D(T). With a BKT transition, kBTc\leq\pi\widetilde D(Tc)/2. Replacing the right-hand side by its zero-temperature value requires an additional monotonic-stiffness assumption. Their derivation couples the vector potential to the kinetic Hamiltonian; its interaction assumptions must accompany applications. 

For the specified two-spin parabolic band, EF=\pi\hbar^2n/m and \widetilde D=\hbar^2n/(4m) give kBTc\leq EF/8. This is a strictly two-dimensional BKT result, not a generic multiband or three-dimensional formula. In an anisotropic sheet the corresponding bound uses \sqrt{\widetilde Dx\widetilde Dy}. Independent density-convention and coordinate-Jacobian checks reproduce these relations; they do not determine a material's input stiffness. 

The BKT jump concerns the renormalized total response at the transition. It does not isolate a geometric share or convert a pairing gap directly into phase stiffness. A mean-field amplitude can remain nonzero after phase coherence has been lost. The  discusses current-window, finite-size and resistance-fit ambiguities that also matter when testing a proposed bound experimentally. 

 Isolated-band constraints

Verma and colleagues examine on-site attraction in a controlled hierarchy w\ll|U|\ll E0, with bandwidth w and isolation gap E0. Projecting to localized Wannier states produces pair hopping and an interaction-dependent current operator. For their trivial-band construction, \widetilde D{\rm low}\leq\widetilde n|U|\Omega/2, where \widetilde n=\min(n,2-n) and \Omega is the Wannier spread in the stated normalization. The Lieb-lattice symmetry sharpens the coefficient; it is not a universal constant for every lattice. 

Their zero-temperature lower bound concerns optical spectral weight and requires the stated long-range-order and correlation assumptions. It is not a general lower bound on finite-temperature superconductivity. Topological bands require care with the Wannier basis: relaxing the Kramers-pair constraint permits localized functions and a generalized overlap bound. Extrapolating the linear interaction trend beyond the isolated-band hierarchy is unjustified; interband physics becomes important. 

 Pair formation is not pair mobility

A simple independent check makes the distinction concrete. An attractive Hubbard dimer was assembled directly in its six-dimensional two-electron Fock space. Sixteen spectra agree with the analytic ground-state energy E0=(-|U|-\sqrt{|U|^2+16t^2})/2. At zero hopping the local pairs have no intersite splitting. In the strong-attraction limit, the low pair-sector splitting approaches 4t^2/|U|, corresponding to pair hopping 2t^2/|U|. Stronger local binding can therefore accompany slower pair motion. The dimer has no thermodynamic transition and supplies no predicted Tc.  

Flat-band geometry can change this mobility argument because overlapping Wannier orbitals generate interaction-mediated pair motion. That is a model-specific route, not permission to discard self-consistency. Peotta and Törmä's geometric response assumes a defined isolated-band and pairing regime. The Chern-trivial Lieb example also demonstrates why nonzero Chern number is not necessary for every geometric contribution. Its existence does not establish superconductivity in an arbitrary flat-band material.  

 Experimental criteria

Measure a total sheet response with units, frequency, device geometry and fitting uncertainties. Tanaka and colleagues infer stiffness from microwave kinetic inductance using a circuit that includes a parallel edge contribution. Their active-region aspect ratio is an assumption in converting the measured inductance to sheet response. A comparison with a conventional estimate may support a geometric interpretation, but it does not directly measure an independently separable geometric component. 

The selected Tanaka author manuscript distinguishes refrigerator base temperature, wired-device temperature and a half-normal-resistance transition. These are separate observables. A finite-frequency stiffness should be connected to the low-frequency, long-wavelength response before applying an equilibrium BKT criterion. Experimental comparison also needs a stated pairing scale, a temperature-dependent stiffness and evidence that sample inhomogeneity or finite size does not dominate the inferred transition.  

 Limits and disputes

Multiband bounds depend on the actual band structure and occupation assumptions; an approximate estimate is not a universal material ceiling. Hazra's three-dimensional discussion does not establish a general linear stiffness bound there. A successful two-dimensional derivation cannot simply be carried into three dimensions with the same prefactor. 

A calculated mean-field stiffness may itself be overstated when internal pairing fields are held fixed during a phase twist. Huhtinen and colleagues show a relaxation correction under their time-reversal and equilibrium assumptions. In the isolated uniform-pairing setting, the relevant integrated metric is minimized over orbital positions. A frozen-field geometric answer can therefore differ qualitatively from the relaxed response. This correction must be considered before interpreting a mean-field value as a usable bound on an experimental transition. 

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The selected original passages, figures and independent algebra are documented, while full projection-error control, interacting response calculations, final-author comparisons and raw experimental data have not all been reviewed. No model temperature in this page is entered as an experimental material transition. The open problem is to obtain useful, controlled limits for realistic multiband and correlated systems, rather than to maximize one isolated formula.    

 Discovery implications

Specify the density, isolation gap, interaction scale, orbital structure and measurement convention before comparing designs. Check whether a change enhances pairing, pair mobility or both, and whether it changes the assumptions behind the calculation. Report the full relaxed response and its uncertainty alongside any decomposition. A useful prediction should identify the observation that would falsify it; a large density of states or geometric metric alone does not meet that standard.

entries.title: Superconductivity: evidence and concepts
entries.summary: A guide to what superconductivity measurements establish, how their limitations differ, and where to explore mechanisms, materials and open questions.
entries.text:
Scope

Superconductivity is a state with characteristic electrical, magnetic and collective behavior. Understanding a new claim requires more than finding a resistance drop or a gap-like feature. Start by asking what was measured, on which sample, under which conditions, and which alternative explanations were tested. This overview links the observable evidence to the wiki's theories, materials and control parameters. It does not assign a microscopic pairing mechanism from one probe or claim that every article has completed scientific acceptance.   

Use ,  and  to compare transport, magnetic response and thermodynamics. Continue to  for excitation spectra and to  for phase-related evidence. These observables constrain different aspects of the state. Agreement on matched samples strengthens a case; one positive result does not automatically supply the missing measurements.    

 Mathematical assumptions

Models turn observations into quantities under explicit assumptions. In a uniform bar carrying homogeneous current, resistivity is inferred from resistance as \rho=RA/L, with cross-sectional area A and voltage-contact separation L. A heterogeneous film or a filamentary path may violate that conversion. A measurement consistent with zero voltage establishes a resistance bound set by current and voltage sensitivity; it does not mathematically demonstrate an infinitely precise zero or determine superconducting volume fraction.  

The simplest local London description gives exponential magnetic screening in a uniform half-space, B(x)=B(0)e^{-x/\lambda}. Penetration depth is not interchangeable with an uncorrected magnetic shielding fraction: sample shape, demagnetization, vortices and measurement history matter. A homogeneous weak-coupling isotropic BCS model also supplies useful reference scales, but its gap and heat-capacity ratios are not definitions that every superconductor must satisfy.   

Distinguish pair formation, global phase coherence and a probe's practical transition criterion. In a two-dimensional regime,  involves phase stiffness and vortex unbinding. A spectroscopic gap or resistance onset can therefore differ from a phase-ordering temperature. A fitted scale must retain its model, dimensionality, current range and uncertainty rather than being relabelled as a universal transition. 

 Experimental criteria

Transport should report contact geometry, applied current, voltage sensitivity, transition width and field dependence. Magnetic evidence should distinguish flux expulsion from shielding, field-cooled from zero-field-cooled protocols, and reversible response from pinning. Thermodynamic evidence should retain background subtraction and sample fraction. Where one probe is impractical, describe the evidence actually obtained and the missing controls rather than either declaring certainty or dismissing a result automatically.   

 tests how changing nuclear mass affects an observed scale, with chemical and structural controls. It does not prove that phonons are the only pairing interaction.  involve orbital, spin and vortex effects; a high field alone does not determine spin-triplet order.  additionally depends on pinning, geometry and an operational electric-field criterion, so it is not a universal material ranking independent of field and temperature.   

 probes electron–hole conversion at an interface, where transparency and the surrounding electronic structure matter.  maps scattering-related spatial modulations and constrains electronic states through a model. Neither an isolated conductance peak nor a Fourier feature independently determines pairing phase or establishes a Majorana mode. Follow the relevant article's probe-specific limitations before interpreting a pattern.  

 and  describe normal-state transport, not a superconductivity test by themselves. Residual resistance, temperature window, carrier weight and scattering anisotropy affect the inference. An observed linear curve is not automatically a direct measurement of a universal relaxation time or a unique quantum-critical mechanism. 

 Limits and disputes

Evidence for a superconducting state, the symmetry of its order parameter, the interaction that produces pairing and the topology of its excitations are different claims. Bulk transport or screening does not alone determine gap phase; normal-state band topology does not alone classify the paired state. Disagreement between probes should be traced to samples, conditions, assumptions and uncertainties before being compressed into a single verdict. The core wiki keeps experiments, models, predictions and hypotheses distinguishable.     

The pinned overview's historical audit label is not a new independent verification. This page reuses the explicitly scoped source checks documented in the linked articles. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including unresolved final-version comparisons, supplementary controls and raw-data analyses. Numerical illustrations establish only their stated algebra and assumptions; they do not certify experimental reproducibility or exhaustive coverage of the field.     

 Discovery implications

Navigate by the question. Start with  and  for interactions, then  for order-parameter constraints. Compare ,  or  with their sample-specific evidence. Use  and  to define the state being tested. These are routes into the evidence, not interchangeable explanations.   

Keep a claim record with material, composition, preparation, pressure, field direction, measurement temperature, transition criterion and source version. Select the next experiment for its ability to distinguish competing interpretations. If a high-pressure, interfacial or transient result lacks a thermodynamic or magnetic cross-check, preserve that limitation in both prose and structured data. A transparent record can be revised as evidence develops without turning an untested hypothesis into a material fact.
